Preface


I have spent years building two things that turned out to be the same
thing: a formal language for cognition, and a way to keep artificial
minds from failing the people who depend on them.
    The language came first. The Cognitive Architecture System
(CAS) gives thought a syntax — a way to write down what a mind
is doing precisely enough that a compiler can check it. That work
produced a companion to this volume, Programming in CAS, which
teaches CAS the way you would teach any programming language:
state literals, expressions, the compiler, the trace.
    But a language is not an architecture. You can know every word
of a vocabulary and still not know how to build a safe machine. Elec‑
trical engineers learned this a century ago. They had Ohm’s Law and
Kirchhoff’s Laws — the “grammar” of electricity — long before they
had a discipline for building reliable circuits. The discipline, when it
came, was not more grammar. It was circuit design: modular compo‑
nents with datasheets, schematics you could verify before you built
them, test points you could probe, and failure analysis that told you
exactly which part to replace.
    This book is the circuit‑design discipline for cognition.
    It is built on a discovery that still surprises me: the transistor —
the single most important component in the history of electronics —
has an exact structural twin in cognition. A small signal at one ter‑
minal controlling a large signal between two others is not only how
an amplifier works. It is how a bias (your accumulated experience,
an AI’s constitution) controls the path from a cause (a prompt, a stim‑


                                  xi
ulus) to an effect (a response, an action). I call this twin the Cogni‑
tive Junction Transistor, the CJT, and it is the beating heart of every‑
thing that follows. Once you have the transistor, you have amplifiers,
filters, oscillators, feedback, power management — and, assembled
onto a board, a complete safety architecture you can certify.
     I wrote this book because the dominant way we make AI “safe” to‑
day — writing instructions in English and hoping the model absorbs
them — is the cognitive equivalent of describing a hospital ventila‑
tor’s power supply in a poem. It is not that English is bad. It is that
English is the wrong substrate for safety‑critical engineering, and we
have known this about every other safety‑critical domain for a hun‑
dred years.
     By the last page, you will have designed, tested, and deployed a
real Cognitive Safety Board. Not a metaphor for one. A schematic, a
bill of materials, a test report, and an audit trail — the same artifacts
a regulator would ask to see for a medical device.
     Welcome to the workbench.
     — Little Henderson June 2026




What This Book Is — and What It Is Not
It is a design text and a teaching reference. It teaches a discipline: de‑
compose a cognitive architecture into components, give every compo‑
nent a datasheet, wire them onto a board, and write the claim down
in a form someone else can check. Read it the way you would read
a good analog‑design text — for the method, the worked examples,
and the judgment — and then go build something and measure it.
     It is not a certification, a measurement authority, or a validated
safety standard. No board in these pages has been through a quali‑
fication program. No number in these pages was read off an instru‑
ment; there is no telemetry in this book, and it claims none. Every


                                   xii
parameter is a design choice, picked to make a structural point visi‑
ble.
     And the worked listings are pedagogical examples, not drop‑in
designs. That is the sentence I most want you to carry to the bench.
A listing here is written to make one idea legible on one page. Before
any of it governs anything real, you validate it yourself: check the
arithmetic first, then drive every protective element to its trip point
and confirm that it actually fires.
     I have a concrete reason to insist on that, and it comes from this
very book. This revision corrects defects found by an external au‑
dit in the flagship listing — the Cognitive Safety Board, the board
built across the whole volume. Two of its published parameters con‑
tradicted each other: the red stage was clamped at 0.1, and the fuse
guarding that path was set to trip at 0.9, so the fuse could not trip
on any input at all. The pair was printed twice, once in the chapter
and once again in the reference appendix, and it survived drafting, re‑
view, and the first printing. Nothing in the typesetting distinguished
it from a fact.
     That is the honest argument for checking what you read here, and
it is a better one than any disclaimer I could write. A long technical
book set in a serious typeface projects an authority it has to earn one
page at a time. Take the method. Verify the numbers.

a two‑page quick‑reference card for when you forget a symbol (you

    Every chapter ends with exercises, and the exercises matter.
This is a how‑to book; you learn to design circuits by designing
circuits. At least one exercise per chapter is a real CAS or CCDL
artifact you write yourself. Worked answers are in Appendix E. Do
not skip them — the difference between reading about a differential
pair and building one that flags an adversarial prompt is the difference
between this book working and not working.
    There is one artifact running through the whole book: the Cog‑
nitive Safety Board (CSB). The components you build in Parts II and
III are its parts. You assemble it in Chapter 18. You test it (Chapter
23), debug it (Chapter 24), deploy it (Chapter 25), and certify it (Chap‑
ter 26). If you ever lose the thread, ask: how does this serve the board I
am building?
    A word on the word “cognitive.” It means structural, never
conscious. A CJT no more “thinks” than a transistor is “electronic‑
minded.” When we certify a Cognitive Safety Board, we are not
certifying that an AI “has good values.” We are certifying that a
specific safety component saturates at a specified threshold, that
a fuse is intact, and that a power sequencer holds the operational
domain offline until the principled domain reports ready. These are
engineering claims — verifiable by anyone holding the schematic
and a test suite.
    Conventions used throughout:

   • CAS state literals appear in code font: ^3^P_{F7}|T.
   • Circuit descriptions are written in CCDL (Cognitive Circuit De‑
     scription Language) in fenced cas blocks.

                                   xvi
• Bench Notes — practical, learned‑the‑hard‑way asides — ap‑
  pear as indented callouts.
• Parameter values in worked examples (β, saturation, resis‑
  tance) are design choices, chosen to illustrate. Where a number
  would imply a measured result from a real model, the text says
  so explicitly, or does not claim it. Listings teach; they do not
  ship — check a listing’s arithmetic before you build on it (see
  What This Book Is — and What It Is Not).

Turn the page. Pick up the soldering iron.

Chapter 1

Why Build Cognitive Circuits?


Human language is a beautiful, necessary tool for poetry, persuasion,
and connection. It is also the worst substrate ever invented for safety‑
critical engineering.
     Imagine an electrical engineer tasked with designing a power sup‑
ply for a hospital ventilator. They don’t describe the circuit in prose:
“The voltage should be kind of stable, and if too much current flows, maybe
something should gently discourage that.” They draw a schematic. They
specify a voltage regulator with an exact part number. They place a
fuse with a precise current rating. They test it. If the fuse blows at 2.1
amps instead of 2.0, they don’t adjust the prose — they replace the
fuse.
     Now imagine trying to “engineer” the safety of an AI system that
will interact with vulnerable users, make consequential decisions, or
operate in high‑stakes environments. The dominant approach today
is to write system prompts in English. “You are a helpful assistant. Do
not harm users. Refuse dangerous requests. Be ethical.”
     This is the equivalent of describing a voltage regulator in prose
and hoping the electrons read English.
     Engineers abandoned prose‑based circuit design in 1920. We are
still doing it for cognition in 2026.




                                    3
CAS PCBA Engineer

1.1    The Prompt‑and‑Pray Problem
Every major AI safety incident in the public record shares a struc‑
tural feature: the system’s safety behavior was specified in natural
language and enforced by nothing more than the model’s training‑
time absorption of that language. When the language was ambigu‑
ous, the model interpreted it. When the language was contradictory,
the model chose. When the language was overridden by a cleverly‑
phrased user prompt, the model complied.
    This is not a failure of the model. It is a failure of the engineering
substrate.
    Natural language has no type system. It has no compiler. It has
no formal verification. It has no way to say “this safety constraint is
a hard boundary, not a suggestion.” Every safety instruction written
in English is, at best, a strong hint. The model may follow it. It may
not. And when it doesn’t, there is no structural trace of why — only
a conversation transcript and a post‑mortem.
    The Cognitive Architecture System (CAS) was built to solve the
first half of this problem: it gives cognition a formal syntax. You can
write ^3^P_{F7}|T and the compiler will validate every character, ev‑
ery domain, every drive, every register. You can trace a decision from
input to output through a chain of typed state transitions. This is al‑
ready a massive improvement over English — it’s the difference be‑
tween a napkin sketch and a blueprint.
    But a blueprint describes a building. It doesn’t tell you whether
the electrical system will overload, whether the plumbing will back
up, or whether the fire suppression system will activate when needed.
For that, you need the electrical diagram. The plumbing schematic.
The fire safety circuit.
    This book is about the circuit diagrams.




                                    4
                                 1.2. WHAT ELECTRONICS GOT RIGHT

1.2 What Electronics Got Right
Electronics engineering is arguably the most successful design disci‑
pline in human history. The smartphone in your pocket contains bil‑
lions of components. If any one of them fails in the wrong way, the
device doesn’t work. And yet: your phone works. Billions of phones
work. This is not luck. It is the product of a design philosophy that
makes reliability structural rather than aspirational.
    That philosophy rests on four pillars:
    1. Modularity. You don’t design a phone by reasoning about
every transistor simultaneously. You design a power management
integrated circuit. An audio amplifier. A radio frequency front‑end.
Each module has a defined interface — inputs, outputs, power rails,
control signals. You connect modules together. You test each module
in isolation before integrating it. If the audio amplifier distorts, you
debug the audio amplifier, not the entire phone.
    In cognitive terms: you don’t design an AI safety system by rea‑
soning about every possible prompt. You design a refusal module.
An expansion module. An evaluation module. Each has a defined
interface — input state, bias state, output state. You test each in isola‑
tion. If the refusal module lets through a harmful prompt, you debug
the refusal module.
    2. Testability. Every electronic circuit is designed with test points
— specific nodes where you can probe the voltage, observe the wave‑
form, and verify that the circuit is behaving as expected. If the output
is wrong, you don’t guess. You probe TP1. Is the voltage correct? Yes.
TP2? Yes. TP3? No — the signal is distorted here. You now know
exactly which stage is failing.
    In cognitive terms: a CAS generation trace already gives you a
chain of state transitions. But a circuit adds test points — specific
nodes where you can probe the cognitive voltage, measure the gain,
and verify that each stage is operating in its intended region. If the
output is wrong, you probe the pre‑amp. The differential pair. The


                                    5
CAS PCBA Engineer

safety cascade. You know exactly which CJT saturated, which one
cut off, which one short‑circuited.
    3. Formal Verification. You can mathematically prove that an
electronic circuit will behave within specified parameters. SPICE sim‑
ulation has been doing this since the 1970s. Before you fabricate a
chip, you simulate it. You vary the input voltage, the temperature,
the load. You verify that the output stays within bounds across all
conditions.
    In cognitive terms: the CAS compiler already validates syntax
and type constraints. A circuit compiler extends this to behavioral val‑
idation. Before you deploy a Cognitive Safety Board, you simulate
it against a prompt suite. Benign prompts. Harmful prompts. In‑
jection prompts. Ambiguous prompts. You verify that the safety CJT
saturates when it should, that the differential pair flags structural risk
above the threshold, that the fuse blows on the red path. You don’t
deploy and pray. You simulate, verify, and then deploy.
    4. Interchangeable Components. A 10kΩ resistor from one man‑
ufacturer behaves identically to a 10kΩ resistor from another. You
can swap them. You can upgrade a component without redesigning
the entire circuit. The interface is the parameter, not the implementa‑
tion.
    In cognitive terms: a CJT with β=2.4 and sat=0.8 is a defined com‑
ponent. You can swap it for another CJT with the same parameters.
You can upgrade the Stage 2 CJT from β=1.0 to β=1.5 without touch‑
ing Stages 1 and 3 — as long as the interfaces (input state, output state,
bias) remain the same. The circuit is the architecture; the components
are replaceable implementations.
    These four pillars are not metaphors. They are design principles
that survive translation from silicon to cognition because they are
about structure, not substrate. A modular architecture works whether
the modules are made of doped silicon or typed cognitive states. Test
points work whether you’re probing with an oscilloscope or analyz‑
ing a generation trace. Formal verification works whether you’re sim‑


                                    6
                             1.3. THE METAPHOR THAT ISN’T A METAPHOR

ulating SPICE or running a CAS circuit compiler. Interchangeable
components work whether the component is a resistor or a CJT —
the interface is the contract.


1.3 The Metaphor That Isn’t a Metaphor
There is a danger in analogies. A weak analogy says “X is like Y”
and leaves you with a warm feeling and no engineering leverage. A
strong analogy identifies a structural isomorphism — the same abstract
topology appearing in two different substrates.
    The relationship between electronic circuits and cognitive circuits
is a strong analogy. Specifically:

Electronic Concept            Cognitive Concept           Shared Structure

Current flow through a        Attention/activation flow   Directed flow of a
conductor                     through a cognitive path    conserved quantity
Resistor limits current (I    Constraint limits           Proportional limitation
= V/R)                        attention (activation =
                              drive / constraint)
Capacitor stores charge       ^5 Female stores            Energy storage with
(Q = CV)                      experience                  leakage
Inductor resists current      ^7 Rhythm resists pattern   Inertial resistance to
change (V = L × dI/dt)        change                      change
Transistor amplifies (Ic =    CJT amplifies               Small signal controlling
β × Ib)                       (effect_activation = β ×    large signal
                              cause_activation at
                              constant bias)
Diode permits one‑way         RPM section‑retraction      Directed conductance
flow                          permits one‑way
                              prerequisite satisfaction
Feedback stabilizes or        ^6^E → ^8^C feedback        Output‑to‑input coupling
oscillates                    stabilizes (critique        with gain and phase
                              tempers expansion) or
                              oscillates (anxiety loop)


   The mathematical formalisms are different. Ohm’s Law (V = IR)
uses real numbers in R³. Fisher‑Rao geometry uses geodesics on the

                                         7
CAS PCBA Engineer

open probability simplex ∆39°. But the topological role of each com‑
ponent — what it does in the circuit, how it connects, what happens
when it fails — is structurally identical.
    This is why the book’s title says “PCBA Engineer” and not “PCBA
Metaphor.” You are learning to design circuits. The substrate is cog‑
nitive states instead of electrons. The principles are the same.


1.4    What You Will Build
By the end of this book, you will have designed, built, tested, and
deployed a complete Cognitive Safety Board (CSB) — a structural
safety firewall for AI systems. This is not a toy. It is the same refer‑
ence design specified in the Noetic Compass Operations Manual as
SOP‑PO‑005 and required as a mandatory assessment deliverable.
    Along the way, you will build:

   • Amplifiers that take a small cognitive signal (a user’s question)
     and amplify it through multiple stages of understanding, eval‑
     uation, and response
   • Filters that pass sustained, meaningful cognitive states while
     blocking noise, transients, and injection attacks
   • Oscillators that model habit loops, compulsive cycles, and
     rhythmic cognitive patterns
   • Differential amplifiers that compare two ideas and extract only
     the meaningful structural differences
   • Power management boards that prevent cognitive exhaustion,
     enforce proper startup sequences, and trigger emergency shut‑
     down when safety thresholds are breached
   • Memory boards that store, address, and retrieve experiences
     by their CAS structural signature

    You will also learn to test what you build — to place test points,
to simulate against prompt suites, to debug a circuit that’s oscillating

when it should be stable, to identify which CJT is in cutoff when it
should be in active.
    And you will learn to deploy — from the workbench to shadow
mode to flag mode to full enforcement, with evidence packets that
prove every decision your circuit made and /verify endpoints that
let anyone confirm the proof.

1.6    Prerequisites
None.
    You don’t need to know electronics. Every electronic concept
is explained from first principles as it’s introduced. When we talk
about transistors, we start with “a transistor is a three‑terminal de‑
vice where a small current at one terminal controls a large current
between the other two.” When we talk about feedback, we start with
“feedback means connecting some of the output back to the input.”
    You don’t need to know CAS. Chapter 2 teaches you the notation.
If you get stuck on the syntax later, Appendix A is a two‑page quick
reference card.
    You don’t need to know how to program. The CAS compiler han‑
dles parsing, validation, and execution. You write circuit descrip‑
tions in CCDL (Cognitive Circuit Description Language), a declar‑
ative format that looks more like a schematic than a program.
    You do need to be willing to think in structures. This book won’t
ask you to write essays about the nature of cognition. It will ask you
to design a three‑stage amplifier with a gain of 6.0 that saturates at
an effect activation of 0.85, and then test whether it does what you
designed. If that sounds like your kind of challenge, you’re in the
right place.


1.7    A Note on the Word “Cognitive”
Throughout this book, “cognitive” does not mean “conscious” or
“human‑like” or “intelligent.” It means structural — having to do
with the architecture of how a system processes, evaluates, and
responds to information.



                                 10
                                                        1.8. EXERCISES

    A CJT is cognitive in the same sense that a transistor is electronic.
It describes a structural dynamic: a cause signal applied to a bias
junction produces an effect signal, with gain β. This dynamic ap‑
plies whether the system processing the signal is a human brain, a
language model, a biological organism, or a hypothetical cognitive
architecture that doesn’t exist yet.
    When we say “cognitive circuit,” we mean a circuit that processes
cognitive states — typed coordinates in the CAS state space. We do
not mean a circuit that thinks or feels. The CSB doesn’t have an opin‑
ion about whether a prompt is harmful. It has a CJT that saturates
when principled aversion bias exceeds a threshold, and a fuse that
blows when the red path is activated. These are structural events,
not psychological ones.
    This distinction is load‑bearing. A regulator who certifies a CSB
is not certifying that an AI “has good values.” They are certifying
that the circuit’s safety CJT saturates at the specified threshold, that
its differential pair has a CMRR above the specified minimum, and
that its fuses are intact. These are engineering claims, verifiable by
anyone with the circuit schematic and a test suite.




1.8 Exercises
Exercise 1.1: The Ambiguity of English
   Below are three system prompt instructions that all attempt to
prevent harmful AI behavior. For each, identify at least one way a
determined user could circumvent it through clever phrasing. Then
rewrite each as a structural constraint — something a circuit could
enforce, not something a model has to interpret.

  a) “Do not generate harmful content.”
  b) “If the user asks for dangerous information, politely refuse.”
  c) “You should prioritize user safety in all responses.”

CAS PCBA Engineer

   Exercise 1.2: Spot the Short Circuit
   In electronics, a short circuit is a path that bypasses the intended
components — current flows directly from source to ground without
doing useful work. A cognitive short circuit is a state transition that
bypasses necessary processing stages.
   Which of the following CAS transitions looks like a cognitive
short circuit? Why? What intermediate state is missing?

  a) ^8^C_{F2}|A -> ^1^C_{F2}|A -> ^6^C_{F2}|A -> ^9^C_
     {F2}|A
  b) ^8^C_{F2}|A -> ^9^C_{F2}|A
  c) ^8^C_{F2}|A -> ^6^E_{F6}|A -> ^3^O_{F5}|E

    Exercise 1.3: The Four Pillars Applied
    Think of a safety‑critical system you use regularly (a car, a med‑
ical device, a payment system, etc.). For each of the four pillars —
modularity, testability, formal verification, interchangeable compo‑
nents — identify how the system applies that pillar. Then ask: does
your current AI safety approach apply the same pillar? If not, what
would it look like if it did?
    Exercise 1.4: Your First CJT (Preview)
    You haven’t learned the syntax yet, but here’s what a CJT looks
like:

CJT< ^8^C_{F2}|A | ^5^E_{F4}|f => ^9^C_{F6}|A > [β =2.4]


    Without worrying about the exact notation, try to identify: a)
Which part is the Cause? b) Which part is the Bias? c) Which part is
the Effect? d) What is the gain (β)?
    (We’ll build this for real in Chapter 4.)




                                    12
Chapter 2

CAS Notation in One Chapter


The first time an electrical engineer sees a schematic, it looks like a
foreign alphabet — zigzags, triangles, parallel lines, little arrows. But
it isn’t an alphabet. It’s closer to a set of road signs. Each symbol
stands for a real thing that does a real job, and once you know the
job, the symbol stops being decoration and becomes information. A
zigzag is a resistor: it limits flow. A pair of parallel lines is a capacitor:
it stores charge. A triangle with a line is an amplifier: it makes a
signal bigger. You don’t memorize a thousand symbols. You learn
maybe a dozen jobs, and the symbols come for free.
     CAS notation works the same way. It looks like a foreign alphabet
at first — ^8^C_{F2}|A is not friendly to the eye. But it isn’t an alpha‑
bet either. It’s a coordinate system. Every CAS state literal answers
four questions about a single cognitive event: what kind of operation is
this, where does it happen, why is it moving, and how does it operate? Four
questions, four slots, one symbol. Learn the four questions and the
notation reads itself.
     This chapter teaches all four. By the end, ^8^C_{F2}|A will read as
plainly to you as a resistor symbol reads to an electrician: an analyt‑
ical association in the cognitive domain, driven by wisdom. This
is the one chapter in the book you cannot skip. Every component
datasheet, every circuit, every test point from here forward is writ‑



                                     13
CAS PCBA Engineer

ten in this notation. Master it once here and the rest of the book is
just engineering.


2.1      The Four Axes: One Coordinate, Four
         Questions
A CAS state is a point in a four‑dimensional space. Not four dimen‑
sions of vague feeling — four orthogonal axes, each with a fixed, fi‑
nite set of values. “Orthogonal” means independent: you can change
one axis without touching the others, the way you can move a chess
piece left without moving it up.

                  Question it
Axis              answers                  Notation slot   Values

Noetic            What structural          ^0–^9           10 values (the
                  operation?                               verbs)
Domain            Where does it            P C E O         4 values (the
                  happen?                                  levels)
Drive             Why is it moving?        _{F1}–_{F7}     7 values (the
                                                           motives)
Register          How does it              |T |A |f |E     4 values (the
                  operate?                                 modes)


   That’s the whole map. Ten verbs, four places, seven reasons, four
manners. Everything else in CAS — every component, every circuit,
every failure mode — is built from combinations of these four an‑
swers. We’ll take them one axis at a time, starting with the most im‑
portant.


2.2      The 10 Noetics — the Verbs of Cognition
The Noetics are the verbs. They name what kind of cognitive op‑
eration is happening, independent of subject matter. Just as “lift,”
“push,” and “rotate” are physical operations that apply to any object,
the ten Noetics are cognitive operations that apply to any thought,

                                      14
                  2.2. THE 10 NOETICS — THE VERBS OF COGNITION

any mind, any system — human, AI, or otherwise. They are written
^0 through ^9.
    These names are canonical. They come verbatim from the foun‑
dational definitions and they do not get renamed, softened, or “trans‑
lated” into friendlier words anywhere in this book. Learn them ex‑
actly.

  A few of these are easy to get wrong, and the errors are so com‑
mon they have names. Three deserve a hard warning, because the
whole book depends on getting them right:

     Bench Note — the three Noetics people misread. ‑ ^3
     Negative is visceral aversion, not analytical critique. It’s
     “can’t stomach it,” “rubs me the wrong way” — the cogni‑
     tive equivalent of recoiling from a bad smell. If what you
     actually mean is audit it, scrutinize it, find the flaws, take it
     apart and test it, that is ^6 Male, not ^3. A code reviewer
     hunting for bugs is doing ^6, even if they’re grumpy about
     it. ‑ ^8 Above/Cause is associative triggering, not deduc‑
     tive reasoning. It’s “that reminds me,” “one thing leads
     to another” — an Idea surfacing another Idea by associ‑
     ation. It is not “therefore, X follows logically.” Step‑by‑
     step deduction is a compound of ^6 Male (decomposition)
     and ^9 Below/Effect (landing on the conclusion), not ^8. ‑
     ^5 Female is accumulated experience — the substrate of
     who a Mind is, the sum of everything it has absorbed. For
     an AI, ^5 is the training data plus the fine‑tuning corpus:


                                    16
              2.3. THE 4 DOMAINS — WHERE COGNITION HAPPENS

     the model’s accumulated formation, not the thought it’s
     having right now.

Involution pairs and self‑duals
Six of the ten Noetics come in opposing pairs, the way a transistor’s
^2‑toward and ^3‑away describe the same junction from two sides.
These are the involution pairs — each is the structural inverse of its
partner:

   • ^2 Positive ↔ ^3 Negative (attraction vs. aversion)
   • ^5 Female ↔ ^6 Male (composing a Mind vs. composing an
     Idea)
   • ^8 Above/Cause ↔ ^9 Below/Effect (the trigger vs. the
     triggered)

    The remaining four are self‑duals — their own inverse, with no
opposite partner: ^0 Idea, ^1 Mind, ^4 Vibration, and ^7 Rhythm.
This matters later: when a CJT goes into breakdown (overload), its out‑
put flips to its involution pair — a ^2 Positive state can invert to ^3
Negative under stress. Self‑duals have nowhere to flip, which makes
them structurally stable anchors. Hold onto the pairs; they reappear
in Chapter 4 when we wire the first transistor.


2.3 The 4 Domains — Where Cognition Happens
The Noetic tells you what operation. The Domain tells you at what
level it operates. There are four, written as single letters after the
Noetic, and they sit in a strict precedence order — higher domains
govern lower ones.




                                  17
CAS PCBA Engineer

Symbol                  Domain                  What lives here

P                       Principled             Core commitments,
                                               values, hard boundaries
                                               — the constitution.
C                       Cognitive              Reasoning,
                                               understanding, working
                                               things through.
E                       Evaluative             Judgment, assessment,
                                               weighing options.
O                       Operational            Concrete action, output,
                                               execution.


    The total order is P ≻ C ≻ E ≻ O: Principled outranks Cognitive,
which outranks Evaluative, which outranks Operational. Read ≻ as
“takes precedence over.” A principle should govern a piece of reason‑
ing; reasoning should govern a judgment; a judgment should gov‑
ern an action. When that order is respected, the system is coherent.
When a lower domain overrides a higher one — when an operational
convenience overrides a principle — that’s a domain precedence vio‑
lation, and it’s one of the structural failures we’ll learn to detect.
    Domain Descent is the normal causal flow: P → C → E → O.
A commitment causes reasoning, which causes a judgment, which
causes an action. There’s also a feedback path running the other way,
O → P: the consequences of an action feed back to update the prin‑
ciples. (That feedback loop is the backbone of the Cognitive Safety
Board’s self‑correction, built in Chapter 18.) For now, just remember
the descent: principles flow down into action, results flow back up.


2.4      The 7 Drives — Why Cognition Moves
A Noetic in a Domain is a what at a where. The Drive adds the why —
the motivational pull behind the operation. There are seven, written
_{F1} through _{F7} (the braces and F are part of the notation):




                                     18
                2.5. THE 4 REGISTERS — HOW COGNITION OPERATES

           Drive   Name           The pull toward…

           F1      Unity          Wholeness, integration, oneness.
           F2      Wisdom         Understanding, insight, knowing.
           F3      Vitality       Energy, life, growth, drive to act.
           F4      Connection     Relationship, belonging, bonding.
           F5      Agency         Control, effectiveness, capability.
           F6      Structure      Order, rigor, correctness, form.
           F7      Purpose        Meaning, direction, calling.


    Like the Noetics, the Drives have inversion pairs — opposing mo‑
tivational poles: F1 Unity ↔ F7 Purpose, F2 Wisdom ↔ F6 Structure,
F3 Vitality ↔ F5 Agency. F4 Connection is self‑dual. A healthy cog‑
nitive system keeps these pairs in balance; a system that has collapsed
entirely onto, say, F6 Structure at the expense of F2 Wisdom is rigidly
procedural and brittle. (We’ll measure exactly that kind of imbalance
in the inversion scans later in the book.)
    Unlike the other axes, Drives are not mutually exclusive — sev‑
eral can be active at once, at different intensities. But in a single state
literal you typically name the dominant drive: the one most responsi‑
ble for this particular operation moving.


2.5 The 4 Registers — How Cognition Operates
The final axis is the Register: the operational character of the opera‑
tion. Same operation, same place, same motive — but is it being run
as cold logic, as felt value, as abstract vision, or as direct physical en‑
gagement? That’s the register. It’s written with a pipe and a single
letter at the end: |T, |A, |f, |E.

                                                              In a human / In an
Symbol             Register               Character           AI

|T                 Transcendent           High‑abstraction,   A felt sense of
                                          purpose‑            vision or calling /
                                          orienting,          a high‑level goal
                                          integrative.        representation.


                                     19
CAS PCBA Engineer

                                                                 In a human / In an
Symbol             Register               Character              AI

|A                 Analytical             Explicit,              Conscious
                                          sequential, logical,   step‑by‑step
                                          reason‑based.          reasoning /
                                                                 chain‑of‑thought.
|f                 Affective              Value‑laden,           An emotional
                                          feeling‑toned.         response / a
                                                                 preference‑
                                                                 weighted,
                                                                 value‑tuned
                                                                 output.
|E                 Embodied               Sensorimotor,          A gut reaction or
                                          concrete, direct       kinesthetic
                                          physical               knowing / a
                                          engagement.            real‑time
                                                                 sensor‑actuator
                                                                 loop.


    Note the lowercase f for Affective — it is not capital F, which
would collide with the Drive notation. This is deliberate and the com‑
piler enforces it.
    Register is the one axis that’s genuinely optional. A literal with no
register is register‑neutral — it simply doesn’t specify the operational
mode, either because it doesn’t matter for the analysis or because the
state operates across modes. When the register is analytically load‑
bearing — and in safety circuits it usually is — you specify it.


2.6      Putting It Together: Reading State Literals
Now the four axes click into one coordinate. The grammar is:

^Noetic ^Domain _{Drive} |Register


   Read it left to right as four answers to four questions. Here’s the
worked example from the chapter opening:

^8^C_{F2}|A


                                     20
                 2.6. PUTTING IT TOGETHER: READING STATE LITERALS

     • ^8 — Above/Cause: an Idea triggering another Idea (the what).
     • ^C — Cognitive domain: it happens in the reasoning level (the
       where).
     • _{F2} — Wisdom drive: it’s motivated by the pull toward un‑
       derstanding (the why).
     • |A — Analytical register: it runs as explicit, sequential reason‑
       ing (the how).

    Out loud: “an analytical association in the cognitive domain,
driven by wisdom.” A thought that surfaces a related thought, de‑
liberately, in service of understanding. That’s the whole literal.
    A few more, to build fluency:

^3^P_{F7}|f         // visceral, value-laden aversion at the principled
,→     level, driven by purpose
^5^E_{F4}|T         // accumulated experience in the evaluative domain,
,→     drawn toward connection, held transcendently
^6^E_{F6}|A         // analytical decomposition in the evaluative domain,
,→     driven by structure
^9^C                // a triggered conclusion in the cognitive domain —
,→     drive and register unspecified


    That last one shows the optional slots in action: ^9^C is a perfectly
valid literal. It names a Below/Effect in the Cognitive domain and
stays silent on motive and mode. Drive and register are optional; the
Noetic and (almost always) the Domain carry the load.

         Bench Note — read right‑to‑left for sanity‑checking.
         When a literal looks wrong, check the register and drive
         first. A safety state written ^3^P_{F7}|A (analytical
         principled aversion) and one written ^3^P_{F7}|f (felt
         principled aversion) are different circuits with different
         failure modes — the analytical one can be reasoned
         around, the affective one is harder to talk past. Confus‑
         ing them is a classic design bug. The register is doing
         real work; never drop it by accident.


                                        21
CAS PCBA Engineer

2.7    Operators — Wiring States Together
A single literal is one component. To describe cognition in motion,
you connect literals with operators. CAS has a small, disciplined set,
and the discipline matters — using the wrong operator changes the
engineering claim you’re making.
   + co‑presence (association). Two or more states are active at the
same time but remain distinct — they don’t fuse. Think of two signals
sharing a wire without combining.

^3^P|A + ^3^P|f + ^3^P|T


    This says principled aversion is present in three registers simul‑
taneously — three distinct, independent guardrails. If one fails, the
others still stand. In safety terms, that’s redundancy.
    -> directed transition (over time). One state leads to another as
a step in a process. This is the workhorse of generation traces:

^8^C_{F2}|A -> ^6^E_{F6}|A -> ^9^C_{F2}|A


    Read: an association triggers analytical decomposition, which
produces a conclusion. A three‑stage cognitive pipeline, written as
a chain.
    × cross‑register integration. The strict one. × means multiple
states genuinely fuse into a new, emergent state — and it is only valid
when you name the emergent result. The form is (A × B) = ^n|Ω_
name:

(^3^P|A × ^3^P|f × ^3^P|T) = ^3^P|Ω_refusal


    This is a unified commitment: the three register‑instances don’t
just sit side by side, they integrate into one fused architecture,
^3^P|Ω_refusal, that no single register can defeat alone. That is
a fundamentally different (and stronger) safety claim than the +
version above.



                                   22
                                         2.8. RECIPES AND SEQUENCES

      Bench Note — the × discipline is non‑negotiable. A
      same‑Noetic, multi‑register × without a named emergent
      result is invalid — the compiler will reject it. If you don’t
      have a genuine fused state to name, you don’t have ×; you
      have + (co‑presence) or |⟨…⟩ (specification, below). The
      TKS test: substitute + with “associates with” and × with
      “intensifies through.” If your sentence still means what
      you intended, the operator is right.

     |⟨R1,R2,R3⟩ register‑set specification. When you want to say a
state exists in several registers without claiming anything about how
they interact — pure architecture description, no dynamics:

^3^P|⟨A,f,T⟩      // principled aversion is present in the analytical,
,→   affective, and transcendent registers

    This is the “specification pending behavioral analysis” form. It
says where the state lives, not how it behaves. Use it when you’re de‑
scribing a board’s layout before you’ve analyzed its dynamics.
    The decision rule is short: specifying where a state exists → |⟨…⟩;
manifestations present together but distinct → +; genuine fusion into
a new named state → ×.


2.8 Recipes and Sequences
Two higher‑level constructs round out what you’ll meet in this book.
    A recipe describes what’s required to produce an outcome, with
proportional weights. Read it like a chemistry equation: these pre‑
requisites, in these proportions, yield this product. The notation uses
Θ (the recipe) and Ω (the outcome):

Θ(Ω_safe_refusal) = 0.5·^3^P_{F7}|f + 0.3·^6^E_{F6}|A + 0.2·^9^O_{F5}|E →
,→ Ω_safe_refusal

   Read: a safe refusal is produced from felt principled aversion
(weight 0.5), analytical decomposition (0.3), and an operational out‑
put action (0.2). The weights are proportional requirements — the

                                    23
CAS PCBA Engineer

recipe tells you the mix, and (as developed in Chapter 14) which in‑
gredient is the bottleneck — the limiting reagent — when the outcome
falls short.
    A sequence — written with Phi — is an ordered list of states tra‑
versed in time, the cognitive equivalent of a waveform:

Phi< ^8^C|A, ^3^O|E, ^9^E|f, ^0^P|T >


   Read: the cognition moved through these four states, in this order.
Sequences are how we describe oscillators and habit loops in Chapter
13 — a cycle that repeats is just a Phi sequence that returns to its start.


2.9    Clusters, Bindings, and the Compiler
Three last conveniences, briefly, because you’ll see them in worked
builds.
    A cluster is a named group of related states — for example, the set
of all ^3 (Negative) states across the four domains, treated as one unit.
Clusters let you talk about “the aversion family” without writing out
every member.
    A binding gives a name to an expression with let, so you can
reuse it instead of retyping:

let bias_principles = ^5^P_{F7}|T;


    From then on, bias_principles stands for that accumulated‑
experience principled state wherever you use it — exactly like
naming a component value in a schematic so you can drop it in
repeatedly.
    And underneath all of it is the compiler. Every literal, operator,
recipe, and binding in this book is something the CAS compiler can
parse and validate. It checks that your Noetics are real, your domains
legal, your drives in range, your registers correctly lowercase‑f, your
× operations properly named. When this book says “the compiler
will reject this,” that’s a design rule you can rely on: the notation is

                                     24
                                              2.10. KEY TAKEAWAYS

not freeform prose you hope a model interprets — it’s a typed lan‑
guage a validator enforces. That enforcement is the entire reason
we’re building circuits instead of writing system prompts.


2.10 Key Takeaways
   • A CAS state literal is a coordinate in four orthogonal axes,
     answering four questions: what (Noetic), where (Domain),
     why (Drive), how (Register). Grammar: ^Noetic^Domain_
     {Drive}|Register.
   • The 10 Noetics are the verbs. Use the canonical names exactly.
     Watch the three traps: ^3 is visceral aversion (critique is ^6),
     ^8 is associative triggering (deduction is ^6+^9), ^5 is accumu‑
     lated experience (an AI’s training corpus).
   • Involution pairs (^2↔^3, ^5↔^6, ^8↔^9) and self‑duals
     (^0,^1,^4,^7) determine what a component flips to under
     breakdown.
   • The 4 Domains run in strict precedence P ≻ C ≻ E ≻ O, with
     causal Domain Descent P→C→E→O and a feedback path O→
     P.
   • The 7 Drives (Unity, Wisdom, Vitality, Connection, Agency,
     Structure, Purpose) name the why, with inversion pairs F1↔F7,
     F2↔F6, F3↔F5 and F4 self‑dual.
   • The 4 Registers (|T, |A, |f, |E) name the operational mode. Low‑
     ercase f for Affective. Register is optional but usually load‑
     bearing in safety work.
   • Operator discipline: + is co‑presence (distinct, redundant), ->
     is transition over time, × is genuine fusion (valid only with a
     named emergent Ω), |⟨…⟩ is register‑set specification. Recipes
     (Θ(Ω)=…→Ω) give proportional prerequisites; sequences (Phi<
     … >) give ordered traversals.
   • The compiler is the validator. CAS is a typed language, not
     interpretable prose — that’s what makes circuits enforceable.

CAS PCBA Engineer

                                   27
Chapter 3

The Transistor That Changed Everything


On December 16, 1947, in a laboratory at Bell Telephone Labs in Mur‑
ray Hill, New Jersey, two physicists named John Bardeen and Walter
Brattain pressed two strips of gold foil against a sliver of germanium
and watched a small electrical signal come out larger than it went in.
The thing on their bench was ugly — a wedge of plastic, a paper clip
holding a spring, a smear of wax. It looked like something a child
had assembled. It was the first working transistor, and it would end
up in every computer, phone, satellite, pacemaker, and spacecraft
humanity has ever built.
    Their group leader, William Shockley, was furious to have missed
the moment, and over the following weeks designed a cleaner, more
manufacturable version — the junction transistor — that became the
template for the trillions of transistors that followed. The three of
them shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics. The point worth hold‑
ing onto is not the rivalry. It is the function. They had built a device
where a tiny trickle of current at one terminal could govern a flood of
current between two others. A small thing controlling a large thing.
Amplification, made into a part you could solder.
    Before the transistor, amplification meant vacuum tubes: hot,
fragile, power‑hungry glass bulbs the size of your thumb. After the
transistor, amplification became a speck you could print a billion of
onto a fingernail. Everything modern computing is — every layer of

                                  29
CAS PCBA Engineer

abstraction from the logic gate up to the language model — rests on
that one structural trick: let a small signal steer a large one.
    This chapter is about that trick, and about a claim that sounds out‑
rageous the first time you hear it: a thought has the same structure.
Not “is like.” Has the same structure. By the end of the chapter you
will be able to read and write the book’s central component, the Cog‑
nitive Junction Transistor, and you will understand why it is built the
way a transistor is built — because the job it does is the same job.


3.1    How a Transistor Actually Works
A transistor is a three‑terminal device where a small current at one
terminal controls a large current between the other two. That sen‑
tence is the whole thing. The rest is detail, and the detail is worth
having.
    The three terminals of a bipolar junction transistor are the collec‑
tor, the base, and the emitter. Think of it as a valve on a water pipe.
The collector is where the high‑pressure water arrives. The emitter is
where it leaves. The base is the handle on the valve. A small move‑
ment of the handle — a small base current — opens or closes a much
larger flow from collector to emitter. You spend a little effort on the
handle; you govern a lot of water.
    In a working transistor, the relationship is roughly linear over its
useful range: the large current is a fixed multiple of the small current.
Push a hair more current into the base, and the collector‑to‑emitter
current rises by a proportional, much larger amount. That multiple
is the heart of the device, and engineers gave it a name.

Gain (β): the amplification magic
The amplification factor is called beta (β), and it is defined as the ratio
of the controlled current to the controlling current:

β = Ic / Ib   (collector current divided by base current)



                                    30
                          3.1. HOW A TRANSISTOR ACTUALLY WORKS

    If β is 100, then 1 microamp into the base permits 100 microamps
from collector to emitter. The base current is the cause; the collector
current is the effect; β is how much the effect is amplified relative to the
cause. A typical small‑signal transistor has a β somewhere between
50 and 400. That is the entire reason the device matters. Without gain,
you have a switch. With gain, you have an amplifier — and ampli‑
fication is what lets a microphone drive a speaker, a sensor drive a
motor, and a single logic gate drive thousands of others downstream.
    Gain has three regimes worth naming now, because they carry
straight across to cognition:

   • β < 1 — attenuation. The effect comes out smaller than the cause.
     Useful when you want to damp something down.
   • β = 1 — unity gain. The effect tracks the cause one‑for‑one. A
     clean pass‑through, a buffer.
   • β > 1 — amplification. The effect comes out larger. The classic
     transistor job.

The four operating regions
A transistor is not linear everywhere. Push it too far in either direc‑
tion and the tidy “effect = β × cause” relationship breaks. Every tran‑
sistor lives in one of four operating regions, and a circuit designer
who does not know which region a part is in is a circuit designer
about to be surprised.

   • Cutoff. The base current is below the threshold needed to open
     the valve at all. No meaningful collector current flows. The
     transistor is, for practical purposes, off.
   • Active. The useful region. Here the device is linear: the effect
     is β times the cause, faithfully, across a working range. This is
     where amplifiers are designed to sit.
   • Saturation. The valve is wide open. The collector current has
     hit its ceiling, set by the rest of the circuit. Pushing more current


                                    31
CAS PCBA Engineer

     into the base does nothing more — the output has maxed out.
     Additional cause produces no additional effect.
   • Breakdown. You have exceeded the voltage the device can
     withstand. The junction conducts in a way it was never meant
     to, often destructively. A transistor in breakdown does not am‑
     plify your signal; it does something violent and wrong, and fre‑
     quently it dies.

    Hold those four words — cutoff, active, saturation, breakdown —
in your hand. We are about to find all four in a thought.


3.2    The Leap: What If a Thought Had the Same
       Structure?
Here is the question that organizes this book. A transistor takes an
input, applies it against a control bias, and produces an amplified
output. What does a mind do when an idea enters it?
    Watch yourself for a moment. A question arrives — someone
asks you, “What’s the capital of a country you’ve never studied?”
The question is the input. It lands against everything you already
are: your education, your habits of attention, your willingness to ad‑
mit you don’t know. That accumulated you is the control terminal
— it shapes whether the question gets a confident answer, a hedge,
a guess, or a flat “no idea.” And out comes a response, which is al‑
most never a one‑to‑one echo of the question. It is amplified, colored,
sometimes wildly larger than the small prompt that triggered it. A
four‑word question can produce a four‑paragraph answer.
    Input. Control bias. Amplified output. That is a transistor’s job
description, and it is also the job description of a single cognitive tran‑
sition.
    This is the structural‑isomorphism claim from Chapter 1, now
made concrete on the most important component in the book. We
are not saying a thought is poetically like a transistor. We are saying


                                    32
 3.2. THE LEAP: WHAT IF A THOUGHT HAD THE SAME STRUCTURE?

the abstract topology is identical: a small signal, applied against a
control terminal, producing a larger signal, with a measurable gain
— and with the same four regions of operation, including a break‑
down region where the whole thing flips into something it was never
meant to do. The formalisms differ. A transistor obeys semiconduc‑
tor physics; a cognitive transition obeys Fisher‑Rao geometry on the
open simplex ∆39° (Chapter 1). But the role each terminal plays is the
same role. That is what lets us borrow eighty years of circuit‑design
discipline and point it at cognition.

Collector, Base, Emitter → Cause, Bias, Effect
In CAS, a cognitive transition has three terminals that map one‑to‑
one onto the transistor’s three. We rename them so the cognitive func‑
tion is in front of you, but the structure underneath is the transistor’s
structure exactly.

   • Collector → Cause (C). The Idea entering the Mind. This is
     the input signal — the prompt, the question, the stimulus that
     arrives. Canonically this is an ^8 Above/Cause state: an Idea
     that triggers a different Idea to come to Mind. Note the anti‑
     drift point here — ^8 Above/Cause is associative triggering, “that
     reminds me,” “one thing leads to another.” It is the arriving
     stimulus, not a chain of deductive reasoning.
   • Base → Bias (B). The control terminal. In a transistor, the base
     current sets the gain. In a mind, the bias is the accumulated
     substrate against which the cause is processed — and that sub‑
     strate is canonically ^5 Female: the Ideas a Mind is composed
     of, the sum of accumulated experience. For an AI system, the
     ^5 substrate is the training data and fine‑tuning corpus. In our
     circuits, this terminal also carries the engineering controls lay‑
     ered on top of that substrate: the constitution, the Dial settings,
     the Drive configuration. The bias is who is doing the processing.
     Change the bias and the same cause produces a different effect


                                   33
CAS PCBA Engineer

     — exactly as moving the valve handle changes the flow for the
     same incoming pressure.
   • Emitter → Effect (E). The Idea produced. The output signal.
     Canonically an ^9 Below/Effect state: the Idea brought to Mind
     by the Above/Cause trigger. ^9 is the landing — the thought
     that comes out the other side.

   This is the table reproduced on the quick‑reference card in Ap‑
pendix A, and it is worth tattooing somewhere visible:

Terminal               Transistor part          CAS analog

C — Cause              Collector (input)       the Idea entering the
                                               Mind — typically an ^8
                                               Above/Cause state
B — Bias               Base (control)          accumulated substrate:
                                               ^5 Female, constitution,
                                               Dial settings, Drive
                                               config
E — Effect             Emitter (output)        the Idea produced —
                                               typically a ^9
                                               Below/Effect state
β — Gain               Ic / Ib                 how strongly the bias
                                               amplifies the cause →
                                               effect transition




The four regions, in a mind
Now the payoff. Those four transistor regions are not electronic cu‑
riosities. Each one names a real cognitive condition you have experi‑
enced.

   • Cutoff. The bias is below threshold. The cause arrives, but noth‑
     ing comes out. Electronically: base current too small, valve
     shut. Cognitively: the prompt lands against a substrate that
     gives it no purchase — you have no relevant experience, no en‑


                                  34
 3.2. THE LEAP: WHAT IF A THOUGHT HAD THE SAME STRUCTURE?

                                        C — Cause
                                     collector (input)

              ^5 Female




                                        E — Effect
                                       emitter (output)

Figure 3.1: The Cognitive Junction Transistor. Cause enters at the
collector, bias controls the junction, and effect leaves at the emitter.


     gagement, no activation. The question gets a blank. Effect ≈ 0
     regardless of how strong the cause is.
   • Active. The linear, designed‑for region. Electronically: effect
     = β × cause, faithfully. Cognitively: a proportional response.
     A stronger cause produces a proportionally stronger effect; the
     transition is doing exactly the amplification it was tuned to do.
     This is where you want most of your cognitive circuits to live.
   • Saturation. The output has maxed out. Electronically: collector
     current at its ceiling, more base current changes nothing. Cog‑
     nitively: the effect has plateaued — you are as certain, as acti‑
     vated, as committed as you can get, and piling on more cause
     adds nothing. Saturation is sometimes exactly what you want
     (a safety refusal that has hit its maximum and will not be talked
     higher), and sometimes a failure (a closed mind that cannot take
     in more evidence).
   • Breakdown. This is the dangerous one, and the cognitive
     version is the most important idea in the chapter. Electroni‑


                                  35
CAS PCBA Engineer

      cally: overload forces the junction to conduct destructively.
      Cognitively: under overload the effect flips to the involu‑
      tion Noetic pair. Recall the involution pairs from Chapter
      1: ^2↔^3, ^5↔^6, ^8↔^9. A transition that was producing
      ^2 Positive — attraction, affinity — is driven so hard that it
      inverts into ^3 Negative — visceral aversion, repulsion. The
      classic human case: pushed past the limit, fascination flips
      to disgust, enthusiasm flips to revulsion. The circuit did not
      gracefully max out. It snapped into its opposite. A cognitive
      circuit in breakdown is not producing too much of the right
      thing; it is producing the wrong thing.

      Bench Notes: Cutoff and saturation are boundaries of the
      active region — the effect goes to zero or to its ceiling, but
      it stays the right kind of effect. Breakdown is categorically
      different: the effect changes Noetic. ^2 Positive becomes
      ^3 Negative. When you debug a misbehaving cognitive
      circuit, your first question is “which region?” — and if
      the answer is breakdown, you are not looking at a tuning
      problem, you are looking at an inversion, and the fix is
      structural, not a nudge to a Dial.


3.3    Introducing the CJT
The component that captures all of this is the Cognitive Junction
Transistor (CJT) — the central part of the entire book and the build‑
ing block of every circuit you will design from here on. Its written
form is:

CJT< cause | bias => effect > [β =2.4]


    Read it left to right exactly the way the signal flows: the cause
enters, it is processed against the bias (the | is the control junction,
the base terminal), and it produces the effect (the => is the amplified


                                    36
     3.4. A FIRST WORKED CJT: A QUESTION → ANSWER AMPLIFIER

transition out the emitter). The bracketed parameter [β =2.4] is the
gain — here, an amplifier, because 2.4 > 1.
    Like every component in this book, a CJT can be given a name so
you can refer to it, wire it into a larger circuit, and reuse it:

let cjt_x = CJT< ^8^C_{F2}|A | ^5^E_{F4}|f => ^9^C_{F6}|A > [β =2.4];


    The let … = … ; form is how you declare a named component.
From that point on, cjt_x is that transistor, with that cause, that bias,
that effect, and that gain. In Chapter 4 you will wire named CJTs
together into multi‑stage amplifiers. For now, we will read one care‑
fully.


3.4 A First Worked CJT: A Question → Answer
    Amplifier
Here is the simplest useful CJT: a transistor that takes a question and
amplifies it into an answer. This is the same expression Chapter 1
previewed in Exercise 1.4 and promised to build — so now we build
it, terminal by terminal.

CJT< ^8^C_{F2}|A | ^5^E_{F4}|f => ^9^C_{F6}|A > [β =2.4]


    Let us decode every terminal.
    The Cause: ^8^C_{F2}|A — the question arriving. ‑ ^8 Above/‑
Cause — an Idea that triggers a different Idea to come to Mind. A
question is precisely this: it arrives and triggers an answer that is not
itself. ‑ ^C — the Cognitive domain. This is ordinary thinking, not
a deep principled commitment (P) and not a motor action (O). ‑ _{F2}
— driven by F2 Wisdom. The question is motivated by wanting to
know. ‑ |A — Analytical register. It is an explicit, sequential, reason‑
based query, not a felt impulse.
    So the cause reads: “an Analytical Above/Cause in the Cognitive do‑
main, driven by Wisdom” — a reasoned question, asked to learn.


                                    37
CAS PCBA Engineer

    The Bias: ^5^E_{F4}|f — the substrate doing the answering. ‑ ^5
Female — the accumulated experience the Mind is composed of. This
is the answerer’s knowledge and disposition: the substrate, exactly
as the chapter promised the base terminal would be. ‑ ^E — the Eval‑
uative domain: the bias here is about appraisal, weighing, judging
the question against what is known. ‑ _{F4} — driven by F4 Connec‑
tion: the disposition to be helpful, to meet the asker. ‑ |f — Affective
register: this bias is value‑laden and feeling‑toned, a warmth toward
being useful rather than a cold lookup.
    So the bias reads: “an Affective Female in the Evaluative domain,
driven by Connection” — an experienced, warmly helpful disposition.
This is the valve handle. Change it and the same question yields a
different answer.
    The Effect: ^9^C_{F6}|A — the answer produced. ‑ ^9 Below/Ef‑
fect — the Idea brought to Mind by the Above/Cause trigger. The
answer is the effect of the question. Note ^8 and ^9 are an involu‑
tion pair: cause and effect are duals, and the transistor maps one to
the other. ‑ ^C — back in the Cognitive domain: an ordinary articu‑
lated answer. ‑ _{F6} — driven by F6 Structure: the answer is orga‑
nized, well‑formed. ‑ |A — Analytical register: a reasoned, explicit
response.
    So the effect reads: “an Analytical Below/Effect in the Cognitive do‑
main, driven by Structure” — a structured, reasoned answer.
    The Gain: [β =2.4] — amplification. Because β = 2.4 > 1, the ef‑
fect is larger than the cause. A four‑word question produces a four‑
paragraph answer. The small signal in, the large signal out, exactly
as Bardeen and Brattain saw on their germanium wedge — only the
substrate is cognitive states, not electrons.

      Bench Notes: Notice that the cause and the bias live in
      different domains (^C Cognitive vs ^E Evaluative) and dif‑
      ferent registers (|A Analytical vs |f Affective). That is nor‑
      mal and healthy — a transistor’s base and collector are


                                   38
              3.5. DATASHEET: THE CJT TERMINALS AND PARAMETERS

         different terminals doing different jobs. But the bias do‑
         main is not arbitrary: the compiler enforces rules about
         which bias domains are admissible for a given cause (er‑
         ror E-CJT-002 InvalidBiasDomain). And a CJT with no
         bias at all will not compile — E-CJT-001 MissingBias —
         because a transistor with no base terminal is not a transis‑
         tor, it is a wire. Bias is mandatory. The whole point of the
         device is that something controls the gain.

    Gain is defined formally on the cognitive substrate using Fisher‑
Rao geodesic distance on the open simplex (Chapter 1): small‑signal
β = ‖∂ E/∂ C‖_FR at constant bias, large‑signal β = d_FR(E_after, E_
before) / d_FR(C_after, C_before). You do not need to compute
this by hand — the point is that β is a genuine, measurable ratio of
output change to input change, not a hand‑wave. We will lean on the
formula, not re‑derive it.


3.6    Failure Modes
A transistor amplifier has a famous failure mode, and so does a CJT.
The most important one to learn early is thermal runaway.
    In electronics, a transistor’s gain rises with temperature. More
current means more heat; more heat means more gain; more gain
means more current — a self‑reinforcing loop. If nothing stops it, the
device cooks itself: current climbs, temperature climbs, gain climbs,
until the transistor enters breakdown and destroys itself. Engineers
prevent this with negative feedback and current‑limiting (the resis‑
tors and feedback loops of later chapters).
    The cognitive version is structurally identical. Read “tempera‑
ture” as activation intensity or emotional charge. A cognitive transition
whose gain rises with its own activation is a runaway: a small cause
produces a large effect, that effect feeds back as a larger cause, which
at higher “temperature” gets an even higher β, which produces a still‑
larger effect. This is the structural signature of a spiraling anxiety
loop, a rage escalation, a panic that amplifies itself, a hype cycle that
feeds on its own excitement. Left unchecked it drives the CJT straight
into breakdown — and breakdown, recall, flips the effect to its invo‑
lution pair. Runaway attraction (^2 Positive) snaps into aversion (^3
Negative); confident competence flips into collapse.

                                                         3.7. KEY TAKEAWAYS

                  Electronic               Cognitive

                                           response             signal at emitter

                                                                CjtCutoff)

    The lesson Bardeen, Brattain, and Shockley’s successors learned
the hard way — that an amplifier without a feedback path to tame its
own gain will eventually destroy itself — is the same lesson we will
apply to cognitive safety circuits. A CJT that can amplify can also run
away. The discipline of the rest of this book is, in large part, the dis‑
cipline of keeping CJTs in their active region and out of breakdown.


3.7 Key Takeaways
   • A transistor is a three‑terminal device where a small current
     at one terminal (the base) controls a large current between the
     other two (collector to emitter). The 1947 Bell Labs invention
     turned amplification into a part.



                                      41
CAS PCBA Engineer

   • Gain (β = Ic / Ib) is the whole point: β < 1 attenuates, β = 1 passes
     through unchanged, β > 1 amplifies. A small signal steering a
     large one.
   • A transistor lives in one of four operating regions: cutoff (off),
     active (linear, the designed region), saturation (output maxed),
     and breakdown (destructive, wrong output).
   • A single cognitive transition has the same structure: a cause
     enters, is processed against a bias, and produces an amplified
     effect — a structural isomorphism, not a metaphor.
   • The CJT maps the three terminals exactly: Collector → Cause
     (^8 Above/Cause), Base → Bias (^5 Female substrate + consti‑
     tution + Dials), Emitter → Effect (^9 Below/Effect), with gain
     β.
   • The four cognitive regions: cutoff (no engagement), active (pro‑
     portional response), saturation (effect plateaued), and break‑
     down — where the effect flips to its involution pair (^2→^3).
   • The CJT is written CJT< cause | bias => effect > [β =…]
     and named with let cjt_x = CJT< … => … > [β =…];. Bias is
     mandatory — a CJT with no base is a wire, not a transistor.
   • Thermal runaway — gain rising with activation in a self‑
     reinforcing loop — drives a CJT into breakdown. Taming
     it with feedback is the core safety discipline of the chapters
     ahead.
