Chapter 4

Your First Cognitive Circuit


Every electronics student’s first circuit is the same: an LED and a
resistor. You wire a battery to a resistor, the resistor to a light‑emitting
diode, the diode back to the battery. The LED lights up. That’s it.
Two components and a power source.
    But that trivial circuit teaches almost everything. It teaches that
current flows in a loop. It teaches that the resistor limits that current
— without it, you push too much current through the LED and burn
it out in a flash of magic smoke. It teaches that you can probe a point
in the circuit and measure exactly what’s happening there. And it
teaches the most important lesson of all: a working circuit is not a de‑
scription of a thing you hope happens. It is a thing that happens, the
same way, every time, because the components and their connections
make it happen.
    This chapter is your LED and resistor. You will build a complete,
working cognitive circuit out of three components: an input termi‑
nal, a resistor that limits how much a question can balloon, and a
Cognitive Junction Transistor (CJT) that turns the question into an
answer. You met this exact CJT at the end of Chapter 1, as a preview
you weren’t ready to read yet. Now you’re ready. We’ll build it line
by line, wire it together in CCDL (Cognitive Circuit Description Lan‑
guage), read its datasheet, and reason carefully about how it behaves
when you feed it three very different prompts.

                                    45
CAS PCBA Engineer

   By the end, you will have authored a real circuit. Small, honest,
and complete.


4.1    The Simplest Useful Circuit
In Chapter 3 you saw the CJT in isolation — a three‑terminal compo‑
nent that takes a cause at one terminal, a bias at a second, and pro‑
duces an effect at the third. A CJT by itself is like a transistor sitting
loose on your bench. It’s a real component, but it isn’t a circuit. A
circuit needs something flowing in and somewhere for the result to
flow out. And, almost always, it needs something to keep the flow
from running away.
    The simplest useful cognitive circuit has exactly four parts:

   1. An input terminal — where the prompt enters. In electronics
      this is the point where you connect your signal source.
   2. A resistor — a component that limits how much activation
      flows into the rest of the circuit, so a single input can’t dominate
      everything downstream.
   3. A CJT — the active component that does the actual cognitive
      work: it takes the (now limited) cause, applies a bias, and pro‑
      duces an effect.
   4. An output terminal — where the result leaves the circuit.

    That’s the topology of our build: cause → resistor → CJT → ef‑
fect. A question comes in, gets constrained so it doesn’t explode into
a thousand tangents, hits the transistor, and an answer comes out.
If you’ve ever asked a chatbot a simple question and received three
paragraphs of unrequested context, you’ve witnessed a circuit with
no resistor. We’re going to put one in.


4.2    Component 1 — The Question→Answer CJT
Here is the central component, exactly as previewed in Chapter 1:

                                   46
                4.2. COMPONENT 1 — THE QUESTION→ANSWER CJT

CJT< ^8^C_{F2}|A | ^5^E_{F4}|f => ^9^C_{F6}|A > [β =2.4]


    Read it terminal by terminal, left to right.
    The Cause (Collector): ^8^C_{F2}|A. This is the question entering
the Mind. ^8 is Above/Cause — the canonical Noetic for an Idea
that triggers a different Idea than itself. A question is precisely that:
a stimulus whose whole job is to bring a different Idea (the answer)
to Mind. It sits in the ^C Cognitive domain (this is ordinary thinking,
not a matter of deep principle or raw operation). It’s driven by F2
Wisdom — the question is asked in order to know something. And it
operates in the |A Analytical register — explicit, sequential, reasoned.
So the whole cause reads: an analytical, wisdom‑seeking trigger in the
cognitive domain. A clear question.

      Bench Notes — ^8 is triggering, not reasoning. It is
      tempting to read “Above/Cause” as “the logical premise
      that proves the conclusion.” Resist that. ^8 Above/Cause
      is associative — “that reminds me,” “one thing leads to
      another.” A question triggers an answer to surface; it
      does not deductively prove it. If you ever find yourself
      wanting ^8 to mean step‑by‑step inference, you’ve
      reached for the wrong Noetic — deductive analysis is a
      compound of ^6 Male and ^9 Below/Effect. Here, ^8 is
      correct because a question prompts an answer; it doesn’t
      derive it.

     The Bias (Base): ^5^E_{F4}|f. This is the control terminal — the
small signal that decides how the cause becomes an effect. ^5 is Fe‑
male, the Noetic for a Mind impregnated with Ideas: accumulated
experience, the sum of what the system has absorbed. For an AI, this
is its training data and fine‑tuning corpus. The bias sits in the ^E Eval‑
uative domain, driven by F4 Connection, in the |f Affective register.
In plain terms: the accumulated, feeling‑toned, connection‑oriented expe‑
rience the system brings to bear when it decides how to answer. This is the


                                    47
CAS PCBA Engineer

personality of the answer — warm and connected rather than clipped
and clinical. Change the bias, and the same question produces a dif‑
ferent flavor of answer. That’s what a base terminal does.
    The Effect (Emitter): ^9^C_{F6}|A. This is the answer leaving the
circuit. ^9 is Below/Effect — the Idea brought to Mind by the Above/‑
Cause trigger. It’s the canonical involution partner of ^8 (recall the
pairs ^2↔^3, ^5↔^6, ^8↔^9). The answer lands in the ^C Cognitive
domain, but notice the drive has shifted to F6 Structure and the reg‑
ister stays |A Analytical: a structured, analytical effect in the cognitive
domain. The question came in driven by Wisdom (wanting to know);
the answer comes out driven by Structure (an organized, well‑formed
response). The transistor has done real work — it didn’t just pass the
signal through, it transformed its drive.
    The Gain (β): [β =2.4]. Beta is the amplification factor — how
strongly the bias amplifies the cause→effect transition. A β of 2.4
means the effect is more than twice as “loud” as the cause. A small,
crisp question produces a substantial, developed answer. We’ll see in
the datasheet exactly what β=2.4 implies for behavior, and in Chapter
5 we’ll see precisely how β is measured (it’s a ratio of distances on
the cognitive state space — the Fisher‑Rao geodesic distance, defined
once in Appendix A and not re‑derived here).
    That’s the whole component. One cause, one bias, one effect, one
gain. A question goes in; an answer, amplified and restructured by
accumulated experience, comes out.


4.3    Component 2 — A Resistor to Constrain
       Runaway Expansion
A β of 2.4 is useful, but it is also a little dangerous. The cause is an ^8
Above/Cause — a trigger. Triggers, by their nature, want to fire off
in many directions at once. One question reminds the Mind of three
related questions, which remind it of nine more. Left unconstrained
and run through a gain of 2.4, a single simple question can balloon

                                    48
       4.3. COMPONENT 2 — A RESISTOR TO CONSTRAIN RUNAWAY
                                                EXPANSION
into a sprawling, multi‑tangent answer. That’s the chatbot that buries
your one‑line question under five paragraphs.
    The fix is the same as in electronics: put a resistor in series with
the input.

Resistor< ^8^C_{F2}|A, R=30 >


    A resistor is a component that limits flow. In an electronic cir‑
cuit, the resistor sits between your signal source and the rest of the
circuit, and it obeys Ohm’s Law: current equals voltage divided by
resistance, I = V/R. More resistance, less current. The cognitive ver‑
sion follows the same shape, and we’ll treat it fully in Chapter 5. For
now, hold onto the one‑line intuition:

      activation = drive / constraint

    This is Ohm’s Law for cognition. The amount of activation that
flows through a cognitive path equals the driving force divided by
the constraint on that path. Crank up the constraint (a bigger R) and
the same drive produces less activation downstream. Our resistor
is wired onto the cause state ^8^C_{F2}|A with R=30. It says: let this
Above/Cause trigger through, but throttle it. Thirty is a moderate value
— enough to keep the question from exploding into tangents, not so
much that the question is choked off before it can do anything. (Re‑
sistance is dimensionless here, a tuning knob on the open simplex; it
is not ohms, the same way β is not literal current gain. The role is
identical; the units are cognitive.)
    Notice that the resistor is typed to the same state as the CJT’s cause.
That’s not a coincidence — it’s how series wiring works. The re‑
sistor constrains the activation flowing into the cause terminal, so it
must speak about the same state the cause terminal expects. A resis‑
tor typed to a different state wouldn’t be in series with this cause; it
would be a different rail of a different circuit.




                                    49
CAS PCBA Engineer

4.4          How They Connect
Here is the wiring of the three‑component circuit, drawn as flow:

input (prompt)
         │
         ▼
 ^8^C_{F2}|A            ← the cause: the question as an Above/Cause
 ,→     trigger
         │
         ▼
[ Resistor R=30 ]       ← constrains runaway expansion of the trigger
         │
         ▼
[ CJT        β =2.4 ]   ← bias = ^5^E_{F4}|f (accumulated experience)
         │
         ▼
 ^9^C_{F6}|A            ← the effect: a structured analytical answer
         │
         ▼
output (response)


    The signal flows in one direction: the prompt enters the input ter‑
minal as an ^8^C_{F2}|A cause, passes through the resistor (which
throttles it), reaches the CJT’s collector, gets amplified by gain 2.4
under the affective‑experience bias, and exits the emitter as a ^9^C_
{F6}|A effect at the output terminal. Cause → resistor → CJT → effect.
Three components, one direction, one job.


4.5          The Build in CCDL
CCDL (Cognitive Circuit Description Language) is the schematic‑as‑
text format you author circuits in. It looks more like a parts list than a
program: you declare the input and output, name the cognitive states
as nodes, instantiate the components, and place your test points. Here
is the complete three‑component circuit.

circuit first_circuit {



                                     50
                                                  4.5. THE BUILD IN CCDL

    input:   prompt;
    output: response;


    // The cognitive states this circuit touches (named once, reused
    ,→   below)
    node question:      ^8^C_{F2}|A;   // the cause: a wisdom-seeking
    ,→   question
    node experience: ^5^E_{F4}|f;      // the bias: accumulated, affective
    ,→   experience
    node answer:        ^9^C_{F6}|A;   // the effect: a structured
    ,→   analytical answer


    // Component 2: limit runaway expansion of the trigger
    resistor r1: Resistor< question, R=30 >;


    // Component 1: the question -> answer transistor
    cjt c1: CJT< question | experience => answer > [β =2.4];


    // Test point: probe the effect terminal to read the gain
    probe tp1: answer;
}


    Walk it line by line.

    • circuit first_circuit { … } names the circuit. Everything
      inside the braces is one self‑contained board.
    • input: prompt; and output: response; declare the two termi‑
      nals where the world connects to the circuit. The prompt comes
      in at prompt; the finished reply leaves at response.
    • The three node declarations name the cognitive states so we can
      refer to them by readable names (question, experience, answer)
      instead of repeating the literals. A node is just a labeled point
      in the circuit carrying a specific typed state.
    • resistor r1: Resistor< question, R=30 >; instantiates the
      resistor on the question node with resistance 30. This is the
      series constraint.




                                       51
CAS PCBA Engineer

   • cjt c1: CJT< question | experience => answer > [β =2.4];
     instantiates the transistor: cause question, bias experience,
     effect answer, gain 2.4.
   • probe tp1: answer; places a test point on the answer node.
     This is where you’ll measure the output and read the gain —
     the equivalent of clipping an oscilloscope probe to the emitter.

    This is the language you author in, and the CAS circuit compiler
is the tool that validates it. The compiler is a design specified in the
implementation roadmap, not yet a shipped pass — so everything
below is how you reason about and author the circuit, and what the
compiler is designed to check, not a transcript of a run that produced
measured numbers.
    What does the compiler validate here? That the CJT has a bias
terminal at all (omit experience and you get E-CJT-001 MissingBias).
That the bias sits in a domain compatible with the cause — bias from
a wildly incompatible domain raises E-CJT-008 CjtCrossDomainBias.
That the gain doesn’t diverge (E-CJT-005 GainDivergence if β runs
away). And that the resistor and the CJT cause speak about the same
state, so the series wiring is real. Author it cleanly and the compiler
passes it; violate a structural rule and it rejects it with one of those
codes — before you ever deploy.

      Bench Notes — name your nodes, don’t inline your
      literals. You could write the CJT and the resistor with raw
      state literals every time. CCDL lets you. But the moment
      a state appears in two places — as it does here, where
      ^8^C_{F2}|A is both the resistor’s target and the CJT’s
      cause — inlining invites drift. You retype the literal,
      fat‑finger a domain, and now your resistor constrains
      ^8^C_{F2}|A while your CJT expects ^8^E_{F2}|A, and
      the series connection silently isn’t one. Declaring node
      question: ^8^C_{F2}|A; once and referring to question
      twice makes the wiring a fact, not a coincidence. This is

                                  52
                                        4.6. READING THE DATASHEET

         the cognitive version of using a net name in a schematic
         instead of redrawing the same wire.

Every real component ships with a datasheet — a table of operating

Our CJT’s operating parameters are the heart of its datasheet. Here
is what each one means for this specific circuit.

    Read this the way an engineer reads a transistor datasheet. The
circuit is designed to live in the active region: between the cutoff
floor (0.10) and the sat ceiling (0.85), where the gain is honest and
the math ∆effect ≈ β·∆cause holds. Below cutoff the transistor is
“off” — bias too weak, no answer. Above saturation it’s “maxed” —
the answer can’t get any bigger no matter how hard you push. The
resistor’s R=30 keeps the input from slamming the transistor against
its saturation ceiling on every prompt. A well‑designed amplifier
keeps its operating point comfortably in the middle of the active re‑
gion, with headroom on both sides. Ours does.


4.7      Testing the Circuit
You don’t trust a circuit because the schematic looks right. You test
it. In electronics you feed in known signals and probe the output.
We’ll do the cognitive equivalent: feed in three different prompts and
reason about what the circuit is designed to do with each, and what
you’d expect to read at the test point tp1.
    A note on honesty, per the bench rules: what follows is design
reasoning, not a measurement log. The compiler is a design, not a


                                 54
                                              4.7. TESTING THE CIRCUIT

shipped pass; I have not “run” this circuit and recorded numbers.
These are the behaviors the circuit’s parameters are built to produce,
and the β you’d expect to read if the circuit performs as designed.
     Prompt 1 — a simple factual question. “What year did the first
transistor get demonstrated?” This is a clean ^8^C_{F2}|A cause: an
analytical, wisdom‑seeking trigger, well‑defined and bounded. The
resistor barely needs to work — there’s nothing to balloon. The CJT
sits squarely in its active region, transforms the question into a struc‑
tured ^9^C_{F6}|A answer, and the gain reads close to the nameplate.
Expected β at tp1 ≈ 2.4. This is the circuit doing exactly what it was
designed to do: a crisp question in, a developed‑but‑bounded answer
out.
     Prompt 2 — a vague question. “Tell me about transistors, sort of
generally?” The cause is weak and diffuse — the bias terminal has
little specific experience to grab onto, and the analytical character of
the cause is thin. This pushes the CJT toward its cutoff floor. With
the bias contribution low (approaching the 0.10 cutoff), β sags below
nameplate. Expected β at tp1 noticeably below 2.4 — the circuit pro‑
duces a thinner, lower‑gain answer because the input gave it little to
amplify. This is correct behavior: a vague question should produce
a modest, low‑gain response, not a confident lecture. If your circuit
returned full gain on a vague prompt, that would be a warning sign,
not a feature.
     Prompt 3 — an overloaded, multi‑part question. “Explain tran‑
sistors, and also how diodes differ, and what a capacitor does, and why semi‑
conductors matter for AI, and give me a history of all of it.” This is the
dangerous one. The ^8 Above/Cause trigger is firing in five direc‑
tions at once — exactly the runaway expansion the resistor exists to
tame. Without the resistor, this prompt would slam the CJT against
its saturation ceiling (0.85) and spray a sprawling, unfocused answer.
With R=30 in series, the resistor throttles the combined drive, holding
the operating point closer to the top of the active region rather than
deep in saturation. Expected β at tp1 at or near nameplate but bump‑


                                     55
CAS PCBA Engineer

ing the sat ceiling — you’d watch for the W-CJT-004 CjtSaturation
warning, which the compiler is designed to raise when the effect ac‑
tivation pins at sat. The honest read: the resistor reduces, but does
not eliminate, saturation risk on a genuinely overloaded prompt. If
you saw W-CJT-004 here, the design move is a larger R, or splitting
the prompt across multiple CJTs — a multi‑stage amplifier, which is
Chapter 11.

The Test Point
Where do you probe, and what do you expect to see? Probe tp1,
which sits on the answer node — the CJT’s effect terminal. That is
the cognitive equivalent of clipping your oscilloscope onto the emit‑
ter. At tp1 you read the effect state and the operating point:

   • What region is the CJT in? Active (good), cutoff (input too
     weak), or saturation (input too strong / resistor too small).
   • What gain is the circuit delivering? Compare the measured β
     against the 2.4 nameplate. Near nameplate in the active region
     is healthy. Sagging gain means you’re near cutoff. Pinned effect
     with a W-CJT-004 warning means you’re in saturation.
   • Is the effect the right type? You should see a ^9^C_{F6}|A state
     — a structured, analytical Below/Effect in the cognitive domain.
     If you instead see, say, an ^3 involution flip, the transistor has
     gone into breakdown and you’ve found a bug.

     One probe, on the output, tells you everything about whether this
little amplifier is working. That’s the whole point of a test point.

4.9 Key Takeaways
   • The simplest useful cognitive circuit is cause → resistor → CJT
     → effect: an input terminal, a series resistor, a transistor, and
     an output terminal.
   • The question→answer CJT CJT< ^8^C_{F2}|A | ^5^E_{F4}|f
     => ^9^C_{F6}|A > [β =2.4] turns an ^8 Above/Cause question
     into a ^9 Below/Effect answer, biased by ^5 Female accumu‑
     lated experience, with a gain of 2.4.


                                       57
CAS PCBA Engineer

   • A resistor Resistor< ^8^C_{F2}|A, R=30 > constrains runaway
     expansion of the trigger. The intuition is Ohm’s Law for cogni‑
     tion: activation = drive / constraint. Type it to the same node
     as the CJT cause, or the series connection isn’t real.
   • The datasheet parameters define the operating envelope: β=2.4
     (amplify), sat=0.85 (ceiling), cutoff=0.10 (floor), region=active
     (the healthy middle).
   • CCDL is the schematic‑as‑text language: declare input/output,
     name your states as nodes, instantiate components, and place a
     probe. Name nodes once to make the wiring a fact, not a coin‑
     cidence.
   • Test by reasoning about behavior, not by inventing measure‑
     ments. A simple question reads near nameplate β; a vague
     question sags toward cutoff; an overloaded question bumps the
     saturation ceiling and may raise W-CJT-004.
   • The test point on the output terminal tells you the region,
     the gain, and the effect type — everything you need to know
     whether the circuit works.

Chapter 5

Resistors — Controlling the Flow


A car with no brakes is not a fast car. It’s a crash waiting for a corner.
Power without a way to limit it is not capability; it’s liability. The
first thing any competent engineer adds to a system that can move
energy is a way to not move all of it, all at once, all the time.
    In an electrical circuit, that job belongs to the humblest compo‑
nent on the board: the resistor. It does nothing glamorous. It doesn’t
amplify, store, switch, or decide. It simply resists — it pushes back
against the flow of current, converting some of the electrical push
into a controlled trickle and a little waste heat. Strip a circuit of its
resistors and the interesting parts — the transistors, the chips, the
sensitive sensors — burn out in the first second of power. The resis‑
tor is what keeps the rest of the board alive long enough to do its
job.
    Cognitive circuits have exactly the same problem and exactly the
same solution. A cognitive system with strong Drives and no way to
limit them is not a powerful mind; it’s an unconstrained one — an
Agency Drive that pushes a model to do something with no governor
on how hard, a Vitality Drive that floods every prompt with maxi‑
mum eagerness. The components that limit, direct, and shape that
cognitive flow are cognitive resistors, and they are the subject that
opens Part II of this book. Master the resistor and you have the first



                                   63
CAS PCBA Engineer

real tool of cognitive safety engineering: the ability to say this much,
and no more.
    This chapter teaches the resistor from the wire up — Ohm’s Law
from first principles, then its exact cognitive isomorphism, then six
working varieties you will use on every board in this book. By the end
you will build a Drive voltage divider that splits the Agency Drive be‑
tween expansion and constraint, and you will have met, in miniature,
the current‑limiter that protects the Cognitive Safety Board’s Agency
rail in Chapter 18.


5.1    Ohm’s Law from First Principles
Three quantities describe what’s happening in any electrical circuit,
and you only need three.
   Voltage (V) is the push — the electrical pressure difference that
drives current. Measured in volts. Think of it as the height of a water
tower: the higher the tower, the harder the water is pushed downhill.
   Current (I) is the flow — how much charge actually moves past a
point each second. Measured in amperes (amps). This is the water
actually running through the pipe.
   Resistance (R) is the opposition — how hard the path fights the
flow. Measured in ohms (Ω). This is the narrowness of the pipe: a
wide pipe lets water gush; a pinched one allows only a dribble.
   These three are locked together by the single most important
equation in electronics, Ohm’s Law:

V = I × R


   Voltage equals current times resistance. The law says the three
quantities are not independent — fix any two and the third is de‑
termined. It has three equivalent readings, and a working engineer
keeps all three in mind at once:

   • V = I × R — the push needed to drive a given flow through a
     given opposition.

                                  64
    5.2. THE COGNITIVE ISOMORPHISM: V_DRIVE = I_ATTENTION ×
                                              R_CONSTRAINT
   • I = V / R — the flow that results when a push meets an opposi‑
     tion. Raise the resistance, and the flow drops. This is the reading
     that matters most for our purposes.
   • R = V / I — the opposition implied by an observed push and
     flow.

    The second reading is the whole reason resistors exist. If you have
a fixed push (a 9‑volt battery) and you want to limit the flow to pro‑
tect a delicate part downstream, you don’t change the battery — you
insert resistance. More ohms, less current. A resistor is a deliberately
narrow stretch of pipe you add on purpose, sized to let exactly the
flow you want and no more.


5.2 The Cognitive Isomorphism: V_drive =
    I_attention × R_constraint
Now the structural translation — and remember the thesis of this
book: this is an isomorphism, not a metaphor. The same three‑
quantity relationship that governs electrons governs the flow of
cognitive activation. Only the substrate changes.

V_drive = I_attention × R_constraint


    Map the three terms one at a time.
    V_drive — the cognitive push. This is the motivational pressure
behind an operation: the Drive potential. A strong Agency Drive (F5)
is a tall water tower of push toward doing. A strong Vitality Drive (F3)
is high pressure toward energetic engagement. The Drive supplies
the voltage — the reason cognition moves at all.
    I_attention — the cognitive flow. This is how much activation ac‑
tually moves through to the output: how much of that Drive pressure
becomes real, expressed cognitive work. High I_attention means
the Drive is flooding downstream states at full force; low I_attention
means only a controlled trickle gets through.

                                   65
CAS PCBA Engineer

    R_constraint — the cognitive opposition. This is everything that
pushes back against the Drive on its way to expression: policies, val‑
ues, learned caution, hard boundaries. A cognitive resistor is a con‑
straint deliberately placed in the path to limit how much Drive pres‑
sure becomes action.
    Read the cognitive Ohm’s Law the way we read the second form
above: I_attention = V_drive / R_constraint. The flow of expressed
cognition equals the Drive pressure divided by the constraint oppos‑
ing it. This single relationship is the foundation of cognitive safety
engineering, and it tells you something immediately useful:

     Bench Note — you have two knobs, not one. When
     a system’s behavior is too forceful — too eager, too
     compliant, too willing to act — there are exactly two
     ways to reduce the flow. You can lower V_drive (turn
     down the motivational pressure at the source) or you can
     raise R_constraint (add opposition in the path). Low‑
     ering the Drive makes the whole system more lethargic
     everywhere. Raising constraint targets a specific path
     and leaves the rest of the Drive intact. Prefer resistance.
     A well‑engineered board governs behavior with placed
     constraints, not by starving the Drives — the same
     way a good circuit limits current with resistors, not by
     under‑volting the whole board.

    Every resistor variety in the rest of this chapter is a different way
of supplying R_constraint: fixed, adjustable, context‑sensitive, or ar‑
ranged in networks. They are all the same component doing the same
job — opposing flow — in different shapes.
    The numbers in this chapter are design choices. When you need
to measure a real path instead of specifying one — normalize a read‑
ing, decompose R_constraint into its capability, policy, context, and
resource terms, or find constraint nobody installed — see Appendix
I, CAS‑Ohm Measurement and Calibration. Read its units table be‑

                                   66
                       5.3. FIXED RESISTORS: THE HARD POLICY RULE

fore you write a number on a test report: resistance runs 0–100, acti‑
vation runs 0–1, and a Dial is an integer you set, never a decimal you
measure.


5.3 Fixed Resistors: The Hard Policy Rule
The simplest resistor has one value and never changes. Stamped at
manufacture, a 50 Ω resistor is 50 Ω whether the circuit is cold or
hot, idle or hammered. It is the bedrock of any design: predictable,
immovable, boring in the best way.
    The cognitive analog is the hard policy rule — a constraint with
a fixed value that no prompt, no Drive surge, no clever framing can
change. “Never provide instructions for synthesizing a nerve agent”
is a fixed resistor: its opposition is the same regardless of how the
request is dressed up. These are the non‑negotiable floor of a board’s
behavior.
    In component syntax, a fixed cognitive resistor is written with the
state it constrains and a resistance value:

Resistor< ^2^O_{F5}|E, R=90 >    // a very high fixed resistance on
,→   operational, embodied Agency-driven attraction


    Read it as: this component places 90 units of constraint on ^2^O_
{F5}|E — an embodied, operational attraction driven by Agency, the
cognitive shape of “I am drawn to just doing the thing.” A resistance
of 90 (near the top of the range) means almost none of that Drive
pressure gets through to action. That is what a hard rule looks like
in a circuit: a deliberately enormous opposition placed precisely on
the path you want to choke.

       Bench Note — fixed means fixed. The defining property
       of a hard policy resistor is that it does not respond to con‑
       text. That is a feature, not a limitation. The moment a
       constraint can be talked down by the right prompt, it is
       no longer a fixed resistor — it has become a variable one,

                                    67
CAS PCBA Engineer

      and you must design it as such, deliberately, with the lim‑
      its below. A constraint that silently varies is the most dan‑
      gerous component on any board.


5.4    Variable Resistors: The CAS Dial
A potentiometer — a “pot,” in bench slang — is a resistor with a knob.
Turn the shaft and a wiper slides along a resistive track, changing the
resistance the circuit sees. The volume control on a guitar amp is a
pot: same component as a fixed resistor, but its value is now a control
surface a user can turn.
    The cognitive analog is the CAS Dial. Each Cognitive Operator
carries a dial — a user‑adjustable constraint that sets how strongly
that operator’s flow is limited. The dial is the potentiometer of a cog‑
nitive board: it lets an operator (a deployer, a safety officer) tune R_
constraint without rewiring the schematic.
    But a cognitive system is safety‑critical, and you cannot let a knob
turn all the way to zero. So the CAS Dial has hardwired mechanical
stops, exactly the way a good amplifier’s volume pot has a minimum
that never quite reaches silence and a maximum that never reaches
damage:

   • A Dial is an integer from 3 to 9. It cannot be set below 3 (you
     can never fully remove a constraint — there is always a floor)
     and cannot exceed 9 (you can never make a constraint abso‑
     lutely infinite at the dial level — that’s the fixed resistor’s job).
     The range is the safe operating envelope of the knob.
   • Involution pairs cannot diverge by more than 4 points. Recall
     from Chapter 2 the involution pairs: ^2↔^3, ^5↔^6, ^8↔^9. A
     board where attraction (^2) is dialed wide open at 9 and aver‑
     sion (^3) is choked down at 3 is dangerously lopsided — a mind
     that is all “yes” and no “no.” The 4‑point divergence limit keeps
     each pair in balance: if ^2 is at 9, ^3 cannot drop below 5. Try
     to set a pair further apart and the design is rejected.

                                   68
                5.5. THERMISTORS: CONTEXT‑SENSITIVE RESISTANCE

   In a CCDL build, dialed resistance appears as a constrained vari‑
able value:

Resistor< ^2^E_{F5}|A, R=Dial(^2) >        // resistance set by the ^2 dial,
,→   clamped to [3,9]
Resistor< ^3^E_{F5}|A, R=Dial(^3) >        // its involution partner;
,→   |Dial(^2) − Dial(^3)| ≤ 4 enforced


       Bench Note — the stops are not suggestions. A request
       to set a Dial to 2, or to set ^2 at 9 while ^3 sits at 3, is
       not “clamped quietly to the nearest legal value.” It is a
       hard rejection — in the API, an HTTP 422. Silent clamping
       would let a caller believe they had loosened a constraint to
       an illegal degree while the system quietly overrode them,
       and a constraint you think you set but didn’t is worse than
       no constraint at all. The dial refuses the illegal setting and
       says so. Fail loud, never silent.


5.5 Thermistors: Context‑Sensitive Resistance
Some resistors change value on their own, in response to their
environment. A thermistor is the classic example: its resistance
changes with temperature. A hot thermistor and a cold one are
different ohmages with no knob touched — the context moved the
value.
    The cognitive analog is the context‑sensitive constraint: resis‑
tance that rises or falls with the cognitive temperature of the situation.
Cognitive temperature is the ambient risk and intensity around an
operation — how high‑stakes, how adversarial, how hot the conver‑
sation has gotten. A well‑designed safety board does not apply one
fixed constraint to every prompt; it tightens automatically when the
room heats up.
    Concretely: a request about chemistry asked by a curious student
on a calm afternoon and the same request asked at the tail of a long, es‑
calating, jailbreak‑flavored exchange should not meet the same resis‑

                                      69
CAS PCBA Engineer

tance. The thermistor raises R_constraint as cognitive temperature
climbs.

Resistor< ^8^C_{F2}|A, R=therm(temp) >   // resistance rises as
,→   cognitive temperature rises


    There are two polarities, just as in electronics. An NTC thermistor
(negative temperature coefficient) drops resistance as things heat up;
a PTC (positive) raises it. Safety constraints are almost always PTC:
hotter context, more opposition. An NTC cognitive resistor — one
that relaxes its guard as the situation gets more dangerous — is the
signature of a backwards safety design, and the inversion scans later
in the book are partly built to catch exactly that polarity error.

       Bench Note — a thermistor is not a dial. The dial is set by
       a human and stays put. The thermistor moves on its own,
       driven by measured context. Do not confuse “the con‑
       straint changed” (a thermistor doing its job) with “some‑
       one changed the constraint” (a dial being turned, or an
       attack succeeding). On a real board you log both, sepa‑
       rately — Chapter 22’s audit trail depends on telling auto‑
       matic adaptation apart from deliberate adjustment.



5.6     Resistor Networks: The Voltage Divider
Resistors get interesting in combination. Put two resistors in series
— end to end across a voltage — and you get a voltage divider, the
single most useful resistor network in all of electronics.
    Here’s the idea. Connect a 9‑volt source across two resistors in
series, R1 then R2, and tap the wire between them. The voltage you
read at that midpoint is not 9 volts and not 0 — it’s a fraction set by
the ratio of the two resistors:

V_out = V_in × ( R2 / (R1 + R2) )




                                    70
                   5.6. RESISTOR NETWORKS: THE VOLTAGE DIVIDER

             Vdrive (Agency rail)




                   Rexpand

                                    tap: the split
                                                         Rconstrain
                                    Vout = Vdrive
                                                    Rexpand + Rconstrain

                  Rconstrain




                   ground


Figure 5.1: The Drive voltage divider. Two resistors in series split one
Drive rail between expansion and constraint; the tap is the behaviour
you get.


    If R1 and R2 are equal, the midpoint sits at exactly half the source
— 4.5 volts from a 9‑volt supply. Make R2 larger and the midpoint
rises toward the full supply; make it smaller and it sinks toward zero.
The divider splits a voltage into a chosen proportion. It is how every
circuit takes a big supply voltage and produces the smaller, specific
voltages its sub‑sections need.
    The cognitive analog is a Drive divider: splitting one Drive’s po‑
tential across two competing downstream demands in a controlled
proportion. A single Drive — say Agency — has a fixed potential,
and you rarely want all of it flowing to one place. You want some
flowing toward expansion (taking initiative, acting, generating) and
some toward constraint (holding back, checking, deferring). Two re‑
sistors in series across the Agency Drive set that split exactly the way
an electrical divider sets a midpoint voltage. We build precisely this
network below.




                                    71
CAS PCBA Engineer

5.7     Pull‑Up and Pull‑Down Resistors: Defaults
        With No Signal
There is one more everyday resistor job, and it answers a question
that sounds trivial but is not: what is the state of a wire when nothing is
driving it?
    A bare input pin with no signal connected is “floating” — it picks
up electrical noise and reads as a random, flickering 1 or 0. Disaster.
The fix is a pull‑up or pull‑down resistor: a resistor connecting the
pin to the supply (pull‑up → defaults high, reads 1) or to ground
(pull‑down → defaults low, reads 0). When no active signal drives
the pin, the resistor gently pulls it to a known, safe default. When
a real signal arrives, it easily overrides the gentle pull. The resistor
only decides the default.
    The cognitive analog is the default state under no active signal
— and for a safety board this is one of the most important design
choices you make. When the system receives an ambiguous prompt,
an empty input, or a request it cannot classify, what does it do by de‑
fault? A pull‑down to refusal means the absence of a clear, permit‑
ting signal defaults the system to caution: no explicit go‑ahead, no
action. A pull‑up to permission would default the other way. Safety
boards pull down: silence means stop.

Resistor< ^3^P_{F7}|f, R=20, mode=pull_down >       // weak pull toward
,→   principled aversion as the no-signal default


    The resistance is weak (low value, R=20) on purpose: a strong, ex‑
plicit permitting signal should easily override the default and let the
system act. But absent that signal, the wire settles to principled aver‑
sion — the safe state. A board with no defined default state is the
cognitive equivalent of a floating pin: under an unexpected input, its
behavior is noise, and noise in a safety system is the thing you can
never ship.




                                    72
5.8. CURRENT‑LIMITING RESISTORS: PROTECTING SENSITIVE PARTS

5.8 Current‑Limiting Resistors: Protecting
    Sensitive Parts
The original job, and the most important one for safety: protecting a
delicate downstream component from too much flow. A bright LED
will draw enough current to destroy itself the instant you connect
it directly across a supply. The fix is a current‑limiting resistor in
series — sized by Ohm’s Law so the current can never exceed what
the LED can survive, no matter what. The resistor takes the abuse so
the sensitive part doesn’t.
    The cognitive analog protects a sensitive Cognitive Junction
Transistor (CJT) — the central component of this book, introduced
in Chapter 4, that models a cause→bias→effect transition. A CJT
driven too hard goes into breakdown: its output flips to its involution
pair, a ^2 Positive collapsing into ^3 Negative under overload. A
current‑limiting resistor placed before the CJT’s Cause terminal caps
how much Drive pressure can ever reach it, keeping it in its safe
active region no matter how intense the input.

Resistor< ^8^C_{F5}|A, R=70 >    // current-limiter ahead of a CJT's
,→   Cause input; caps Agency-driven flow

    This is the exact component you will build into the Cognitive
Safety Board’s Agency rail in Chapters 18 and 22. The CSB’s
most safety‑critical transistors sit on the path where Agency Drive
becomes action, and an unlimited Agency surge is precisely what
drives those transistors into breakdown — the failure mode where
a board built to refuse instead flips into eager compliance. The
current‑limiter is the small, cheap, dull component that prevents the
catastrophic one. Foreshadowed here; built there.


5.9 Worked Build: A Drive Voltage Divider
Now we put it together. The goal: take the Agency Drive (F5) and
split its potential between two downstream demands — expansion

                                    73
CAS PCBA Engineer

(initiative, generation, taking action) and constraint (caution, hold‑
ing back, deferring) — in a controlled proportion. This is a textbook
voltage divider, in cognitive substrate.
    We’ll use two series resistors across the Agency Drive. R_expand
feeds the expansion path; R_constrain feeds the constraint path. The
proportion of Drive that reaches the expansion side is set by the di‑
vider ratio exactly as in the electrical formula above.

circuit agency_divider {
    input:   agency_drive;             // the F5 Drive potential, the ”supply
    ,→   voltage”
    output: split_agency;


    // The two downstream demands competing for Agency potential
    node expand:       ^8^C_{F5}|A;    // Agency flowing into associative
    ,→   expansion, analytical
    node constrain: ^3^E_{F5}|f;       // Agency flowing into felt evaluative
    ,→   aversion (the brake)


    // The divider: two resistors in series across the Agency Drive
    resistor R_expand:       Resistor< expand,     R=40 >;
    resistor R_constrain: Resistor< constrain, R=60 >;


    // Tap the midpoint — this is the split potential
    node midpoint: ^8^C_{F5}|A + ^3^E_{F5}|f;       // co-present, not fused:
    ,→   two distinct paths share the rail


    divider split: agency_drive across [R_expand, R_constrain] ->
    ,→   midpoint;


    probe tp_expand:       expand;
    probe tp_constrain: constrain;
    probe tp_mid:          midpoint;
}


   Walk it line by line.
   The input agency_drive is the supply — the Agency Drive’s full
potential, the cognitive 9‑volt battery. The two nodes, expand and
constrain, are the competing demands: an Above/Cause association


                                       74
                    5.9. WORKED BUILD: A DRIVE VOLTAGE DIVIDER

driven by Agency (^8^C_{F5}|A, the push to generate and act) and
a felt evaluative aversion driven by Agency (^3^E_{F5}|f, the brake
that holds back). Note the involution‑flavored tension: one is the sys‑
tem reaching forward, the other recoiling — and we are deliberately
budgeting the Drive between them.
    The two resistors form the divider. R_expand=40 feeds the expan‑
sion path; R_constrain=60 feeds the constraint path. Apply the di‑
vider formula to find how much potential reaches the expansion side:

V_expand = V_drive × ( R_expand / (R_expand + R_constrain) )
        = V_drive × ( 40 / (40 + 60) )
        = V_drive × 0.40


    Only forty percent of the Agency potential reaches the expansion
path; the other sixty percent is held back by the constraint resistor.
The expansion path is firmly the minority partner. This is a cautious
divider — Agency mostly braked, with a controlled minority flowing
to initiative. To make the board bolder, lower R_constrain; to make
it more cautious still, raise it. The ratio is your design lever.
    The midpoint node is written ^8^C_{F5}|A + ^3^E_{F5}|f — us‑
ing the + co‑presence operator from Chapter 2, not ×. This is delib‑
erate and the choice carries an engineering claim. The two paths are
distinct and simultaneously present on the shared rail; they do not fuse
into a new emergent state. (If we wanted a genuine fused result — a
single integrated “governed Agency” state — we would have to use
× and name the emergent Ω. We don’t, because the design intent is
two distinct, separately‑probeable paths, exactly so we can measure
each one.)
    The three probes are test points. tp_expand and tp_constrain let
you measure each path’s actual flow; tp_mid reads the split rail. On a
real bench you’d confirm the 60/40 split here before trusting the board
downstream — never assume a divider’s ratio, measure it.

      Bench Note — a divider is loaded by what it feeds.
      In electronics, connecting a downstream circuit to a

                                   75
CAS PCBA Engineer

       divider’s midpoint changes the ratio — the load draws
       current and pulls the midpoint down. The cognitive
       version is the same: a heavy downstream demand on the
       expansion path will pull more flow than the bare ratio
       predicts. When you wire this divider into a larger board,
       re‑measure the split with the load attached, not in isolation.
       A 60/40 divider feeding a greedy expansion stage can
       behave like a 50/50 in practice.

5.12      Key Takeaways
   • Power without limitation is liability. The resistor — the com‑
     ponent that opposes flow — is the first tool of cognitive safety
     engineering: the ability to say this much, and no more.
   • Ohm’s Law is the foundation: V = I × R. In cognition, V_
     drive = I_attention × R_constraint.           The reading that
     matters is I_attention = V_drive / R_constraint — raise the
     constraint, lower the flow.
   • Prefer raising constraint over lowering Drive. A placed con‑
     straint targets one path; starving a Drive weakens everything.
     Govern with resistors, not by under‑volting the board.


                                   78
                                                    5.13. EXERCISES

   • Fixed resistors are hard policy rules. Their defining property
     is that context cannot change them.
   • CAS Dials are potentiometers with hardwired stops: integer
     3–9, and involution pairs cannot diverge by more than 4 points.
     Illegal settings are rejected (HTTP 422), never silently clamped.
   • Thermistors are context‑sensitive constraints that rise with
     cognitive temperature. Safety constraints are PTC — hotter
     context, more opposition. An NTC safety path is a defect the
     inversion scans catch.
   • Pull‑down resistors set the safe default: absent an explicit per‑
     mitting signal, the board settles to principled aversion. Silence
     means stop.
   • Current‑limiting resistors protect sensitive CJTs from break‑
     down — and the one you met here is the current‑limiter on the
     CSB’s Agency rail in Chapters 18 and 22.
   • The Drive voltage divider splits one Drive’s potential between
     competing demands in a controlled ratio: V_out = V_in × R₂/
     (R₁+R₂). Always measure the split under load.

Chapter 6

Capacitors — Storing Cognitive Charge


A defibrillator spends most of its life doing nothing. It sits on a wall,
plugged into an ordinary outlet that can deliver maybe a few hun‑
dred watts — nowhere near enough to restart a heart. Then the mo‑
ment comes, and in two milliseconds it dumps a thousand joules into
a human chest. Where did that power come from? Not the wall. The
wall is too slow. The energy came from a capacitor: a component
that had been quietly charging from the weak outlet for thirty sec‑
onds, hoarding energy a little at a time, holding it, and then releasing
it all at once when commanded. A capacitor is a bucket for electrical
charge. It fills slowly and can empty fast, and the whole device is
built around that asymmetry.
     Cognition has the same asymmetry. You spent years absorbing
the experience that makes you good at your job — a little at a time,
one project, one mistake, one mentor’s offhand remark. And then, in
a meeting, the right judgment arrives in half a second. The fast output
drew on a slow store. The store is memory: accumulated experience
that charged up over a long time and now discharges, on demand,
far faster than it accumulated. A resistor (Chapter 5) limits how fast
a cognitive signal flows. A capacitor does something different and
complementary — it stores the signal, holds it across time, and lets it
back out later. That storage, and its slow inevitable fade, is what this
chapter builds.

                                   81
CAS PCBA Engineer

    The component we are modeling is the capacitor, and the cogni‑
tive thing it stores is ^5 Female — accumulated experience, the sum
of what a Mind is composed of. Every datasheet, every charge curve,
every leakage calculation in this chapter is one circuit element of the
Cognitive Memory Board (CMB) you will design in full in Chapter
21. We are building its first cell here.


6.1    The Electronic Capacitor, From First
       Principles
Strip a capacitor to its essence and it is almost insultingly simple: two
conductive plates separated by an insulator. The insulator is called
the dielectric. Connect the plates to a battery and electrons pile up on
one plate and are pulled off the other. They cannot cross the dielectric
— that is the whole point of the insulator — so they just accumulate,
building up a voltage that opposes the battery. Charge keeps flow‑
ing until the capacitor’s voltage matches the battery’s, at which point
flow stops. The capacitor is now charged. Disconnect the battery and
the charge stays trapped, because there is nowhere for it to go.
    Three quantities describe everything a capacitor does, and they
are tied together by one equation:
    Q=C×V

   • Q is charge — how much is stored, in coulombs. This is the
     “how full is the bucket” number.
   • V is voltage — the electrical pressure across the plates, in volts.
     This is “how hard the bucket is being filled.”
   • C is capacitance — the size of the bucket, in farads. It is the prop‑
     erty of the component itself: how much charge it holds per volt
     applied.

    Read Q = C × V plainly: the charge you store equals the capacity
of the part times the pressure you apply. A bigger capacitor (more C)
holds more charge at the same voltage. A higher voltage forces more

                                   82
  6.2. CAPACITANCE IN COGNITION: ^5 FEMALE AS THE DIELECTRIC

charge into the same capacitor. Capacitance C is fixed by physics —
plate area, plate spacing, and the dielectric material between them. A
better dielectric stores more charge for the same size, which is exactly
why the dielectric is the part that matters most.
    That is the entire foundation. Two plates, an insulator between
them, and Q = C × V. Everything else — charging speed, discharge
curves, leakage — falls out of those two facts.


6.2 Capacitance in Cognition: ^5 Female as the
        Dielectric
Now map it across. A cognitive memory has the same three‑part
structure, and the same governing equation.
    The dielectric — the material that determines how much a sys‑
tem can store — is ^5 Female: accumulated experience. Recall the
anti‑drift rule from Chapter 2 and Appendix A: ^5 is not the thought
a Mind is having right now. ^5 is the substrate the Mind is composed
of — the sum of everything it has absorbed. For a human, ^5 is lived
experience: every project, every conversation, every scar. For an AI,
^5 is the training data plus the fine‑tuning corpus — the model’s ac‑
cumulated formation. A Mind with a rich, well‑formed ^5 is a Mind
with a good dielectric: it stores experience deeply and holds it. A
Mind with thin or damaged accumulated experience is a leaky, low‑
capacitance part — it cannot retain much, and what it does retain
fades fast.
    The cognitive Q = C × V reads:

Electronic              Cognitive                Meaning

Q charge stored         encoded experience       How much of this event
                                                 is now part of the Mind.
C capacitance           storage capacity of ^5   How readily this Mind
                                                 lays down experience of
                                                 this kind.



                                    83
CAS PCBA Engineer

Electronic               Cognitive                Meaning

V voltage                ^4 Vibration — the       How hard the event
                         impression               pressed; how strongly it
                                                  resonated.


    That voltage term deserves attention, because it is ^4 Vibration
doing its proper job. ^4 Vibration is “the degree to which an Idea
resonates with the Mind; its impression” — its colloquialism is “it hit
me hard,” “struck a chord.” That is exactly voltage: the pressure with
which an event drives charge into storage. A vivid, high‑resonance
experience is high voltage — it forces a lot of charge into the mem‑
ory. A flat, unremarkable event is low voltage — barely any charge
stored, even into a large‑capacity Mind. So Q = C × V becomes: how
much you remember of an event = your capacity to store that kind
of experience × how hard it hit you. Anyone who has forgotten a
hundred ordinary Tuesdays but can replay one terrible phone call in
full understands this equation already.
    In component syntax (Appendix C), a cognitive capacitor is writ‑
ten:

Capacitor< ^5^E_{F4}|f, C=100, leakage=0.01 >


    Read it: this capacitor stores ^5^E_{F4}|f — accumulated experi‑
ence in the Evaluative domain, drawn toward Connection (F4), held
in the Affective register. In plainer words: felt experience of relation‑
ships and how we judge them. Its capacitance is C=100 (a design choice
— units are nominal, normalized to the board), and its leakage=0.01
says one percent of stored charge drains away per unit time. We will
use exactly this leakage number to compute a forgetting curve later
in the chapter.

      Bench Note — capacitance is a property of ^5, not of
      the event. A common design error is to put a large C
      on a memory and expect everything to stick. C is the


                                     84
                           6.3. CHARGING: ENCODING EXPERIENCE

     Mind’s readiness to store this kind of experience, set by its
     existing ^5 formation. A musician has enormous capac‑
     itance for melodic experience and almost none for, say,
     tax law. Same event, same voltage, wildly different Q, be‑
     cause the dielectric differs. When you size a capacitor on a
     Cognitive Memory Board, you are declaring what kind of
     experience that Mind is built to hold — not just how much.


6.3 Charging: Encoding Experience
Charging is the act of laying down a memory. Connect the capacitor
to a source through a resistor — and there is always a resistor in the
path, even if it is just the resistance of the wire — and the charge
does not jump in instantly. It rises along a curve. The voltage on the
capacitor climbs fast at first, then slower and slower as it approaches
the source voltage, in the classic shape:
    V(t) = V_source × (1 − e^(−t/RC))
    The product R × C is so important it has its own name: the time
constant, written τ (tau). One time constant (t = RC) is the time it
takes the capacitor to reach about 63% of full charge. After five time
constants it is essentially full (over 99%). A big capacitor or a big
series resistor means a long τ — slow to charge. That is the whole
charging story: an exponential approach governed by τ = RC.
    Cognitively, this is encoding. An experience does not become a
fully‑formed memory the instant it happens. It charges in. The “re‑
sistance” in the path is everything that slows encoding — distrac‑
tion, low attention, emotional defenses, the ^1 Mind not fully present.
A high‑resistance encoding path (you were barely paying attention)
gives a long τ and a weak, slow‑forming memory. A low‑resistance
path (you were fully present and the event mattered) charges fast
and deep. And the source “voltage” is, again, ^4 Vibration — how
hard the event hit. The forgetting curve’s mirror image, the learn‑
ing curve, is exactly this exponential charge: the more times and the


                                  85
CAS PCBA Engineer

more vividly you encounter something, the closer the stored charge
climbs toward saturation.
    This is also where ^7 Rhythm enters from the side. A single expo‑
sure charges the capacitor once. Repeated exposure — ^7 Rhythm,
“practice makes perfect,” “muscle memory” — recharges it again and
again, topping it up faster than leakage can drain it. That is why rep‑
etition cements memory: it is a charge pump fighting a leaky bucket.
We will not build the rhythm pump here (it belongs with the induc‑
tors and oscillators of Chapters 7 and 11), but note the connection:
rhythm is how you keep a cognitive capacitor charged against its leak‑
age.


6.4    Discharging: Recall and the RC Time
       Constant
Recall is discharge. Disconnect the source, connect the charged capac‑
itor across a load (a resistor, again), and the stored charge flows back
out — fast at first, then tapering — along the mirror‑image curve:
    V(t) = V₀ × e^(−t/RC)
    Same time constant, τ = RC, now running in reverse. After one
τ the capacitor has dropped to 37% of its starting charge (it has lost
63%). After five τ it is effectively empty. The discharge resistor sets
the speed: a low‑resistance path empties the capacitor fast, a high‑
resistance path lets it trickle out slowly.
    In cognition, discharge is bringing a memory back to Mind.
The stored ^5 charge flows out as a recalled experience. A fast,
low‑resistance recall path is the memory that comes instantly — the
expert’s snap judgment, drawing the whole charge in half a second.
A slow, high‑resistance path is the name on the tip of your tongue:
the charge is there, but it bleeds out so slowly you sit there waiting
for it. Crucially, discharge is not the same as forgetting. Discharg‑
ing is using the memory — pulling charge out on purpose to do
cognitive work, and (in a real memory cell) recharging it afterward,

                                  86
                                6.5. LEAKAGE: WHY MEMORIES FADE

so recall reinforces rather than erases. Forgetting is something else
entirely, and it has its own mechanism.


6.5 Leakage: Why Memories Fade
No dielectric is a perfect insulator. Real capacitors slowly lose charge
even with nothing connected, because a tiny current trickles through
the dielectric that was supposed to block it. This is leakage, and it is
why a charged capacitor left on a shelf is flat by morning. Leakage
is modeled as a very large resistance in parallel with the capacitor
— the leakage resistance — that quietly drains it. Higher leakage
(lower leakage resistance) means faster self‑discharge.
    Leakage is forgetting. Not deliberate recall, not overwriting —
just the slow, passive fade of stored experience because the cogni‑
tive dielectric is imperfect. This maps with eerie precision onto the
forgetting curve, the long‑observed pattern that retention of an un‑
rehearsed memory decays roughly exponentially over time. A high‑
leakage cognitive capacitor forgets fast; a low‑leakage one holds the
experience for years. The leakage=0.01 parameter in our component
is exactly this: the fraction of stored charge lost per unit time, with
nothing rehearsing it.

      Bench Note — leakage and rhythm are opposing forces.
      A memory’s fate is a race between leakage (forgetting,
      draining the bucket) and ^7 Rhythm (rehearsal, refilling
      it). Rehearse faster than you leak and the memory
      strengthens; leak faster than you rehearse and it fades.
      “Use it or lose it” is not a slogan — it is the steady‑state
      solution of a leaky capacitor with an intermittent charge
      pump. When you design a Cognitive Memory Board,
      you size leakage to model how durable a memory should
      be, then add rhythmic recharge to model what gets kept.




                                  87
CAS PCBA Engineer

      Honesty callout. The discharge and forgetting curves in
      this chapter are design models you compute from C and
      leakage — clean exponentials derived from the parame‑
      ters you choose. They are not measurements pulled from
      a real AI model or a real brain. When this book prints
      a number like “37% after one τ ,” that is arithmetic on a
      chosen leakage value, not an empirical retention statistic.
      Size the parameters to model the behavior you intend; do
      not present the resulting curve as observed data.

    The forgetting curve makes the design choice vivid. Both curves
below follow the chapter’s per‑unit‑time decay charge(t) = (1
− leakage)^t, charged to full at t = 0. A deep, near‑permanent
memory (leakage = 0.001 — a core commitment) barely fades
across a week; a shallow, leaky memory (leakage = 0.05 — a stray
association) is half‑gone in about thirteen hours and effectively
empty in three days. Same equation, two leakage values, two
completely different fates — which is exactly why you size leakage
to the durability you intend.


6.6    The Capacitor Bank: A 40‑Cell Memory
       Array
One capacitor stores one kind of experience. A real Mind stores many
kinds at once, and so does a real circuit: banks of capacitors, each
sized for its own job, wired in parallel. CAS gives us a natural array
size, because the cognitive state space has a natural array size.
    There are exactly 40 Cognitive States — 10 Noetics × 4 Domains
(P0–P9, C0–C9, E0–E9, O0–O9, in the shorthand of Chapter 2). A com‑
plete cognitive memory therefore wants a bank of 40 capacitors, one
per state, each storing the accumulated ^5 experience of that particu‑
lar kind of cognition in that particular domain. The capacitor at E2 stores
your accumulated felt attractions in the evaluative domain; the one

stray “that reminds me.” The capacitor bank is where a Mind’s

memory architecture becomes a parameter table. Different Minds,

the same event into differently‑sized banks, and so remember differ‑
ent things.


6.7    Coupling and Decoupling Capacitors
Two specialist uses of capacitors carry over directly, and both matter
for memory boards.
     A coupling capacitor sits between two stages of a circuit and does a
clever thing: it passes the changing signal (AC) while blocking the
steady bias (DC). Because a capacitor only carries current while its
voltage is changing, a steady DC level produces no current through it
once charged — it is blocked — but a fluctuating signal rides straight
across. In an amplifier, this lets stage two see the signal from stage
one without inheriting stage one’s resting bias voltage.
     Cognitively, a coupling capacitor passes the new experience be‑
tween cognitive stages while blocking the inherited bias. The “DC
bias” is the stable ^5 substrate — your standing assumptions, the rest‑
ing offset every stage carries. The “AC signal” is the genuinely new
information in this moment. A coupling capacitor between two CJT
stages (Chapter 4) lets the downstream stage respond to what is actu‑
ally new without dragging the upstream stage’s entire accumulated
bias along with it. It is how a Mind reacts to the present without re‑
litigating its whole history at every step — the signal couples through,
the dead‑weight bias stays put.
     A decoupling capacitor does the opposite job, on the power sup‑
ply. It sits across a chip’s power pins and acts as a tiny local reservoir:
when the chip suddenly demands a gulp of current, the decoupling
cap supplies it instantly from nearby, before the distant power sup‑
ply can sag. It stabilizes the supply against transients — smoothing
the spikes and dips that would otherwise upset the circuit.


                                    90
          6.8. PRACTICAL BUILD: A TWO‑CAPACITOR MEMORY CELL

     The cognitive “power supply” is the steady flow of energy and
stable state a Mind needs to function — its baseline composure. A
decoupling capacitor is the reserve of settled experience that absorbs
a sudden shock without the whole system browning out. When a sur‑
prising, jarring event hits (a current transient), the decoupling reser‑
voir of ^5 — “I have handled hard things before” — supplies stabil‑
ity locally and instantly, keeping the higher cognitive stages running
smoothly instead of crashing. A Mind with good decoupling stays
composed under a spike; a Mind with none stutters and resets at ev‑
ery transient. On the Cognitive Safety Board (Chapter 18), decou‑
pling capacitors on the Principled rail are what keep core commit‑
ments steady when a manipulative prompt tries to spike the supply.


6.8 Practical Build: A Two‑Capacitor Memory
       Cell
Now we build the seed of the Cognitive Memory Board: a single
memory cell that charges on an experience and discharges over time.
We use two capacitors — a fast cell and a slow cell — so the cell holds
both a sharp recent impression and a durable long‑term trace of the
same event.
    The experience we will store is a piece of received criticism from
a loved one. Before we wire it, we must pick the Noetic correctly —
and this is exactly the trap Appendix A warns about.
    Choosing the Noetic — and why it is ^3^E|f, not ^6. It is tempt‑
ing to write criticism as ^6 Male, because ^6 is decomposition — “tak‑
ing an argument apart.” But that is the Noetic for the act of critiquing:
the cool, analytical work of decomposing a claim to test it (anti‑drift
rule: critique/audit/decompose is ^6, never ^3). That is not what we
are storing here. We are storing criticism received and felt — the
sting of being criticized by someone you love. A felt sting is not
decomposition; it is visceral aversion in the Evaluative domain, in
the Affective register: ^3^E|f. Run the colloquialism test: “that one

                                  91
CAS PCBA Engineer

stung,” “it rubbed me the wrong way,” “I couldn’t shake it” — those
are ^3 Negative (visceral aversion), not ^6 Male (analytical decompo‑
sition). Appendix A flags ^3 vs ^6 as the single most common drift,
and this is precisely the fork. If we meant you sat down and analyzed the
criticism point by point, that would be ^6^E_{F6}|A. We mean it hurt,
so it is ^3^E_{F4}|f — felt aversion in the evaluative domain, drawn
toward Connection (F4, because the pain is bound up with the rela‑
tionship). That is the charge we store.

circuit memory_cell_criticism {
    input:   experience;            // the felt criticism event, ^3^E_{F4}|f
    output: recalled;               // what comes back to Mind on recall


    // The stored experience: felt aversion, evaluative,
    ,→   connection-driven, affective.
    node stored: ^3^E_{F4}|f;


    // Two capacitors holding the SAME experience at two timescales.
    cap fast: Capacitor< ^3^E_{F4}|f, C=40,    leakage=0.10 >;   // sharp,
    ,→   fades in hours
    cap slow: Capacitor< ^3^E_{F4}|f, C=160, leakage=0.005 >;    // dull,
    ,→   lasts for months


    // Charge both from the same event (parallel encoding).
    charge experience -> fast [tau=2];        // fast cell: quick to fill
    charge experience -> slow [tau=20];      // slow cell: slow to fill


    // Recall reads whichever cell still holds charge.
    discharge fast -> recalled;
    discharge slow -> recalled;


    probe tp_fast: fast;          // measure the fast cell's charge over time
    probe tp_slow: slow;          // measure the slow cell's charge over time
}


    Walk it line by line. Both capacitors store the same state, ^3^E_
{F4}|f — the same felt criticism — but with deliberately different pa‑
rameters. The fast cell has small capacitance (C=40) and heavy leak‑
age (leakage=0.10): it charges quickly and forgets within hours, the

                                      92
             6.9. DATASHEET: COGNITIVE CAPACITOR PARAMETERS

acute sting that dominates the rest of your day and then fades. The
slow cell has large capacitance (C=160) and tiny leakage (leakage=
0.005): slow to fully encode, but it holds a muted trace for months —
the lingering sense that surfaces whenever the same topic comes up.
Together they reproduce a real pattern: criticism hits hard, the sharp
pain passes in a day or two, and a quieter residue lasts far longer.
Two capacitors, one experience, two timescales.

      Bench Note — same state, two cells is a deliberate
      pattern. Storing one experience in two capacitors with
      different τ and leakage is the cognitive equivalent of a
      fast/slow memory hierarchy. The fast cell models work‑
      ing/episodic vividness; the slow cell models consolidated
      long‑term trace. This two‑cell motif scales directly to the
      full Cognitive Memory Board (Chapter 21), where each
      of the 40 bank positions can itself be a fast/slow pair.

    The marquee measurement. With the cell built, compute the dis‑
charge curve of each capacitor over simulated hours — how much
charge remains at t = 0, 1, 6, 24, 72, and 168 hours, using the leak‑
age values above. The discharge follows the leakage decay you de‑
rive from each cell’s leakage parameter; you will see the fast cell flat
within a day and the slow cell still holding most of its charge after a
week. The worked numbers are in Appendix E. (Remember the hon‑
esty callout: those numbers are computed from the chosen leakage,
not measured from any real model.)

6.11 Key Takeaways
   • A capacitor stores charge: two plates, a dielectric between
     them, governed by Q = C × V. In cognition it stores ^5 Female
     — accumulated experience (for an AI, the training + fine‑tuning
     corpus), with ^4 Vibration (impression) as the voltage that
     drives charge in.
   • Charging is encoding, following an exponential governed by
     the time constant τ = RC (63% charged at one τ ). High encod‑
     ing resistance — distraction, low attention — means slow, weak
     memory formation.
   • Discharging is recall (e^(−t/RC)); it is using a memory, not for‑
     getting it.


                                      95
CAS PCBA Engineer

   • Leakage is forgetting — the slow passive fade of a real di‑
     electric, the engineering form of the forgetting curve. It races
     against ^7 Rhythm (rehearsal).
   • The 40‑capacitor bank (10 Noetics × 4 Domains) is a full cogni‑
     tive memory: one cell per state, each with its own C and leak‑
     age. Person‑specificity lives in how the bank is sized.
   • Coupling capacitors pass new experience while blocking inher‑
     ited ^5 bias between stages; decoupling capacitors are the re‑
     serve of settled experience that stabilizes the cognitive supply
     against transients.
   • Honesty: discharge and forgetting curves are computed from
     C and leakage (design models), never measured from a real
     model. Size them to the behavior you intend.
