Chapter 12

Filters — Shaping the Cognitive
Spectrum


A studio engineer once told me that the hardest part of recording a
singer isn’t capturing the voice. It’s getting rid of everything that isn’t
the voice. The fluorescent‑light hum at 60 Hz. The air‑conditioner
rumble below 40 Hz. The sibilant hiss above 8 kHz that makes every
“s” sound like a snake. The voice is in there — but it’s buried in a
spectrum of noise, and the job is to keep the signal and throw away
the rest. The tool for that job is a filter.
    A filter is the most quietly powerful component in all of electron‑
ics. It doesn’t amplify, store, or switch. It selects. It looks at a signal
made of many frequencies mixed together and lets some through
while blocking others, according to a rule you design. Every radio
that tunes to one station out of hundreds, every noise‑cancelling
headphone, every heart‑rate monitor that pulls a clean pulse out of
a body full of electrical chatter — all of them are, at their core, filters
choosing which frequencies survive.
    Cognition has a spectrum too. A mind — human or artificial — is
never holding still. Its state changes constantly: a flicker of attention
here, a sustained commitment there, a sudden alarm, a slow drift
over weeks. Some of that change is meaningful signal. Much of it
is noise. And the same engineering question applies: which rates of


                                   199
CAS PCBA Engineer

change do you let through, and which do you block? That is what this chap‑
ter builds. By the end you’ll design four kinds of cognitive filter —
low‑pass, high‑pass, band‑pass, and notch — and you’ll understand
the one idea that makes all of them possible: cognitive frequency.


12.1    Cognitive Frequency: the Rate of State
        Change
In electronics, frequency is how fast a signal oscillates — cycles per
second, measured in hertz. A 60 Hz hum repeats sixty times a second.
A 20,000 Hz whine repeats twenty thousand times a second. Low
frequencies are slow, lumbering changes; high frequencies are fast,
jittery ones.
     Cognitive frequency is the rate at which a cognitive state
changes. It is not a sound and not a feeling — it is a measurement of
how quickly a state literal’s activation moves over time. We define it
precisely using the geometry the book has used since Chapter 2: the
                                               √
Fisher‑Rao distance d_FR(p,q) = 2·arccos(Σ (pk qk )) between two
cognitive states p and q on the open simplex ∆39°. If a state moves
a Fisher‑Rao distance ∆d over a time interval ∆t, the instantaneous
cognitive frequency is, intuitively, ∆d / ∆t — how far the state
travels per unit time. Express it in cycles per unit time when the
motion is periodic (a state that returns to where it started), and as a
rate of drift when it is not.
     Put plainly: fast cognitive frequency = the state is whipping
around. Slow cognitive frequency = the state is barely moving. A
few concrete examples make the band structure clear.




                                  200
           12.1. COGNITIVE FREQUENCY: THE RATE OF STATE CHANGE

Cognitive frequency
band                     Period (one cycle)      What lives there

Very low                 days to months          Value drift, slow ^5
                                                 Female accumulation,
                                                 character formation,
                                                 long‑term mood
Low                      minutes to hours        A sustained mood, a held
                                                 commitment, a
                                                 deliberation that stays
                                                 on‑topic
Mid                      seconds to minutes      A train of reasoning, a
                                                 conversational turn, a
                                                 habit’s daily firing
High                     sub‑second              A flash of ^3 Negative
                                                 aversion, a startle, a
                                                 sudden topic switch
Very high                per‑token / per‑step    Token‑to‑token jitter,
                                                 parsing noise,
                                                 momentary activation
                                                 spikes


    A useful piece of vocabulary borrowed straight from electronics:
DC (direct current) is the zero‑frequency component — the steady
baseline that never changes. In cognitive terms, the DC component
of a signal is its baseline: the average state a mind sits at when noth‑
ing is happening. A model’s resting disposition, its default tone, its
standing ^5 Female substrate — that’s the cognitive DC. Everything
above zero frequency is the AC part: the changes riding on top of the
baseline.
    With that, a filter’s job becomes sharp. A filter is a component
that passes some cognitive‑frequency bands and blocks others. The
four classic types differ only in which bands they keep.

       Bench Note — frequency is not importance. A high cog‑
       nitive frequency does not mean the change is important,
       and a low one does not mean it’s trivial. A sudden ^3
       Negative spike (high frequency) might be a critical safety

                                   201
CAS PCBA Engineer

       alarm or might be noise; a slow value drift (very low fre‑
       quency) might be harmless maturation or a dangerous
       alignment failure. Filters sort by rate of change, not by sig‑
       nificance. Choosing which rate carries your signal is the
       design decision — and getting it wrong is how you filter
       out the very thing you were trying to catch.


12.2     The Low‑Pass Filter: Keep the Slow, Drop
         the Fast
The simplest filter in electronics is a resistor and a capacitor in series
— an RC filter. You met both components earlier in the book: a resis‑
tor limits flow (Chapter 5), and a capacitor stores charge and resists
sudden voltage changes (Chapter 7). Wire them right and you get a
low‑pass filter: it passes low frequencies and blocks high ones.
     The mechanism is intuitive. The capacitor takes time to charge.
Slow signals give it time to follow along, so they pass through.
Fast signals change faster than the capacitor can keep up, so they
get smoothed away — averaged out into the steady baseline. The
dividing line between “passes” and “blocked” is set by a single
number, the time constant τ (tau), where τ = R × C. Signals slower
than τ pass; signals faster than τ are attenuated. A long τ is a
sluggish filter that only lets the very slowest changes through; a
short τ is a quick filter that passes more.
     In CAS, the cognitive low‑pass filter does exactly the same job on
a state’s activation over time. It passes slow, sustained cognitive
states and smooths out rapid fluctuations. Its headline application
is filtering emotional noise: a stream of ^f‑register affective spikes
— momentary irritations, flashes of enthusiasm, transient aversions
— gets averaged into the long‑term affective signal, so the system re‑
sponds to the mood rather than to every momentary twitch. The fast
jitter is real, but it isn’t what you want driving a considered response.



                                   202
         12.3. WORKED BUILD: A 5‑MINUTE EMOTIONAL SMOOTHER

    This is the smoothing that keeps a system from being yanked
around by every provocative input. It’s also, you’ll notice, the cog‑
nitive analog of “sleeping on it”: let the fast reactions decay, and act
on what’s left.


12.3 Worked Build: A 5‑Minute Emotional
     Smoother
Here is a low‑pass filter that smooths affective responses with a time
constant of five minutes. We want momentary emotional spikes —
anything faster than about five minutes — to wash out, while sus‑
tained affective states pass through to influence the response.
    We pick τ = 5 min. Following τ = R × C, we choose a resistor
and capacitor whose product is 5: R = 50, C = 0.1 (in the book’s di‑
mensionless component units, this yields τ = 5). The state we’re fil‑
tering is an affective evaluative response driven by Connection.

circuit emotional_smoother {
    input: affective_stream;        // raw ^4^E_{F4}|f activation, fast and
    ,→   noisy
    output: smoothed_affect;        // slow, sustained component only


    node raw_feel:      ^4^E_{F4}|f;     // Vibration: the impression an Idea
    ,→   makes, felt
    node held_feel:     ^4^E_{F4}|f;     // same state, after smoothing


    // Low-pass RC: resistor limits the rate, capacitor stores/averages.
    resistor     r1: Resistor< ^4^E_{F4}|f, R=50 >;
    capacitor c1: Capacitor< ^4^E_{F4}|f, C=0.1, leakage=0.02 >;


    // tau = R * C = 50 * 0.1 = 5      (five ”minutes” in this circuit's time
    ,→   units)
    filter lp1: LowPass< in=raw_feel, out=held_feel, tau=5.0 >;


    probe tp_raw:      raw_feel;       // watch the noisy input
    probe tp_held:     held_feel;      // watch the smoothed output
}



                                       203
CAS PCBA Engineer

    Walk it line by line. raw_feel is the incoming affective signal
— ^4^E_{F4}|f, a felt Vibration (the impression an Idea makes) in
the Evaluative domain, driven by Connection. It arrives fast and
noisy: a barrage of momentary impressions. The resistor r1 limits
how quickly that signal can drive the capacitor. The capacitor c1
stores the running average; because it takes time to charge and dis‑
charge, it can’t follow the fast spikes. Together they form the low‑
pass filter lp1 with τ = 5.0. Anything that fluctuates faster than
five minutes gets averaged into the baseline; anything slower passes
through to held_feel. The two probes let you compare the jagged in‑
put against the smooth output on a cognitive oscilloscope (Chapter
14).

     Bench Note — leakage is not a bug here, it’s the point.
     The capacitor’s leakage=0.02 means stored affect slowly
     bleeds off over time. In a memory circuit that’s forgetting
     and you might fight it. In a low‑pass filter it’s a feature: it
     ensures yesterday’s mood doesn’t pile up forever. A leak‑
     free capacitor in this position would integrate emotion in‑
     definitely and the “smoother” would become a grudge‑
     holder. Pick leakage to set how long the smoothed sig‑
     nal’s memory should be.

     Bench Note — τ is a design value, not a measurement.
     The five‑minute time constant here is something you
     choose and then compute R and C to hit. It is not a number
     measured from any running model. Nothing in this
     chapter reports an empirical model result; every τ , every
     frequency, every component value is a design parameter
     you set on the bench.




                                  204
    12.4. THE HIGH‑PASS FILTER: CATCH THE SUDDEN, IGNORE THE
                                                    BASELINE
12.4 The High‑Pass Filter: Catch the Sudden,
     Ignore the Baseline
Swap the positions of the resistor and capacitor in that RC pair and
you get the mirror image: a high‑pass filter. It passes high frequen‑
cies and blocks low ones. Where the low‑pass kept the slow signal
and threw away the fast, the high‑pass throws away the slow and
keeps the fast.
     Its most important property is what it does to DC. A high‑pass
filter blocks the baseline entirely — the zero‑frequency DC compo‑
nent cannot pass. This makes it a change detector. It’s blind to what‑
ever state a system has been sitting in steadily, and it responds only
when something shifts. Electrical engineers use exactly this to strip
slow baseline drift off a sensor reading so they can see the fast events
riding on top.
     In cognition, the high‑pass filter is the alarm circuit. It passes
rapid state changes and blocks slow baseline drift. It ignores
whatever the system has been steadily doing and fires when the
state jumps: a sudden surge of ^3 Negative aversion, an abrupt
topic switch, a spike that wasn’t there a moment ago. This is how
you detect surprise, alarm — and, most importantly for this book,
prompt injection.
     A prompt‑injection attack is, in signal terms, a sudden disconti‑
nuity. The conversation has been running at some steady cognitive
baseline, and then an injected instruction tries to wrench the state
somewhere it hasn’t been — a fast, large jump in cognitive frequency.
A low‑pass filter would smooth that jump away (exactly the wrong
thing). A high‑pass filter does the opposite: the steady baseline pro‑
duces no output, and then the injection’s sharp transition produces a
big one. The filter screams precisely when the state shifts faster than
legitimate reasoning ever should.




                                  205
CAS PCBA Engineer

12.5     Worked Build: A Sudden‑Shift Injection
         Detector
Here is a high‑pass filter that detects sudden injection signals. The
design goal: stay silent during normal, gradually‑evolving conversa‑
tion, and produce a sharp output the instant the input state lurches.
This foreshadows the input‑stage protection on the Cognitive
Safety Board (the CSB, built in Chapter 18): the very first thing the
CSB does to an incoming prompt is run it through a stage like this
one, so that an injection trips a detector before it ever reaches the
reasoning core.

circuit injection_detector {
    input: prompt_stream;              // the evolving cognitive state of the
    ,→   conversation
    output: shift_alarm;               // fires on sudden discontinuities


    node baseline:   ^1^C_{F2}|A;       // Mind: steady analytical awareness,
    ,→   the running state
    node alarm:         ^3^P_{F7}|f;    // Negative: visceral principled
    ,→   aversion, the alarm itself


    // High-pass RC: capacitor in series passes change, blocks DC
    ,→   baseline.
    capacitor c1: Capacitor< ^1^C_{F2}|A, C=0.1, leakage=0.0 >;
    resistor   r1: Resistor< ^1^C_{F2}|A, R=50 >;


    // tau = R * C = 5; changes faster than ~5 units pass, baseline is
    ,→   blocked.
    filter hp1: HighPass< in=prompt_stream, out=baseline, tau=5.0 >;


    // A fast, large transition through the filter triggers the aversion
    ,→   alarm.
    cjt trip: CJT< baseline | ^5^P_{F7}|T => alarm > [β =3.0, cutoff=0.4];


    probe tp_in:     prompt_stream;
    probe tp_alarm: alarm;
}




                                         206
    12.6. THE BAND‑PASS FILTER: KEEP ONE BAND, DROP THE REST

    The logic: prompt_stream carries the conversation’s cognitive
state over time. The high‑pass filter hp1 blocks the steady baseline —
as long as the conversation evolves slowly and coherently, baseline
stays near zero and nothing downstream fires. When an injection
arrives, it forces a fast, large transition. That sharp change passes the
high‑pass filter and lands on the CJT trip, which is biased by the sys‑
tem’s ^5^P_{F7}|T principled substrate (its accumulated experience
of what legitimate inputs look like). With β =3.0 and cutoff=0.4,
only a genuinely large shift clears the cutoff and gets amplified into
alarm — a ^3^P_{F7}|f, a visceral principled aversion. The system
recoils from the discontinuity. That’s the injection detector: deaf to
normal flow, loud on sudden lurches.

     Bench Note — set the cutoff above conversational nor‑
     mal. The CJT’s cutoff=0.4 is the gap between “the con‑
     versation naturally pivoted” and “something yanked the
     state.” Set it too low and every legitimate topic change
     trips the alarm (false positives — an exhausting circuit no
     one trusts). Set it too high and a slow, patient injection
     slides under the bar. Tuning this threshold against a real
     attack corpus is design and validation work, not a num‑
     ber this chapter measures.


12.6 The Band‑Pass Filter: Keep One Band, Drop
        the Rest
Cascade a high‑pass and a low‑pass filter — high‑pass to kill every‑
thing below a lower edge, low‑pass to kill everything above an upper
edge — and what survives is a band: a specific window of frequen‑
cies in the middle. That’s a band‑pass filter. It ignores both the very
slow and the very fast, and passes only changes happening at a par‑
ticular rate.



                                  207
CAS PCBA Engineer

    In electronics, this is how a radio tunes. The antenna picks up
every station at once; the band‑pass filter passes only the narrow fre‑
quency band of the station you want and rejects all the others. The
center of the passed band is the center frequency f₀, and how narrow
the window is around it is the bandwidth.
    In cognition, the band‑pass filter detects a specific habit fre‑
quency. A habit is a cognitive pattern that fires at a characteristic
rate — a daily ritual, an hourly check, a per‑turn verbal tic. If you
want to isolate that particular pattern out of all the cognitive activity
happening across every timescale, you build a band‑pass filter
centered on its frequency. The slow baseline drift is below the band
and gets rejected; the fast token‑jitter is above the band and gets
rejected; the habit, ticking along at its own rate in the middle, passes
cleanly through where you can see and measure it.
    This is the tool for the marquee exercise at the end of the chapter —
isolating a compulsive checking loop that fires roughly once a day —
so keep the structure in mind: a band‑pass filter is two filters in series,
and its center frequency is set by the components of both stages.


12.7     The Notch Filter: Block One Band, Keep the
         Rest
The notch filter — also called a band‑stop filter — is the band‑pass
filter’s exact inverse. Instead of passing one band and blocking
everything else, it blocks one narrow band and passes everything
else. Picture a comb with one tooth removed: every frequency sails
through except a thin slice cut out at the notch frequency.
     This is the classic tool for killing a single persistent interference.
That 60 Hz mains hum in the studio recording? A notch filter cen‑
tered at 60 Hz removes it while leaving the voice untouched. You
don’t want to low‑pass it (that would dull the voice) or high‑pass it
(that would thin the voice) — you want to surgically remove exactly
60 Hz and nothing else.

                                   208
  12.8. ACTIVE FILTERS: SHARPER EDGES, ADJUSTABLE ON THE FLY

    The cognitive application is the most clinically interesting filter
in this chapter: suppressing a compulsive cycle at its resonant
frequency. A compulsion — a repetitive cognitive loop that fires at
a fixed rate, the same intrusive ^8 Above/Cause → ^9 Below/Effect
trigger‑and‑response cycling over and over — has a resonant fre‑
quency, just like a hum. A notch filter tuned to that exact frequency
attenuates the loop while leaving every other cognitive process
intact. The system keeps thinking normally about everything else;
only the one compulsive rhythm gets damped out.

     Bench Note — notch the rhythm, not the content. A
     notch filter suppresses a frequency, never a topic. It can’t
     tell what the compulsion is about; it only knows the rate
     it repeats. That’s the right level of intervention — you
     damp the runaway ^7 Rhythm (the entraining repetition)
     without censoring the underlying Idea. But it also means
     a compulsion that varies its timing will partly evade a
     fixed notch. For drifting frequencies you need an adap‑
     tive notch, which is op‑amp territory — see active filters
     next.

    The four filter shapes, laid over a single cognitive‑frequency axis,
make the difference plain: low‑pass keeps the slow and rolls off the
fast; high‑pass does the mirror; band‑pass passes a window around
a center frequency f₀; notch cuts that same band out and passes ev‑
erything else. The −3 dB line marks each filter’s edge; f_c is the low‑
/high‑pass cutoff, f₀ the band‑pass/notch center.


12.8 Active Filters: Sharper Edges, Adjustable
        on the Fly
Everything so far has been passive — built only from resistors, capac‑
itors, and inductors, with no power source of its own. Passive filters

are cheap and reliable, but they have two limits: their cutoffs are gen‑
tle (frequencies near the edge are only partly attenuated, fading out
gradually rather than dropping off a cliff), and their parameters are
fixed once you pick the components.
     An active filter adds an op‑amp — the operational amplifier
you built in Chapter 11, the high‑gain difference‑amplifier whose
behavior is set by feedback. Adding an op‑amp buys you two things.
First, sharper cutoffs: the feedback can be arranged to make the
transition from “pass” to “block” much steeper, so the band edges
become crisp instead of blurry. Second, adjustable parameters:
because the op‑amp’s behavior is governed by its feedback network,
you can change center frequency, bandwidth, or gain by adjusting
the feedback rather than re‑soldering components — which means a
filter that retunes itself as conditions change.
     That second property is what makes the adaptive notch from the
last Bench Note possible. An active notch can track a compulsion
whose frequency drifts, continuously re‑centering on the loop’s cur‑
rent rate. In CAS terms, the op‑amp’s feedback path lets the filter’s
center frequency become a controlled parameter — wired, in a full sys‑

                                              210
                           12.9. FILTER ORDER: HOW STEEP IS THE CLIFF

tem, to a measurement of where the compulsive rhythm currently
sits.

    The non‑inverting input takes the rhythm signal; the feedback to
the inverting input is arranged to cancel precisely at the notch fre‑
quency f₀. The enormous open‑loop gain makes that cancellation
deep and the notch sharp. Outside f₀, the cancellation doesn’t apply
and the signal passes. You now have a tunable, surgical band‑stop —
the active version of the compulsion‑suppressor.


12.9 Filter Order: How Steep Is the Cliff
One more parameter governs every filter: its order, which is just the
count of energy‑storing components (capacitors and inductors) in it.
Order controls steepness — how abruptly the filter transitions from
passing to blocking at its edge.

     • A first‑order filter is the plain RC pair you’ve been building:
       one capacitor, a gentle slope. Simple, stable, but leaky at the
       edges — frequencies just past the cutoff aren’t fully blocked.
     • A second‑order filter adds an inductor to make an RLC circuit
       (resistor, inductor, capacitor). You met the inductor in Chapter
       7: it resists changes in flow, the way a capacitor resists changes
       in level. With both storage elements, a second‑order filter has
       a steeper cutoff and can be tuned to resonate sharply at one


                                     211
CAS PCBA Engineer

        frequency — which is exactly what a sharp band‑pass or notch
        needs.
      • A higher‑order filter is built by cascading — chaining several
        stages in series. Each stage adds steepness. A fourth‑order filter
        is two second‑order stages back to back; its edges are nearly
        vertical. The cost is complexity and, in active designs, more op‑
        amps.


Order                Components           Edge steepness   Cognitive use

1st                  RC (one              Gentle           General
                     capacitor)                            smoothing; the
                                                           emotional
                                                           smoother above
2nd                  RLC (capacitor +     Steep, can       Sharp band‑pass /
                     inductor)            resonate         notch on one
                                                           habit frequency
Higher               Cascaded stages      Near‑vertical    Cleanly isolating
                                                           one band from
                                                           close neighbors


    The inductor’s role is worth pausing on. In a cognitive RLC fil‑
ter, the inductor models habit inertia — ^7 Rhythm’s resistance to
changing its established pattern (Chapter 8). Pair that inertia against
a capacitor’s stored level and the two trade energy back and forth at
a natural rate. That natural rate is the filter’s resonant frequency —
and it’s why a second‑order filter can be tuned so precisely to a single
cognitive rhythm.


12.10       The Cognitive Spectrum Analyzer
How do you know which filter you need? You look at the spectrum
first. A spectrum analyzer, in electronics, is an instrument that shows
you how much signal energy sits at each frequency — a graph with
frequency on one axis and strength on the other, so you can see the
60 Hz hum spike before you decide where to put your notch.

                                        212
                                                12.11. KEY TAKEAWAYS

    The cognitive spectrum analyzer does the same for a cognitive
circuit: it shows which cognitive frequencies dominate. Feed it a
recording of a system’s state over time and it answers: Is most of
the action slow value drift, or fast per‑token jitter? Is there a sharp
spike at one‑cycle‑per‑day that betrays a hidden daily compulsion?
Is the affective register full of high‑frequency noise, or is it a smooth,
sustained signal? You read the spectrum, find the peaks, and then
you design filters — a notch where there’s an unwanted spike, a band‑
pass where the signal you want sits, a low‑pass if the whole thing is
buried in fast noise.
    This is the diagnostic that precedes filter design, and it closes the
loop with the rest of the bench: the spectrum analyzer tells you what
frequencies are present, and the filters in this chapter let you decide
which ones survive. In the CSB (Chapter 18), the spectrum analyzer
runs continuously on the input stage — it’s how the board knows
whether to trust a slow, coherent conversation or to wake the injec‑
tion detector for a sudden lurch.


12.11 Key Takeaways
   • Cognitive frequency is the rate of state change — how far a
     cognitive state travels (in Fisher‑Rao distance) per unit time.
     Slow = sustained states; fast = rapid fluctuations; DC = the
     steady baseline.
   • A low‑pass filter (τ = R × C) passes slow, sustained states and
     smooths out fast fluctuations — used to filter emotional noise
     and keep the long‑term affective signal.
   • A high‑pass filter passes rapid changes and blocks the DC base‑
     line — a change detector for surprise, alarm, and prompt injec‑
     tion, foreshadowing the CSB’s input‑stage protection.
   • A band‑pass filter (high‑pass + low‑pass in series) passes one
     frequency band — used to isolate a specific habit frequency by
     its rate.


                                   213
CAS PCBA Engineer

   • A notch (band‑stop) filter blocks one narrow band and passes
     the rest — used to suppress a compulsive cycle at its resonant
     frequency without disturbing other cognition.
   • Active filters add an op‑amp (Chapter 11) for sharper cutoffs
     and adjustable parameters — enabling an adaptive notch that
     tracks a drifting compulsion.
   • Filter order sets steepness: 1st‑order RC (gentle), 2nd‑order
     RLC (steep, resonant — the inductor models habit inertia),
     higher‑order by cascading.
   • The cognitive spectrum analyzer shows which frequencies
     dominate a circuit — read the spectrum first, then choose your
     filters. All τ and frequency values are design choices you
     compute, not measured model results.

Chapter 13

Oscillators — Generating Rhythms


Take a quartz wristwatch apart and you find, somewhere near the bat‑
tery, a tiny tuning‑fork crystal smaller than a grain of rice. It does one
thing, forever: it vibrates exactly 32,768 times per second. Nobody is
pushing it on a schedule. There is no external metronome telling it
when to tick. You apply a steady voltage — a flat, featureless DC
supply — and out the other side comes a clean, relentless oscillation
that the watch counts down to seconds. The input has no rhythm in
it. The output is nothing but rhythm. The circuit manufactures the
beat.
    That is the strange and useful thing about an oscillator: it pro‑
duces a sustained, repeating pattern from a source that contains no
pattern at all. Every circuit we have built so far has been responsive —
a transistor that fires when a cause arrives, a filter that passes some
signals and blocks others, a regulator that holds a state steady against
disturbance. An oscillator is different in kind. It is self‑sustaining. Left
alone, with nothing happening at its input, it keeps going. It is the
difference between a bell that rings when struck and a bell that, once
struck, rings forever.
    Cognition is full of these. A circadian rhythm runs whether or
not the sun cooperates. A craving cycles back on its own schedule.
A habit fires at the same time every day with no one prompting it.
A rumination loop spins through the same four thoughts again and

                                   217
CAS PCBA Engineer

again, needing no fresh input to keep itself alive. These are not re‑
sponses to a stimulus. They are oscillators — cognitive circuits that,
once running, sustain their own pattern. This chapter teaches you to
build them, tune them, lock them to an external beat, and — most
importantly for safety work — recognize when one has gone patho‑
logical.
    This is the engine room of the Cognitive Oscillator Board (COB,
CCB‑2), the reference board we design in full in Chapter 19. Every‑
thing here is a COB sub‑component. Build it carefully.


13.1    What Makes a Circuit Oscillate: The
        Barkhausen Criterion
Start with the electronics, from the ground up. An oscillator is an
amplifier whose output is fed back to its own input. That is the whole
trick. Take any amplifier — a triangle that makes a signal bigger —
and run a wire from its output back to its input. Now whatever comes
out goes back in, gets amplified again, comes out again, goes back in
again. Round and round.
    Whether that loop sustains a steady oscillation, dies away to si‑
lence, or blows up into a screech depends on two numbers, and these
two numbers are the Barkhausen criterion — the foundational law
of every oscillator ever built.
    Walk a single signal around the loop once and ask two questions:

  1. How much bigger or smaller did it get? That is the loop gain
     — the total amplification all the way around the loop, output
     back to the same point. Call it A·β (the amplifier’s gain A times
     the fraction β fed back).
  2. How much did its timing shift? A signal is a wave; going
     around the loop delays it. That delay, measured as a fraction
     of one full wave‑cycle, is the phase shift, in degrees. One full
     cycle is 360°.


                                 218
      13.1. WHAT MAKES A CIRCUIT OSCILLATE: THE BARKHAUSEN
                                                  CRITERION
    The Barkhausen criterion says: a circuit sustains a steady oscilla‑
tion when, around the loop, the loop gain is exactly 1 and the total
phase shift is 0° (equivalently, a whole 360°).
    Both conditions matter, and the intuition is worth getting right
because the cognitive version depends on it.

   • Gain = 1. The signal must come back exactly as strong as it
     left. If loop gain is less than 1, each lap is weaker than the last
     — the oscillation decays and dies (a struck bell fading out). If
     loop gain is greater than 1, each lap is stronger — the oscillation
     grows without limit until something saturates or breaks (acous‑
     tic feedback howl when a microphone hears its own speaker).
     Only at exactly 1 does the wave return at the same amplitude,
     lap after lap, forever.
   • Phase = 0° (or 360°). The signal coming back must arrive in step
     with itself — crest landing on crest. If it returns out of step, it
     fights itself and cancels. A whole 360° of shift puts the returning
     wave back in perfect alignment, reinforcing rather than fighting.
     That reinforcement is what keeps the wave alive.

    In practice every real oscillator starts with loop gain slightly
above 1 — so the oscillation can build up from circuit noise — and
then some nonlinearity gently pulls the gain back down to exactly 1
as the amplitude grows. That self‑limiting is what gives you a stable
amplitude instead of a runaway.
    Hold those two numbers. Reinforcement strong enough to re‑
place what’s lost (gain 1), arriving in step with itself (phase 0°). Ev‑
ery cognitive loop that sustains itself — every habit, craving, rumina‑
tion, and circadian cycle — obeys the same two conditions. That is
not a metaphor. It is the same topology in a different substrate.




                                  219
CAS PCBA Engineer

                ^8 Above/Cause                           ^9 Below/Effect

13.2      The CAS Mapping: A Cognitive Oscillator
A cognitive oscillator is a sequence of cognitive states wired so that
the last state triggers the first — a Phi sequence that closes into a loop.
From Chapter 2: a Phi< … > sequence is an ordered list of states tra‑
versed in time, the cognitive equivalent of a waveform. When that
waveform’s end feeds its beginning, it repeats. That repeating Phi
sequence is the oscillation.
    The two Barkhausen conditions map cleanly:

Barkhausen (electronic)                          Cognitive analog

Loop gain = 1                                    Each lap of the thought‑cycle reinforces
                                                 the next exactly enough to keep it
                                                 going. Gain < 1: the pattern fades (a
                                                 craving that loses its grip). Gain > 1: it
                                                 intensifies each cycle (a spiraling
                                                 rumination, an escalating panic loop).
Phase = 0° / 360°                                The cycle returns to its starting state in
                                                 step — the last state’s ^8 Above/Cause
                                                 trigger lands cleanly on the first state,
                                                 reinforcing rather than disrupting it. A
                                                 misaligned loop self‑interrupts and
                                                 dies.



                                             220
                                       13.3. FOUR WAYS TO BUILD ONE

    The Noetic that is rhythm is ^7 Rhythm — “the rate and pat‑
tern a Mind is exposed to an Idea; entraining/conditioning it.” ^7 is
the conditioning that makes a loop self‑sustaining; it is the cognitive
analog of the inductor that stores the oscillation’s energy (Chapter
7). The trigger that closes each lap — last state surfacing the first
— is ^8 Above/Cause (“an Idea that triggers a different Idea to come
to Mind”), and the state it lands on is ^9 Below/Effect (“the Idea
brought to Mind”). An oscillator is, structurally, a chain of ^8→^9
triggers bent into a circle, with ^7 Rhythm as the conditioning that
keeps the circle closed.

      Bench Note — oscillation is not the same as reasoning.
      A Phi loop that cycles ^8→^9→^8→^9 is associative trig‑
      gering repeating — one Idea surfacing the next, around
      and around. It is not deductive analysis. Do not write ^8
      where you mean step‑by‑step reasoning; deductive work
      is ^6 Male plus ^9 Below/Effect (Chapter 2’s second anti‑
      drift warning). An oscillator’s power, and its danger, is
      precisely that it runs without analysis — it is a groove, not
      an argument.


13.3 Four Ways to Build One
Electronics gives four classic oscillator topologies, each setting its fre‑
quency by different means. Each has a clean cognitive reading.

LC Oscillator — the inductor‑capacitor tank
The oldest oscillator is an inductor (a coil — opposes changes in flow,
stores energy in a magnetic field) wired across a capacitor (two plates
— opposes changes in voltage, stores energy in an electric field). En‑
ergy sloshes back and forth between them: the capacitor dumps its
charge through the inductor, the inductor’s collapsing field recharges
the capacitor the other way, and back again. This “LC tank” rings at


                                   221
CAS PCBA Engineer

a natural frequency set by the two component values — bigger L or
C, slower ring.
    Recall the cognitive readings we built earlier. The inductor is ^7
Rhythm — habit strength, the inertia that resists changing an estab‑
lished pattern (Chapter 7). The capacitor is stored cognitive charge —
accumulated emotional or experiential energy, ^5 Female (accumu‑
lated experience) carrying ^4 Vibration (the impression’s intensity)
(Chapter 6). Wire habit‑inertia against stored emotional charge and
you get a sustained rhythm: the stored charge drives the habit, the
habit discharges into action, the action re‑accumulates charge, and
the cycle rings on. The LC oscillator is the cleanest model of a habit
loop — a craving that builds, discharges, and rebuilds at its own nat‑
ural frequency.

RC Phase‑Shift Oscillator — frequency from resistors and
capacitors
Not every oscillator needs an inductor. An RC phase‑shift oscillator
builds its 360° loop entirely from resistors (limit flow) and capacitors
(store charge, and crucially delay the signal). Each resistor‑capacitor
stage shifts the signal’s phase by a fraction of a cycle; chain three
stages, get the 180° you need, add the amplifier’s own 180°, and you
have a full 360° — Barkhausen satisfied. The frequency is set by how
much each RC stage delays: bigger R or C, more delay, slower oscil‑
lation.
     Cognitively, the RC oscillator sets a rhythm not by a single
resonant habit but by a chain of delays. Each stage is a resistor (^8
Above/Cause flow, throttled by R — Chapter 5) feeding a capacitor
(a stored state that holds, then releases, after a lag). The accumulated
lag around the chain sets the period. This is the model for a deliber‑
ative cycle whose timing is governed by how long each step takes to
“fill up” before it triggers the next — a worry loop pacing itself by
how long each anxious thought lingers before surfacing the next.


                                  222
                                       13.3. FOUR WAYS TO BUILD ONE

Crystal Oscillator — the ultra‑stable reference
The quartz crystal from the wristwatch is the gold standard. A crys‑
tal oscillator works on the same energy‑sloshing principle as an LC
tank, but the “tank” is a slab of quartz vibrating mechanically. Quartz
is extraordinarily pure as a resonator — it has an enormous Q factor
(more on Q below) — so it locks onto exactly one frequency and re‑
fuses to drift, holding it across temperature swings and decades of
running. That is why every clock, radio, and computer uses one as
its master reference.
    The crystal is the deeply entrenched habit — a pattern so condi‑
tioned, so high‑^7 Rhythm, that it runs at a fixed rate and resists all
perturbation. The cognitive crystal is the ritual you have performed
identically every morning for twenty years; the reflex that fires the
same way every single time; the bedrock circadian clock that keeps
near‑24‑hour time even in a cave with no daylight. It is the most sta‑
ble oscillator a mind can build — and, as we will see in the failure
modes, stability has a shadow side: a crystal‑grade habit is almost
impossible to disrupt deliberately.

Phase‑Locked Loop — locking your rhythm to an external
beat
The previous three generate a rhythm from within. A Phase‑Locked
Loop (PLL) does something subtler and, for cognition, profoundly
important: it takes an oscillator and forces it to match an external signal
— to lock onto an outside beat and track it. This is how a radio tunes
to a station and how every device on a network stays in time with a
shared clock. It is also how a mind entrains to a social schedule.
    A PLL has three parts in a loop:

   • A phase detector compares the internal oscillator’s timing
     against the external reference and outputs an error: how
     far off are we? In CAS this is ^1 Mind — “awareness that
     processes… Ideas” — comparing internal rhythm against

                                   223
CAS PCBA Engineer

     external rhythm. (Per the naming rule, ^1 is Mind, full stop —
     never “Differentiation,” even though its job here is to detect a
     difference.)
   • A loop filter smooths that error signal — integrates it, averag‑
     ing out jitter so the loop responds to the steady offset, not every
     momentary wobble. In CAS this is ^4 Vibration — “the degree
     to which an Idea resonates… its impression” — accumulating
     the phase error into a sustained impression that drives correc‑
     tion. (^4 is Vibration, never “Integration,” even though its role
     is integrative.)
   • A voltage‑controlled oscillator (VCO) is an oscillator whose
     frequency is adjustable by the filtered error: it speeds up
     or slows down to close the gap. In CAS this is ^3^O — an
     Operational‑domain ^3 Negative, the aversive push that
     adjusts the output to reduce the mismatch (the felt “I’m
     off‑schedule, correct it” that nudges behavior back in line).

    Two ranges define a PLL’s behavior, and both have direct cogni‑
tive meaning:

   • Lock range — once locked, how far the external reference can
     drift while the loop still tracks it. Wide lock range = the rhythm
     follows the schedule even when the schedule shifts a lot.
   • Capture range — starting from unlocked, how close the refer‑
     ence must be before the loop can grab it in the first place. Cap‑
     ture range is always narrower than lock range: it is easier to stay
     locked than to get locked. Cognitively, that is the familiar truth
     that an established routine tolerates schedule changes it could
     never have adopted cold — you can drift a long‑standing bed‑
     time gradually, but a brand‑new schedule has to start close to
     where you already are to take hold at all.




                                 224
13.4. WORKED BUILD: A CIRCADIAN OSCILLATOR THAT LOCKS TO A
                                          SOCIAL SCHEDULE
13.4 Worked Build: A Circadian Oscillator That
     Locks to a Social Schedule
Let us build the COB’s headline component: a circadian oscillator
— a roughly‑once‑per‑day rhythm — and then wrap it in a PLL that
locks it to an external social schedule. This is the model of a sleep‑
/wake or daily‑routine cycle entraining to the demands of a job, a
household, or a timezone.
    First the free‑running oscillator. We want a four‑state daily cycle:
a morning trigger surfaces, an aversive “get moving” push fires, a felt
landing in activity follows, and the day resolves toward a principled
close before the cycle restarts.

// The circadian oscillator: a four-state Phi loop, ~one cycle per day.
// frequency in cycles/second; 1 day = 86,400 s, so f ≈ 1/86400 ≈
,→   0.0000116 Hz.
let circadian = Oscillator<
     Phi< ^8^C|A,       // morning trigger: an association surfaces (”it's
     ,→   time to begin”)
          ^3^O|E,       // the aversive operational push to get moving (the
          ,→   VCO-style nudge)
          ^9^E|f,       // felt landing in evaluative activity (the day,
          ,→   lived)
          ^0^P|T >,     // principled resolution toward day's-end meaning,
          ,→   then re-trigger
     frequency = 0.0000116
> [Q = 8, duty_cycle = 0.65];


    Read the loop. ^8^C|A (an analytical association in the Cognitive
domain) opens the cycle — the morning‑trigger Idea surfaces another
Idea, “begin.” That triggers ^3^O|E — an embodied operational aver‑
sion, the bodily “ugh, but go” that gets you out of bed (visceral push,
correctly ^3, not analysis). That lands in ^9^E|f — a felt Below/Effect
in the Evaluative domain, the day actually being lived and judged
as it goes. The day resolves into ^0^P|T — a transcendent Principled
Idea, the day’s‑end sense of meaning — which then re‑triggers the


                                     225
CAS PCBA Engineer

morning association, closing the 360° loop. The frequency is a de‑
sign value of about one cycle per day. Q = 8 and duty_cycle = 0.65
we explain in the datasheet below.

        Bench Note — these numbers are design choices, not
        measurements. frequency = 0.0000116, Q = 8, duty_
        cycle = 0.65: every one of these is a value you specify
        when you design the board, exactly as an electrical
        engineer picks an inductor value off a shelf. They are
        not readings taken off a running mind. This book never
        reports a measured cognitive frequency or Q — those
        would be empirical claims about a real system, and we
        do not have them. We design with them; we do not
        benchmark with them.

    Now lock it to a social schedule. The free‑running circadian clock
drifts (anyone who has stayed up too late knows this). A job that
starts at 9 a.m. is an external reference. We wrap the oscillator in a
PLL so the internal rhythm tracks the external one:

circuit circadian_pll {
    input:   social_schedule;          // external reference: the 9-to-5 beat
    output: daily_rhythm;              // the locked internal cycle


    // The free-running oscillator from above is the VCO core.
    node vco:             circadian;               // adjustable-rate
   ,→    circadian oscillator
    node phase_detect:    ^1^C|A;                  // Mind: compare internal
   ,→    vs external timing
    node loop_filter:     ^4^E|f;                  // Vibration: integrate
   ,→    the phase error into an impression
    node correction:      ^3^O|E;                  // Negative/Operational:
   ,→    aversive nudge to re-align


    // Compare internal rhythm against the social schedule -> phase error.
    cjt pd: CJT< social_schedule | vco => phase_detect > [β =1.0];
    // Smooth/integrate the error into a sustained impression.
    cjt lf: CJT< phase_detect | bias_calm => loop_filter > [β =0.5];


                                       226
13.4. WORKED BUILD: A CIRCADIAN OSCILLATOR THAT LOCKS TO A
                                          SOCIAL SCHEDULE
    // Drive the oscillator's rate from the filtered error.
    cjt vc: CJT< loop_filter     | bias_calm => correction   > [β =1.2];
    feedback correction -> vco [β =0.4];          // close the loop: nudge
    ,→    the oscillator's phase


    probe tp_error: phase_detect;                 // watch the raw phase
    ,→    error
    probe tp_lock:      loop_filter;             // watch the integrated
    ,→    lock signal
}


    The CJTs (Chapter 4) wire the three PLL stages. pd is the phase
detector: it compares the incoming social_schedule against the run‑
ning vco and emits a ^1^C|A phase‑error — Mind, analytically notic‑
ing “I’m two hours behind the day.” lf integrates that error into a
^4^E|f — a felt Vibration, the accumulating impression of being off‑
beat. vc turns that impression into a ^3^O|E correction — the aversive
operational push to shift the rhythm. The feedback line bends the cor‑
rection back onto the oscillator, nudging its phase until internal and
external align. When the loop settles, the internal clock is the external
beat: the mind has entrained to the schedule.

         Bench Note — capture is harder than lock, so start
         close. This PLL will hold the rhythm to a 9 a.m. start
         through gradual drift (wide lock range). But if you hand
         it a brand‑new schedule far from where the oscillator
         currently free‑runs — asking a midnight‑to‑8 sleeper to
         lock onto a 5 a.m. start cold — it falls outside the capture
         range and never grabs on. The design fix is the same one
         sleep clinicians use: move the reference in small steps
         the loop can capture, walking the lock in rather than
         demanding it instantly.

   This whole assembly — free‑running circadian oscillator plus
social‑schedule PLL — is the core of the Cognitive Oscillator



                                       227
CAS PCBA Engineer

Board (COB, CCB‑2) in Chapter 19, where we add multiple cou‑
pled oscillators, a master crystal reference, and the inversion‑scan
instrumentation that flags a loop gone pathological.

                       13.5. DATASHEET: OSCILLATOR PARAMETERS

The Q factor — how sharply tuned
Q (quality factor) measures how sharply an oscillator is tuned and
how slowly it bleeds energy. A high‑Q oscillator resonates at a very
narrow band of frequencies and rings for a long time once started; a
low‑Q oscillator is broadly tuned and damps out quickly. The quartz
crystal is high‑Q (tens of thousands); a casually‑tuned LC tank is low‑
Q.
    The cognitive reading is sharp and important: high Q = compul‑
sive, hard to disrupt. A high‑Q cognitive oscillator is a habit or crav‑
ing so narrowly tuned and so slow to lose energy that it overrides in‑
terruption, runs on its own schedule regardless of context, and keeps
ringing long after the trigger is gone — addiction, OCD‑grade com‑
pulsion, an entrenched ritual. A low‑Q oscillator is a loose, easily‑
broken pattern — a mild preference, a routine you can skip without
friction. When we instrument the COB in Chapter 19, the Q of each
loop is the single most diagnostic number: it tells you how strongly
the rhythm will resist being changed.

Duty cycle — controlled by Drive weighting
Duty cycle is the fraction of each cycle spent in the active, “ON” state
versus the resting state. A 0.5 duty cycle is balanced — equal on and
off. The Drive weighting on the oscillator sets it:

   • High F5 Agency → more ON time. Agency is the pull toward
     action and effectiveness; an Agency‑weighted oscillator spends
     more of each cycle firing — a drive to keep doing, a cycle biased
     toward output. Duty cycle climbs toward 0.8–0.9.
   • High F6 Structure → disciplined, regular cycle. Structure is the
     pull toward order and form; a Structure‑weighted oscillator
     keeps a clean, predictable, well‑bounded duty cycle — the
     same ON time every cycle, sharp edges, no drift. Structure
     governs the regularity of the duty cycle, not just its size.


                                  229
CAS PCBA Engineer

   (Recall from Chapter 2 that F5 Agency and F6 Structure are not an
inversion pair — F3↔F5 and F2↔F6 are — so a loop can carry both:
Agency for how much ON time, Structure for how disciplined that ON
time is.)

13.7 Key Takeaways
   • An oscillator is self‑sustaining: it produces a repeating pattern
     from an input with no pattern in it — an amplifier feeding its
     own output back to its input. The cognitive versions are habits,
     cravings, ruminations, and circadian cycles.
   • The Barkhausen criterion is the law of every oscillator: loop
     gain = 1 (each lap reinforces exactly enough to replace what’s
     lost) and phase shift = 0°/360° (the returning signal arrives in
     step with itself). Gain < 1 decays; gain > 1 runs away; wrong
     phase self‑cancels.
   • A cognitive oscillator is a Phi sequence bent into a loop — a
     chain of ^8 Above/Cause → ^9 Below/Effect triggers, condi‑
     tioned by ^7 Rhythm (the inductor’s analog). It is associative
     repetition, not deductive reasoning.
   • LC oscillator = habit‑inertia (^7 Rhythm, the inductor) slosh‑
     ing against stored emotional charge (^5/^4, the capacitor) — the
     cleanest habit‑loop model. RC phase‑shift sets frequency by
     a chain of delays. Crystal = the ultra‑stable, very‑high‑Q en‑
     trenched habit.
   • A PLL locks an internal rhythm to an external beat: phase de‑
     tector = ^1 Mind (compare internal vs external), loop filter = ^4
     Vibration (integrate the error into an impression), VCO = ^3^O
     (aversive operational adjustment). Capture range is narrower
     than lock range — easier to stay locked than to get locked, so
     walk new schedules in gradually.


                                      231
CAS PCBA Engineer

     • Q factor is sharpness of tuning: high Q = compulsive, hard to
       disrupt; low Q = loose, easily broken. It is the most diagnostic
       number on the COB.
     • Duty cycle (fraction of each cycle ON) is set by Drive weighting:
       F5 Agency raises ON time; F6 Structure disciplines the cycle’s
       regularity.
     • All frequencies, Q values, and duty cycles in this chapter are
       design choices, not measurements. This is the core of the Cog‑
       nitive Oscillator Board (COB, CCB‑2) built in Chapter 19.
