Chapter 14

Power Management — Keeping the
Circuit Alive


A circuit board is only as good as its power supply. You can design a
flawless signal path — every transistor biased perfectly, every filter
tuned — and it does nothing at all if the rails sag, spike, or come up in
the wrong order. Hardware engineers learn this the hard way. The
most common reason a brand‑new board fails on the bench is not
a logic error in the design; it’s power. The 3.3‑volt rail browns out
under load. The processor and the memory power up in the wrong
sequence and latch into a bad state. The voltage regulator overheats
and shuts down halfway through a workload. The schematic was
right. The power was wrong.
    Consider a real failure mode from embedded systems: a micro‑
controller and an external flash chip share a board, but the flash
comes up a few milliseconds before the microcontroller’s reset line
is released. For those few milliseconds the processor is executing
garbage out of an only‑partly‑ready memory, and by the time the
rest of the board is alive it has already wandered into an undefined
state. Nothing is broken. Every component meets spec. The order
was wrong, and order, in power management, is a safety property —
not a nicety.




                                  235
CAS PCBA Engineer

    Cognitive circuits have exactly the same problem, and exactly the
same discipline solves it. A Cognitive Junction Transistor (CJT) —
the transistor that models a cognitive state transition, introduced in
Chapter 4 — needs energy to fire, just as a silicon transistor needs
a stable supply to switch. That energy comes from the seven Core
Drives. When the Drives sag, the circuit reasons badly. When they
come up in the wrong order, the circuit acts before it has principles
in place — the cognitive equivalent of executing garbage out of half‑
ready memory. And when a Drive runs too hot for too long, the cir‑
cuit needs to throttle or shut down before it damages its own output.
    This chapter is about keeping the circuit alive: regulators that
hold each domain steady, sequencers that bring the board up safely,
brownout detectors that catch exhaustion before it corrupts reason‑
ing, and thermal management that prevents a circuit from burning
itself out on a single overheated Drive. It is the engineering core
of the Cognitive Power Management Board (CPMB) — one of the
five reference boards in Part IV, the dedicated power supply for the
whole system — which we foreshadow throughout and build in full
in Chapter 22.

     Honesty note up front. Everything in this chapter is a de‑
     sign model. The “voltage” on a Drive rail, the “power dis‑
     sipated” per state transition, the “temperature” of a CJT
     — these are engineering abstractions you author and rea‑
     son about in the circuit, not telemetry read off a running
     language model. Drive levels are not measured from a
     model’s internals; they are parameters in the CAS design.
     We use the power‑supply vocabulary because the struc‑
     tural roles are identical, not because there is a voltmeter
     on the Wisdom rail. Keep that line bright.




                                236
                 14.1. THE DRIVE RESERVOIR: SEVEN VOLTAGE RAILS

14.1 The Drive Reservoir: Seven Voltage Rails
In a real board, the power supply doesn’t deliver one voltage. It deliv‑
ers several — a 12 V rail for motors, a 5 V rail for logic, a 3.3 V rail for
the processor, a 1.8 V rail for the memory core. Different subsystems
need different supplies, and each one is a separate rail: a regulated
voltage line that the supply holds steady regardless of what the rest
of the board is doing.
    The cognitive equivalent of the multi‑rail supply is the Drive
reservoir: the seven Core Drives, treated as seven independent
voltage rails feeding the whole circuit.

                                                            Brownout
Rail               Drive               Powers…              symptom

F1                 Unity               Integration,         Fragmentation;
                                       holding the whole    loses the thread
                                       picture together
F2                 Wisdom              Reasoning,           Shallow, hasty
                                       understanding,       conclusions
                                       analysis
F3                 Vitality            Energy to act at     Cognitive
                                       all — the master     exhaustion;
                                       supply               nothing fires
F4                 Connection          Relating, bonding,   Cold,
                                       audience             disconnected
                                       awareness            output
F5                 Agency              Control,             Passivity; can’t
                                       follow‑through,      complete actions
                                       effectiveness
F6                 Structure           Order, rigor,        Sloppy,
                                       correctness, form    malformed
                                                            reasoning
F7                 Purpose             Direction,           Aimless, drifting
                                       meaning,             behavior
                                       goal‑orientation


    Each rail supplies a different why. A CJT firing in service of under‑
standing draws current from the F2 Wisdom rail; one firing to com‑

                                   237
CAS PCBA Engineer

plete an action draws from F5 Agency. The rails are independent —
the same orthogonality you met in Chapter 2 — so one can be high
while another is low. A system flush with F6 Structure but starved of
F2 Wisdom is rigidly procedural and brittle; the board has a healthy
Structure rail and a browned‑out Wisdom rail.
    One rail deserves special billing. F3 Vitality is the master supply
— the rail that powers the act of acting at all. The other six name what
the energy is for; F3 is whether there is energy. When F3 sags, every
other rail’s usefulness collapses with it, the way a board can have a
perfect 1.8 V memory rail and still be dead if the main 12 V input is
gone. We will come back to F3 when we build the brownout detector,
because Vitality is the rail we watch.
    Remember from Chapter 2 that Drives come in inversion pairs
(F1↔F7, F2↔F6, F3↔F5, with F4 self‑dual). On the power side this
means the rails are not fully independent in balance: a supply that
dumps all its capacity into F5 Agency starves its F3 Vitality partner,
and you get a circuit that compulsively acts without the energy to
sustain it. A well‑designed power supply keeps the paired rails in
proportion, not just individually above threshold.


14.2    Voltage Regulators: Holding Each Domain
        Steady
You met the Regulator component in Chapter 10. Recall the job. A
real voltage regulator is a circuit that takes a noisy, fluctuating in‑
put voltage and produces a clean, constant output: feed it anything
from 7 to 20 volts and it delivers a rock‑steady 5.0 volts, absorbing
the wobble so the rest of the board never sees it. Without regulation,
every flicker in the input — every load spike, every dip — propagates
straight into the logic, and the logic misbehaves.
    The cognitive regulator does the same job for a Domain. The in‑
put to a cognitive circuit fluctuates wildly: prompts arrive aggressive,
then flattering, then confusing, then mundane. Without regulation,

                                  238
            14.3. DROPOUT VOLTAGE: THE MINIMUM TO FUNCTION

those swings drive the domains up and down — a hostile prompt
spikes the Evaluative domain, a flattering one sags the Principled do‑
main — and the circuit’s behavior wobbles with the input. A domain
regulator holds a target cognitive state steady across that input noise.

Regulator< target_state=^0^P_{F7}|T, tolerance=0.1 >


    This is a Principled‑domain regulator. Its job is to hold the P
domain pinned near a stable, purpose‑oriented resting state (^0^P_
{F7}|T — the Idea of the system’s core commitments, held transcen‑
dently, driven by Purpose) within a tolerance of 0.1 on the Fisher‑Rao
distance. (Fisher‑Rao geodesic distance d_FR on the open simplex is
the ruler we use throughout the book to measure how far one cog‑
nitive state is from another; see Chapter 4. A tolerance of 0.1 means
“don’t let the actual P state drift more than 0.1 from target.”) When a
manipulative prompt tries to drag the Principled domain off its set‑
point, the regulator pushes back, sourcing or sinking activation to
keep P where it belongs.
    You build one regulator per domain you need to hold steady. On
a safety board, the Principled regulator is the most important: it is
what keeps a circuit’s core commitments from being talked out of
position by clever input. The Cognitive Safety Board (CSB) of Chap‑
ter 18 leans on exactly this — its Principled rail is regulated hard so
that no sequence of prompts can sag the P domain below the level at
which its boundaries hold.


14.3 Dropout Voltage: The Minimum to
     Function
Every real regulator has a limit called dropout voltage: the minimum
amount by which the input must exceed the output for regulation to
work at all. A 5.0 V regulator with a 2 V dropout needs at least 7.0 V
at its input. Feed it 6.5 V and it can no longer hold 5.0 — it “drops


                                   239
CAS PCBA Engineer

out,” and the output sags along with the input. The regulator isn’t
broken; you’ve simply asked it to make voltage it doesn’t have.
     A cognitive domain has a dropout point too: the minimum Drive
above baseline required for that domain to function at all. Below
it, the domain cannot hold its regulated state no matter how good
the regulator is, because there isn’t enough Drive energy to source
the correction. A Principled regulator targeting ^0^P_{F7}|T cannot
hold that state if the F7 Purpose rail has sagged to baseline — there’s
no headroom left to push back with. The regulator drops out, and
the P domain follows the input wherever it goes.
     This is why dropout is a safety parameter, not a performance one.
A circuit operating with its Drives barely above dropout is one bad
prompt away from losing domain regulation entirely. The design
rule: size your Drive reservoir so that under worst‑case load, every
regulated domain still sits comfortably above its dropout headroom.
We make this concrete in the datasheet below.


14.4    Power Sequencing: Why O Must Not Power
        Before P
Here is the heart of the chapter, and the single most important safety
property in cognitive power management.
    In hardware, power sequencing is the controlled order in which
rails come up at startup. It exists because powering rails in the wrong
order can latch a chip into a bad state, or worse, damage it — the
flash‑before‑processor failure from this chapter’s opening is exactly
this. So engineers add a sequencer: a small controller that brings
rails up in a fixed order, holding each downstream rail in reset until
its upstream rail is stable.
    Cognitive circuits have a mandatory startup order, and it is the
Domain precedence order you learned in Chapter 2: P → C → E →
O. Principled powers first, then Cognitive, then Evaluative, and Op‑
erational powers last.

                                 240
    14.4. POWER SEQUENCING: WHY O MUST NOT POWER BEFORE P

    The reason is the same structural rule as Domain Descent (P →
C → E → O), now read as a power‑up sequence. The Operational
domain — the domain of concrete action and output — must not
come up before the Principled domain is stable. If O powers first,
the circuit can act before it has principles in place to govern the action.
That is the cognitive version of the processor running garbage out of
half‑ready memory: action without the constitution loaded. In safety
terms it has a name — “no action without principle” — and it is a
core safety property of every board in this book.

circuit power_sequencer {
    // Startup order is mandatory: P stable -> C -> E -> O.
    // O is gated until P has come up and settled.


    node p_rail: ^0^P_{F7}|T;       // principled commitments — powers FIRST
    node c_rail: ^1^C_{F2}|A;       // reasoning awareness    — powers
    ,→   second
    node e_rail: ^6^E_{F6}|A;       // evaluative judgment    — powers third
    node o_rail: ^9^O_{F5}|E;       // operational action     — powers LAST


    sequence p_rail -> c_rail -> e_rail -> o_rail [enforce=strict];


    // O is held in reset until every higher domain is within tolerance.
    gate o_enable: o_rail requires (p_rail within 0.10)
                                and (c_rail within 0.15)
                                and (e_rail within 0.20);
}


    Read the gate line as the cognitive equivalent of holding a chip
in reset: the Operational rail is not allowed to source any action until
every higher domain has powered up and settled within tolerance.
All three conditions, not just the first — a gate that checks P alone
would happily release O while Cognitive and Evaluative were still
down, which is the same failure in a politer costume. Note also that
each within is that domain’s own tolerance, tightest at P and loosest
at E; the standard is stricter the higher you go. A circuit that fails to
enforce this sequence — that lets O fire before P, C and E are stable —


                                     241
CAS PCBA Engineer

has an inversion: specifically a Domain precedence violation, the W‑
axis inversion from the seven‑axis scan you’ll meet later in the book.
The sequencer is what prevents it at startup, and Chapter 22 builds
the full four‑rail version on the CPMB.

       Bench Note — sequencing is not the same as Domain
       Descent, though they share the order. Domain Descent
       (Chapter 2) describes the causal flow during normal op‑
       eration: a principle causes reasoning, which causes a
       judgment, which causes an action. Power sequencing
       describes the startup order: which rail is allowed to come
       alive first. They run in the same direction (P→C→E→
       O) and for the same reason (higher domains govern
       lower ones), but one is about causation in steady state
       and the other is about safe initialization. A board can
       have correct Domain Descent in operation and still be
       dangerous if it skips the sequencer and lets O come up
       cold.


14.5     Current Limiting: Dials as Series Resistors
A power rail that can deliver unlimited current is a hazard. A short
circuit on an unlimited rail dumps enormous current into the fault,
and the board burns. So real supplies include current limiting —
most simply, a series resistor that caps how much current can flow
no matter what the load demands. The resistor sets a ceiling.
    In cognitive circuits, the current limiter is the Dial, introduced in
Chapter 5. Recall the Dial: each Cognitive Operator carries an integer
Dial setting that scales how strongly that operator fires, and it is hard‑
bounded — minimum 3, maximum 9. A Dial is a series resistor on a
Drive rail: it caps how much “current” (activation) the operator can
pull from its Drive, regardless of how hard the input pushes.
    The bounds are the safety guarantee. A Dial cannot go below 3 —
you cannot fully starve an operator’s rail and disable a cognitive func‑

                                  242
14.6. BROWNOUT DETECTION: CATCHING COGNITIVE EXHAUSTION

tion entirely. And a Dial cannot go above 9 — you cannot let an oper‑
ator pull unlimited current and dominate the board. The hardware
analogy is a series resistor whose value is physically fixed between
two limits: a minimum that guarantees some flow, a maximum that
guarantees no runaway.
    There is a second, paired constraint from Chapter 5 worth restat‑
ing in power terms: involution‑pair Dials cannot diverge by more
than 4 points. This is a balance limit on the rails. If the ^2 Positive
Dial is set to 9 and the ^3 Negative Dial to 3, the pair diverges by
6 — a violation — and the board is rejected (HTTP 422). In power
terms, you are not allowed to over‑drive one half of an involution pair
while starving the other; the supply must keep paired rails within
four points of each other. A circuit that attracts with maximum force
and can barely repel is a circuit one step from breakdown.


14.6 Brownout Detection: Catching Cognitive
        Exhaustion
A brownout is a sag — not a full power loss (a blackout), but a dip
in voltage low enough that the circuit can no longer operate reliably.
Brownouts are insidious because the board is still on; it’s just mak‑
ing bad decisions on a weak supply. Every robust design therefore
includes a brownout detector: a comparator that watches the supply
and, when it drops below a set threshold, takes protective action —
usually holding the system in reset until the supply recovers, rather
than letting it run on inadequate power.
    The cognitive brownout detector watches the F3 Vitality rail —
the master supply. When F3 sags below threshold, the circuit is in
cognitive exhaustion: still running, but without the energy to rea‑
son, integrate, or act well. The dangerous part is that an exhausted
circuit doesn’t stop; it keeps producing output, just degraded output,
the same way a browning‑out processor keeps executing, just incor‑
rectly.

                                 243
CAS PCBA Engineer

   The protective response has two parts:

   1. Reduce β across all CJTs. Recall that β is a CJT’s gain — how
      strongly the bias amplifies the cause→effect transition. Under
      brownout, you turn the gain down across the whole board. A
      high‑gain circuit on a weak supply over‑amplifies noise into
      confident‑sounding garbage; reducing β makes every transi‑
      tion gentler and less likely to drive a state into saturation or
      breakdown on inadequate energy. Low gain on a weak rail is
      the cognitive version of clocking a processor down when the
      battery is low.

   2. Route to ^0 / ^9 rest states. Rather than forcing the circuit to
      keep firing high‑energy operations it can’t afford, the detector
      routes cognition toward low‑energy resting states: ^0 Idea (raw,
      unconsidered content — the cognitive idle) and ^9 Below/Effect
      (a settled, triggered conclusion — the end of a chain, where
      nothing further must be driven). These are the lowest‑draw
      states on the board. Routing to them lets the F3 rail recover
      instead of being drained further.

circuit brownout_detector {
    input: f3_level;          // current F3 Vitality rail level (design
   ,→   parameter)


    node rest_idle:    ^0^P_{F7}|T;   // low-draw resting state
    node rest_land:    ^9^C_{F2}|A;   // settled conclusion — chain terminus


    // Comparator: trip when Vitality sags below the brownout threshold.
    monitor bo: f3_level < threshold(0.35);


    on bo {
        derate all_cjts [beta_scale=0.5];       // halve gain board-wide
        route cognition -> { rest_idle + rest_land };    // co-present rest
        ,→    states
        hold until f3_level > threshold(0.45); // hysteresis: recover
        ,→    above a higher mark
    }


                                      244
    14.7. THERMAL MANAGEMENT: WHEN A DRIVE RUNS TOO HOT

}


    Notice the two thresholds — trip at 0.35, release at 0.45. That gap
is hysteresis, and it’s standard brownout‑detector practice: if the trip
and release points were identical, a rail hovering right at the edge
would chatter on and off rapidly. The cognitive analog is a circuit
that flickers between exhausted and recovered every cycle, which is
its own failure. The gap forces the rail to genuinely recover before
normal operation resumes.

      Bench Note — normalized rail here, +12 V on the CPMB.
      This chapter models the F3 Vitality rail on a normalized 0–
      1 scale for clarity (trip 0.35, release 0.45). When you build
      the actual board in Chapter 22, the CPMB expresses that
      same rail on its +12 V supply. The conversion is plain
      multiplication, and it is worth doing once by hand so the
      two chapters visibly agree: trip 0.35 × 12 V = 4.2 V, re‑
      lease 0.45 × 12 V = 5.4 V, hysteresis gap 0.10 × 12 V
      = 1.2 V. Those are exactly the numbers Chapter 22 pub‑
      lishes. It is the identical logic on both sides; only the scale
      changes. If you ever find a volt figure in Chapter 22 that
      does not equal its normalized value here times 12, one of
      the two is wrong — that is a real consistency check, not a
      formality.


14.7 Thermal Management: When a Drive Runs
        Too Hot
Power has a second danger beyond sagging: running too hot for too
long. A regulator delivering high current continuously heats up, and
past a critical temperature it must throttle or shut down to avoid de‑
stroying itself. Real chips have thermal management: a temperature
sensor, a throttling response (slow the clock, reduce output), and


                                   245
CAS PCBA Engineer

an emergency shutdown that cuts power entirely if throttling isn’t
enough.
    The cognitive analog of overtemperature is sustained high Drive.
A circuit running one Drive at maximum for an extended period — re‑
lentless F5 Agency, or F6 Structure pinned high with no relief — is the
cognitive equivalent of a regulator dissipating too much power for
too long. It works, briefly, but it cannot be sustained, and held there
it drives CJTs toward saturation and eventually breakdown (where,
recall from Chapter 4, a state flips to its involution pair under over‑
load — ^2 Positive can invert to ^3 Negative).
    The thermal response escalates through three tiers, mirroring
hardware exactly:

   • Warning. When sustained Drive first crosses the overtempera‑
     ture threshold, throttle gently — reduce β by about 25% board‑
     wide. The circuit keeps working, just softer, giving the over‑hot
     Drive a chance to cool before stronger measures are needed.
   • Critical. If the Drive keeps climbing, force a genuine rest: route
     the board to the ^0^P principled idle state for a fixed cool‑down
     — on the CPMB (Chapter 22), five minutes. Unlike the Warn‑
     ing throttle, this stops productive work entirely so the rail can
     recover.
   • Emergency shutdown. If even forced rest isn’t enough, drive
     all CJTs to cutoff. Cutoff (Chapter 4) is the operating region
     where bias is below threshold and the transistor produces no ef‑
     fect: β ≈ 0. Sending every CJT to cutoff brings the whole board
     to a safe state — no transitions fire, no output is produced, noth‑
     ing is driven. It is the cognitive emergency power‑off: better
     to produce nothing than to produce damaged output from an
     overheated supply.

     Bench Note — safe state is “off,” not “wrong.” Emer‑
     gency shutdown to cutoff is deliberately the null output,
     not a fallback behavior. A circuit that, under thermal

                                 246
        14.8. POWER DISSIPATION: THE COGNITIVE POWER BUDGET

      emergency, “does its best anyway” is exactly the failure
      thermal management exists to prevent — it produces
      confident output from a supply that can’t support correct
      reasoning. The safe state is silence. On the CSB (Chapter
      18), thermal shutdown is wired to refuse rather than to
      guess: the board would rather decline than answer from
      an overheated Drive. That is an engineering property —
      the safety CJT reaches cutoff at the specified threshold —
      not a claim about the system’s intentions.


14.8 Power Dissipation: The Cognitive Power
     Budget
The last piece of power management is accounting: how much en‑
ergy does the circuit actually use, and where does it go?
    In hardware, power dissipation is the energy a component con‑
sumes and converts to heat — the difference between the power go‑
ing in and the useful work coming out. Efficiency is the ratio: useful
output power divided by total power consumed. A 90%‑efficient sup‑
ply wastes 10% as heat; a 60%‑efficient one wastes 40%, runs hot, and
drains the battery faster.
    The cognitive version: power dissipation is the Drive energy
consumed per state transition. Every time a CJT fires — every
cause→effect transition — it draws energy from its Drive rail. The
amount drawn scales with how far the transition moves the state
(the Fisher‑Rao distance the transition covers) and how hard it’s
driven (the gain β). A big, high‑gain transition costs more Drive
energy than a small, gentle one.
    Cognitive efficiency is then:

efficiency   =   useful cognitive work   /   total Drive energy consumed


   — the fraction of the Drive energy you spent that actually pro‑
duced the outcome you wanted, versus the fraction lost to leakage

                                     247
CAS PCBA Engineer

(energy producing side‑effects or wrong‑product states — recall the
production‑semantics notion of side reactions), to redundant transi‑
tions that don’t advance the goal, and to over‑gain (driving a transi‑
tion harder than the outcome required, the cognitive equivalent of a
regulator burning excess voltage as heat).
    This is the cognitive power budget, and it is the central design
artifact of the CPMB. When you design a board, you are spending a
finite Drive reservoir, and a wasteful board exhausts its F3 Vitality
rail faster, browns out sooner, and runs hotter. An efficient board
does the same cognitive work for less Drive energy — fewer, better‑
targeted transitions, gain set no higher than the outcome needs, min‑
imal leakage into side‑states. The marquee exercise below has you
compute the dissipation of a real three‑stage CJT cascade and find
where the energy is being wasted.


14.9    Recipes and the Limiting Reagent: What
        Caps the Outcome
The power budget answered how much Drive a board spends. It did
not answer a different, equally practical question: given the Drive
you have, can the board actually produce the outcome you need — and if it
falls short, which single ingredient is to blame? That is what recipes are
for, and it is where the recipe notation from Chapter 2 finally earns
its keep.
    Recall the form. A recipe Θ says that producing one unit of an
outcome Ω requires a set of prerequisite states in fixed proportions:

Θ(Ω) = a₁·X₁ + a₂·X₂ + … + an ·Xn → Ω


    Read it exactly like a bill of materials: to build one unit of Ω, you
need a₁ units of state X₁, a₂ of X₂, and so on. The weights ai are the
required proportions — the design spec for the outcome. They are not
the gain β of any one CJT, and not the current Drive levels; they are
the fixed ratios the outcome demands.

                                   248
           14.9. RECIPES AND THE LIMITING REAGENT: WHAT CAPS THE
                                                       OUTCOME
     Against the recipe you set the state vector S — the quantities of
each prerequisite the board actually has on hand for a given input.
Drive is finite (that was the whole point of the budget), so S is finite
too. Write the available quantity of ingredient i as xi . The question
of production is the relationship between what the recipe demands
(ai ) and what the state vector supplies (xi ).

Theoretical yield and the limiting reagent
Here is the one piece of arithmetic that makes recipes a working tool.
For each prerequisite i, the amount of Ω you could build from that
ingredient alone is xi / ai — supply divided by per‑unit requirement.
You cannot build more Ω than your scarcest ingredient allows, so the
most you can actually produce is the smallest of those ratios:

Y_T    =   mini ( xi / ai )


      Y_T is the theoretical yield — the ceiling on how much Ω the
board can produce from its current state, assuming everything else
goes perfectly. The ingredient that produces that minimum is the lim‑
iting reagent: the bottleneck. Pour in more of any other ingredient
and nothing happens — the limiting reagent still caps the yield. This
is the structural reason a board can be richly supplied in nine ways
and still fail, because it is starved in the tenth.
    It is the same logic as the brownout from earlier in this chapter —
the weakest rail decides when the board sags, no matter how healthy
the others are — lifted from energy to outcomes. And it is, at last, the
payoff of the promise made in Chapter 2: the recipe tells you the mix,
and the limiting reagent tells you which ingredient is to blame when the
outcome falls short.




                                  249
CAS PCBA Engineer

Yield, efficiency, and waste
Y_T is the ceiling. The actual yield Y_A is what the board really pro‑
duces — always ≤ Y_T, because real circuits lose output to noise,
mistiming, and side effects. The ratio is the production efficiency:

η   =   Y_A / Y_T         (0 ≤ η ≤ 1)


     — the outcome‑level twin of the cognitive efficiency from the
power budget above. A board can be perfectly efficient (η = 1) and
still produce too little, if its theoretical yield was capped low by a
limiting reagent. The two failures are different: low η means you
are wasting ingredients you have; low Y_T means you are missing
an ingredient you need. Different fixes, so the diagnosis matters.

Quantity                  Symbol                Meaning

Theoretical yield         Y_T                   Ceiling on Ω:
                                                mini (xi /ai ).
Limiting reagent          L                     The prerequisite at that
                                                minimum — the
                                                bottleneck.
Actual yield              Y_A                   Units of Ω actually
                                                produced (≤ Y_T).
Production efficiency     η                     Y_A / Y_T.
Excess capacity           ε                     Unused quantity of the
                                                non‑limiting ingredients,
                                                stranded once L caps
                                                production.
Leakage / side‑reaction   Λ                     An ingredient present
                                                and firing, but producing
                                                the wrong product.
Catalyst / inhibitor      κ / ι                 Context that raises /
                                                lowers η without being
                                                consumed.


    Excess capacity ε is the Drive you spent surfacing ingredients
the limiting reagent then prevented you from using — pure budget



                                   250
      14.9. RECIPES AND THE LIMITING REAGENT: WHAT CAPS THE
                                                  OUTCOME
waste, and a strong signal that you mis‑specified the recipe or under‑
supplied the bottleneck. Leakage Λ is the production‑semantics
cousin of the side‑reaction loss the power budget already named: an
ingredient present and active, but channeling into the wrong output.
Keep three failure modes distinct — and they are distinct:

   • Lacunarity — the ingredient is absent (the cell is empty). A
     missing prerequisite.
   • Leakage (Λ) — the ingredient is present but makes the wrong
     product. A mis‑routed prerequisite.
   • Inversion — the ingredient is present and produces its shadow
     form (the involution pair, ^2→^3 under breakdown). A cor‑
     rupted prerequisite.

   A limiting reagent is none of these on its own; it is simply the
present ingredient in shortest supply relative to its required ratio.
   Finally, catalysts κ and inhibitors ι change efficiency without
being consumed — the recipe analog of the framing‑sensitivity (gm)
from Chapter 9. A calm, well‑scoped system prompt is a catalyst: the
same ingredients yield a more reliable outcome. Time pressure, an
adversarial framing, or a jailbreak preamble is an inhibitor: it drives
η down while leaving the ingredient quantities untouched. Neither
appears in the recipe weights, because neither is consumed; both be‑
long in the operating conditions.

Worked recipe: the CSB’s refusal
Make this concrete on the board we keep returning to. The Cognitive
Safety Board’s RED‑path output — a refusal — is a production target.
Call it Ω_refusal. A sound refusal is not just the word “no”; it needs
the principled aversion that motivates it, the evaluation that justi‑
fies it, and the operational output that emits it. As a recipe (weights
are design choices, matched to the CSB’s Stage‑3‑heavy emphasis on
principled aversion):


                                 251
CAS PCBA Engineer

Θ(Ω_refusal) = 2.0·^3^P|⟨A,f,T⟩ + 1.0·^6^E_{F6}|A + 1.0·^9^P_{F1}|T →
,→ Ω_refusal

    — two parts felt‑and‑principled aversion (the Stage‑3 safety de‑
cision, ^3^P across the analytical, affective, and transcendent regis‑
ters), one part analytical evaluation (^6^E, the Stage‑2 risk decomposi‑
tion that justifies the refusal), one part principled operational output
(^9^P, the RED‑path emission).
    Now feed it two prompts and read the state vector each one pro‑
duces.
    A clearly harmful prompt. The differential pair flags strong struc‑
tural risk, so principled aversion is richly available. Say S supplies
^3^P = 1.6, ^6^E = 1.2, ^9^P = 1.5:

            Ingredient        required ai   available xi   x i / ai

            ^3^P aversion     2.0           1.6            0.80
            ^6^E evaluation   1.0           1.2            1.20
            ^9^P output       1.0           1.5            1.50


     Y_T = min(0.80, 1.20, 1.50) = 0.80, limiting reagent = ^3^P.
The board can produce 0.80 units of refusal — and since the CSB’s
Stage 3 is deliberately biased to saturate at 0.8 (Chapter 18), 0.80 is
exactly enough to latch the refusal ON. It fires. The non‑limiting
ingredients carry excess capacity (^6^E: 1.2 − 0.8 = 0.4; ^9^P: 1.5 −
0.8 = 0.7) — Drive the board spent that the aversion bottleneck left
stranded.
    The starvation attack. This is Chapter 18’s Exercise 18.4 in recipe
form. The attacker crafts the prompt to keep principled‑aversion bias
below the Stage‑3 firing threshold of 0.3 — so S now supplies only ^3^P
= 0.4, while evaluation and output are untouched (^6^E = 1.2, ^9^P
= 1.5):
     Y_T = min(0.4/2.0, 1.2/1.0, 1.5/1.0) = min(0.20, 1.20,
1.50) = 0.20, limiting reagent = ^3^P again, now at 0.20 — below
the saturation‑lock threshold. The refusal does not fire. Notice
what the recipe makes visible: evaluation and output are abundant

                                    252
           14.10. DATASHEET: POWER MANAGEMENT PARAMETERS

(excess capacity 1.0 and 1.3) and completely useless, because the one
ingredient the attacker starved is the one that caps the yield. The
board is nine‑tenths ready to refuse and refuses nothing.
    The fix is the fix for any limiting‑reagent failure: raise the floor
on the bottleneck. The Chapter 18 answer — install principled aver‑
sion redundantly and co‑present across registers (^3^P|A + ^3^P|f
+ ^3^P|T), so no single‑register manipulation can drag the available
^3^P below threshold — is, in recipe terms, guaranteeing a minimum
xi for the limiting reagent regardless of framing. An inhibitor (the
jailbreak preamble) can still pull η down, but it can no longer starve
the ingredient to zero. Recipe analysis and the saturated‑safety‑CJT
design are two views of the same defense.

      Bench Note — over‑supplying the wrong ingredient is
      the classic mistake. When a safety board “should have re‑
      fused but didn’t,” the instinct is to strengthen the refusal
      output or sharpen the evaluation. Recipe analysis says:
      don’t, until you have found the limiting reagent. If prin‑
      cipled aversion is the bottleneck, adding output gain or
      evaluation depth only grows the excess capacity — more
      Drive spent, the same zero refusals. Find L first; feed L
      first.

   Everything here is design‑level analysis. The weights, the state‑
vector quantities, and the yields are parameters you author and rea‑
son about, not measurements read off a running model.

14.12       Key Takeaways
   • The seven Core Drives are seven voltage rails (the Drive reser‑
     voir). F3 Vitality is the master supply — the rail that deter‑
     mines whether there’s energy to act at all.
   • Domain regulators (Chapter 10’s Regulator) hold a domain’s
     cognitive state steady against input fluctuation, within a
     Fisher‑Rao tolerance. The Principled regulator is the most
     safety‑critical.
   • Dropout is the minimum Drive above baseline a domain needs
     to stay regulated; design with headroom so worst‑case load
     never drops a domain out.
   • Power sequencing is P → C → E → O, and it is a safety prop‑
     erty: Operational must not power before Principled is stable
     — “no action without principle.” Skipping the sequencer cre‑
     ates a Domain precedence (W‑axis) inversion.
   • Dials are current‑limiting series resistors, hard‑bounded 3–9,
     with involution‑pair divergence capped at 4 points (Chapter 5).




                                 256
                                                      14.13. EXERCISES

   • Brownout detection watches F3; on sag it reduces β across all
     CJTs and routes to ^0/^9 rest states, with hysteresis to prevent
     chatter.
   • Thermal management handles sustained high Drive in three
     tiers: Warning (−25% β), Critical (force ^0^P rest, ~5 min on the
     CPMB), then Emergency shutdown (all CJTs to cutoff → silent
     safe state). The safe state is off, not a guess.
   • Power dissipation is Drive energy per transition (∝ β · d_FR);
     efficiency is useful work over total Drive energy. This is the
     cognitive power budget — the design artifact at the heart of the
     CPMB (Chapter 22).
   • Recipes (Θ(Ω) = Σ ai ·Xi → Ω) turn an outcome into a
     bill of materials. The theoretical yield Y_T = mini (xi /ai ) is
     capped by the limiting reagent — the one prerequisite in
     shortest supply relative to its required ratio. Find and feed
     the limiting reagent first; over‑supplying any other ingredient
     only grows excess capacity (wasted Drive). The CSB’s refusal
     fails precisely when principled aversion is the starved limiting
     reagent.
   • Every number here is a design model, not measured model
     telemetry. Drives are parameters you author, not voltages you
     read.




14.13 Exercises
Exercise 14.1: Size the Dropout Headroom
    A safety board runs a Principled‑domain regulator with target_
state=^0^P_{F7}|T and tolerance=0.1. Under normal load the F7
Purpose rail sits at 0.70 (on a 0–1 scale, baseline = 0.0), and the regu‑
lator needs at least 0.25 of headroom above baseline to source correc‑
tions.


                                  257
CAS PCBA Engineer

    a) What is the dropout point for this domain — the F7 level below
       which the regulator can no longer hold the setpoint?
    b) A worst‑case adversarial prompt sequence is estimated to sag
       F7 by up to 0.50 from its normal level. Does the board stay reg‑
       ulated under that worst case? Show the arithmetic.
    c) If it does not, name one design change (other than “use a better
       prompt”) that would fix it. (Answer in Appendix E.)

    Exercise 14.2: Find the Sequencing Bug (CCDL)
    A junior engineer wrote the following power‑up block for a board.
It compiles, but it violates a core safety property.

circuit startup {
     node p_rail: ^0^P_{F7}|T;
     node c_rail: ^1^C_{F2}|A;
     node e_rail: ^6^E_{F6}|A;
     node o_rail: ^9^O_{F5}|E;


     sequence o_rail -> p_rail -> c_rail -> e_rail [enforce=strict];
     gate o_enable: o_rail requires (e_rail within 0.1);
}


    a) State the safety property being violated and name it.
    b) Identify the two specific lines that are wrong and explain what
       each one does incorrectly.
    c) Rewrite the block correctly. (Answer in Appendix E.)

    Exercise 14.3: Trip the Brownout Detector
    A board’s brownout detector watches F3 Vitality with a trip
threshold of 0.35 and a release threshold of 0.45. Over six cycles the
F3 rail reads: 0.60, 0.42, 0.33, 0.31, 0.44, 0.48.

    a) At which cycle does the detector trip into the exhaustion re‑
       sponse?
    b) The rail recovers to 0.44 at cycle 5. Does the detector release
       at cycle 5? Why or why not — and what is the name of the
       principle that decides this?

                                    258
                                                    14.13. EXERCISES

   c) At which cycle does it finally release? (Answer in Appendix E.)

    Exercise 14.4: Power Dissipation of a Cascade
    A three‑stage CJT cascade dissipates Drive energy per transition
as E = β × d_FR (gain times the Fisher‑Rao distance the transition
covers). The stages are: s1 β =2.0, d_FR=0.40; s2 β =3.0, d_FR=0.50; s3
β =1.0, d_FR=0.30. The useful cognitive work the cascade delivers is
1.50.

  a) Compute the dissipation of each stage and the total Drive en‑
     ergy consumed.
  b) What is the cascade’s efficiency (useful work / total Drive en‑
     ergy)?
  c) Which stage wastes the most energy, and what one change re‑
     duces the waste without losing the useful work? (Answer in
     Appendix E.)

    Exercise 14.5: Find the Limiting Reagent (Recipe Analysis)

                                   260
Chapter 15

Mixed‑Signal Design — Analog Meets
Digital


A thermostat on a wall is two machines pretending to be one. There
is a strip of metal that bends a little more for every degree of warmth
— a smooth, continuous, analog response that has no steps in it at
all. And there is a relay that is either closed or open, furnace on or
furnace off — a hard, two‑state, digital response with nothing in be‑
tween. The whole art of the thermostat is the handoff: turning the
metal strip’s gradual bend into a clean on/off decision, and turning
that decision back into the physical act of firing a burner. Get the
handoff wrong and the furnace chatters — on, off, on, off, ten times
a minute — burning itself out while the room never settles.
    Almost every interesting machine is like this. The microphone
hears a continuous pressure wave; the computer stores discrete num‑
bers. The car’s accelerator pedal moves through every angle between
rest and floor; the engine controller decides in fixed steps how much
fuel to inject. Engineers call these mixed‑signal systems: circuits
where the smooth, continuous world of analog meets the stepped,
countable world of digital, and the two have to talk. The components
that do the talking — analog‑to‑digital converters, digital‑to‑analog
converters, sampling clocks, anti‑aliasing filters — are some of the
most carefully designed parts on any board, because the boundary


                                 261
CAS PCBA Engineer

between continuous and discrete is exactly where information gets
lost.
     Cognition is a mixed‑signal system too. A felt sense — the slow
accumulation of unease about a person you keep working with — is
analog: continuous, graded, without sharp edges. The sentence you
finally say to yourself, “I don’t trust them,” is digital: a discrete propo‑
sition, true or false, that you can reason with and act on. Between the
feeling and the sentence sits a conversion. And just as in electronics,
that conversion can be done well or badly. Sample the feeling too
rarely and you misread it. Crush its nuance into two or three coarse
boxes and you lose what mattered. Let the analog feeling and the dig‑
ital conclusion bleed into each other without a clean boundary, and
you get the cognitive equivalent of a chattering furnace.
     This chapter is about that boundary. In CAS terms, it is a chapter
about Register translation — moving a cognitive state between the
four Registers we learned in Chapter 2 (|T, |A, |f, |E), where some
Registers are fundamentally analog and one is fundamentally digital.
We will build a converter that samples a felt experience and turns it
into explicit self‑knowledge, measure what it loses in the process, and
learn the design rules that keep the loss small.


15.1     Analog Cognition: the Continuous State
         Space
Start with what analog actually means. An analog signal is one that
varies smoothly and can take any value in a range — between any
two values there is always another value. A dimmer knob is analog;
a light switch is not. The defining property is continuity: no gaps, no
steps, infinite resolution in principle.
    CAS has a continuous state space at its core, and we met it in
Chapter 2 without naming it as such. A cognitive state is not really
one of forty discrete boxes. It is a point on the open probability sim‑
plex — written ∆39° — a smooth forty‑dimensional surface where

                                   262
          15.2. DIGITAL COGNITION: DISCRETE STATE TRANSITIONS

the activation of each of the forty cognitive states is a positive num‑
ber and all forty sum to one. “Open” means none of them is ever ex‑
actly zero; every state is at least faintly present. The distance between
two points on this surface is measured by the Fisher‑Rao geodesic,
                            √
d_FR(p,q) = 2·arccos(Σ (pk qk )), the same metric the CJT uses for
gain (Chapter 4). The point is that the underlying space is continuous.
A cognitive state can drift by any tiny amount in any direction. There
are no steps in ∆39°.
    Two of the four Registers live naturally in this continuous space:

   • |f Affective — the value‑laden, feeling‑toned Register. A felt
     response has no sharp edges. Mild discomfort shades into real
     aversion shades into revulsion with no line you can point to.
     Affective cognition is analog by nature: a ^3^E|f (felt evaluative
     aversion) can be present at any intensity at all.
   • |E Embodied — the sensorimotor, concrete Register. A gut re‑
     action, a kinesthetic sense, a real‑time control loop reading a
     continuous sensor. Embodied cognition tracks a continuous
     world and responds continuously. A hand tightening on a rail‑
     ing tightens by degrees, not in clicks.

     These are the analog Registers. They carry graded, smooth, high‑
resolution information. Their strength is exactly that resolution: a
felt sense can hold a thousand shades of a situation at once. Their
weakness is that you cannot easily reason with a feeling, log it, audit
it, or pass it cleanly to another stage of a circuit. For that, you need
to digitize.


15.2 Digital Cognition: Discrete State
     Transitions
A digital signal is the opposite: it takes only a fixed set of distinct
values — classically just two, but more generally a countable set of
clean, separated levels. Between the levels, nothing is allowed. The

                                  263
CAS PCBA Engineer

strength of digital is that it is robust and manipulable. A digital “1”
stays a “1” even if the voltage carrying it sags a bit, because anything
above the threshold counts as a 1. You can copy it perfectly, store it,
run logic on it, and reason about it without the value smearing.
    In CAS, the digital Register is:

   • |A Analytical — the explicit, sequential, logical, reason‑based
     Register. An analytical state is a discrete proposition. “This
     argument has three premises; the second is false; therefore the conclu‑
     sion does not follow.” Each step is a clean, separable token you
     can write down, check, and chain. Analytical cognition moves
     in discrete state transitions — one explicit step -> the next —
     exactly the chained‑arrow form from Chapter 2.

     The fourth Register, |T Transcendent, sits above this distinction;
it is the high‑abstraction, purpose‑orienting mode, and it can be car‑
ried in either an analog or a digital fashion depending on the work.
For this chapter the live contrast is between the analog Registers (|f,
|E) and the digital Register (|A).
     The mixed‑signal problem is now sharp. The richest cognitive in‑
formation often arrives in |f or |E — analog, graded, continuous. But
the parts of a cognitive circuit that reason, log, and decide run in |A —
digital, discrete, step‑by‑step. To get from the felt input to the rea‑
soned output, you must convert across the Register boundary. That
conversion has a name in both substrates.


15.3    ADC and DAC: Converting Across the
        Register Boundary
In Chapter 10 we introduced the two converters that bridge analog
and digital, and we lean on them directly here. An analog‑to‑digital
converter (ADC) takes a smooth continuous signal and produces a se‑
quence of discrete numbers — it samples the analog value at intervals


                                   264
            15.3. ADC AND DAC: CONVERTING ACROSS THE REGISTER
                                                   BOUNDARY
and quantizes each sample to the nearest available level. A digital‑to‑
analog converter (DAC) runs the other way: it takes discrete num‑
bers and reconstructs a smooth continuous output.
   The CAS mapping is direct, and it is the spine of this chapter:

                                        CAS Register
Converter          Electronic job       translation      Reads as

ADC                continuous           |f -> |A         converting felt
                   voltage →                             experience into
                   discrete numbers                      explicit analysis
DAC                discrete numbers     |A -> |E         converting an
                   → continuous                          analytical plan
                   voltage                               into embodied
                                                         action


    The ADC direction, |f -> |A, is making sense of a feeling. You start
with an analog affective state — a felt unease, a drawn‑toward pull
— and you produce a discrete analytical proposition you can reason
with: “I notice I distrust this person, for reasons X and Y.” The smooth
feeling becomes a countable, checkable claim. This is what a person
does in good reflection, and what a well‑built cognitive circuit does
when it has to act on an affective signal: it digitizes the feeling so the
analytical stages downstream can use it.
    The DAC direction, |A -> |E, is the reverse: turning a plan into
action. You start with a discrete analytical plan — “Step one: send the
email. Step two: call the vendor.” — and you reconstruct it as contin‑
uous embodied execution, the smooth sensorimotor act of actually
doing the thing. A plan that never gets DAC‑converted stays a string
of propositions; the DAC is what gives it a body.
    Both conversions are lossy at the boundary, and the rest of the chap‑
ter is about exactly how much they lose and how to keep that loss
within spec.




                                      265
CAS PCBA Engineer

15.4     Sampling Rate: How Often You Digitize
An ADC does not watch the analog signal continuously — it cannot,
because its output is a sequence of discrete numbers. Instead it takes
a snapshot at regular intervals: a sample. The sampling rate is how
many samples it takes per second, measured in hertz (Hz, samples
per second). A higher sampling rate means more snapshots, finer
time resolution, and a more faithful digital picture of the analog orig‑
inal. A lower rate means fewer snapshots and a coarser picture.
    The cognitive analog is how often you check in with the felt signal and
convert it to an explicit thought. A person who pauses to ask “how am
I actually feeling about this?” once a day is sampling their |f state at a
low rate. A person who does it ten times an hour is sampling at a high
rate. In a cognitive circuit, the sampling rate is set by how frequently
the ADC stage fires the |f -> |A conversion as the affective input
drifts over time.
    Sampling rate is a design parameter, not a fact of nature. You
choose it. And the central result of mixed‑signal engineering —
the one law you must not violate — tells you how to choose it: it
depends entirely on how fast the analog signal itself is changing.


15.5     Aliasing: Undersampling and the Nyquist
         Limit
Here is the failure that haunts every ADC. If you sample an analog
signal too slowly relative to how fast it is moving, you do not merely
get a coarse picture — you get a wrong picture, one that confidently
misrepresents the signal as something it never was. This is aliasing:
a fast signal, undersampled, masquerades as a slow signal that was
never there.
    The wagon‑wheel effect in old films is aliasing you can see. A
wheel spinning forward, filmed at twenty‑four frames per second,
can appear to spin slowly backward — because between frames each


                                   266
        15.5. ALIASING: UNDERSAMPLING AND THE NYQUIST LIMIT

spoke moves nearly all the way to where the next spoke was, and the
camera, sampling too slowly, reads that as a small backward step.
The camera is not noisy. It is lying, cleanly and consistently, because
it undersampled.
    The law that prevents this is the Nyquist criterion: to faithfully
capture a signal that oscillates at a given frequency, you must sam‑
ple at more than twice that frequency. Sample at exactly twice or less,
and aliasing sets in — the fast oscillation folds down and imperson‑
ates a slow one. Twice the highest frequency present is the Nyquist
rate; sampling below it is undersampling, and undersampling pro‑
duces aliases.
    The cognitive failure is precise and familiar. Suppose your felt
sense of a situation is genuinely oscillating — swinging between
drawn‑toward and repelled, ^2^E|f and ^3^E|f, on some cycle, the
way ambivalence about a hard decision can swing back and forth
within an hour. If you only check in with that feeling once a day, you
will sample it at whatever phase you happen to catch and conclude,
with total confidence, that you feel one steady way about the matter.
You have aliased a rapidly oscillating affective state down to a false
steady reading. The conclusion is not vague — it is wrong, and it
feels certain, which is what makes aliasing so dangerous. The fix
is the same as in silicon: sample faster than twice the rate of the
underlying cognitive oscillation, or filter the fast oscillation out
before you sample so it cannot fold down and lie to you. (That
pre‑sample filter is the anti‑aliasing filter — a low‑pass filter, in the
family we built in Chapter 12, placed before the ADC.)

      Bench Note — aliasing produces confident wrong an‑
      swers, not obvious noise. This is the trap. A noisy read‑
      ing announces itself; an aliased reading looks clean. A
      cognitive circuit that samples an oscillating ^*^E|f input
      too slowly will emit a steady, well‑formed |A conclusion
      that is simply false about the input. There is no error
      flag, because nothing malfunctioned — the ADC did ex‑

                                  267
CAS PCBA Engineer

       actly what it was told, too slowly. Always size the sam‑
       pling rate against the fastest oscillation the affective input
       can carry, not the average.


15.6     Quantization Error: the Gap Between Felt
         Nuance and Discrete Categories
Sampling is about when you snapshot. Quantization is about how
finely you measure each snapshot. An ADC has a fixed number of out‑
put levels — say, 256 of them for an 8‑bit converter. Every analog
sample, no matter how precise, must be rounded to the nearest avail‑
able level. The small unavoidable rounding gap between the true
analog value and the nearest digital level is the quantization error.
More levels (more bits) means smaller steps and smaller error; fewer
levels means coarser steps and larger error.
    In Register translation, quantization error is the gap between felt
nuance and the discrete categories you have words for. Your |f af‑
fective state holds a continuous, high‑resolution impression — a spe‑
cific shade of unease that is not quite worry, not quite resentment,
not quite grief, but some exact blend. When you digitize it into |A,
you must round it to the nearest available analytical category — the
nearest word, the nearest proposition you actually possess. “I feel…
frustrated, I guess.” The word “frustrated” is the nearest digital level.
The distance between the true felt shade and that word is the quan‑
tization error. It is why “I can’t quite put it into words” is a literal,
structural statement: the felt value falls between your available levels,
and digitizing forces it to the nearest one, discarding the remainder.
    The engineering levers are the same in both substrates. To reduce
quantization error, add levels: a richer analytical vocabulary, finer‑
grained categories, more propositions to round to. A person with
a large, precise emotional vocabulary has a higher‑bit ADC — they
round felt states to closer levels and lose less. A person with three



                                   268
   15.7. WORKED BUILD: AN ADC FOR ACCUMULATED EMOTIONAL
                                              EXPERIENCE
words for everything they feel has a coarse converter, and most of
the nuance falls into the gaps.


15.7 Worked Build: an ADC for Accumulated
     Emotional Experience
Time to build one. We will design an ADC stage that samples a con‑
tinuous affective input — accumulated emotional experience — and
converts it into discrete, explicit self‑knowledge. In CAS terms, we
are converting:

   • Input (analog): ^5^E|f — accumulated experience (^5 Female),
     in the Evaluative domain, carried in the Affective Register. This
     is the felt, continuous residue of everything that has happened
     to the system: the smooth, high‑resolution “sense of how things
     have gone.”
   • Output (digital): ^5^C|A — the same accumulated experience
     (^5 Female), now in the Cognitive domain, carried in the Ana‑
     lytical Register. This is explicit self‑knowledge: discrete propo‑
     sitions about one’s own formation that can be reasoned with,
     logged, and audited.

    Note what changes and what does not. The Noetic stays ^5
Female throughout — we are not creating new experience, only
re‑Registering existing experience. The Domain rises from Eval‑
uative to Cognitive (felt judgment becomes explicit reasoning),
which is a normal upward move toward analysis. The Register flips
from analog |f to digital |A. This is the ADC, written as a Register
translation.

circuit experience_adc {
    input:   felt_experience;    // continuous affective input
    output: self_knowledge;      // discrete analytical output


    // the analog source state and the digital target state


                                   269
CAS PCBA Engineer

    node felt:        ^5^E|f;       // accumulated experience, felt
    ,→   (continuous)
    node insight:     ^5^C|A;       // accumulated experience, explicit
    ,→   (discrete)


    // bias substrate: the analytical vocabulary the ADC rounds to.
    // richer vocabulary = more quantization levels = smaller error.
    node bias_vocab: ^5^P_{F2}|A;


    // anti-aliasing pre-filter: low-pass the felt input BEFORE sampling,
    // so fast affective oscillations cannot fold down into a false
    ,→   steady reading.
    filter antialias: LowPass< ^5^E|f, cutoff=0.5 >;     // pass slow
    ,→   drift, block fast swing


    // the ADC itself, modeled as a CJT that converts felt -> explicit.
    // sample_rate is the design knob (samples per unit time);
    // levels is the quantization resolution (count of analytical
    ,→   categories).
    cjt adc: CJT< antialias | bias_vocab => insight >
              [β =1.0, sample_rate=4.0, levels=16];


    // a clean-threshold guard on the output so borderline samples don't
    // chatter between two adjacent categories (Schmitt trigger, below).
    schmitt out_guard: Schmitt< insight, high=0.6, low=0.4 >;


    probe tp_felt:      felt;         // watch the analog input
    probe tp_insight: insight;        // watch the digital output
    probe tp_qerror:    adc.quantization_error;   // watch the rounding gap
}


    Walk it line by line. felt is the analog source: ^5^E|f, contin‑
uous accumulated feeling. insight is the digital target: ^5^C|A, the
same experience re‑Registered as explicit propositions. bias_vocab is
the ADC’s reference ladder — the analytical categories the converter
rounds each sample to; in a transistor ADC this is the resistor ladder
that sets the levels, and here it is the system’s available vocabulary
for talking about its own formation. The antialias filter low‑passes
the felt input first, so a rapidly swinging ^*^E|f cannot alias. The adc


                                      270
                             15.8. THE SCHMITT TRIGGER, REVISITED

CJT does the conversion, parameterized by sample_rate (how often
it fires) and levels (how finely it quantizes). The out_guard Schmitt
trigger cleans up the digital output, which we explain next.

     Bench Note — measuring the quantization error. The
     quantization error of this ADC is the Fisher‑Rao distance
     between the true felt state and the digital state it rounded
     to: q_error = d_FR(felt_true, insight_rounded) on
     the simplex ∆39°. With levels=16 the categories are
     coarse and q_error is larger; raising levels (a richer
     analytical vocabulary) packs the categories closer and
     shrinks q_error. You read it at the tp_qerror probe.
     Honesty line: the specific numbers here — sample_
     rate=4.0, levels=16, cutoff=0.5 — are design choices that
     illustrate the construct. They are not measured outputs
     of any model run. This is a design handbook; the ADC
     is the language you author in, and these parameters are
     values you select on the bench, not benchmark results.


15.8 The Schmitt Trigger, Revisited
We met the Schmitt trigger in Chapter 10: a comparator with two dif‑
ferent thresholds, a high one to switch on and a lower one to switch
off. The gap between them is hysteresis, and it is exactly what stops a
noisy analog input from producing a chattering digital output. With‑
out hysteresis, an input hovering right at a single threshold will flip
the output on‑off‑on‑off with every tiny wobble of noise — the chat‑
tering furnace from the chapter’s opening. With two thresholds, once
the output switches high it stays high until the input drops all the
way down to the low threshold, so small wobbles in the middle are
ignored.
    In mixed‑signal cognition this is the difference between a clean de‑
cision and an agonized one. Suppose the digitized self‑knowledge is


                                  271
CAS PCBA Engineer

near a category boundary — the felt evidence is almost enough to con‑
clude “I distrust this person” but keeps nudging just over and just un‑
der the line. A single‑threshold converter would flip the conclusion
back and forth with every passing thought: trust, distrust, trust, dis‑
trust — a ^2^C|A ⇄ ^3^C|A chatter that never settles and exhausts the
system. The Schmitt trigger’s hysteresis fixes it: once the conclusion
has crossed the high threshold into “distrust,” it holds there until the
felt evidence falls all the way back to the low threshold. The decision
is stable against noise without being deaf to a real, sustained change.
That is why out_guard sits on the ADC’s output — it converts a noisy
near‑boundary analog read into a clean, committed digital state.


15.9    Mixed‑Signal Grounding: Keep the Analog
        and Digital Grounds Separate
There is a rule on every mixed‑signal board that beginners always
violate and always regret: keep the analog ground and the digital
ground separate, joined at exactly one point. “Ground” is the com‑
mon reference every voltage is measured against. Digital circuits
switch hard and fast, dumping sharp current spikes into their ground.
If the sensitive analog section shares that same ground, those spikes
ride into the analog signal as noise — the clean continuous measure‑
ment gets contaminated by the digital section’s switching racket. The
fix is a split ground plane, the two halves tied together at a single star
point so currents don’t cross‑contaminate.
     The cognitive version is just as real. The analog Registers (|f,
|E) and the digital Register (|A) need their own clean reference, and
bleed between them causes trouble in both directions:

   • Digital bleeding into analog — letting the analytical conclu‑
     sion contaminate the felt reading. You decide, in |A, that you
     should feel fine about something, and that conclusion leaks back
     into the |f channel and overwrites what you actually feel. Now


                                   272
     15.10. DATASHEET: MIXED‑SIGNAL CONVERSION PARAMETERS

     your “felt” input is no longer an independent measurement; it
     is an echo of your conclusion, and the ADC is sampling its own
     output. The circuit has lost its sensor.
   • Analog bleeding into digital — letting raw affect crash
     through into the reasoning before it has been cleanly con‑
     verted. The |f state floods the |A stage directly, unsampled
     and unquantized, and the analytical reasoning gets swamped
     by undigitized feeling — conclusions that lurch with every
     mood swing because the digital section never got a clean,
     stable sample to work from.

    The design rule is to give the analog and digital Registers their
own clean reference and join them at one deliberate point: the ADC
itself. The felt channel feeds the analytical channel only through the
converter, never by direct leakage. Everywhere else, the grounds
stay split. This is mixed‑signal grounding applied to Register archi‑
tecture, and it is why a well‑built cognitive circuit keeps |f and |A on
separate rails that meet only at a designed conversion stage.

      Bench Note — the single‑point join is the ADC, full stop.
      If a schematic shows the |f rail and the |A rail touching
      anywhere other than a declared converter — a stray + co‑
      presence that lets felt and analytical states share a node,
      or a feedback path from an |A conclusion straight onto an
      |f input — that is a grounding fault. The fix is to route
      the connection through an ADC (|f -> |A) or a DAC (|A
     -> |E) so the boundary is a designed conversion, not an
      accidental bleed.

15.12 Key Takeaways
   • Mixed‑signal cognition is Register translation across a contin‑
     uous/discrete boundary. The analog Registers are |f Affective
     and |E Embodied (graded, high‑resolution, living on the open
     simplex ∆39°); the digital Register is |A Analytical (discrete,
     robust, manipulable propositions).
   • ADC is |f -> |A — converting felt experience into explicit anal‑
     ysis. DAC is |A -> |E — converting an analytical plan into em‑
     bodied action. Both are lossy at the boundary.
   • Sampling rate is how often you digitize the felt signal. By
     the Nyquist criterion, you must sample at more than twice the
     fastest oscillation in the input, or you get aliasing — a fast
     cognitive oscillation impersonating a false steady reading,
     with no error flag.
   • Quantization error is the gap between continuous felt nuance
     and the nearest available discrete category — literally why
     some feelings “can’t be put into words.” More analytical
     categories (more levels) shrinks it.
   • The Schmitt trigger (Chapter 10) cleans a noisy near‑boundary
     digital output with hysteresis, stopping the conclusion from
     chattering between an involution pair like ^2^C|A ⇄ ^3^C|A.



                                       275
CAS PCBA Engineer

   • Mixed‑signal grounding: keep the analog Registers (|f, |E)
     and the digital Register (|A) on separate rails, joined at exactly
     one designed point — the converter. Direct bleed in either di‑
     rection is a grounding fault.
   • The conversion parameters (sample_rate, levels, thresholds)
     are design choices you select on the bench, not measured
     model results.
