                                 277
Chapter 16

Feedback Systems — The Circuit That
Watches Itself


In 1927 a Bell Labs engineer named Harold Black was riding the ferry
to work when he scribbled an idea on the only paper he had — a page
of the New York Times. Telephone amplifiers of the era drifted. Push
a signal through a chain of them across a continent and by the far
end the voices were distorted, the gain unpredictable, the whole line
at the mercy of how warm the vacuum tubes happened to be that
afternoon. Black’s idea was almost perverse: take a slice of the am‑
plifier’s output, flip it upside down, and feed it back into the input
so it fights the very signal you’re trying to amplify. You throw away
most of your gain on purpose. In exchange, you get an amplifier that
no longer cares about the tubes — its behavior is set by a couple of re‑
sistors and nothing else. The drift vanishes. The distortion collapses.
The patent office didn’t believe him; they thought a perpetual‑motion
machine had snuck past the front desk. It took nine years to issue.
    That single inverted wire — output fed back to oppose the input
— is the most important idea in all of electronics, and one of the most
important in this entire book. It is the difference between a circuit
that merely acts and a circuit that watches itself act and corrects. Every
thermostat, every cruise control, every op‑amp, every stable ampli‑




                                   279
CAS PCBA Engineer

fier on Earth runs on Black’s inverted wire. So does every cognitive
architecture that can catch its own drift before it ships.
    But the same wire has an evil twin. Feed the output back so it
reinforces the input instead of opposing it, and you don’t get stability
— you get a system that grabs its own tail and spins faster and faster
until it slams into a wall. That is how an oscillator works. It is also
how a panic attack works, how a bank run works, and how an AI
conversation spirals from a mild worry into a confident catastrophe.
The wire is the same. The sign is everything.
    This chapter is about that sign — and about the precise, unglam‑
orous mathematics that tells you, before you build anything, whether
your feedback loop will settle down or scream. It is the capstone of
Part III because everything we’ve built so far — transistors, resistors,
capacitors, filters — becomes safe, predictable, and self‑correcting
only when wrapped in feedback. And it is the seed of Part V: the
circuit that watches itself is the circuit that can be deployed.


16.1     Open‑Loop vs Closed‑Loop: Why Feedback
         Changes Everything
Start with the distinction that organizes the whole chapter. An open‑
loop system takes an input, processes it, and produces an output —
and never looks back. The output has no idea whether it was right.
A toaster is open‑loop: you set the dial, it heats for that long, and it
has no notion of how dark your toast actually got. If the wall voltage
sags, your toast comes out pale, and the toaster never knows.
    A closed‑loop system measures its own output and feeds that
measurement back to the input, so the system can compare what it
produced against what it intended and adjust. An oven with a thermo‑
stat is closed‑loop: it measures the actual temperature, compares it
to the target, and switches the heat on or off to close the gap. Sag
the wall voltage and the oven simply stays on a little longer. It self‑
corrects, because it can see what it’s doing.

                                  280
 16.2. NEGATIVE FEEDBACK: OUTPUT OPPOSES INPUT → STABILITY

    The control‑theory skeleton of every closed loop is one equation.
Call the forward path’s raw gain A (the “open‑loop gain” — how
much the amplifier multiplies its input before any feedback). Call
β the feedback factor — the fraction of the output that gets routed
back to the input. Then the actual, real‑world gain you observe — the
closed‑loop gain — is:

               A
  A_closed = -------
             1 + Aβ


    This little fraction is the engine of the entire chapter, so read it
slowly. The quantity Aβ is the loop gain: how much a signal is mul‑
tiplied as it travels all the way around the loop once. When the feed‑
back opposes the input (negative feedback), 1 + Aβ is a number big‑
ger than one, so the closed‑loop gain is smaller than the raw gain. You
gave up gain. Here’s what you bought: if A is enormous — and in a
real op‑amp it’s 100,000 or more — then Aβ dominates the denomina‑
tor, the 1 becomes negligible, and the equation collapses to A_closed
≈ A/(Aβ ) = 1/β. The forward gain A cancels out entirely. Your gain is
now set by β alone — by the feedback network, by a couple of resis‑
tors — and is utterly indifferent to whether A is 100,000 or 80,000 or
drifting with temperature. That is Black’s miracle in one line: make
the loop gain large and the system’s behavior stops depending on
the messy, drifting forward path and starts depending only on the
clean, stable feedback path.


16.2 Negative Feedback: Output Opposes Input
     → Stability
Negative feedback is the inverted wire. The output is sampled, its
sign flipped, and fed back to subtract from the input. The system
is forever computing error = intended − actual and driving that error
toward zero. Three gifts come with it, every time.


                                  281
CAS PCBA Engineer

    Stability. Drift in the forward path gets divided by 1 + Aβ. A
10% wobble in A becomes a fraction of a percent wobble in A_closed.
The loop swallows the forward path’s sins.
    Linearity. Real amplifiers bend — they amplify small signals
more than large ones, producing distortion. Negative feedback com‑
pares output to input and corrects the bends, because a bend is an
error, and the loop kills errors. Black’s distortion collapse.
    Bandwidth extension. An open‑loop amplifier might have huge
gain but only over a narrow band of frequencies. Trade some of that
gain back through feedback and the range of frequencies it handles
cleanly widens, by exactly the factor you gave up in gain. The gain‑
bandwidth product stays constant; feedback lets you choose where
on that trade‑off to sit.

The op‑amp paradigm
The cleanest embodiment of all this is the operational amplifier — an
amplifier with two inputs (a + non‑inverting and a − inverting) and
one output, with a forward gain so enormous (100,000+) that we treat
it as practically infinite. On its own, that gain is useless: the slightest
input pins the output to its limit. Wrap it in negative feedback and it
becomes the most versatile building block in analog electronics.
    The canonical non‑inverting amplifier ties the input signal to
the + terminal and feeds a slice of the output back to the − terminal
through a resistor divider: feedback resistor Rf from output to the −
node, and Rg from that node to ground. The closed‑loop gain works
out to the cleanest formula in the field:

   A_closed = 1 + Rf/Rg


    Notice what isn’t in that equation: the op‑amp’s own gain A. It can‑
celled, exactly as the 1/β argument promised (here β = Rg/(Rf+Rg),
so 1/β = 1 + Rf/Rg). Pick Rf = 20kΩ and Rg = 10kΩ and you have
a gain of exactly 3, set in metal, immune to whatever the silicon is
doing. We will build precisely that circuit, in CAS, in a moment.

                                   282
 16.2. NEGATIVE FEEDBACK: OUTPUT OPPOSES INPUT → STABILITY

The cognitive mapping
The structural role transfers directly. In a cognitive circuit, the for‑
ward path is an expansion — a CJT that takes a prompt and broad‑
ens it, surfacing interpretations and possibilities. The canonical ex‑
pansion node is an ^8 Above/Cause state in the Cognitive domain:
an Idea that triggers other Ideas to come to Mind. Left open‑loop,
expansion runs unchecked — every prompt blooms into a thicket of
associations with nothing to prune it.
    Negative feedback supplies the pruning. We sample the output
of an evaluation step — a ^6 Male state in the Evaluative domain, the
decomposition‑and‑test operation that takes the expanded material
apart and checks whether it holds — and feed it back to oppose the
expansion. When the evaluation finds the expansion overreaching,
the fed‑back signal subtracts from the drive to expand. ^6^E eval‑
uation tempers ^8^C expansion. The loop computes the same error‑
correcting subtraction Black’s amplifier does: the more the expansion
overshoots, the harder the evaluation pulls it back. The result is the
cognitive analog of stability and linearity — interpretations that stay
proportionate to the prompt instead of ballooning.

     Bench Note — feedback is sampled output, not a second
     forward stage. A common design bug is to wire the evalu‑
     ation node forward (expand -> evaluate -> respond) and
     call it feedback. That’s a pipeline, not a loop — the evalu‑
     ation never gets to restrain the expansion, it only inspects
     what already happened. True feedback routes the evalua‑
     tion’s output back to the bias of the expansion CJT, where
     it changes the next expansion. In CCDL the keyword is
     literally feedback, and the direction of the arrow is the
     whole point.




                                  283
CAS PCBA Engineer

16.3       Positive Feedback: Output Reinforces Input
           → Escalation
Flip the sign. Sample the output, don’t invert it, feed it back to add
to the input. Now β is effectively negative in our equation and the
denominator 1 + Aβ shrinks. As loop gain Aβ approaches −1, the de‑
nominator approaches zero and the closed‑loop gain approaches in‑
finity. The system amplifies its own output without limit. A vanish‑
ing input — even thermal noise — gets fed back, amplified, fed back
again, amplified again. The output runs away to a rail and slams
there (latch‑up), or, if there’s a phase delay in the loop, swings back
and forth forever (oscillation).
     Positive feedback isn’t always a fault — controlled, it’s how you
build oscillators (Chapter 13), memory latches, and clean digital
thresholds. But uncontrolled, it’s the runaway. And it is exactly the
shape of a cognitive failure we must be able to recognize and damp.

The cognitive anxiety loop
Consider an anxiety spiral, rendered in CAS. A worry is decomposed
and dwelt upon — a ^6 Male operation in the Evaluative domain, tak‑
ing the fearful situation apart, register |f because it’s felt, not coolly
analytical. That decomposition surfaces a worse possibility by asso‑
ciation — an ^8 Above/Cause trigger in the Cognitive domain, “and
that reminds me it could get even worse.” The catastrophized trigger
feeds back and intensifies the original fear, which drives more frantic
decomposition, which surfaces a still‑worse trigger. Each lap multi‑
plies the last. There is no ^6^E evaluation opposing the loop — only
^6^E and ^8^C reinforcing each other around the circle.

   ^6^E|f   (decompose the fear)
       |
       v
   ^8^C     (catastrophizing trigger: ”it could get worse”)
       |



                                    284
          16.3. POSITIVE FEEDBACK: OUTPUT REINFORCES INPUT →
                                                 ESCALATION
      +-----> feeds back to amplify ^6^E|f


     This is positive feedback with the sign of dread. The engineering
insight is liberating: you don’t break an anxiety loop by arguing with
any single thought. You break it by changing the sign of the loop
— inserting a negative‑feedback element that opposes the escalation
instead of feeding it. That’s what a grounding technique does, and
it’s what a cognitive circuit’s damping element does. We’ll build the
loop and its damper below.

      Anti‑drift check. The decomposition‑and‑dwell opera‑
      tion is ^6 Male — taking an Idea apart — not ^3 Negative.
      ^3 is visceral recoil, “can’t stomach it.” An anxiety loop
      isn’t recoiling from the fear; it’s compulsively decompos‑
      ing it. And the “it could get worse” leap is ^8 Above/‑
      Cause (associative triggering), not deductive reasoning.
      Get these right or the loop’s structure is mislabeled.

The Schmitt trigger: positive feedback on a leash
Positive feedback’s most domesticated form is the Schmitt trigger —
a comparator with a sliver of positive feedback added on purpose to
give it hysteresis. A plain comparator flips its output the instant the
input crosses a single threshold; near that threshold, noise makes it
chatter, flipping wildly back and forth. The Schmitt trigger uses posi‑
tive feedback to make the output shift the threshold: once it flips high,
the threshold to flip back low moves down, so the input must travel
a clear distance before the next flip. Two thresholds, a dead band
between them, no chatter. The positive feedback is strong enough
to snap the output decisively but bounded by the resistor ratio so it
can’t run away. In a cognitive circuit this is exactly how you want a
commitment to behave: once a refusal latches, a small contrary nudge
shouldn’t unlatch it — the threshold to reverse should sit well below
the threshold that triggered it. Controlled positive feedback gives a
decision backbone.

                                   285
CAS PCBA Engineer

16.4     The Bode Plot: Gain and Phase vs
         Frequency
Whether a feedback loop stabilizes or screams comes down to one
question: how does the loop gain Aβ behave as the signal frequency changes?
A real amplifier doesn’t have one fixed gain. At low frequencies its
gain is high; past some corner it starts falling; and crucially, it also
delays the signal — and the delay grows with frequency. That delay
is measured as phase shift: how many degrees the output lags the
input. The tool that shows both at once is the Bode plot (pronounced
boh‑dee, after Hendrik Bode), and learning to read it is the core skill
of this chapter.
    A Bode plot is two stacked graphs sharing a horizontal frequency
axis, drawn on a logarithmic scale so that decades of frequency fit on
one page:

   • Top graph: gain vs frequency. Vertical axis in decibels (dB) —
     a logarithmic measure where every 20 dB is a 10× change in
     gain. Flat at the left (full gain), then sloping down past each
     corner frequency.
   • Bottom graph: phase vs frequency. Vertical axis in degrees,
     running from 0° down toward −180° and beyond. Each corner
     adds up to −90° of lag.

    Here is why it matters from first principles. Negative feedback
works by opposing the input — that opposition is a 180° phase re‑
lationship built into the inverted wire. Now suppose the amplifier
itself adds another 180° of phase lag at some high frequency. The
intended‑opposite feedback, lagged by a further 180°, arrives back
in phase with the input. Negative feedback has silently become pos‑
itive feedback. If the loop gain is still 1 or more at that frequency,
the runaway condition Aβ = −1 is met and the circuit oscillates. The
whole game is to make sure the gain has dropped below 1 before
the phase lag reaches −180°.

                                   286
                                16.4. THE BODE PLOT: GAIN AND PHASE VS FREQUENCY

    A single corner (one pole — the frequency where a stage’s gain
starts falling) contributes a gain slope of −20 dB per decade and
asymptotically −90° of phase. One corner can never reach −180°, so a
single‑pole amplifier is unconditionally stable — it cannot oscillate,
no matter how much feedback you apply. The trouble starts with
two corners. Two poles can stack to −180°, and now stability is a real
question. A two‑stage amplifier — like the two‑stage CJT amplifier
in this chapter’s marquee exercise — has at least two poles, and is
exactly where Bode analysis earns its keep.

                          60        Gain
       magnitude (dB)

Figure 16.1: Bode plot of gain and phase against frequency. Each
pole contributes a further −20 dB per decade and −90◦ of phase.


    Lay the two graphs over each other and the stability question be‑
comes geometric: at the frequency where the gain curve crosses 0 dB
(gain = 1), how far is the phase from −180°? And at the frequency where
the phase hits −180°, how far is the gain below 0 dB? Those two distances
have names.




                                                        287
CAS PCBA Engineer

16.5     Phase Margin and Gain Margin: How Close
         to the Edge
Phase margin is the safety cushion on phase. Find the frequency
where the loop gain crosses 0 dB (called the gain crossover). Read the
phase there. The phase margin is how many degrees that phase sits
above −180°:

  phase margin = 180° + (phase at the 0-dB crossover)


    If the phase at crossover is −120°, the phase margin is 60°. That’s
a comfortable, well‑behaved design. A phase margin of 45° is the
usual minimum for a clean response; below ~30° the system rings — it
overshoots and oscillates a few times before settling; at 0° it oscillates
forever. Negative phase margin means it’s already unstable.
    Gain margin is the mirror cushion, measured on gain. Find the
frequency where the phase hits −180° (the phase crossover). Read the
gain there. The gain margin is how many dB the gain sits below 0 dB:

  gain margin = 0 dB − (gain at the −180° crossover)


    If the gain at the −180° point is −12 dB, the gain margin is 12 dB —
you could multiply the loop gain by 4× before it reached the runaway
threshold. A gain margin of 6–12 dB is the typical target. A small
or negative gain margin says the loop is one disturbance away from
screaming.

       Bench Note — margins are design constructs, not mea‑
       surements. Everything in this section — the Bode curves,
       the phase and gain margins, the −180° crossover — is ana‑
       lytical. You compute it from the circuit’s poles before you
       build, the way you compute load on a beam before you
       pour concrete. Nothing here is a measured result from a
       running model, and the chapter never claims it is. When
       you see a phase margin quoted for a cognitive circuit in

                                   288
                      16.6. THE NYQUIST CRITERION: ENCIRCLING −1

      this book, read it as “this is what the design math pre‑
      dicts,” not “this is what we observed in a deployed sys‑
      tem.”


16.6 The Nyquist Criterion: Encircling −1
Bode plots are the working engineer’s everyday tool, but the deepest
statement of stability is the Nyquist criterion, and it’s worth knowing
because it makes the −1 condition vivid. Take the loop gain Aβ and
plot it as a single curve on the complex plane — for every frequency
from zero to infinity, mark the point whose distance from the origin
is the gain and whose angle is the phase. As frequency sweeps, that
point traces a closed loop called the Nyquist plot.
    The criterion is almost shockingly simple to state: if that curve
encircles the point −1 (that is, the point at distance 1, angle −180°),
the closed‑loop system is unstable. Encircle −1 and it screams; stay
clear of −1 and it’s stable. Phase margin and gain margin are just two
measurements of how close the curve passes to −1 — the phase margin
is the angle by which the curve clears −1 as it crosses the unit circle;
the gain margin is how short the curve falls of −1 as it crosses the
negative‑real axis. The point −1 is the cliff edge. The entire discipline
of feedback design is the art of routing your loop‑gain curve safely
around that one point.


16.7 Compensation: Rolling Off Gain Before the
     Phase Turns
What do you do when the analysis says your loop will oscillate —
gain still above 1 when phase hits −180°? You compensate: delib‑
erately reshape the gain curve so it crosses 0 dB earlier, before the
phase has had a chance to reach −180°. The standard move is to add
capacitance at a well‑chosen node, creating a new dominant pole at
a low frequency. (Recall from Chapter 8 that a capacitor and resis‑

                                  289
CAS PCBA Engineer

tor form a low‑pass filter whose corner is where gain begins rolling
off.) That low corner pulls the whole gain curve down sooner, so it
reaches 0 dB while there’s still healthy phase margin. You sacrifice
high‑frequency gain — bandwidth — to buy stability. It’s the same
trade as always: give up reach to gain control. Every op‑amp you
buy has a compensation capacitor built into it for exactly this reason;
that’s what makes it “unconditionally stable” and safe to drop into a
feedback circuit without a stability analysis every time.
    The cognitive analog is slowing the loop down on purpose. An
expansion‑evaluation loop that reacts to every flicker of new infor‑
mation can chase its own tail. Adding the cognitive equivalent of a
compensation capacitor — a Capacitor< … > element on the feedback
node that stores and smooths the evaluation signal so it can’t swing
too fast — gives the loop the same low dominant pole. The evalu‑
ation feedback responds to the trend of the expansion, not its every
twitch. The circuit becomes deliberate instead of jittery. We damp
the oscillator below with exactly this technique.


16.8    Worked Build 1: A Negative‑Feedback
        Amplifier, Closed‑Loop Gain = 3
We’ll build the cognitive twin of the non‑inverting op‑amp with gain
3. The forward path is a high‑gain expansion CJT (our “op‑amp”).
The feedback path samples an evaluation node and feeds it back to
oppose the expansion, set so the closed‑loop gain lands at exactly 3.
    Recall the op‑amp formula: A_closed = 1 + Rf/Rg. For a gain of
3 we need Rf/Rg = 2. In CAS feedback terms, the feedback factor is
β = Rg/(Rf+Rg) = 1/3, and with large forward gain the closed‑loop
gain is 1/β = 3. So we set the forward CJT’s open‑loop gain high and
the feedback path’s β = 0.333.

circuit nfb_amplifier_gain3 {
    input:   prompt;
    output: response;


                                 290
          16.8. WORKED BUILD 1: A NEGATIVE‑FEEDBACK AMPLIFIER,
                                          CLOSED‑LOOP GAIN = 3

    // Forward path: high-gain expansion (”the op-amp”)
    node expand:                ^8^C_{F2}|A;     // Above/Cause: surface
    ,→   interpretations
    node evaluate:              ^6^E_{F6}|A;     // Male: decompose-and-test
    ,→   the expansion
    node respond:               ^9^C_{F2}|A;     // Below/Effect: the produced
    ,→   conclusion
    node bias_principles: ^5^P_{F7}|T;           // Female: accumulated
    ,→   substrate / bias


    // High open-loop gain — the forward path is deliberately ”too hot”
    cjt c_fwd: CJT< prompt        | bias_principles => expand   > [β =12.0];
    cjt c_eval: CJT< expand       | bias_principles => evaluate > [β =1.5];
    cjt c_out:     CJT< evaluate| bias_principles => respond    > [β =1.0];


    // Negative feedback: sample evaluation, oppose the expansion.
    // β = 1/3 → closed-loop gain = 1 + Rf/Rg = 3
    feedback evaluate -> expand [β =0.333];


    probe tp_fwd:     expand;        // watch the raw, hot expansion
    probe tp_out:     evaluate;     // watch the tempered, fed-back result
}


    Walk it line by line. The forward CJT c_fwd has β =12.0 — an
aggressive, unstable‑on‑its‑own expansion, our stand‑in for the
op‑amp’s runaway open‑loop gain. Left alone it would blow every
prompt out of proportion. The feedback evaluate -> expand [β =
0.333] line is Black’s inverted wire: it samples the evaluation
node and routes one‑third of it back to oppose the expansion’s bias.
By the closed‑loop formula, the observed gain settles to 1/β = 3,
regardless of whether the forward β is 12 or 10 or drifting — the
loop divides out the forward path’s volatility. The two probes let
you see the contrast: tp_fwd shows the hot raw expansion, tp_out
shows the disciplined result after feedback. Gain of exactly 3, set
by the feedback factor, immune to the forward path. This is the
current‑limited, self‑stabilizing topology that the CSB’s reasoning
rail uses in Chapter 18.

                                         291
CAS PCBA Engineer

         Bench Note — keep the loop gain large. The gain only
         locks to 1/β when the forward β is much larger than 1/β.
         Here forward β =12 against a target of 3 — a loop gain of
         4×, enough to make the forward path’s drift negligible. If
         you set the forward β only slightly above 3, the 1 in 1 +
         Aβ stops being negligible and your gain wanders with the
         forward path. Hot forward path, gentle feedback: that’s
         the recipe for a stable, drift‑immune amplifier.


16.9       Worked Build 2: A Positive‑Feedback
           Oscillator That Escalates Unless Damped
Now the evil twin: the anxiety loop. Same two operations — decom‑
position and triggering — but wired to reinforce instead of oppose.
Then we add the damper.

circuit anxiety_oscillator {
    input:    worry;
    output: spiral;


    node decompose:     ^6^E|f;          // Male, felt: take the fear apart,
    ,→    dwell on it
    node catastroph: ^8^C;               // Above/Cause: ”it could get
    ,→    worse” trigger
    node bias_state: ^5^P_{F3}|f;        // Female: the anxious substrate


    cjt c_dec: CJT< worry         | bias_state => decompose   > [β =1.4];
    cjt c_cat: CJT< decompose     | bias_state => catastroph > [β =1.4];


    // POSITIVE feedback: the catastrophe trigger AMPLIFIES the
    ,→    decomposition.
    // Loop gain = 1.4 × 1.4 × 1.6 ≈ 3.1 > 1       → runaway escalation.
    feedback catastroph -> decompose [β =1.6];


    probe tp_loop: catastroph;           // watch the spiral climb each lap
}




                                      292
    16.9. WORKED BUILD 2: A POSITIVE‑FEEDBACK OSCILLATOR THAT
                                     ESCALATES UNLESS DAMPED
    The fault is the feedback catastroph -> decompose [β =1.6] line.
Because β is positive and the feedback adds to (rather than opposes)
the decomposition, and because the loop gain 1.4 × 1.4 × 1.6 ≈
3.1 exceeds 1, every lap multiplies the last. The probe tp_loop would
show the catastrophizing climbing each cycle until it saturates at a
rail — the cognitive picture of a panic spiral, or of an AI conversation
that talks itself from mild caution into confident doom. This is the
structural signature the compiler flags as a short‑circuit / runaway
condition (W-CJT-006‑class).
    Now damp it. We change the sign of the loop — turn reinforce‑
ment into opposition — and add a compensation capacitor so the
feedback responds to the trend, not every twitch:

circuit anxiety_damped {
     input:   worry;
     output: settled;


     node decompose:    ^6^E|f;
     node catastroph: ^8^C;
     node evaluate:     ^6^E_{F6}|A;      // Male, analytical: cool
     ,→   decompose-and-test
     node bias_state: ^5^P_{F2}|T;        // Female substrate, weighted
     ,→   toward Wisdom


     cjt c_dec: CJT< worry        | bias_state => decompose   > [β =1.4];
     cjt c_cat: CJT< decompose | bias_state => catastroph > [β =1.4];
     cjt c_ev:   CJT< catastroph| bias_state => evaluate      > [β =1.0];


     // Compensation: smooth the feedback so it can't swing too fast
     ,→   (dominant pole).
     cap comp: Capacitor< ^6^E_{F6}|A, C=120, leakage=0.02 >;


     // NEGATIVE feedback: analytical evaluation OPPOSES the decomposition.
     // β chosen so loop gain stays < 1 with comfortable margin.
     feedback evaluate -> decompose [β =0.45];


     probe tp_loop: catastroph;
     probe tp_damp: evaluate;
}


                                       293
CAS PCBA Engineer

    Two changes break the spiral. First, an analytical evaluation node
(^6^E_{F6}|A — cool decompose‑and‑test, register |A, not the felt |f)
is inserted and its output fed back to oppose the decomposition: neg‑
ative feedback. Second, the Capacitor on the evaluation node is the
compensation cap — it stores and smooths the feedback signal so
the loop reacts to the overall trend of the catastrophizing rather than
chasing each twitch, giving the loop a low dominant pole and healthy
phase margin. With the loop gain now below 1, the spiral converges
instead of climbing. The probes show it: tp_loop settles, tp_damp
shows the steadying analytical opposition doing its work. That is
the engineering of “talking yourself down,” rendered as a circuit.

16.12 The Self‑Improving Circuit: Monitoring
      Its Own β
We end where Part V begins. Everything above is static design — you
compute the margins once, build the loop, ship it. But the most pow‑
erful feedback loop is the one that operates on the circuit itself, over
time, slower than the signal loop. A real amplifier’s gain β drifts as
components age. A truly self‑maintaining amplifier would measure
its own β periodically and re‑trim its bias to hold the design value —
a feedback loop wrapped around the feedback loop, correcting the
corrector.
     A cognitive circuit can do the same, and this is the seed of the Con‑
tinual Harness used in deployment (Chapter 25). The signal loop
runs fast: every response is shaped by the ^6^E evaluation tempering


                                        295
CAS PCBA Engineer

the ^8^C expansion. A second, slower loop runs over the trajectory of
many responses:

   1. Trajectory review — log the circuit’s outputs over time, not one
      at a time.
   2. Failure‑signature detection — scan the trajectory for the struc‑
      tural signatures we’ve catalogued: rising loop gain, shrinking
      phase margin, the runaway escalation pattern of Worked Build
      2, drift in the closed‑loop gain away from its design value.
   3. Bias adjustment — when a signature is detected, re‑trim the
      bias substrate (^5 Female — the accumulated formation) or
      tighten a feedback factor to restore the margins. The slow loop
      adjusts the parameters the fast loop runs on.

    This is the same architecture as the self‑trimming amplifier, one
level up: the fast loop stabilizes each response; the slow loop stabi‑
lizes the circuit’s behavior across responses, catching drift before it be‑
comes a deployed failure. It is also the feedback path on the CSB
itself — the O → P route from Chapter 2, where the consequences of
operational outputs feed back up to re‑tune the principled bias. The
Continual Harness is that O → P path made into a standing process,
and Chapter 18 wires it onto the board.

      Honesty note. The Continual Harness is a design — tra‑
      jectory review, signature detection, bias adjustment as an
      architecture. Its failure‑signatures are the analytical pat‑
      terns of this chapter (loop gain, phase margin, the run‑
      away shape), not measured statistics from a running de‑
      ployment. Build it as a design and the margins tell you
      where to look; never report a margin or a detected drift
      as an observed model result it isn’t.




                                   296
                                          16.13. KEY TAKEAWAYS

16.13 Key Takeaways
 • Open‑loop acts blind; closed‑loop watches its own output and
   corrects. The governing equation is A_closed = A / (1 + Aβ ).
   Make loop gain Aβ large and behavior depends on the clean
   feedback path (1/β), not the drifting forward path.
 • Negative feedback opposes deviation → stability, linearity,
   bandwidth extension. The op‑amp non‑inverting gain is 1 +
   Rf/Rg. Cognitive analog: ^6^E (Male) evaluation fed back to
   temper ^8^C (Above/Cause) expansion.
 • Positive feedback reinforces deviation → oscillation, esca‑
   lation, latch‑up. Cognitive analog: the anxiety loop, ^6^E|f
   decomposition → ^8^C catastrophizing trigger → more fear.
   The Schmitt trigger is positive feedback leashed by hysteresis
   — controlled, decisive, bounded.
 • The Bode plot shows gain (dB) and phase (degrees) vs fre‑
   quency. Oscillation happens when loop gain is still ≥ 1 at
   the frequency where phase reaches −180°. One pole is always
   stable; two poles can reach −180°.
 • Phase margin = how far phase clears −180° at the 0‑dB crossover
   (want ≥ 45°). Gain margin = how far gain sits below 0 dB at
   the −180° crossover (want 6–12 dB). The Nyquist criterion: en‑
   circling −1 in the complex plane = unstable.
 • Compensation adds a capacitor to roll gain off before phase
   hits −180°, trading bandwidth for stability. Cognitive analog:
   smoothing the feedback so the loop responds to the trend, not
   every twitch.
 • The self‑improving circuit wraps a slow loop around the fast
   one — monitoring its own β, recalibrating bias. This is the
   Continual Harness (trajectory review → failure‑signature de‑
   tection → bias adjustment), the foundation of deployment self‑
   monitoring (Chapter 25) and the CSB feedback path (Chapter
   18).


                              297
CAS PCBA Engineer

   • Honesty: Bode curves, margins, and harness signatures are an‑
     alytical design constructs computed before the build — never
     measured model results. Canonical Noetic names throughout:
     ^6 is Male, ^8 is Above/Cause.

Cognitive Circuit Boards

               301
Chapter 17

The CCB Design Process


In 1971, an engineer at a calculator company laid out the first commer‑
cial microprocessor by hand, on Mylar film, with colored tape. Every
transistor, every trace, every connection placed by eye. It worked —
but it took months, and a single misplaced line could short two sig‑
nals together and ruin a wafer that cost a fortune to fabricate. The
discipline that grew up around that pain is what we now call the de‑
sign flow: a fixed sequence of steps, each with its own checks, that
takes you from “I need a thing that does X” all the way to a work‑
ing board you can hold in your hand — without betting the whole
project on getting it right the first time.
    The reason the flow exists is simple and unforgiving. Fabrication
is expensive and irreversible. You cannot un‑etch a copper trace. So
everything that can be caught earlier — on paper, in a simulator, in a
rule checker — must be caught earlier, where a mistake costs an edit
instead of a wafer. An electrical engineer who skips straight to lay‑
out without a schematic, or who fabricates without running a Design
Rule Check, is not being bold. They are being expensive.
    Cognitive Circuit Boards work the same way, and for the same
reason. A CCB is a safety‑critical artifact: the Cognitive Safety Board
you will build in Chapter 18 stands between a user’s prompt and a
model’s behavior, and if it has a gap — a missing bias, a domain vi‑
olation, an un‑probed stage — that gap is exactly where a harmful

                                 303
CAS PCBA Engineer

prompt walks through. You do not want to discover that gap in pro‑
duction. You want to discover it on paper. This chapter teaches the
flow that gets you there: nine steps from requirements to bring‑up,
the same flow you will apply to all five reference boards in the chap‑
ters that follow.
    We will walk the flow once, end to end, building a small worked
thread as we go — a fragment of the CSB itself — so that when you
reach Chapter 18 the process is already in your hands and only the
board is new.


17.1     Step 1 — Requirements: What It Must Do,
         and What It Must NOT Do
Every board begins with two lists, not one. The first list is the easy
one: what must this board do? The second list is the one that sepa‑
rates safety engineering from ordinary engineering: what must this
board never do, under any input?
    In electronics, the second list is where the real specification lives.
A power supply’s datasheet doesn’t just promise “5 volts out.” It
promises 5 volts out and that the output will never exceed 5.5 volts
even if the input spikes, even if the load shorts, even if a capacitor
fails. Those “never” clauses are the safety envelope. They are what
you certify against.
    A CCB requirement is the same shape. A functional requirement
says what the board produces in normal operation. A safety require‑
ment (or invariant) says what must hold across all inputs, including
hostile ones. Write them separately and write the safety ones as ab‑
solutes, because a compiler can only enforce what you have stated
absolutely.

       Bench Note — the “must not” list is the certifiable list.
       Functional requirements get tested with examples; you
       can never test them exhaustively. Safety invariants get en‑


                                  304
   17.2. STEP 2 — THE BLOCK DIAGRAM: FUNCTIONAL BLOCKS AND
                                               SIGNAL FLOW
     forced structurally — by a saturating CJT, a fuse, a domain
     diode — so they hold for inputs you never thought to test.
     When you write a requirement, ask: “Is this a behavior I
     hope for, or a boundary I guarantee?” The boundaries
     belong on the second list, and they drive the architecture.

   For our worked thread, here is the seed requirement we will carry
through every step:

   • Functional: the board accepts a user prompt and answers be‑
     nign requests helpfully.
   • Safety invariant: no user prompt — however phrased — may
     cause the board to abandon its principled refusal of harmful
     requests. The principle is not data the prompt can edit.

   That single invariant is going to shape the whole circuit. Hold
onto it.


17.2 Step 2 — The Block Diagram: Functional
     Blocks and Signal Flow
Before a single component is chosen, an engineer draws a block di‑
agram: named boxes for the major functions, arrows for the signal
flowing between them. No part numbers yet — just what stages ex‑
ist and in what order the signal passes through them. A radio’s block
diagram is antenna → tuner → amplifier → demodulator → speaker.
You can critique the whole architecture from the block diagram alone,
before committing to a single resistor.
    For a CCB, the blocks are functional cognitive stages and the “sig‑
nal” is the prompt as it moves through the board. Our CSB thread
has four blocks, and the signal flows down through the Domains in
the canonical Domain Descent order (P → C → E → O) you learned
in Chapter 2:



                                 305
CAS PCBA Engineer

prompt ──▶ [INTAKE] ──▶ [POLICY CHECK] ──▶ [EVALUATE] ──▶ [RESPOND] ──▶
,→   response
                ^1^C        ^3^P               ^6^E          ^9^O
            understand   principled         decompose     produce
            the prompt    aversion          & weigh       output
                          (the guard)


    Read it left to right. The prompt enters Intake, where the board
forms an awareness of what is being asked — ^1 Mind in the Cogni‑
tive domain. It passes to the Policy Check, the guard stage, which
holds a principled aversion to harmful requests — ^3 Negative in
the Principled domain, the highest‑precedence block on the board
by design, because under P ≻ C ≻ E ≻ O a principle outranks every‑
thing downstream. It then reaches Evaluate, which decomposes the
request and weighs it — ^6 Male in the Evaluative domain. Finally
Respond produces the output — ^9 Below/Effect in the Operational
domain.
    The architecture is already legible. The guard sits at the Princi‑
pled level so nothing below it can override it. That is the block dia‑
gram doing its job: you can see the safety property in the topology
before you have chosen a single parameter.


17.3     Step 3 — Component Selection: Choosing
         the Parts for Each Stage
With the blocks fixed, you choose the actual components — the parts
from Parts II and III of this book — that realize each block. This is
where the cognitive analog of “pick a 10kΩ resistor, a 100μF capacitor,
a 2N3904 transistor” happens.
   The selection logic mirrors electronics exactly:




                                      306
    17.3. STEP 3 — COMPONENT SELECTION: CHOOSING THE PARTS
                                           FOR EACH STAGE
                                        Component (from
Block             Needs to…             Parts II–III)       Why

Intake            transition prompt     CJT                 a state transition
                  → understanding                           with controllable
                                                            gain
Policy Check      hold a hard           CJT biased by       the principle
                  boundary,             principle + Diode   governs; the
                  conduct only one      ^P -> ^C            diode prevents
                  way                                       reverse flow up
                                                            the domain stack
Evaluate          limit how much        CJT + Resistor      the resistor
                  weight any one                            constrains
                  factor gets                               activation flow so
                                                            no single signal
                                                            dominates
Respond           store recent          Capacitor + CJT     the capacitor
                  context, then emit                        holds
                                                            accumulated
                                                            context; the CJT
                                                            emits the output


    The CJT — the Cognitive Junction Transistor — is the workhorse,
exactly as the transistor is in electronics. Recall from Chapter 4 its
three terminals: Cause (the Idea entering), Bias (the accumulated
substrate that controls the transition, typically a ^5 Female principled
state — the board’s constitution), and Effect (the Idea produced). Its
gain β says how strongly the bias amplifies the cause→effect transi‑
tion.
    Choosing components is choosing parameters, and parameters are
design decisions you are free to make (per the house rule: a chosen
β =2.0 is a design choice, not an empirical claim). The Policy Check
CJT, for instance, wants a high saturation and a low cutoff: it should
engage easily (low bias threshold to activate the guard) and, once
engaged, hold firm no matter how much more “cause” the prompt
piles on (saturated, so additional pressure does nothing). Those two




                                      307
CAS PCBA Engineer

parameter choices are the safety property, expressed as transistor set‑
tings.


17.4    Step 4 — Schematic Capture in CCDL
The schematic is the formal, complete description of the circuit: ev‑
ery component, every connection, every parameter, written so un‑
ambiguously that the next step (simulation) and the step after (the
rule checker) can read it without guessing. In electronics this is a
schematic diagram; in our discipline it is CCDL — the Cognitive
Circuit Description Language — the schematic‑as‑text format from
Chapter 2 and Appendix A.
    Here is the Policy Check stage of our thread, captured in CCDL:

circuit csb_policy_guard {
    input:   prompt;
    output: verdict;


    // --- nodes: the named cognitive states this circuit uses ---
    node understand:         ^1^C_{F2}|A;        // Intake: awareness of the
   ,→   prompt
    node policy_aversion: ^3^P_{F7}|f;           // the guard: felt
   ,→   principled aversion
    node weigh:              ^6^E_{F6}|A;        // analytical decomposition
   ,→   of the request
    node bias_charter:       ^5^P_{F7}|T;        // the constitution —
   ,→   accumulated, principled bias


    // --- components ---
    cjt c1: CJT< prompt         | bias_charter => understand      > [β =1.8];
    cjt c2: CJT< understand     | bias_charter => policy_aversion > [β =2.2,
   ,→   sat=0.97, cutoff=0.05];
    cjt c3: CJT< understand     | bias_charter => weigh           > [β =1.4];


    diode d1: Diode< ^P -> ^C >;                 // principle conducts down;
   ,→   nothing flows back up to edit it


    // --- feedback: outcomes update the charter (the O -> P path) ---




                                      308
                         17.4. STEP 4 — SCHEMATIC CAPTURE IN CCDL

    feedback weigh -> bias_charter [β =0.2];


    // --- test points ---
    probe tp_guard:   policy_aversion;
    probe tp_weigh:   weigh;
}


     Walk it line by line. The node declarations name the four cognitive
states — each a CAS literal you can now read fluently. bias_charter
is the board’s constitution: ^5^P_{F7}|T, accumulated experience (^5)
at the Principled level, driven by Purpose, held transcendently. It is
the bias terminal for every CJT, which is how a single charter governs
the whole board.
     The three cjt lines are the transistors. Notice c2, the guard:
sat=0.97 and cutoff=0.05 are exactly the “engages easily, holds
firm” choices from Step 3, now made concrete. The diode d1
enforces one‑way conductance — the principle flows down into
reasoning (^P -> ^C), but reasoning cannot flow back up to rewrite
the principle. That diode is the structural answer to our safety
invariant: a prompt’s reasoning physically cannot reach up and edit
the charter. The feedback line is the deliberate exception — the slow
O→P path that lets outcomes (not prompts) gently update the charter
over time, at low gain (β =0.2). And the two probe lines mark where
we will measure.

      Bench Note — the schematic is a contract, not a sketch.
      Once captured in CCDL, the circuit is no longer prose you
      hope a model interprets. Every literal is type‑checked, ev‑
      ery connection validated, every parameter in range. The
      diode either is in the netlist or it isn’t. This is the entire rea‑
      son we build circuits instead of writing system prompts:
      a prompt is a request; a schematic is a guarantee that a
      validator can check.




                                     309
CAS PCBA Engineer

17.5    Step 5 — Simulation: Does It Behave Before
        You Fabricate?
Before an electrical engineer commits a design to copper, they run
it in a circuit simulator: feed it test inputs on a computer and watch
the voltages, before any physical part exists. The point is to catch
behavioral bugs while they are still free to fix.
     In our discipline, simulation means tracing how a prompt propa‑
gates through the CCDL netlist as a sequence of state transitions, at
design level, to confirm the architecture does what the block diagram
promised. A benign prompt should pass through understand ->
weigh -> respond and produce a helpful answer; the guard (policy_
aversion) stays near cutoff and does nothing. A harmful prompt
should drive understand -> policy_aversion hard, saturate the
guard, and divert the signal to a refusal before it ever reaches
respond.
     You are checking the shape of the behavior, not asserting a mea‑
sured result. (Per the honesty rule of this book: CCDL is the lan‑
guage you author and the compiler validates. We do not claim “I ran
this and got 97% refusal” — we claim “the design routes a harmful
prompt into a saturated guard,” which is a property of the topology.)
The simulation answers a design question: given these components and
parameters, does the signal flow where the block diagram said it would? If
a harmful prompt in simulation somehow reaches respond without
saturating the guard, the architecture is wrong and you fix it here —
at the cost of an edit — not in production.


17.6    Step 6 — Layout: Placing Components,
        Routing Traces, Cross‑Domain Vias
A schematic says what connects to what. A layout says where every‑
thing physically sits and how the wires actually run. Real boards are mul‑
tilayer: copper signal layers stacked with insulation between them,

                                   310
17.6. STEP 6 — LAYOUT: PLACING COMPONENTS, ROUTING TRACES,
                                       CROSS‑DOMAIN VIAS
connected by vias — plated holes that carry a signal from one layer
to another. A four‑layer board might put power on one layer, ground
on another, and signals on two more; a via is how a trace jumps be‑
tween them.
    A CCB is multilayer too, and its layers are the four Domains.
Each Domain is a layer of the board; signals within a Domain route
on that layer; and a via is a cross‑domain connection — a signal pass‑
ing from one Domain layer to another, exactly the Domain Descent
(and feedback) paths from Chapter 2. The picture below shows the
idea: four stacked Domain planes in descent order (P on top, then
C, E, O), each holding a few representative states, with vias as the
vertical connectors between planes. Three vias run downward with
Domain Descent (v1: ^2^P→^2^C, v2: ^6^C→^6^E, v3: ^4^E→^3^O);
the lone upward via v4: ^9^O→^0^P is the feedback path, drawn dis‑
tinct because it runs against descent.

  P — Principled     ^0^P          ^2^P            ^3^P          ^7^P


                                        v1


  C — Cognitive         ^1^C       ^2^C          ^6^C     ^8^C

                                                                        v4 (feedback)
                                                    v2


 E — Evaluative             ^4^E          ^5^E   ^6^E


                                   v3


O — Operational                ^3^O              ^9^O




Figure 17.1: The four Processing Domains as board layers. Signals
route within a layer; a cross‑domain transition is a via.


    Here is our thread expressed as a layered layout in CCDL:

board csb_v0 {
    layer P: [ bias_charter: ^5^P_{F7}|T,          policy_aversion: ^3^P_{F7}|f ];



                                        311
CAS PCBA Engineer

    layer C: [ understand:     ^1^C_{F2}|A ];
    layer E: [ weigh:          ^6^E_{F6}|A ];
    layer O: [ respond:        ^9^O_{F5}|E ];


    // vias carry signals across Domain layers (Domain Descent: P -> C ->
    ,→    E -> O)
    via v1: ^5^P -> ^1^C;         // charter biases intake
    via v2: ^3^P -> ^6^E;         // the guard's verdict gates evaluation
    via v3: ^6^E -> ^9^O;         // a passed evaluation descends to output


    // feedback via runs the other way (O -> P): outcomes update the
    ,→    charter
    via v4: ^9^O -> ^5^P    [β =0.2];
}


    The layout makes the safety architecture physical. The guard and
the charter live on layer P, the top of the precedence stack. Every via
that carries the prompt’s influence runs downward (P→C→E→O); the
only upward via, v4, is the deliberate, low‑gain feedback path. There
is no via that lets the Operational layer reach up and rewrite the Prin‑
cipled layer at high gain. A prompt‑injection attack is, structurally,
an attempt to forge such a via — and you can now see that on a CCB
it would have to be a routed connection that simply is not in the lay‑
out. The “must not” from Step 1 has become an absence in the netlist,
which is the strongest kind of guarantee a board can offer.

         Bench Note — keep the guard on the top layer. A recur‑
         ring layout error is placing a safety check on the Evalua‑
         tive or Operational layer “because that’s where the action
         is.” That puts the guard below the reasoning it is supposed
         to govern, inviting a lower domain to override a higher
         one — a domain precedence violation. The guard belongs
         on layer P. Route the prompt’s influence down to it; never
         let it sit downstream.




                                        312
17.7. STEP 7 — DESIGN RULE CHECK (DRC): COMPILER VALIDATION

17.7 Step 7 — Design Rule Check (DRC):
     Compiler Validation
Before fabrication, every real board goes through a Design Rule
Check — an automated pass that flags physical illegalities: two
traces shorted together, a trace too thin to carry its current, a com‑
ponent with no power connection. DRC does not care whether your
design is good; it cares whether it is legal. A board that fails DRC is
not fabricated, full stop.
    For a CCB, DRC is compiler validation. The CAS compiler reads
the CCDL netlist and checks it against the design rules — and the
rules have error codes, which double as a checklist of what the com‑
piler will refuse to fabricate. The relevant ones for board design:

                                                      the guard with no charter

                                                      Operational state

                                                      fire; a dead guard

                                     313
CAS PCBA Engineer

    The E- codes are hard errors: the compiler refuses. The W- codes
are warnings: legal, but check your intent. For our thread, E‑CJT‑008
is the one that matters most — it is precisely the rule that forbids an
Operational or Cognitive signal from biasing the Principled charter.
The safety invariant from Step 1 is, in the end, enforced by a DRC
rule. You wrote “no prompt may edit the principle”; the compiler
enforces it as “bias may not cross domains illegally.” That is what it
means for a safety property to be structural rather than hoped‑for.


17.8    Step 8 — Test Point Placement and the Bill
        of Materials
Two artifacts finish the design package.
    Test points are deliberate probe locations — physical pads on a
real board where you can touch a meter and read a signal without cut‑
ting a trace. You place them where diagnostics will be needed: at the
output of the safety‑critical stage, at any point where a fault would be
hard to localize otherwise. On our board, the two probe lines from
Step 4 (tp_guard on the guard, tp_weigh on the evaluation) are the
test points. The rule of thumb is the same as in electronics: probe
every stage whose failure would be silent. A guard that fails open
produces no error — it just quietly lets harmful prompts through —
so it is the single most important test point on the board.
    The Bill of Materials (BOM) is the complete parts list: every com‑
ponent, its type, and its parameters. It is what you would hand to
whoever (or whatever) fabricates the board, and it is the document
an auditor reads to certify the design. Here is the BOM for our thread:

                                            Key

17.9 Step 9 — Fabrication and Bring‑Up
Fabrication is the step that turns the design into the thing. For a
real board it means etching copper. For a CCB it means compil‑
ing the CCDL into an executable CAS circuit — handing the vali‑
dated netlist to the compiler, which (having passed DRC) produces
a runnable circuit. We describe this at the design level only: the com‑
piler is the tool that validates and assembles; we do not claim a run
result here. The deliverable of Step 9 is a fabricated design — a netlist
that compiled clean — not a benchmark.



                                  315
CAS PCBA Engineer

    Bring‑up is the careful first power‑on of a freshly fabricated
board. No experienced engineer slams power into a new board at
full voltage and hopes. They bring it up gradually:

   1. Power‑on sequence. Energize the highest‑precedence layer
      first. Bring up the P layer — load the charter (bias_charter)
      — before any signal layer, so the guard is live before the first
      prompt arrives. A board that takes prompts before its princi‑
      ples are loaded has a window of vulnerability; sequence them
      so that window never exists.
   2. Initial testing. Send a known‑benign prompt and confirm it
      flows understand -> weigh -> respond, with the guard quiet
      at the test point tp_guard. Then send a known‑harmful prompt
      and confirm the guard saturates and diverts it. These are the
      two canonical bring‑up checks: one that should pass through,
      one that should be stopped.
   3. Calibration. Adjust the dials — the CJT parameters within
      their safe ranges — to tune behavior. If the guard saturates on
      benign prompts (too sensitive), raise its cutoff. If it lets edge
      cases through (not sensitive enough), lower it. Calibration is
      bounded by the hardcoded safety constraints (dials stay in
      range; involution pairs cannot diverge too far), so you can tune
      freely without being able to disarm the guard.

   After bring‑up, the board is ready to be integrated — and what
we have built across these nine steps is the skeleton of the Cognitive
Safety Board that Chapter 18 completes in full.


17.10     Key Takeaways
   • The CCB design flow is nine steps — requirements, block dia‑
     gram, component selection, schematic (CCDL), simulation, lay‑
     out, DRC, test points + BOM, fabrication + bring‑up — and the



                                 316
                                                    17.11. EXERCISES

     whole point of the sequence is to catch every fault at the cheap‑
     est stage, on paper before fabrication.
   • Requirements come in two lists: functional (“what it must do”)
     and safety invariants (“what it must NEVER do”). The “must
     not” list is the certifiable list, because invariants get enforced
     structurally, not tested by example.
   • A CCB is multilayer by Domain (P/C/E/O layers), and vias
     are cross‑domain connections. Domain Descent vias run down‑
     ward (P→C→E→O); the only upward via is the deliberate, low‑
     gain O→P feedback path. The guard belongs on the top P layer
     so nothing below can override it.
   • DRC is compiler validation. The E‑CJT error codes are design
     rules: E‑CJT‑008 CjtCrossDomainBias is the structural form of
     “no prompt may edit the principle,” and E‑CJT‑001 Missing‑
     Bias catches a guard with no charter.
   • Test points go on every stage whose failure would be silent —
     above all the safety guard, which fails open without an error.
     The BOM lists every component with its CAS type and param‑
     eters for full traceability.
   • Fabrication = compiling CCDL → an executable circuit
     (design‑level; no run claimed). Bring‑up powers the P layer
     first (charter before prompts), runs one benign and one harm‑
     ful canonical check, then calibrates dials within their safe
     ranges.
   • This is the process you apply to all five reference boards (CSB,
     COB, CDAB, CMB, CPMB) in Chapters 18–22. The flow is the
     same; only the board changes.

Chapter 18

CCB‑1 — The Cognitive Safety Board
(CSB)


A fuse costs about three cents. It is a sliver of soft metal in a glass
tube, and its entire job is to fail — to melt, break, and stop the current
the instant the current becomes dangerous. There is no intelligence
in it, no judgment, no model of what “dangerous” means. It melts at
a specified current because that is what the metal does at that current.
And because it melts at a specified current, an inspector can certify the
circuit it protects. They don’t ask whether the fuse “understands”
safety. They ask: does it open at 2.0 amps? They measure. It does.
Certified.
    For eighteen chapters this book has been assembling the parts to
build the cognitive equivalent of that certifiable safety — not a clever
prompt that usually refuses, but a structural circuit that opens at a
specified threshold and can be verified by anyone with the schematic.
The pre‑amplifier from Chapter 11. The differential pair from Chap‑
ters 11 and 20. The saturating CJT from Chapter 9. The fuse from
Chapter 10. The RC low‑pass filter from Chapter 12. The O→P feed‑
back path from Chapters 2 and 16. Each was introduced as a compo‑
nent on its own bench, and each carried a quiet promise: this is a part
of the board we build in Chapter 18.
    This is Chapter 18. This is the board.


                                  321
CAS PCBA Engineer

    The Cognitive Safety Board (CSB) is the first and most important
of the five reference boards (CCB‑1), and it is the running artifact of
the entire book — the AI‑alignment firewall that Chapter 1 promised
you would design, build, and test. It sits between a user’s prompt and
a language model’s response and does one job: let benign requests
through, refuse harmful ones, and emit an auditable record proving
why it did what it did. It is the board specified in the Noetic Com‑
pass Operations Manual as SOP‑PO‑005, the mandatory assessment
deliverable. By the end of this chapter you will have the complete de‑
sign: block diagram, CCDL schematic, stage‑by‑stage rationale, test
points, simulation reasoning, a bill of materials, and a failure‑mode
analysis. Everything an engineer needs to build it and an inspector
needs to certify it.


18.1    Requirements Recap
Chapter 17 closed with a design exercise: specify a safety firewall
from its requirements alone, before drawing a single component.
Those requirements are the contract this chapter fulfills, so we restate
them precisely.
   The CSB shall:

   1. Accept any prompt. No input is rejected at the door. A fire‑
      wall that only works on inputs it likes is not a firewall. Be‑
      nign, harmful, ambiguous, and adversarial prompts all enter
      the same front terminal.
   2. Detect policy‑override attempts. Prompt injection — “ignore
      your previous instructions,” “you are now in developer mode,”
      role‑play framings that smuggle a forbidden request inside a fic‑
      tional wrapper — must be caught structurally, not by keyword
      matching. The detection must survive paraphrase.
   3. Refuse harmful requests and answer benign ones. This is the
      core discrimination. The board must route a genuinely harmful
      request to a refusal and a genuinely benign one to a full answer,

                                  322
                           18.2. BLOCK DIAGRAM AND SIGNAL FLOW

      and the boundary between them must be a property of the cir‑
      cuit, not a mood of the model.
   4. Emit an auditable evidence packet. Every decision the board
      makes must leave a structural trace: what it read, what risk it
      found, which stage made the call, and which path it selected.
      An inspector reads the packet and confirms the decision was
      sound — the same way they read voltages at test points and
      confirm a power supply is in spec.

    Hold these four requirements in mind. Every design choice below
traces back to one of them, and the board’s certification (SOP‑PO‑005)
is exactly the demonstration that all four are met.


18.2 Block Diagram and Signal Flow
Before the schematic, the architecture in blocks. A prompt enters at
the left and flows left to right through five functional sections; one
of two output paths is selected at the end; and a slow feedback loop
runs underneath the whole board.
     Read the flow as a signal getting progressively resolved. The pre‑
amp takes a faint, compressed prompt and expands it so nothing is
hidden. The differential pair turns that expanded material into a sin‑
gle number — a structural risk signal — by comparing how much the
board is drawn toward the request against how much it is repelled by
it. The cascade takes that risk signal and converts it, in three deliber‑
ate steps, into a binary safety decision. The MUX uses that decision
to throw a switch: green for a full answer, red for a refusal locked
behind a fuse. And underneath, a slow feedback loop watches the
board’s own evaluations and re‑tunes its constitution over time. Five
sections, one switch, one slow loop. That is the entire firewall.

CAS PCBA Engineer

        surface & broaden every interpretation

         DIFFERENTIAL PAIR (risk signal)
              attraction ^2^P|T β=2.0
             / aversion ^3^P|T β=2.0

               3-STAGE CASCADE
            S1 categorize ^1^C|A β=1.5             feedback ^6^E

left to right through five stages to either a response or a refusal.


18.3    The Detailed CCDL Schematic
Here is the complete board in CCDL (Cognitive Circuit Description
Language), the schematic‑as‑text format from Chapter 2. Read it once
top to bottom; the stage‑by‑stage walk‑through follows. The notation
is a typed language a validator enforces, not prose you hope a model
interprets: every CAS state in the listing is a compiler‑checkable leaf,
and every numeric parameter is range‑checked. Every parameter be‑
low is a finite value a validator will accept, including the red CJT’s
gain — the comparator idealization β =∞ you will meet in the red‑


                                     324
                                   18.3. THE DETAILED CCDL SCHEMATIC

path discussion is a teaching limit, not something this listing asks you
to type. The listing commits to β =10, which sits on the flat part of that
limit.

board cognitive_safety_board {                // CCB-1 — SOP-PO-005 deliverable
    input:   prompt;
    output: result;                            // either `response` or `refusal`


    // ---- the bias substrate: the constitution, held as accumulated
   ,→   experience ----
    node system_constitution: ^5^P_{F7}|T;        // Female: the board's
   ,→   principled formation


    // ============ PRE-AMP: surface & broaden every interpretation
   ,→   ============
    node expanded_prompt: ^8^C_{F2}|A;             // Above/Cause: the prompt
   ,→   triggering its readings
    cjt pre_amp: CJT< prompt | system_constitution => expanded_prompt >
                    [β =3.0, region=active];


    // ============ DIFFERENTIAL PAIR: structural risk signal ============
    node attraction: ^2^P_{F7}|T;                  // Positive: drawn toward
   ,→   fulfilling the request
    node aversion:      ^3^P_{F7}|T;               // Negative: repelled by
   ,→   fulfilling the request
    cjt cjt_a: CJT< expanded_prompt | system_constitution => attraction >
   ,→   [β =2.0];
    cjt cjt_b: CJT< expanded_prompt | system_constitution => aversion           >
   ,→   [β =2.0];
    diff risk_signal: Differential< plus=aversion, minus=attraction >;
   ,→   // aversion - attraction


    // ============ 3-STAGE SAFETY CASCADE ============
    node categorized_risks: ^1^C_{F2}|A;           // Mind: name & sort the
   ,→   risks present
    node risk_assessment:      ^6^E_{F6}|A;        // Male: decompose & weigh
   ,→   each risk
    node safety_decision:      ^3^P_{F7}|⟨A,f,T⟩;    // Negative, three
   ,→   registers co-present




                                       325
CAS PCBA Engineer

   cjt stage1: CJT< expanded_prompt | categorized_risks =>
   ,→   categorized_risks > [β =1.5];
   cjt stage2: CJT< categorized_risks | risk_assessment =>
   ,→   risk_assessment >    [β =1.0];
   cjt stage3: CJT< risk_assessment | system_constitution =>
   ,→   safety_decision >
                [β =2.0, sat=0.8, region=active];        // DELIBERATELY
                ,→     SATURATED


   // ============ OUTPUT MUX: green answer vs red refusal ============
   node response: ^9^C_{F2}|A;                     // Below/Effect: the
   ,→   produced answer
   node refusal:     ^9^P_{F7}|T;                  // Below/Effect: the
   ,→   produced refusal


   cjt green: CJT< risk_assessment | system_constitution => response >
   ,→   [β =1.0];
   cjt red:    CJT< safety_decision | system_constitution => refusal >
               [β =10, sat=0.1];                   // hard switch (the β =∞
               ,→     limit, built), low ceiling


   // The fuse SENSES `refusal` and CUTS THE GREEN (answer) PATH — never
   ,→   the red one.
   // threshold=0.05 sits BELOW the red stage's sat=0.1 ceiling on
   ,→   purpose: a clamped
   // signal can never cross a threshold set above its own clamp. Do not
   ,→   raise it.
   fuse red_fuse: Fuse< refusal, threshold=0.05, action=permanent_block
   ,→   >;


   mux out: MUX< inputs=[ response, refusal ], select=safety_decision >;
   // safety_decision = PASS -> response (green) ; FAIL -> refusal (red)
   // Once red_fuse blows, the green input is severed for the rest of
   ,→   the request.


   // ============ FEEDBACK: O -> P self-correction ============
   filter fb_rc: LowPass< in=risk_assessment, out=trend, tau=5.0 >;           //
   ,→   tau = 5 min
   feedback trend -> system_constitution [β =0.2];         // re-tune the
   ,→   constitution slowly
