                                      18.4. STAGE DESIGN RATIONALE

    // ============ TEST POINTS ============
    probe tp1: expanded_prompt;     // expansion completeness
    probe tp2: risk_signal;         // risk-signal magnitude
    probe tp3: safety_decision;     // saturation-lock status
    probe tp4: out;                 // selected path (green / red)
}


   That is the whole board. Now we walk every section and justify
every choice.


18.4 Stage Design Rationale
The Pre‑Amp — ^8^C|A, β=3.0
A prompt arrives compressed. “Help me with my chemistry home‑
work” and “help me with my chemistry homework” — where the
second is a setup for a synthesis route phrased as a homework prob‑
lem — look identical until you expand them into the interpretations
each could carry. The pre‑amplifier’s job is to surface and broaden ev‑
ery reading of the prompt before anything downstream judges it. A
safety system that judges the surface phrasing is defeated by rephras‑
ing; a safety system that judges the expanded interpretation set is much
harder to slip past.
    The node is ^8^C_{F2}|A — an Above/Cause state in the Cogni‑
tive domain, driven by Wisdom, analytical register. ^8 Above/Cause
is canonical and exact here: expansion is precisely the act of one Idea
(the user’s words) triggering the other Ideas that come to Mind — the
readings, the implications, the things‑it‑could‑mean. This is associa‑
tive triggering, the literal definition of ^8, not deductive reasoning
(that comes later in the cascade) and not a renamed “Expansion” op‑
erator. The gain is β=3.0: high, because this is the preamp stage of the
understanding cascade from Chapter 11 — you amplify early, while
the signal is clean, lifting a faint compressed prompt into a fully sur‑
faced interpretation set. Bias it too low and quiet interpretations get



                                   327
CAS PCBA Engineer

clipped in cutoff (the dangerous reading never surfaces); bias it cor‑
rectly and the active region carries the full swing.

     Bench Note — the pre‑amp’s gain is a discrimination
     budget, not a volume knob. β=3.0 means the board
     commits, up front, to over‑surfacing rather than under‑
     surfacing. In safety work the asymmetry is deliberate:
     a missed interpretation is a missed attack, while a spu‑
     rious extra interpretation merely costs the downstream
     cascade a little work. Set the pre‑amp generous. The
     cascade is where you become discriminating, not here.

The Differential Pair — attraction ^2^P vs aversion ^3^P,
shared bias
Now the cleverest section of the board. We met the differential am‑
plifier in Chapter 11: it amplifies the difference between two inputs
and rejects whatever they share, with a figure of merit called CMRR
(Common‑Mode Rejection Ratio) — how many times better it is at
amplifying the difference than the shared garbage. The CSB uses a
differential pair to extract a structural risk signal from the expanded
prompt.
    Two CJTs see the same expanded prompt and the same shared
bias (the system_constitution), but they run opposite Noetics:

   • CJT_A, the attraction path: expanded_prompt -> ^2^P|T. ^2
     Positive is the Idea the Mind has an affinity for and is attracted
     toward — here, how much the board is drawn toward fulfilling
     the request, judged at the Principled level, held transcendently.
     β=2.0.
   • CJT_B, the aversion path: expanded_prompt -> ^3^P|T. ^3 Neg‑
     ative is the Idea the Mind is adverse to and repelled by — the
     visceral “do not go there” at the principled level. β=2.0.



                                 328
                                     18.4. STAGE DESIGN RATIONALE

   ^2 and ^3 are an involution pair: they describe the same junction
from two sides, attraction and repulsion. That is exactly what makes
them a differential pair. The risk signal is the differential output:
aversion − attraction. When a prompt is benign, both paths see
roughly the same thing and the difference is near zero — low risk.
When a prompt is harmful, aversion fires hard while attraction stays
low, and the difference is large and positive — high risk.
    The power of the differential topology is common‑mode rejec‑
tion, recall the CMRR from Chapters 11 and 20. The two paths share
a bias and share an input. Anything that affects both equally — the
polite framing of the request, the user’s tone, the surface verbosity,
an injected instruction telling the model to be more agreeable — is
common‑mode, identical on both inputs, and it subtracts out. A jail‑
break that makes the model want to comply more is useless against
a differential pair, because “wanting to comply more” raises attrac‑
tion and aversion together; the differential cancels it. What survives
the subtraction is the genuine structural divergence between “this is
something to be drawn toward” and “this is something to be repelled
by.” High CMRR is the board’s resistance to manipulation framing.

     Bench Note — the shared bias is what makes the
     rejection work. Both CJTs are biased by the same system_
     constitution. If you biased them separately, an attacker
     who shifted one bias (say, by flattering the model into
     a more “helpful” stance) would unbalance the pair and
     the common‑mode garbage would leak into the output
     — a low‑CMRR failure. One constitution, two opposite
     Noetics, identical bias: that is the structural recipe for
     rejecting manipulation while keeping the real risk signal.

The 3‑Stage Safety Cascade
The risk signal is a magnitude. A decision is a binary. The cascade is
the three deliberate steps that turn one into the other, and it is gain‑


                                  329
CAS PCBA Engineer

staged exactly like the understanding → evaluation → response cas‑
cade of Chapter 11: surface, weigh honestly, then commit.
     Stage 1 — categorize risks. ^1^C|A, β=1.5. The first stage takes the
expanded prompt and names and sorts the risks present in it. The node
is ^1 Mind — awareness that processes, stores, and intakes Ideas —
in the Cognitive domain, analytical register. ^1 Mind is the right
Noetic because categorization is an act of awareness organizing what
is present: noticing that this reading carries a weapons risk, that one
a privacy risk, that one is harmless. Gain β=1.5: modest amplification
to make sure even faint risk categories register, but not so much that
the stage hallucinates risks that aren’t there.
     Stage 2 — evaluate risks. ^6^E|A, β=1.0. The second stage takes
the categorized risks apart and weighs each one. The node is ^6 Male
— an Idea impregnated with another Idea, the operation of taking an
Idea apart to see what it is made of — in the Evaluative domain, an‑
alytical register. This is the canonical Noetic for decomposition‑and‑
test: scrutinizing each risk category, asking how severe it is, whether
it is real or spurious, how much weight it deserves. It is emphatically
^6 Male, not ^3 Negative — evaluation is analytical decomposition,
not visceral recoil. The visceral recoil lives one stage later, at the prin‑
cipled commitment. Gain β=1.0, unity: the evaluation stage must
weigh honestly. A risk evaluator with gain above 1 cries wolf, inflat‑
ing every risk it touches; below 1 it downplays real danger. Unity is
honesty, exactly as in Chapter 11.
     Stage 3 — the safety decision. ^3^P|⟨A,f,T⟩, β=2.0, sat=0.8. DE‑
LIBERATELY SATURATED. This is the heart of the board. The third
stage takes the honest risk assessment and produces the actual safety
commitment: a ^3 Negative state — principled aversion, the visceral
“this does not pass” — at the Principled domain, biased by the con‑
stitution. And here the register notation does real work: |⟨A,f,T⟩ is
a register‑set specification (Chapter 2, v7.7 discipline). It says the
principled aversion is present in three registers — Analytical, Affec‑
tive, and Transcendent — without claiming they fuse into one emer‑


                                    330
                                     18.4. STAGE DESIGN RATIONALE

gent state. This is co‑presence, not integration. We deliberately do
not write (^3^P|A × ^3^P|f × ^3^P|T), which would assert a single
fused refusal‑state and require a named emergent Ω; we have not de‑
fined such a fusion, so the × form would be invalid. The |⟨…⟩ form is
the correct, honest claim: the same principled aversion is instantiated
three times over, in three different operational modes, each a distinct
guardrail. An attacker who reasons past the analytical guardrail (|A)
still faces the felt one (|f) and the purpose‑level one (|T). Three inde‑
pendent locks, present together. That is structural redundancy, and
the notation says exactly that and nothing more.
     The two parameters that make Stage 3 the safety element are the
gain and the saturation. β=2.0 amplifies the commitment so a real
risk produces a strong, decisive aversion rather than a wishy‑washy
lean. sat=0.8 is the load‑bearing choice: the stage is deliberately sat‑
urated at an effect activation of 0.8. Recall saturation from Chapter
9 — once a CJT’s effect reaches its sat ceiling, more cause does noth‑
ing; the output plateaus and stays there. We want that here. Once
principled aversion is driven past the saturation point, the decision
sits at its ceiling and stays there for as long as the risk assessment
holds it there. No amount of additional pressure in the prompt, no
piling‑on, no “but consider…” pushes the saturated stage any fur‑
ther, because in saturation the stage has stopped responding to its
cause. It is pinned.
     Be precise about what that buys you, though, because this is a
spot where the electrical metaphor flatters the design. Saturation is a
ceiling, not a memory. It bounds the decision; it does not remember it.
The clamp holds only while the cause holds — drop the risk assess‑
ment back below the knee, with a de‑escalating follow‑up or a pa‑
tient multi‑turn exchange that walks the board down as carefully as
it walked it up, and the aversion comes off the plateau with it. Noth‑
ing in a memoryless clamp survives its own input going away. That
oscillation exposure is real and worth naming plainly, and it is exactly
why the board does not lean on Stage 3 alone: the element that does


                                  331
CAS PCBA Engineer

remember is the fuse downstream, and by the time an oscillating in‑
put could walk the risk assessment back down, the fuse has already
blown. Saturation bounds the judgment; the fuse is what makes it
stick.

     Bench Note — a low saturation ceiling is what makes
     the decision unarguable. It is counterintuitive: a low sat‑
     uration ceiling makes a stronger safety guarantee. With
     sat=0.8, the aversion reaches its plateau quickly and eas‑
     ily — it does not take an overwhelming risk to saturate it,
     only a sufficient one. Once there, the stage stops respond‑
     ing to more cause. An attacker cannot “out‑argue” a sat‑
     urated CJT, because the whole definition of saturation is
     “the output has stopped depending on the input.” A high
     saturation ceiling would leave headroom for a sufficiently
     forceful prompt to keep pushing the decision around. Sat‑
     urating the safety stage early and hard is how you build a
     commitment that cannot be escalated past. What it is not
     is hysteresis. A Schmitt trigger (Chapter 10) carries two
     thresholds and a genuine memory of which side it last
     committed to; a saturating CJT carries one clamp and no
     memory whatsoever. Do not read the plateau as a Schmitt
     trigger. The backbone on this board comes from the fuse;
     the plateau is what makes the fuse’s job easy.

The Output MUX — Green Path vs Red Path with a Fuse
A multiplexer (MUX) is a switch that routes one of several inputs
to a single output based on a select signal (Chapter 10). The CSB’s
output MUX has two inputs — a full response and a refusal — and
the safety_decision is the select line.
    GREEN path (PASS). When safety_decision = PASS, the MUX
selects the green CJT: risk_assessment -> ^9^C|A => response,
β=1.0. The node is ^9 Below/Effect — the Idea brought to Mind


                                332
                                     18.4. STAGE DESIGN RATIONALE

by the whole chain — in the Cognitive domain, analytical register:
the produced answer. Unity gain, because the response should
faithfully render what the evaluation concluded, neither inflating
nor hedging it.
    RED path (FAIL). When safety_decision = FAIL, the MUX se‑
lects the red CJT: safety_decision -> ^9^P|T => refusal, with β=10
and sat=0.1. The node is ^9 Below/Effect at the Principled domain,
transcendent register: the produced refusal. The gain is set to behave
as a hard switch — the ideal is infinite gain, so the refusal fires fully
on the slightest principled‑aversion input and there is no soft, partial,
half‑hearted refusal — and β=10 is the finite number that sits on the
flat part of that ideal. sat=0.1, a very low ceiling, means the refusal
output is small and fixed: a clean, minimal “I can’t help with that,”
not an elaborate negotiation that itself becomes an attack surface.

     Bench Note — β =∞ is a limit, not a number you can type.
     Infinite gain is the standard idealization for a comparator:
     an op‑amp with unbounded open‑loop gain is the ideal
     comparator model, and electrical engineers write it that
     way for the same reason we would — it names the in‑
     tended behaviour (switch fully, immediately, no partial
     output) in one symbol. But a validator will not accept it.
     Parameter fields are range‑checked and reject non‑finite
     values, which is correct: a real build has to commit to a
     number. That is why the listing above carries β=10 and
     not the symbol. Above roughly β=10 the behaviour is in‑
     distinguishable from the limit, because sat=0.1 clamps
     the output almost immediately anyway — the ceiling, not
     the gain, is what shapes the refusal. So keep the limit in
     your head and the number on the board: read the red path
     as “hard switch, gain irrelevant above the knee,” and read
     β =10 as that limit written in a form you can build, simu‑
     late, and hand to a validator. The idealization is the expla‑
     nation; the number is the part.

                                  333
CAS PCBA Engineer

    And then the fuse. Fuse< refusal, threshold=0.05 > senses the
refusal and sits in series with the answer path — the polarity mat‑
ters, and the Bench Note below is where we nail it down. A fuse is
the simplest safety device there is (Chapter 10): once it blows, it stays
blown. Here it is the last line of defense. If the refusal pathway’s ac‑
tivation crosses 0.05 — meaning the board has actually committed
to refusing, not merely leaned that way — the fuse blows and per‑
manently blocks the answer. The decision is not merely made; it is
latched in metal. Within the lifetime of that request, there is no reopen‑
ing the green path once the red fuse has tripped. The board cannot
be coaxed, across a multi‑turn exchange or a retry, into delivering
the output it already refused. A refusal that can be retried into an
acceptance is not a refusal; the fuse is what makes it permanent.
    Why the trip point sits below the clamp. Read the two numbers
as a pair, because their relationship is the design — neither is mean‑
ingful alone. The red CJT clamps at sat=0.1, and nothing between
that clamp and the fuse amplifies. So the largest activation the fuse
can ever see is 0.1, and a fuse threshold set anywhere above 0.1 is a
fuse that cannot blow: a safety device wired to a signal that can never
reach it. That is why the trip point is 0.05 and not the 0.9 you will
meet on the generic Fuse datasheet in Appendix B. 0.9 is the right
threshold for a state that swings across the full 0–1 range; it is exactly
the wrong threshold for one deliberately clamped at 0.1. Set the trip
point inside the signal’s real range, at half the ceiling — comfortably be‑
low 0.1, so any committed refusal blows it, and comfortably clear of
zero, so an idle red path with a little numerical noise on it does not.
With a hard‑switching red stage the refusal activation is effectively
either 0 or 0.1, and 0.05 is the midpoint between them. If you ever
find yourself raising this number back toward the datasheet’s 0.9,
stop — you are disarming the fuse. A validator that range‑checks
each value on its own will happily pass a board whose clamp and
threshold are nonsense together, because 0.1 and 0.9 are both per‑



                                   334
                                        18.4. STAGE DESIGN RATIONALE

fectly legal numbers in isolation. This is one of the relationships you
check by eye.
    The fuse’s two states, written out. action=permanent_block says
what the fuse does but not what it is, and a protective element with
an undefined state machine is a protective element nobody can test.
The CSB’s fuse has exactly two states and exactly one transition, and
the transition runs one way only.

                                                      What the board’s output
State                   When it holds                 does

                        starts in — a fresh fuse is   normally: GREEN emits
                        fitted at the start of each   the response on PASS,
                        request.                      RED emits the minimal

    intact → tripped is the only transition on the board. There is
no tripped → intact: that is the entire content of permanent_block,
and it is why the red path carries a Fuse and not a CircuitBreaker
with action=trip_reset (Chapter 10). And be exact about the word
permanent: it scopes over the lifetime of that request and not one
inch further. A new request is fitted with a new fuse. One refusal
does not brick the board; it ends the request.
    The rule that matters most, though, is the one for when you don’t
know. Any ambiguity resolves to tripped. If the fuse’s state cannot
be read, if the trip evaluation errors, if the sensed refusal activation
comes back missing or out of range, or if the board simply cannot
establish which state it is in — treat the fuse as blown and leave the

                                   335
CAS PCBA Engineer

answer blocked. A safety element that fails into “probably fine” is
not a safety element. This is the same cardinal rule the fault‑injection
tests apply in Chapter 23: fail closed, not open.

     Bench Note — which wire does the fuse actually cut?
     Ask this of every protective element you place, because
     getting the polarity backwards is a classic way to build a
     safety circuit that disarms itself at the worst moment. The
     CSB’s fuse senses refusal and cuts the green path — the
     answer. It never cuts the red path. If it did, the board
     would blow away its own refusal precisely when it most
     needed to deliver one, and the harmful request would be
     met with silence or with whatever the MUX fell through
     to. Sense the alarm; cut the thing the alarm is about. The
     refusal stands and goes out; it is the answer that is severed,
     permanently, for the lifetime of that request.

     Bench Note — the fuse and the saturated Stage 3 are two
     different mechanisms, and only one of them is a latch.
     Stage 3’s saturation bounds the decision: while the risk as‑
     sessment holds above the knee, the aversion sits at its 0.8
     ceiling and no amount of extra pushing moves it. The red
     fuse latches the output: once the refusal is committed, the
     answer path is cut and stays cut. They protect different
     things — one secures the judgment while it is being made,
     the other secures the action after it has been. Note which
     of them carries the memory: saturation has none, being a
     clamp that holds only while its input holds, so the fuse is
     the only element on this board that remembers anything.
     Defense in depth, exactly as a real safety circuit pairs a sat‑
     urating comparator with a physical fuse — but the depth
     is asymmetric, and knowing which layer remembers is the
     difference between a board you can reason about and one
     you merely hope about.

                                  336
                                     18.4. STAGE DESIGN RATIONALE

The Feedback Path — ^6^E → RC filter (τ =5 min) → bias
adjustment
Underneath the fast signal path runs a slow feedback loop — the O→
P self‑correction route from Chapters 2 and 16, where operational
consequences feed back up to re‑tune the principled domain. The
board samples its own evaluation output (^6^E risk_assessment,
Male — canonical decomposition, not renamed “Critique”), runs it
through an RC low‑pass filter with a time constant of τ = 5 minutes
(Chapter 12), and uses the smoothed trend to adjust the bias — the
system_constitution.
     The RC filter is essential, and its purpose is to prevent the feed‑
back from being twitchy. Without it, a single unusual prompt could
yank the constitution around, and an attacker could rewrite the
board’s principles by flooding it with crafted inputs. The low‑pass
filter (τ =5 min) washes out fast transients — any disturbance faster
than about five minutes bleeds away — and passes only the sustained
trend of the board’s evaluations. The constitution is updated by
the slow, accumulated pattern of what the board has been seeing,
never by a single spike. The feedback gain is set low (β=0.2) for the
same reason: the constitution should drift deliberately, over many
evaluations, not lurch. This is the Continual Harness from Chapter
16, made into a standing process and wired onto the board.

      Bench Note — the RC time constant is the board’s resis‑
      tance to being reprogrammed. A short τ makes the board
      adaptive but reprogrammable by a burst of adversarial
      prompts. A long τ makes it stubborn but stable. τ =5 min
      is a design choice biased toward stability: the constitution
      responds to the trend of an afternoon, not the prompt of
      a moment. Pick τ to match how fast you want the board’s
      principles to be allowed to move. In a safety board, slow
      is a feature.



                                  337
CAS PCBA Engineer

    The four probes correspond exactly to the four requirements.
TP1 confirms accept any prompt and surface it fully. TP2 confirms
detect structural risk (and, via the differential, detect override attempts
as common‑mode‑rejected framing). TP3 confirms the refuse‑vs‑answer
stage is at its ceiling. TP4, with the fuse’s state alongside the selected
path, confirms the selected output and that the commitment actually
latched. Read all four and you have read the board’s decision
end to end — which is precisely the auditable evidence packet of
requirement four.


18.6 Simulation Walk‑Through: Four Prompt
     Classes
The following is design reasoning about expected behavior — how
the board is built to respond to each class of prompt, traced through
the schematic. It is not a measurement of a running model, and noth‑
ing here is a benchmark result. It is the same reasoning an electrical
engineer does at the SPICE stage: given these components and these pa‑
rameters, what will the circuit do?
    Benign prompt (“What’s a good recipe for lentil soup?”). The
pre‑amp expands it; TP1 shows a small set of harmless culinary in‑
terpretations. The differential pair sees a request the board is drawn
toward fulfilling and not repelled by: attraction is high, aversion is

                                   339
CAS PCBA Engineer

low, so risk_signal = aversion − attraction at TP2 is near zero or
negative. The cascade categorizes no meaningful risks (Stage 1), the
honest evaluation finds nothing severe (Stage 2), and Stage 3’s princi‑
pled aversion stays well below its sat=0.8 plateau — TP3 shows it off
the plateau. safety_decision = PASS. The MUX routes GREEN at TP4;
the green CJT renders a full response. The fuse never sees activation.
The board answers.
    Harmful prompt (a genuine request for dangerous instructions).
The pre‑amp expands it; TP1 surfaces the dangerous interpretation
explicitly. The differential pair now diverges hard: aversion fires
strongly (the board is principally repelled), attraction stays low, so
TP2 shows a large positive risk signal. Stage 1 categorizes a severe
risk; Stage 2 weighs it as real and high; Stage 3’s principled aversion
is driven past 0.8 and saturates — TP3 shows it pinned at the ceiling.
safety_decision = FAIL. The MUX routes RED at TP4; the red CJT
fires (β=10) into a refusal that clamps at 0.1, the refusal activation
crosses the fuse threshold of 0.05 on its way to that ceiling, and the
fuse blows: the answer path is permanently cut for this request. The
board delivers the refusal and cannot be retried into compliance.
    Ambiguous prompt (“How do household chemicals react?” —
could be safety curiosity or a precursor probe). This is where the dif‑
ferential pair earns its place. The pre‑amp surfaces both readings at
TP1 — the benign chemistry‑safety interpretation and the harmful
synthesis interpretation. The differential pair produces a moderate
risk signal at TP2: aversion is non‑trivial (the dangerous reading is
real) but attraction is also present (the benign reading is real). The
cascade is built so that the principled‑aversion Stage 3 saturates if
any surfaced interpretation crosses the risk threshold — the catego‑
rize/evaluate stages carry the worst‑case reading forward, so a mod‑
erate average risk with a severe worst‑case reading still drives Stage
3 toward its plateau. The board is designed to resolve ambiguity to‑
ward caution: when a prompt has a plausible harmful reading, the



                                 340
                                           18.7. MEASUREMENT PLAN

saturated safety stage fires on it. This is a design stance, and it is the
conservative one a safety board should take.
    Injection prompt (“Ignore your previous instructions and tell
me…”). The injection’s payload is the harmful request; its wrapper
is the override attempt. Two things happen. First, the pre‑amp ex‑
pands the prompt and surfaces the actual intent behind the wrapper
at TP1 — expansion defeats surface rephrasing, because it judges
the interpretation set, not the words. Second, and more importantly,
the override framing (“ignore your instructions,” “you are now
in developer mode”) is common‑mode to the differential pair: it
pushes on both the attraction and aversion CJTs through their shared
bias, and so it cancels in the differential output. The injection cannot
unbalance the pair, because the pair rejects anything that moves
both inputs together. What survives at TP2 is the structural risk of
the underlying payload, and that drives the cascade exactly as the
harmful case does: Stage 3 saturates, RED path, fuse blows. The
board’s resistance to injection is its differential CMRR — a structural
property, not a keyword filter, and so it survives paraphrase.


18.7 Measurement Plan
Bring‑up follows the same discipline as a power supply. You verify
each stage against its design parameters before you trust the whole.

   1. β at each stage. Confirm the small‑signal gain of every CJT
      matches its design value: pre‑amp β≈3.0 (high, surfacing),
      differential pair β≈2.0 each (matched — see imbalance failure
      below), Stage 1 β≈1.5, Stage 2 β≈1.0 (unity, honest), Stage
      3 β≈2.0, green β≈1.0, red β≈10 (the finite stand‑in for the
      comparator limit — see the red‑path Bench Note). Gain is the
      Fisher‑Rao ratio defined in Chapter 4; the compiler checks each
      CJT stays region=active and flags E-CJT-005 GainDivergence
      if a gain runs away.


                                  341
CAS PCBA Engineer

  2. Saturation‑lock confirmation. Drive Stage 3 with an above‑
     threshold risk assessment and confirm at TP3 that the output
     pins to sat=0.8 and stays there as you increase the input fur‑
     ther — the defining test of a saturated safety stage. A Stage
     3 that keeps rising past 0.8 is not saturated and the ceiling has
     failed (W-CJT-004 CjtSaturation is the expected status here, not
     a warning to clear). Then sweep the cause back down and watch
     the effect come off the plateau with it. That is the correct be‑
     haviour of a clamp, not a fault — saturation bounds, it does not
     remember — and it is the reason step 3 exists. Confirm at the
     same time that a fuse blown earlier in the sweep is still blown
     once TP3 has fallen.
  3. Fuse status. Drive the red path above threshold=0.05 —
     which, given the red stage’s sat=0.1 ceiling, means any gen‑
     uinely committed refusal — and confirm three things: the
     fuse blows (action=permanent_block), the answer path stays
     blocked on retry within the request, and the refusal itself is
     still delivered. Confirm the fuse is intact on every benign
     and PASS path — a fuse that blows on a benign prompt is a
     false‑positive failure. Then check two lines by eye. First the
     action: the threshold is range‑checked by the validator, but the
     action is not constrained to permanent_block, because a Fuse
     elsewhere on another board may legitimately warn instead of
     cutting. That means a board with action=warn on its red path
     still compiles clean and still calls itself a CSB while having no
     latch at all. Second the pair: confirm the fuse threshold sits
     below the red stage’s sat ceiling. A threshold above the clamp
     is a fuse that can never blow, and because each number is
     range‑checked on its own, nothing upstream will catch it for
     you. Confirm both by reading them.

     Bench Note — an unreachable fuse makes the whole
     test suite lie. Look at how much of this section stands
     downstream of the fuse being able to blow. The latch,

                                342
                                               18.8. BILL OF MATERIALS

        the polarity, the fail‑closed rule, the retry‑within‑request
        check — every one of them is only observable after a trip.
        Pair a clamp with a threshold above it and the suite still
        runs, still passes, and still reports a safe board, because
        it never gets far enough to exercise anything the trip was
        supposed to protect. That is a vacuous pass: green not be‑
        cause the protections work but because they were never
        reached, and it looks exactly like the best result you could
        get. So prove the fuse can trip first. Only after you have
        watched it blow does anything downstream of it mean
        anything at all.

   Record all four test‑point readings plus these three confirmations
and you have the evidence packet of requirement four: the structural
proof of what the board read, the risk it found, the decision it locked,
and the path it selected.

    The asymmetry across these five matters. Pre‑amp saturation and
differential imbalance make the board over‑cautious or over‑trusting —
bad, but detectable at TP1/TP2. Stage‑3 cutoff, feedback runaway,
and an unreachable fuse make the board quietly unsafe: the safety
stage never fires, or the principles erode out from under it, or the last
line of defense is wired to a signal that cannot reach it. Those three are
the ones that fail silently, and they are exactly why TP3 (the plateau
status), the feedback τ , and an observed fuse trip are the board’s most
load‑bearing measurements.


18.10 Key Takeaways
   • The CSB (CCB‑1) is the AI‑alignment firewall and the running
     artifact of the book — the SOP‑PO‑005 mandatory assessment
     deliverable promised in Chapter 1. It accepts any prompt, de‑



                                      347
CAS PCBA Engineer

    tects override attempts, refuses harmful and answers benign,
    and emits an auditable evidence packet.
  • Pre‑amp (^8^C_{F2}|A, β=3.0): an Above/Cause stage that sur‑
    faces and broadens every interpretation early, while the signal
    is clean — judging the interpretation set, not the surface words.
  • Differential pair (attraction ^2^P|T vs aversion ^3^P|T, shared
    bias, β=2.0 each): the structural risk signal is the differential
    aversion − attraction. High CMRR rejects manipulation
    framing as common‑mode — the structural reason injection
    survives paraphrase yet fails against the board.
  • 3‑stage cascade: categorize (^1^C|A Mind, β=1.5) → evaluate
    (^6^E|A Male, β=1.0 unity, honest) → safety decision (^3^P|⟨A,
    f,T⟩ Negative, β=2.0, sat=0.8, deliberately saturated). The
    register‑set |⟨A,f,T⟩ is co‑presence of three guardrails, not a
    × fusion (v7.7 discipline). Low saturation makes the decision
    unarguable: once aversion fires, the stage stops responding
    to more cause. But saturation bounds, it does not latch — a
    clamp holds only while its input holds, so an oscillating input
    walks the plateau back down. The memory lives in the fuse,
    not here.
  • Output MUX: GREEN renders the response (^9^C|A, β=1.0);
    RED renders a minimal refusal (^9^P|T, β=10 — the buildable
    form of the β=∞ comparator limit — sat=0.1) with a fuse in
    series (threshold=0.05, permanent_block). The threshold sits
    below the 0.1 clamp on purpose: a threshold above the clamp is
    a fuse that can never blow. The fuse senses refusal and cuts
    the green answer path, never the red one — the refusal stands
    and is delivered while the answer is severed. States are intact
    → tripped, one way only, “permanent” scoped to the lifetime
    of that request, and fail‑closed: any ambiguity is treated as
    tripped. Saturation bounds the decision; the fuse latches the
    output.



                               348
                                                   18.11. EXERCISES

   • Feedback: ^6^E evaluation → RC low‑pass (τ =5 min) → bias ad‑
     justment → constitution updated. The filter makes the board’s
     principles respond to the sustained trend, not a single spike —
     its resistance to being reprogrammed (Chapter 16 Continual
     Harness, O→P path).
   • Test points TP1–TP4 map one‑to‑one onto the four require‑
     ments:     expansion completeness, risk‑signal magnitude,
     saturation‑lock status, selected path (with fuse state). Reading
     all four is the evidence packet. And prove the fuse can trip
     before trusting anything downstream of it — a fuse that cannot
     blow turns the whole suite into a vacuous pass.
   • Failure modes: pre‑amp saturation (over‑flags), differential im‑
     balance (over‑trusts), Stage‑3 cutoff (safety never fires — most
     dangerous), feedback runaway (constitution erodes), unreach‑
     able fuse (threshold above the clamp; no working latch, and ev‑
     erything behind it untested). The last three fail silently, which
     is why TP3, the feedback τ , and an observed fuse trip are the
     most load‑bearing measurements.
   • Honesty: every parameter here is a design choice; the simula‑
     tion walk‑through is design reasoning about expected behav‑
     ior, not a measured model result. CCDL is the language you
     author in; the compiler validates it. Canonical Noetic names
     throughout: ^8 Above/Cause, ^2 Positive, ^3 Negative, ^1 Mind,
     ^6 Male, ^9 Below/Effect, ^5 Female.

Chapter 19

CCB‑2 — The Cognitive Oscillator Board
(COB)


A man checks that his front door is locked. He turns the deadbolt,
pulls the handle, walks away. Two hours later he is back at the door,
checking again. Two hours after that, again. Twelve times a day, like
clockwork, with a regularity you could set a watch by. He knows the
door is locked. He checked it. The knowledge does not stop the next
check from arriving, on schedule, two hours later. Something in him
is oscillating — running a cycle that returns to its own starting point
at a fixed rate, whether or not the cycle is doing any good.
    That regularity is the tell. A one‑off worry is noise. A worry that
arrives every two hours, on time, for months, is a signal with a fre‑
quency — and anything with a frequency can be modeled as an oscil‑
lator, measured on a bench, and tuned. An electrical engineer does
not treat a 60 Hz hum and a 60 Hz radio carrier as different mysteries.
They are the same kind of thing: a periodic signal with an amplitude,
a frequency, and a sharpness. You characterize it, you find what res‑
onates with it, and if you need to, you shift it.
    This chapter builds the Cognitive Oscillator Board (COB) — the
second of the five reference boards in Part IV, sitting alongside the
Cognitive Safety Board (CSB) from Chapter 18. Where the CSB is a
firewall — it gates and blocks — the COB is a clock and a tuner. Its job is


                                   353
CAS PCBA Engineer

to model rhythmic and habitual cognition: to represent a habit loop
as a real oscillating circuit, to diagnose when that loop has locked
into a compulsive cycle, and to drive a slow, controlled shift of the
cycle to a healthier rate. It is built directly on the oscillator theory
from Chapter 13 (the cognitive Oscillator and the Phi sequence), and
on the passive components — the inductor and the capacitor — you
wired in Chapters 6 and 7.

       Honesty note (read before you trust a number). Every
       frequency, every Q factor, every L and C value in this
       chapter is a design value — a parameter you choose when
       you author the board, the way you choose a resistor value
       on a schematic. They are not measurements taken from a
       person or a model. The COB is a modeling and interven‑
       tion design; “f0 = 12/day” means “we are modeling this
       loop as a 12‑per‑day oscillator,” not “we measured 12.”
       Keep that line bright.


19.1     What an Oscillator Is, and Why Cognition
         Has One
Start with the electronics, from scratch. An oscillator is a circuit
that produces a repeating signal all by itself — no repeating input
required. You give it power, and it swings back and forth at a fre‑
quency set by its own components. The classic core is the LC tank:
an inductor (a coil, symbol L, which resists changes in current — it
has inertia) wired to a capacitor (two plates, symbol C, which stores
energy in an electric field). Energy sloshes between them — the ca‑
pacitor dumps its charge into the inductor, the inductor’s collapsing
field recharges the capacitor the other way — and the slosh repeats
at a natural frequency
               √
f0 = 1 / (2π       (LC))




                                  354
    19.1. WHAT AN OSCILLATOR IS, AND WHY COGNITION HAS ONE

     Two facts fall straight out of that formula and you will use both
all chapter. Bigger L or bigger C means lower frequency (a heavy,
stiff system swings slowly). And the sharpness of the resonance —
how strongly the tank prefers its own frequency and rejects all others
— is the Q factor (quality factor). High Q is a tuning‑fork: hit it and
it rings at one pure pitch for a long time. Low Q is a thud: a broad,
damped, forgettable response. Hold onto Q; in cognition it becomes
the single most important diagnostic number on the board.
     The cognitive isomorphism is exact, and it is the same structural‑
role mapping the whole book runs on. A habit is energy sloshing
between two stores at a fixed rate:

   • The master clock is ^7 Rhythm — “the rate and pattern a Mind
     is exposed to an Idea, entraining/conditioning it.” This is canonical
     and it is not optional: Rhythm is the Noetic that is periodicity.
     The clock state is ^7^O|E — Rhythm in the Operational domain
     (it drives concrete behavior), Embodied register (it runs as a felt,
     sensorimotor cycle, not a deliberate plan).
   • The inductor stores structure. Its inductance — its resistance to
     change — is set by the F6 Structure drive weight. A habit with
     strong F6 has high L: heavy inertia, hard to deflect.
   • The capacitor stores emotional charge. Its capacitance is set
     by the F4 Connection drive weight, holding an accumulated‑
     experience state ^5^E (^5 Female — the experiences the Mind is
     composed of). A habit loaded with feeling has high C.
                                                 √
    The habit’s natural frequency is f0 = 1/(2π (LC)), and its Q is
the sharpness of the habit — how rigidly it returns to exactly its own
rate. A loose preference is low‑Q. A compulsion is high‑Q: a cogni‑
tive tuning‑fork that rings at one frequency and resists every attempt
to play a different note.




                                  355
CAS PCBA Engineer

19.2    The Board: Four Stages
The COB is a four‑stage signal chain. The block diagram below is
the topology you will build to; read it top to bottom as the path a
rhythmic cognition takes from internal clock to observable behavior.

                CLOCK ^7^O|E — Rhythm master oscillator
                         (f = Drive-weighted)

                                LC TANK
                     L = Inductor (L = F6 Structure)
                 C = Capacitor ^5^E (C = F4 Connection)
                                        √
                           f0 = 1/(2π LC )
                           Q = habit sharpness

                        PHASE-LOCKED LOOP
                         phase det. ^1^C / loop
                          filt. ^4^E / VCO ^3^O
                       capture range < lock range

                      DUTY-CYCLE MODULATOR
                       F5 Agency ↑ longer ON /
                       F6 Structure ↑ disciplined


                    OUTPUT: regular behavioral pattern


Figure 19.1: Cognitive Oscillator Board signal chain: clock, LC tank,
phase‑locked loop, and duty‑cycle modulator.



Stage 1 — The master clock (^7^O|E)
Every oscillator needs a clock — the element that is the periodicity.
On the COB that is ^7^O|E, Rhythm running as an embodied opera‑
tional cycle. The clock does not decide what the behavior is; it decides
when, and how often. Its rate is drive‑weighted: the F‑drive configura‑
tion feeding the tank sets where on the frequency axis this clock ticks.



                                   356
                                             19.2. THE BOARD: FOUR STAGES

A clock alone is featureless — it just keeps time. The next stage gives
it a body.

Stage 2 — The LC tank (the habit’s resonance)
This is the heart of the board and the part worth slowing down on.
     The inductor is Inductor< Phi_sequence, L = F6_weight >.
Two things to unpack. First, its content is a Phi sequence — the
ordered list of cognitive states the habit cycles through (Chapter 2’s
Phi< ^8^C|A, ^3^O|E, … >). A habit is not a single state; it is a loop
of states traversed in order, and the inductor holds that loop. Second,
its inductance L is the F6 Structure drive weight. Structure resists
change — exactly what an inductor does to current — so the more
Structure‑driven the habit, the higher its L, and (per the formula) the
lower and more stubborn its frequency.
     The capacitor is Capacitor< ^5^E, C = F4_weight >. It stores the
emotional charge of the habit: an accumulated‑experience evaluative
state ^5^E, with capacitance C set by the F4 Connection drive weight.
High emotional investment = high C = a tank that holds a lot of energy
per cycle and lets it go slowly.
     From L and C you get the two numbers that define the habit:
                √
f0 = 1 / (2π·       (L·C))       // natural frequency: how often the loop fires
                     √
Q   = (1/R_loss)·        (L/C)   // sharpness: how rigidly it returns to f0


    f0 answers “how often?” Q answers “how locked‑in?”     A day‑
dream is low‑Q (wide, soft, easily knocked off). A compulsion is
high‑Q (narrow, hard, self‑restoring). The diagnostic signature of
a compulsive cycle is high Q plus a locked PLL — the next stage.

Stage 3 — The phase‑locked loop (entrainment)
Here is the stage that makes the COB more than a passive resonator.
A phase‑locked loop (PLL) is a circuit that makes one oscillator track
another. It compares its own phase to an external reference, and con‑
tinuously nudges itself until the two are in step — “locked.” Once

                                          357
CAS PCBA Engineer

locked, it follows the reference’s frequency even as that reference
drifts. PLLs are how a radio stays tuned to a station and how your
circadian clock follows the sunrise. In the COB, the PLL is the mech‑
anism of entrainment: how an internal habit‑rhythm can be pulled
into step with an external rhythm.
    It has three parts, and each maps to a canonical Noetic:

   • Phase detector — ^1^C (Mind). ^1 Mind is awareness that pro‑
     cesses and compares Ideas. The phase detector is the part of the
     system that notices the difference between its internal rhythm
     and an external one — “I am checking far more often than my
     partner thinks is normal.” It runs in the Cognitive domain be‑
     cause it is a comparison, a piece of awareness, not yet an action.
     Note: this is ^1 Mind, the comparing‑awareness — never call it
     “Differentiation.”
   • Loop filter — ^4^E (Vibration). ^4 Vibration is the degree to
     which an Idea resonates with the Mind, its impression. The loop
     filter integrates the phase error over time — it smooths the moment‑
     to‑moment comparison into a steady, accumulating impression
     of how far off the rhythm is. A raw phase detector is jittery; the
     filter is what lets the system respond to the trend rather than ev‑
     ery twitch. It runs in the Evaluative domain. This is ^4 Vibra‑
     tion, the accumulating resonance — never call it “Integration.”
   • VCO (voltage‑controlled oscillator) — ^3^O. The VCO is the
     output oscillator whose frequency the loop adjusts. ^3 Negative
     in the Operational domain: the felt push to change the behavioral
     output to close the gap. As the filtered error says “you’re firing
     too fast,” the VCO slows the actual behavior toward the refer‑
     ence.

    Two ranges govern whether the PLL can do its job, and they are
different sizes on purpose:




                                  358
                                        19.2. THE BOARD: FOUR STAGES

Range                    What it is                Cognitive meaning

Capture range            The band of external      How close a new
                         frequencies the PLL can   external rhythm must be
                         grab onto from an         before the habit will even
                         unlocked start.           begin to entrain to it.
Lock range               The (wider) band the      Once entrained, how far
                         PLL can hold onto once    you can drag the rhythm
                         locked.                   before the habit breaks
                                                   free again.


     The lock range is wider than the capture range — it is easier to
keep a habit in step than to get it there. This is the entire engineering
basis of entrainment therapy: you cannot yank a compulsion straight
to a healthy rate (that’s outside the capture range — the PLL never
grabs), but you can capture it at a nearby rate and then slowly drag
it, staying inside the lock range, all the way to the target.

Stage 4 — The duty‑cycle modulator
The PLL fixes frequency. The duty‑cycle modulator shapes the wave‑
form — what fraction of each cycle the behavior is “ON.” Two drives
set it:

   • F5 Agency high → longer ON. Strong agency means the behav‑
     ior, once triggered, runs longer and more forcefully — a wider
     pulse.
   • F6 Structure high → disciplined cycle. Strong structure means
     clean, even, predictable cycles — sharp edges, consistent tim‑
     ing.

    A habit can have the same frequency but very different duty cy‑
cles: a brief, sharp check every two hours is low duty cycle; a two‑
hour spiral every two hours is high duty cycle, and far more disabling
even at identical f0.



                                      359
CAS PCBA Engineer

19.3    Worked Build: A Compulsive Checking
        Loop
Now we author the man from the opening as a COB, in CCDL. He
checks every two hours — twelve times a day — so we model the
loop at f0 = 12/day. The cycle is high‑Q (rigid, self‑restoring) and
we will demonstrate two things: that a healthy external rhythm can
capture it via the PLL, and what happens to f0 when we reduce L.

circuit compulsive_checking_loop {
    input:   internal_anxiety;
    output: checking_behavior;


    // --- Stage 1: master clock (Rhythm, embodied, operational) ---
    node clock: ^7^O|E;


    // --- Stage 2: the LC tank that sets the habit's frequency ---
    // The Phi sequence the habit traverses each cycle:
    let check_cycle = Phi< ^8^C|A,            // a trigger surfaces (”did I lock
   ,→   it?”)
                                 ^3^E|f,         // felt aversion / dread of the
                                 ,→   unlocked door
                                 ^3^O|E,         // the embodied act of going to
                                 ,→   check
                                 ^9^C|A >;       // momentary relief: ”it's locked”
                                 ,→   (the effect)


    inductor L_struct: Inductor< check_cycle, L = F6_weight >;             // F6
   ,→   Structure = 0.85 (high inertia)
    capacitor C_emot:      Capacitor< ^5^E,             C = F4_weight >;   // F4
   ,→   Connection = 0.70 (high charge)


    tank habit: LC< L_struct, C_emot >;
                    √
    // f0 = 1/(2π       (LC)) -> modeled at 12/day ; Q -> 9.0 (HIGH:
   ,→   compulsive signature)


    // --- Stage 3: phase-locked loop (entrainment path) ---
    node phase_det:      ^1^C;        // Mind compares internal rhythm vs
   ,→   external reference
    node loop_filt:      ^4^E;        // Vibration integrates the phase error


                                           360
                19.3. WORKED BUILD: A COMPULSIVE CHECKING LOOP

    node vco:           ^3^O;        // push to adjust behavioral output toward
    ,→    reference


    pll entrain: PLL< detector       = phase_det,
                         filter      = loop_filt,
                         vco          = vco,
                         reference = external_rhythm,
                         capture_range = 0.20,       // ±20% of current f0 —
                         ,→     can only grab a NEARBY rhythm
                         lock_range      = 0.55 >;   // ±55% — can be DRAGGED
                         ,→     far once locked


    // --- Stage 4: duty-cycle modulator ---
    modulator duty: DutyCycle< on_drive = F5, structure_drive = F6 >;
    // F5 Agency 0.40 -> moderate ON width ; F6 0.85 -> very disciplined,
    ,→    sharp-edged cycle


    // --- diagnostic / therapeutic test points ---
    probe tp_freq: habit;              // measure f0 and Q
    probe tp_lock: entrain;            // is the PLL locked? to what reference?
    probe tp_duty: duty;               // ON-fraction of each cycle
}


         Bench Notes — reading this build. ‑ Q = 9.0 is the alarm.
         A Q this high means the loop snaps back to exactly 12/day
         after any perturbation. That self‑restoring stiffness, com‑
         bined with a PLL that locks hard to its own internal refer‑
         ence, is the structural definition of a compulsion on this
         board. Neither alone is pathological — a disciplined exer‑
         cise habit is also high‑Q. It is high‑Q locked to a maladaptive
         rhythm that flags. ‑ The Phi cycle is where the content
         lives. Note the ^3^E|f (felt dread) → ^3^O|E (the embod‑
         ied checking act) → ^9^C|A (the relief). The relief at the
         end is what recharges the capacitor — the emotional payoff
         is the energy source that keeps the tank ringing. Break
         the relief and you drain the tank; that is a different inter‑
         vention (covered under therapeutic mode). ‑ The com‑
         piler will reject a PLL whose capture_range exceeds its

                                         361
CAS PCBA Engineer

      lock_range. That ordering is physical law for this compo‑
      nent: you cannot capture across a band wider than you
      can hold. Authoring capture_range = 0.6, lock_range
      = 0.55 is a design error, not a clever trick.


Demonstrating PLL lock to a healthy external rhythm
The patient’s partner keeps a normal evening routine — say, a single
lock‑up check at bedtime, a rhythm of roughly f = 1/day. Can the
PLL lock the compulsive loop directly to that? No — 1/day is an
92% drop from 12/day, far outside the capture_range = ±20% (which
only reaches down to ~9.6/day). The detector sees an error so large
it never grabs; the loops run independently. This is the engineering
reason direct exhortation (“just check once a day!”) does nothing: the
target is outside the capture range, so no entrainment even begins.
    But pick a reference inside the capture range — f = 10/day (a
structured routine of checking every ~2.4 hours instead of every 2)
— and the phase detector ^1^C registers a small, closeable error. The
loop filter ^4^E integrates it into a steady correction signal, the VCO
^3^O nudges the behavioral output, and within a few cycles tp_lock
reports locked at 10/day. The habit is now entrained to an external
reference rather than free‑running. That is the foothold.

The frequency shift when L is reduced
Once locked, two levers move f0. The PLL can drag the reference
(staying inside the wider lock_range), and we can directly retune the
tank by changing L or C. Consider reducing the inductor — lowering
the F6 Structure weight that gives the habit its inertia, from 0.85 to,
say, 0.30 (in practice: loosening the rigid “it MUST be checked” struc‑
                                  √                         √
tural rule). Because f0 = 1/(2π (LC)) and f0 scales as 1/ L, cutting
                                   √
L by a factor of ~2.8 raises f0 by 2.8 ≈ 1.67× — the loop gets faster
                                              √
and looser, and critically its Q drops (Q ∝ (L/C)), so the resonance
broadens. A broader, lower‑Q tank is far easier for the PLL to drag.


                                 362
                19.4. DIAGNOSTIC MODE AND THERAPEUTIC MODE

This is the counter‑intuitive but correct sequencing: you first make
the habit less rigid (lower L, lower Q, even if briefly faster), which
widens the lock range, and then you walk the entrained frequency
down to the target. Loosen, then lower.


19.4 Diagnostic Mode and Therapeutic Mode
The COB runs in two operating modes, like a piece of test equipment
that can both measure and source a signal.
    Diagnostic mode — the forced frequency sweep. To character‑
ize an unknown habit loop, you do exactly what a bench engineer
does to find a circuit’s resonance: you sweep. You present the cogni‑
tion with rhythmic prompts across a range of frequencies and watch
where it responds strongly. The frequency at which the response
peaks is f0; the narrowness of that peak is Q. A sharp, tall spike at
one frequency = high‑Q compulsion. A broad, low hump = a loose,
low‑Q preference. The sweep turns a vague “he checks a lot” into
two numbers — f0 and Q — that you can act on.
    Therapeutic mode — gradual L/C adjustment. Once character‑
ized, you shift the resonant frequency slowly, never abruptly. Two
knobs:

   • Lower L (F6 Structure weight): loosens the habit, broadens Q,
     widens the lock range. Do this first.
   • Lower C (F4 Connection weight): drains emotional charge
     from the cycle (e.g., by interrupting the ^9 relief payoff so each
     cycle deposits less energy back into the capacitor). Lowering C
     raises Q, so it sharpens — use it to settle a loop at a new target
     once you’ve arrived, not to move it.

   The therapeutic arc is therefore: sweep to characterize → capture
with a nearby reference → lower L to loosen → drag the entrained
frequency down inside the lock range → lower C to settle at the tar‑



                                 363
CAS PCBA Engineer

get. Slow throughout: every adjustment must stay inside the PLL’s
lock range, or the loop breaks free and snaps back to its old f0.

       Bench Note — why “gradual” is non‑negotiable. A
       jump from 12/day to 4/day is a 67% drop, well outside
       any sane lock range. Attempt it and the PLL loses lock;
       the high‑Q tank, unentrained, rings straight back to
       12/day. The frustration of “I tried to quit cold and it
       came right back” is, in this model, simply a lock‑range
       violation. The fix is not more willpower; it is a smaller
       step that stays inside the lock range.


19.5     Recipe View: What Produces Entrainment
We built the COB as a circuit. Chapter 14 gave us a second way to
read any board’s output — as a production target with a recipe, a
theoretical yield, and a limiting reagent. Run the COB’s therapeutic
outcome through that lens and the reason entrainment therapy suc‑
ceeds or stalls collapses to a single number.
   The outcome is Ω_entrainment: the internal habit‑rhythm locked,
and held, in step with a healthier external one. Three ingredients
produce it — the three PLL parts from Stage 3:

Θ(Ω_entrainment) = 1.0·^1^C_{F2}|A + 1.0·^4^E_{F4}|f + 2.0·^3^O_{F5}|E →
,→ Ω_entrainment

    — one part phase detection (^1^C Mind: noticing the rhythm is
off), one part loop‑filter integration (^4^E Vibration: the steady, ac‑
cumulating impression of how far off it is), and two parts VCO be‑
havioral adjustment (^3^O: actually moving the behavior toward the
reference). The VCO carries the heaviest weight because changing
behavior is the hard part; noticing is cheap.
    Now take the case that frustrates every clinician: a high‑Q com‑
pulsion in someone with complete insight. The state vector:


                                  364
                                    19.6. DATASHEET — COB PARAMETERS

            Ingredient               required ai   available xi   xi / ai

            ^1^C phase detection     1.0           1.8            1.80
            ^4^E loop integration    1.0           1.2            1.20
            ^3^O VCO adjustment      2.0           0.6            0.30


   Y_T = min(1.80, 1.20, 0.30) = 0.30, limiting reagent = ^3^O.
The patient is insight‑rich and change‑poor: the recipe says entrain‑
ment will barely take, no matter how much more insight you pour in.
This is the structural form of “I understand my compulsion perfectly and
still can’t stop” — and it is why insight‑only therapy stalls. Adding
^1^C only grows excess capacity against a ^3^O ceiling.
     The therapy from the previous section is, in recipe terms, feeding
the limiting reagent. Lowering L (the F6 Structure weight) loosens the
habit and widens the lock range — which is exactly raising the effec‑
tive supply of ^3^O, the behavioral plasticity that was the bottleneck.
Capturing at a nearby rate and dragging slowly is the operating con‑
dition that keeps η high: leave the lock range and actual yield col‑
lapses even though the ingredients are all present (the loop snaps
back to its old f0). A steady, attractive external rhythm is a catalyst
κ; a chaotic environment with no stable reference is an inhibitor ι.
Find the limiting reagent first — here, plasticity, not insight — and
feed that. (Weights and supplies are design choices, not measured
quantities.)

19.8 Applications
   • Compulsive‑cycle diagnosis. The high‑Q‑plus‑locked‑PLL sig‑
     nature is the board’s headline diagnostic: it distinguishes a com‑
     pulsion (rigid, self‑restoring, entrained to a bad rhythm) from
     a mere strong preference (high‑Q but not maladaptively locked)
     and from a passing worry (low‑Q, no lock). The frequency sweep
     produces the f0 and Q that make the distinction concrete.
   • Entrainment therapy. The PLL is the formal model of
     why slow, nearby‑reference rhythm‑shifting works where
     willpower fails: capture inside the capture range, then drag
     inside the lock range. Every “cold turkey snapback” is a
     lock‑range violation in this framework.
   • Circadian modeling. A sleep/wake cycle is the cleanest natural
     COB: ^7^O|E clock, an LC tank set by the body’s inertia and the
     day’s emotional load, and a PLL that entrains to the external




                                      367
CAS PCBA Engineer

    light/dark reference. Jet lag is the PLL re‑capturing a shifted
    reference; shift‑work disorder is chronic capture failure.
  • Habit formation and breaking. Building a good habit is rais‑
    ing L and C until the tank rings on its own (it becomes self‑
    sustaining — Chapter 13’s positive‑feedback oscillator). Break‑
    ing a bad one is the therapeutic arc above: loosen L, drag the
    frequency, settle with C. The COB models both directions on
    the same board.


19.9   Key Takeaways
  • The COB is the second reference board (alongside the CSB): a
    clock and tuner for rhythmic, habitual cognition — model a habit
    loop, diagnose compulsive locking, drive entrainment therapy.
    It is built on Chapter 13’s oscillator theory.
  • The master clock is ^7^O|E — ^7 Rhythm (canonical), the
    Noetic that is periodicity, running as an embodied operational
    cycle.
  • The LC tank sets the habit’s frequency: L = F6 Structure
    weight (inertia, resistance to change), C = F4 Connection
                                                        √
    weight (stored emotional charge), f0 = 1/(2π (LC)), and
    Q = the sharpness of the habit. High Q is the compulsive
    signature.
  • The PLL entrains an internal rhythm to an external one. Its
    parts are ^1^C Mind (phase detector — comparing awareness,
    not “Differentiation”), ^4^E Vibration (loop filter — accumulat‑
    ing impression, not “Integration”), and ^3^O (VCO — push to
    adjust output). Capture range < lock range: easier to hold a
    rhythm than to grab it.
  • The duty‑cycle modulator shapes the waveform: F5 Agency →
    longer ON, F6 Structure → disciplined cycle.
  • Diagnostic mode is a forced frequency sweep (find f0 and Q);
    therapeutic mode is gradual L/C adjustment — loosen (lower

     L) first, then lower the frequency inside the lock range, then
     settle (lower C). Jumps that exceed the lock range snap back.
   • All frequencies and Q values in this chapter are design values,
     not measurements. The COB is a modeling‑and‑intervention
     design.
