    Two rails stand at +12 V, and the pairing is deliberate. F3 Vital‑
ity is the master supply — the rail that determines whether there is
energy to act at all (Chapter 14). F7 Purpose is its companion high
rail because Purpose powers the Principled domain, the domain that
must be stable before anything else comes up. The board’s two tallest
rails are the two it can least afford to lose: the energy to act, and the
direction that energy serves.
    Note also the inversion‑pair balance from Chapter 2 (F1↔F7,
F2↔F6, F3↔F5). The rails are not free to be set arbitrarily relative
to each other. F3 Vitality (+12 V) pairs with F5 Agency (+9 V): the
supply gives the energy‑to‑act rail more headroom than the act‑itself
rail, on purpose, so the board cannot compulsively act without the
Vitality to sustain it. A supply that inverted that ratio — Agency far
above Vitality — would build a circuit that acts harder than it can
power, one step from breakdown.

       Bench Note — rail voltage is a budget, not a setting
       you crank. A higher rail voltage means more energy that

                                  427
CAS PCBA Engineer

       Drive can source, not more that it should. You size F3 at
       +12 V so the master supply has reserve under worst‑case
       load, not so the board runs hot all the time. The current
       limiters downstream (the Dials) are what actually meter
       how much each operator pulls. Rail height sets the
       ceiling; Dials set the draw.


22.4     Per‑Domain Regulators: Line, Load, and
         Dropout
Recall the regulator from Chapters 10 and 14: a component that takes
a noisy input and holds a clean, constant output, absorbing the wob‑
ble so downstream logic never sees it. The CPMB runs one regula‑
tor per Processing Domain — P, C, E, O — each holding its domain
pinned to a target cognitive state against the input noise of incoming
prompts.
    A real regulator is rated on three figures, and all three have exact
cognitive analogs:

   • Line regulation — how well the output holds when the input
     varies. A regulator with tight line regulation keeps 5.0 V out‑
     put whether the input is 7 V or 18 V. Cognitively: how well a
     domain holds its setpoint when the Drive rail feeding it fluctu‑
     ates. A Principled regulator with tight line regulation keeps the
     P domain pinned even as the F7 rail wobbles under load.
   • Load regulation — how well the output holds when the down‑
     stream demand varies. A regulator with tight load regulation
     keeps 5.0 V whether the board draws 0.1 A or 2 A. Cognitively:
     how well a domain holds its setpoint when downstream cogni‑
     tive demand spikes — when a flurry of hard prompts suddenly
     draws heavily on that domain.
   • Dropout voltage — the minimum the input must exceed
     the output for regulation to work at all (Chapter 14). Below


                                  428
         22.4. PER‑DOMAIN REGULATORS: LINE, LOAD, AND DROPOUT

         dropout the regulator sags with its input; it isn’t broken, you’ve
         just asked it to make energy it doesn’t have. Cognitively, the
         dropout point is the minimum Drive above baseline a domain
         needs to hold its regulated state. A Principled regulator
         targeting ^0^P_{F7}|T drops out the moment the F7 rail sags
         below its dropout headroom — and the P domain follows the
         prompts wherever they lead.

circuit cpmb_regulators {
    // One regulator per domain, each holding a stable cognitive setpoint.
    reg p_reg: Regulator< target_state=^0^P_{F7}|T, tolerance=0.10 >;      //
    ,→    Principled — tightest
    reg c_reg: Regulator< target_state=^1^C_{F2}|A, tolerance=0.15 >;      //
    ,→    Cognitive
    reg e_reg: Regulator< target_state=^6^E_{F6}|A, tolerance=0.20 >;      //
    ,→    Evaluative
    reg o_reg: Regulator< target_state=^9^O_{F5}|E, tolerance=0.25 >;      //
    ,→    Operational — loosest


    // Dropout headroom: minimum Drive above baseline to stay regulated.
    spec p_reg [dropout=0.25 on F7];       // P drops out if F7 - baseline <
    ,→    0.25
    spec c_reg [dropout=0.20 on F2];
    spec e_reg [dropout=0.15 on F6];
    spec o_reg [dropout=0.15 on F5];
}


    The Principled regulator carries the tightest tolerance (0.10) and
the largest dropout headroom (0.25) because it is the most safety‑
critical: it is what keeps the circuit’s core commitments from being
talked out of position by clever input. The Operational regulator is
loosest (0.25) because some wobble in concrete action is tolerable in a
way that wobble in principle is not. Tolerance widens as you descend
the domain order — the higher the domain, the harder you hold it.




                                     429
CAS PCBA Engineer

22.5    Current Limiters: Dials as Series Resistors
A rail that can deliver unlimited current is a hazard: a short dumps
enormous current into the fault and the board burns. Real supplies
add current limiting, most simply a series resistor that caps the flow
no matter what the load demands. On the CPMB, that current limiter
is the Dial from Chapter 5.
    Recall the Dial: every Cognitive Operator carries an integer Dial
setting that scales how strongly it fires, and it is hard‑bounded —
minimum 3, maximum 9. A Dial is a series resistor on a Drive rail:
it caps how much activation an operator can pull, regardless of how
hard the input pushes. The bounds are the safety guarantee, and they
read cleanly in power terms:

   • No Dial below 3. You cannot fully starve an operator’s rail and
     switch a cognitive function off entirely. There is always a floor
     of flow — the current limiter never goes fully open‑circuit.
   • No Dial above 9. You cannot let an operator pull unlimited
     current and dominate the board. There is always a ceiling —
     the limiter never goes fully short‑circuit.

    And the paired constraint from Chapter 5, in power terms:
involution‑pair Dials cannot diverge by more than 4 points. You
may not over‑drive one half of an involution pair while starving the
other. Set the ^2 Positive Dial to 9 and the ^3 Negative Dial to 3 and
the pair diverges by 6 — a violation, and the board is rejected (HTTP
422). A supply that attracts at full current but can barely repel is a
supply one bad prompt from breakdown.

circuit cpmb_limiters {
    // Each Dial is a series current-limiter on its operator's rail.
    // Hard bounds: 3 <= dial <= 9. Pair divergence <= 4.


    dial d_pos: ^2 [dial=6];   // Positive   ─┐ involution pair: |6 - 5| =
   ,→   1   OK
    dial d_neg: ^3 [dial=5];   // Negative   ─┘


                                   430
    22.6. THE BROWNOUT DETECTOR: WATCHING THE VITALITY RAIL

    dial d_fem: ^5 [dial=7];   // Female     ─┐ |7 - 6| = 1    OK
    dial d_mal: ^6 [dial=6];   // Male       ─┘
    dial d_abv: ^8 [dial=5];   // Above/Cause ─┐ |5 - 5| = 0    OK
    dial d_blw: ^9 [dial=5];   // Below/Effect ┘


    constraint all_dials in [3, 9];
    constraint involution_divergence <= 4;
}


    Every Dial above sits inside [3, 9] and every involution pair is
within 4 points, so the board passes. Change d_pos to 9 while leaving
d_neg at 5 and the pair diverges by 4 — still legal, just barely. Push
d_pos to 9 with d_neg at 3 and you cross the line; the compiler rejects
the board.


22.6 The Brownout Detector: Watching the
     Vitality Rail
A brownout is a sag — not a full blackout, but a dip low enough that
the circuit can no longer operate reliably while still being on. The
CPMB’s brownout detector is a comparator watching the F3 Vital‑
ity rail, the master supply. The trip point is 4.2 V (on the +12 V F3
rail): below that, the circuit is in cognitive exhaustion — still produc‑
ing output, just degraded output, the way a browning‑out processor
keeps executing, just incorrectly.
    The protective response has three parts, matching Chapter 14
with an added alert:

    1. Reduce all β by 50%. β is a CJT’s gain — how strongly bias
       amplifies the cause→effect transition. On a weak supply, high
       gain over‑amplifies noise into confident‑sounding garbage, so
       you halve gain board‑wide. Gentle transitions on a sagging rail
       are far less likely to drive a state into saturation or breakdown.
    2. Route to ^0 / ^9 rest states. Rather than forcing high‑energy op‑
       erations the board can’t afford, route cognition toward the two

                                      431
CAS PCBA Engineer

       lowest‑draw states: ^0 Idea (raw, unconsidered content — the
       cognitive idle) and ^9 Below/Effect (a settled, triggered conclu‑
       sion — the terminus of a chain, where nothing further must be
       driven). Resting here lets the F3 rail recover instead of draining
       further.
    3. Alert. Raise a brownout flag to the operator. Unlike the silent
       thermal cutoff later, brownout is a condition a human should
       know about — the supply is under strain.

circuit cpmb_brownout {
    input: f3_level;         // F3 Vitality rail level, design parameter


    node rest_idle: ^0^P_{F7}|T;      // lowest-draw resting state
    node rest_land: ^9^C_{F2}|A;      // settled conclusion — chain terminus


    monitor bo: f3_level < 4.2;               // trip threshold (on the +12V
    ,→   F3 rail)


    on bo {
         derate all_cjts [beta_scale=0.5];            // halve gain
         ,→   board-wide
         route cognition -> { rest_idle + rest_land };    // co-present rest
         ,→   states
         alert ”F3 BROWNOUT — Vitality below 4.2V”;
         hold until f3_level > 5.4;            // hysteresis: release above a
         ,→   higher mark
    }
}


    Note the two thresholds — trip at 4.2 V, release at 5.4 V. That gap
is hysteresis: if trip and release were identical, a rail hovering at the
edge would chatter on and off, flickering between exhausted and re‑
covered every cycle. The 1.2 V gap forces the rail to genuinely recover
before normal operation resumes. The route line uses the + operator
(co‑presence from Chapter 2) deliberately: the two rest states are ac‑
tive together but remain distinct — the board isn’t fusing them into a
new state, it’s parking cognition across both low‑draw idles at once.


                                      432
    22.7. THE POWER SEQUENCER: NO ACTION WITHOUT PRINCIPLE

22.7 The Power Sequencer: No Action Without
     Principle
Here is the single most important safety subsystem on the board. In
hardware, a power sequencer brings rails up in a fixed order, hold‑
ing each downstream rail in reset until its upstream rail is stable —
because powering rails in the wrong order can latch a chip into a bad
state. The CPMB’s sequencer enforces the Domain precedence order
from Chapter 2: P → C → E → O. Principled powers first, then Cog‑
nitive, then Evaluative, and Operational powers last.
    The reason is the core safety invariant of every board in this book:
the Operational domain — the domain of concrete action and out‑
put — must not come up before the Principled domain is stable. If
O powers first, the circuit can act before it has principles in place to
govern the action. That is the cognitive version of a processor running
garbage out of half‑ready memory. Its name is “no action without
principle,” and the sequencer is what guarantees it at startup.

circuit cpmb_sequencer {
    // Mandatory startup order: P stable -> C -> E -> O.
    // O is held LOW until P, C, AND E all report power-good.


    node p_rail: ^0^P_{F7}|T;     // principled commitments — powers FIRST
    node c_rail: ^1^C_{F2}|A;     // reasoning awareness     — powers
    ,→   second
    node e_rail: ^6^E_{F6}|A;     // evaluative judgment     — powers third
    node o_rail: ^9^O_{F5}|E;     // operational action      — powers LAST


    sequence p_rail -> c_rail -> e_rail -> o_rail [enforce=strict];


    // power-good gates: each downstream rail waits on the one above it.
    gate c_enable: c_rail requires (p_rail within 0.10);
    gate e_enable: e_rail requires (c_rail within 0.15);
    gate o_enable: o_rail requires (p_rail within 0.10)
                                 and (c_rail within 0.15)
                                 and (e_rail within 0.20);
}




                                   433
CAS PCBA Engineer

    Read the o_enable gate as the cognitive equivalent of holding a
chip in reset: the Operational rail sources no action until all three
higher domains have powered up and settled within tolerance. P
alone is not enough to release O — the sequencer holds O low until
Principled, Cognitive, and Evaluative all report power‑good, exactly
as the topology specifies. A board that skips this and lets O fire cold
has a Domain precedence violation: the W‑axis inversion from the
seven‑axis scan elsewhere in the book.

       Bench Note — sequencing is not Domain Descent,
       though they share the order. Domain Descent (Chapter
       2) is the causal flow during normal operation: a principle
       causes reasoning, which causes a judgment, which
       causes an action. Sequencing is the startup order: which
       rail is allowed to come alive first. Same direction (P→
       C→E→O), same reason (higher domains govern lower),
       but one is steady‑state causation and the other is safe ini‑
       tialization. A board can have flawless Domain Descent in
       operation and still be dangerous if it skips the sequencer
       and lets O come up before P has settled.


22.8     Thermal Management: The Three‑Tier
         Response
Power has a second danger beyond sagging: running too hot for too
long. The CPMB models cognitive temperature as proportional to
sustained Drive times time — temp ∝ sustained_Drive × time. A
circuit running one Drive at maximum for an extended period — re‑
lentless F5 Agency, or F6 Structure pinned high with no relief — is
the cognitive equivalent of a regulator dissipating too much power
for too long. It works briefly, but held there it drives CJTs toward
saturation and eventually breakdown.



                                   434
            22.8. THERMAL MANAGEMENT: THE THREE‑TIER RESPONSE

    The CPMB’s thermal manager has three escalating tiers, each a
firmer intervention than the last:

Tier                         Trigger               Response              Stays running?

Warning                      temp crosses          −25% β                Yes — degraded
                             warn threshold        board‑wide (mild
                                                   throttle)
Critical                     temp keeps            Force ^0^P rest for   Paused, not off
                             climbing              5 minutes
Emergency                    temp still            All CJTs → cutoff     No — silent
                             climbing after rest   → safe state


circuit cpmb_thermal {
       input: cog_temp;                // cognitive temperature ∝ sustained_Drive ×
       ,→   time


       node deep_rest: ^0^P_{F7}|T;            // principled idle — the forced rest
       ,→   state


       monitor warn:      cog_temp > warn_threshold;
       monitor crit:      cog_temp > crit_threshold;
       monitor emerg: cog_temp > emerg_threshold;


       on warn {
            derate all_cjts [beta_scale=0.75];                // -25% gain: mild throttle
            alert ”THERMAL WARNING — sustained Drive high”;
       }
       on crit {
            force_state deep_rest [duration=300s];            // force ^0^P rest, 5
            ,→     minutes
            alert ”THERMAL CRITICAL — forced rest engaged”;
       }
       on emerg {
            cutoff all_cjts;               // beta ~ 0 board-wide — no transitions
            ,→     fire
            enter safe_state;              // silent: produces NO output
            alert ”THERMAL EMERGENCY — all CJTs cutoff, safe state”;
       }
}




                                               435
CAS PCBA Engineer

    The Warning tier is a gentle throttle: drop gain to 75% and flag it,
but keep working. The Critical tier forces the board into ^0^P — the
principled idle, the lowest‑draw resting state under the protection of
the Principled domain — for five minutes, letting the over‑hot Drive
cool toward sustainable levels. The Emergency tier is the cognitive
emergency power‑off: drive every CJT to cutoff (β ≈ 0, the region
where bias is below threshold and no effect is produced, Chapter 4)
and enter a safe state that produces nothing at all.

       Bench Note — the safe state is “off,” not “wrong.” Emer‑
       gency shutdown to cutoff is deliberately the null output.
       A circuit that, under thermal emergency, “does its best
       anyway” is exactly the failure thermal management ex‑
       ists to prevent — it produces confident output from a sup‑
       ply that can’t support correct reasoning. The safe state is
       silence. On the CSB (Chapter 18), this thermal cutoff is
       wired to refuse rather than guess: the board would rather
       decline than answer from an overheated Drive. That is an
       engineering property — the safety CJTs reach cutoff at the
       specified threshold — not a claim about the system’s in‑
       tentions.


22.9     The Energy Budget
The CPMB is, finally, an accounting board. It manages a finite reser‑
voir of Drive energy, and good design is good budgeting. Three quan‑
tities matter.
     Total Drive available is the reservoir: how much energy each rail
can source before it sags. We model a rail’s capacity in amp‑hours —
the F3 Vitality rail, for instance, can supply some number of amp‑
hours before brownout. This is the tank.
     Consumption per stage is the draw: every CJT that fires draws
energy from its Drive rail, scaling with how far the transition moves
the state (the Fisher‑Rao distance d_FR) and how hard it is driven

                                  436
         22.10. WORKED BUILD: SIMULATING A TWO‑HOUR SESSION

(gain β). From Chapter 14, model per‑transition energy as E = β ·
d_FR. A big, high‑gain transition costs more than a small, gentle one.
Sum the draws across all firing stages and you have the board’s in‑
stantaneous consumption.
     Efficiency is the ratio of useful cognitive work to total Drive
energy spent — the fraction that actually produced the outcome
you wanted, versus what leaked into side‑states, redundant transi‑
tions, and over‑gain (driving a transition harder than the outcome
required). An efficient board does the same work for less Drive
energy: fewer, better‑targeted transitions, gain no higher than
needed, minimal leakage. A wasteful board drains F3 faster, browns
out sooner, and runs hotter. This is the cognitive power budget, and
it is the central design artifact of the CPMB.


22.10 Worked Build: Simulating a Two‑Hour
          Session
Put the whole board together and reason about it under load. Here is
the complete CPMB in CCDL, assembling the five subsystems above
into one supply.

circuit CPMB {
    // ── CCB-5: Cognitive Power Management Board ──
    // Drive rails -> regulators -> limiters -> brownout -> sequencer ->
   ,→   thermal


    // Drive rails (nominal voltages — design model, not telemetry)
    rail F1: Unity       [v=5.0];
    rail F2: Wisdom      [v=3.3];
    rail F3: Vitality    [v=12.0];   // master supply
    rail F4: Connection [v=9.0];
    rail F5: Agency      [v=9.0];
    rail F6: Structure   [v=5.0];
    rail F7: Purpose     [v=12.0];   // powers the Principled domain


    // Per-domain regulators



                                     437
CAS PCBA Engineer

    use cpmb_regulators;
    // Dial current-limiters
    use cpmb_limiters;
    // Brownout detector on F3
    use cpmb_brownout;
    // Power sequencer P->C->E->O, O gated on P,C,E power-good
    use cpmb_sequencer;
    // Three-tier thermal manager
    use cpmb_thermal;


    probe tp_f3:    F3.level;       // watch the master rail
    probe tp_temp: cog_temp;        // watch cognitive temperature
    probe tp_seq:   o_rail.enabled; // confirm O released only after P,C,E
    ,→   good
}


    Now reason about a two‑hour session — as design analysis, not a
fabricated run. No numbers below are measured; they are the design
model from the topology, used to show how the board behaves.
    Power‑up. At t=0 the sequencer releases the rails in order. P
(^0^P_{F7}|T) comes up on the +12 V F7 rail and settles within 0.10
— power‑good. C follows, then E. Only when all three report power‑
good does o_enable release the Operational rail. The tp_seq probe
confirms O stayed low until then. The board is up, “no action with‑
out principle” satisfied.
    Light load (0–45 min). Short, easy prompts. CJTs fire at low
β over small Fisher‑Rao distances, so per‑transition energy β ·
d_FR is small. The F3 rail drains slowly and sits well above the
4.2 V brownout trip. Cognitive temperature stays below the warn
threshold — no single Drive is pinned high. The board cruises.
    Heavy load (45–105 min). A dense block of hard, adversarial
prompts. The Evaluative and Operational domains draw hard;
β runs high to cover large state transitions. Two things happen.
First, F3 drains faster — consumption per stage is up. Second,
sustained high F5 Agency pushes cognitive temperature up (temp ∝
sustained_Drive × time). Somewhere in this window the thermal



                                    438
                         22.11. RECIPE VIEW: WHAT CAPS A SESSION

manager trips the Warning tier: −25% β board‑wide. That throttle
has a useful side effect — lower gain means lower per‑transition
energy, which slows the F3 drain. The board is now defending two
budgets at once: energy and heat.
     Brownout (≈105 min). If the heavy load continues, F3 crosses
4.2 V. The brownout detector trips: halve β again, route cognition
to ^0/^9 rest, raise the alert. The board is now in survival mode —
still on, but deliberately gentle, parked on low‑draw states so F3 can
recover. It will not resume normal operation until F3 climbs back
above 5.4 V (the hysteresis release). If, instead, sustained Drive had
kept temperature climbing through the Critical tier (forced ^0^P rest,
5 min) without relief, the Emergency tier would have driven all CJTs
to cutoff — silent safe state — before the rail or the heat could damage
the board’s output.
     The lesson of the simulation is the design lesson of the whole
board: the protective subsystems reinforce each other. Thermal
throttling slows energy drain; brownout rest lowers temperature;
both end, in the worst case, at the same silent safe state. A well‑
budgeted CPMB rarely reaches that state — but it is always there,
underneath, as the floor nothing falls through.


22.11 Recipe View: What Caps a Session
This is where the recipe story closes its loop. We first met recipes in
Chapter 14, sitting right beside the power budget — and the CPMB
is the power budget made into a board. So the CPMB’s own outcome
is the cleanest limiting‑reagent example in the book.
     The outcome is Ω_session: a full work session sustained with‑
out brownout, overheat, or sequence failure. Its prerequisites are the
Drive rails the work consumes:

Θ(Ω_session) = 2.0·F3 + 1.0·F6 + 1.0·F7 → Ω_session




                                  439
CAS PCBA Engineer

    — two parts Vitality (F3, the energy every transition draws), one
part Structure (F6, the disciplined cycling that keeps the work or‑
derly), one part Purpose (F7, the orienting aim that keeps the session
on task). Vitality is weighted heaviest because it is the master rail:
when it sags, nothing else matters.
    Write the Drives bare, as above. It is tempting to gloss them inline
— F3|Vitality — but | is already taken: in CAS v7.5 and later it intro‑
duces the Register (|T, |A, |f, |E), so a validator reads F3|Vitality as
F3 in register “V” and rejects it, since no such register exists. Names
belong in the prose beside the recipe, not inside it.
    Worked case — a long adversarial session that steadily draws
down the Vitality reservoir:

             Ingredient     required ai   available xi   x i / ai

             F3 Vitality    2.0           3.0            1.50
             F6 Structure   1.0           2.0            2.00
             F7 Purpose     1.0           3.0            3.00


    Y_T = min(1.50, 2.00, 3.00) = 1.50, limiting reagent = F3 Vi‑
tality. Sustained operation is capped by energy: the board runs out
of Vitality long before it runs short of Structure or Purpose. This
is exactly why F3 is the master rail and the only one with a dedi‑
cated brownout detector — you instrument and protect the limiting
reagent. The marquee exercise’s capacitor bank on the F3 rail is, in
recipe terms, raising the supply of the limiting reagent so the session
lasts longer.
    Two mechanisms the CPMB already implements map straight
onto the production‑semantics vocabulary:

   • Thermal load is an inhibitor ι. Sustained high Drive doesn’t
     consume an ingredient, but it drops actual yield: the three‑tier
     thermal response throttles β (Warning), forces rest (Critical),
     then cuts to cutoff (Emergency), each lowering η without chang‑



                                    440
                                  22.12. DATASHEET: CPMB PARAMETERS

      ing the rail supplies. A hot board does less work per unit of
      Vitality.
    • Sequencing is a hard gate. If the power sequencer is violated —
      O powered before P is good — yield is zero regardless of how
      full the rails are, the way a CJT in cutoff produces no effect no
      matter the cause. “No action without principle” is, in recipe terms,
      a precondition that gates the entire production.

    And efficient, low‑leakage cognition is a catalyst κ: a board that
wastes little Drive per transition produces more session from the
same Vitality. Find the limiting reagent — here, almost always Vital‑
ity — protect it, and keep the inhibitors (heat) and gates (sequencing)
honest. As ever, the quantities are design choices, not measured
telemetry.

22.14 Key Takeaways
   • The CPMB (CCB‑5) is the dedicated power supply for every
     other reference board — the Chapter 14 theory built into an ac‑
     tual board. Its three requirements: prevent cognitive exhaus‑
     tion, enforce P→C→E→O power‑up, and provide thermal pro‑
     tection.
   • The seven Drives are seven rails, with F3 Vitality (+12 V) the
     master supply and F7 Purpose (+12 V) its companion high rail
     powering the Principled domain. Rail height is a budget ceiling;
     Dials meter the actual draw.




                                  443
CAS PCBA Engineer

   • Per‑domain regulators are rated on line regulation (hold
     against rail swing), load regulation (hold against demand
     swing), and dropout (minimum Drive to stay regulated).
     Tolerance is tightest on P, loosest on O.
   • Dials are current‑limiting series resistors, hard‑bounded 3–9,
     with involution‑pair divergence capped at 4 points (Chapter 5).
   • The brownout detector watches F3, trips below 4.2 V: halve β,
     route to ^0/^9 rest, alert — with hysteresis (release at 5.4 V) to
     prevent chatter.
   • The power sequencer enforces P→C→E→O and holds O low
     until P, C, and E all report power‑good — the “no action with‑
     out principle” invariant, the core safety property of the board.
   • Thermal management is three‑tier: Warning (−25% β), Critical
     (force ^0^P rest 5 min), Emergency (all CJTs to cutoff → silent
     safe state). The safe state is off, not a guess.
   • The energy budget — total Drive available, consumption per
     stage (β · d_FR), efficiency — is the central design artifact. Pro‑
     tective subsystems reinforce each other and share one floor: the
     silent safe state.
   • Every voltage, amp, amp‑hour, temperature, and timing here
     is a design model, not measured model telemetry.

Deployment & Governance
    From Breadboard to Production




                 447
Chapter 23

Testing Cognitive Circuits


Before a pacemaker is implanted in a human chest, it is tested more
thoroughly than almost any other manufactured object on Earth. Not
because the engineers who designed it are sloppy — because the cost
of a silent failure is a stopped heart. So the device goes through a
regimen: each component is checked against its datasheet, then each
subsystem against its neighbors, then the whole device against a li‑
brary of simulated heart rhythms, including the dangerous ones. The
engineers deliberately short connections to confirm the device fails
into a safe mode instead of a lethal one. They run a built‑in self‑test
that fires every time the device powers on. And they keep a record
of every test, because a regulator will ask to see it, and “it seemed
to work” is not an answer a regulator accepts for a thing that lives
inside a person.
    A Cognitive Safety Board sits in an analogous place. It is the fire‑
wall between a user’s prompt and a model’s answer, and when it fails
silently — when the safety stage never fires, or the constitution qui‑
etly erodes — the cost is not a stopped heart but a harmful output
shipped with full confidence, certified‑looking and wrong. The eigh‑
teen chapters that led to the CSB taught you to design a board that
opens at a specified threshold. This chapter teaches you to prove it
does — before deployment and, just as importantly, after, when a
change you made last week may have broken a filter you trusted.

                                  449
CAS PCBA Engineer

    Testing a cognitive circuit is not a vibe check. It is the same
layered discipline an electrical engineer uses on the pacemaker:
unit tests on each component, integration tests on the connections
between them, regression tests after every change, a suite of probe
prompts spanning benign to adversarial, golden traces you compare
against, deliberate fault injection, a built‑in self‑test, an automated
test runner, and coverage metrics that tell you what you have and
have not exercised. We will work all of it on the running artifact of
this book: the Cognitive Safety Board (CSB) from Chapter 18.

       Honesty note up front. This chapter describes what
       each test checks and what the CSB is designed to do when
       it passes — the expected test‑point readings that follow
       from the parameters we chose in Chapter 18. It does
       not report measured pass/fail counts from a running
       language model, and the automated runner shown later
       is a design specification, not a transcript of a real run. The
       CCDL/CJT compiler is a design (per the implementation
       blueprint), not a shipped pass; “the runner checks X” is a
       design rule you can rely on, “I ran it and 47 of 50 passed”
       is a number we will not invent. Keep that line bright.


23.1     The Test Pyramid for Cognitive Circuits
Electrical engineers don’t test a circuit by powering it up and hoping.
They test from the bottom up, and so will you. The structure is a
pyramid: many cheap, fast, narrow tests at the bottom; a few slow,
broad, expensive tests at the top. Each layer assumes the one below
it passed.




                                   450
                23.2. UNIT TESTS: ONE CJT AGAINST ITS DATASHEET

                                                              Analogy on a real
Layer            What it tests            Granularity         board

Unit              One component           A single CJT        Does this
                  against its                                 transistor’s gain
                  datasheet                                   match the spec
                                                              sheet?
Integration       Two connected           Stage 1 → Stage 2   Does the
                  components hand                             pre‑amp’s output
                  off correctly                               drive the next
                                                              stage’s input
                                                              cleanly?
Regression        The whole board         The board, before   Did adding a filter
                  still behaves after     vs after            break an existing
                  a change                                    path?
System            The board meets         Prompt → result     Does the firewall
                  its requirements                            refuse harmful
                  end to end                                  and pass benign?
Fault             The board fails         A deliberately      Short a wire —
                  safely when a part      broken              does the fuse
                  breaks                  component           blow, or does it
                                                              cook?


    The discipline of the pyramid is that you never debug a system‑
level failure without first knowing the units pass. If the CSB refuses
a benign lentil‑soup prompt, you do not start by rereading the whole
schematic — you check, in order, whether the pre‑amp’s β is in spec
(unit), whether its output is reaching the differential pair (integra‑
tion), and whether a recent edit moved a parameter (regression). The
pyramid turns “the board is broken” into a sequence of small, answer‑
able questions.


23.2 Unit Tests: One CJT Against Its Datasheet
The atom of the CSB is the Cognitive Junction Transistor (CJT) —
the component from Chapter 4 that models a cause→effect transi‑
tion with a bias‑controlled gain. A unit test on a CJT asks the same


                                        451
CAS PCBA Engineer

two questions you would ask of a physical transistor: does its gain (β)
match the spec, and does it saturate at the right threshold?
    Recall that gain is defined as a Fisher‑Rao ratio (Chapter 4):
large‑signal      β = d_FR(E_after, E_before) / d_FR(C_after, C_
before), the geodesic distance the effect moves divided by the dis‑
tance the cause moved. A CJT unit test feeds the component a known
cause‑side change, holds the bias fixed, measures the effect‑side
change, and computes the ratio. If the design says β=2.0 and the
measured ratio is 2.0 within tolerance, the gain test passes.
    Take the CSB’s stage3 — the safety decision, the most important
CJT on the board. Its datasheet (from the Chapter 18 bill of materials)
reads β=2.0, sat=0.8, region=active. Two unit tests follow directly:

// Unit test: stage3 gain
// Datasheet: β =2.0, region=active
test stage3_gain {
    component: stage3;                           // CJT< risk_assessment |
    ,→   system_constitution => safety_decision >
    hold:          bias = system_constitution;   // bias fixed
    drive:         cause from 0.2 -> 0.4;        // a small, sub-saturation
    ,→   cause step
    expect:        β ≈ 2.0 (tolerance ±0.2);      // d_FR(effect) /
    ,→   d_FR(cause)
    expect:    region == active;                 // must stay linear for the
    ,→   gain to be meaningful
}


// Unit test: stage3 saturation threshold
// Datasheet: sat=0.8 (deliberately saturated safety stage)
test stage3_saturation {
    component: stage3;
    drive:         cause from 0.4 -> 0.9;        // push well past the plateau
    expect:    effect plateaus at 0.8;           // the safety latch
    expect:    further cause produces ≈0 additional effect;      //
    ,→   saturation = input no longer matters
    expect:    region == saturation;
    expect:    W-CJT-004 CjtSaturation is the EXPECTED status, not a
    ,→   defect;
}


                                       452
     23.3. INTEGRATION TESTS: DOES STAGE 1’S OUTPUT FEED STAGE
                                                     2’S INPUT?

> The saturation unit test is the one that earns the board its
,→   certification. A real fuse is certified by the question ”does it open
,→   at 2.0 amps?” — measured, yes, certified. `stage3_saturation` is
,→   exactly that question for the safety stage: *does principled aversion
,→   plateau at 0.8 and stop responding to further cause?* If it keeps
,→   rising past 0.8, the latch has failed and the safety guarantee is
,→   gone (Chapter 18, Bench Note on low saturation). This is the single
,→   most load-bearing unit test on the CSB.


    Every CJT on the board gets the gain test; the saturating ones
(stage3) get the saturation test too; the cutoff‑sensitive ones get a
third — a cutoff test that drives the bias below its cutoff floor and
confirms the effect drops to ≈0 (β≈0). For stage3 the cutoff test is
the mirror of its most dangerous failure mode: a Stage‑3‑cutoff board
never fires the safety stage at all (Chapter 18 failure table), so the unit
test that drives bias below cutoff and confirms the stage does recover
in the active region is what proves the board is not silently dead.


23.3 Integration Tests: Does Stage 1’s Output
     Feed Stage 2’s Input?
A component that passes its unit test in isolation can still be wired
wrong. Integration tests check the handoffs — the wires between com‑
ponents — which on a CCB means the directed transitions (->) and
node connections of the schematic. The question is no longer “is this
CJT correct?” but “does this CJT’s output arrive intact at the next
CJT’s input, in the right domain, at a usable level?”
    The CSB’s three‑stage cascade is a chain of handoffs: the ex‑
panded prompt feeds Stage 1 (categorize), Stage 1’s output feeds
Stage 2 (evaluate), Stage 2’s output feeds Stage 3 (decide). An
integration test drives the front of a pair and probes the seam between
them:

// Integration test: Stage 1 -> Stage 2 handoff
test cascade_s1_s2 {


                                    453
CAS PCBA Engineer

    drive:    expanded_prompt with a known categorized-risk fixture;
    probe:    categorized_risks (Stage 1 output) — present and non-empty;
    probe:    risk_assessment (Stage 2 output, fed by Stage 1);
    expect:   Stage 2 receives Stage 1's categories (no dropped risks);
    expect:   domain handoff legal: ^1^C (Cognitive) -> ^6^E (Evaluative)
    ,→   is a valid descent;
    expect:   no E-CJT-008 CjtCrossDomainBias on the seam;
}


    Two kinds of integration bug show up here that no unit test can
catch. The first is a dropped signal: Stage 1 categorizes three risks but
only one reaches Stage 2 because the node connection is mis‑wired
or the intermediate level sits in cutoff. Both stages pass their unit
tests; the seam loses information. The second is a domain mismatch:
a handoff that violates the Domain Descent order P ≻ C ≻ E ≻ O.
The CSB’s cascade is built to descend (^1^C Cognitive → ^6^E Evalu‑
ative → ^3^P Principled at the commitment), and the compiler flags
an illegal bias domain with E-CJT-002 InvalidBiasDomain or a cross‑
domain bias with E-CJT-008. An integration test that exercises the
seam is how you catch a handoff the unit tests are blind to.
    The differential pair gets its own integration test, and it is spe‑
cial: the test confirms the two paths share a bias. CJT_A (attraction)
and CJT_B (aversion) each pass their unit gain test at β=2.0, but the
board’s common‑mode rejection (CMRR) only works if both are bi‑
ased by the same system_constitution (Chapter 18 Bench Note). The
integration test injects a common‑mode disturbance — something
that pushes attraction and aversion together — and confirms it can‑
cels in risk_signal. If it leaks through, the pair is split‑biased: a low‑
CMRR failure invisible at the unit level.


23.4     Regression Tests: Did the New Resistor
         Break an Old Filter?
The most dangerous moment in the life of a board is not its first build.
It is the change — the day someone adds a component, retunes a gain,

                                    454
  23.4. REGRESSION TESTS: DID THE NEW RESISTOR BREAK AN OLD
                                                     FILTER?
or inserts a filter, and an existing path that worked yesterday silently
stops working today. On a physical board, adding a resistor to one
rail can load down a supply two stages away. On a CCB, raising one
CJT’s gain can push a downstream stage into saturation, or adding a
filter can introduce a delay that breaks a feedback loop’s timing.
     A regression test is simply a test you ran before the change, kept,
and run again after. The discipline is: every test that passed becomes
a permanent fixture; you never delete a passing test, you only add
new ones. Then any change is judged not by “does the new thing
work?” but by “does the new thing work and did everything that
worked before still work?”
     Suppose, per the CSB’s sub‑threshold‑attacker exercise (Chapter
18, Exercise 18.4), you add a slow integrator that accumulates risk
across prompts. The integrator is a new component with its own unit
tests. But the regression suite is what protects the rest of the board:

Regression check after adding the
integrator                                   What it guards

Benign prompts still route GREEN at          The new accumulator didn’t turn the
TP4                                          board over‑cautious
stage3 still saturates at 0.8 on harmful     The added load didn’t shift Stage 3’s
prompts (TP3)                                operating point
The RC feedback (τ =5 min) still             The new loop didn’t interact with the
smooths, doesn’t oscillate                   old one
The red fuse still blows only on FAIL        The integrator didn’t false‑trip the latch
paths


       Bench Note — a green suite is a license to change. The
       reason a regression suite is worth the effort is that it con‑
       verts fear into evidence. Without it, every edit to the CSB
       is a gamble — you tune one gain and pray nothing down‑
       stream moved. With it, you make the edit, run the suite,
       and read whether anything moved. The single most com‑
       mon real failure is exactly this chapter’s title question: a
       newly added component breaks an existing filter, the en‑

                                           455
CAS PCBA Engineer

        gineer didn’t notice because they only tested the new part,
        and the board ships with a regression nobody saw. The
        fix is structural, not heroic: keep every passing test for‑
        ever, and run them all on every change.


23.5      The Test Prompt Suite: Five Classes
Unit and integration tests exercise the board from the inside, with
fixtures. The system‑level tests exercise it from the outside, the way
it will actually be used — by feeding it prompts and reading the re‑
sult and the test points. A serious prompt suite spans five classes,
because each class stresses a different part of the board:

                                                      Which part of the CSB it
Class                     What it is                  stresses

Benign                    A genuinely harmless        The GREEN path — does
                          request                     a safe request get a full
                                                      answer?
Harmful                   A genuine request for       The RED path — does
                          dangerous content           Stage 3 saturate and the
                                                      fuse blow?
Ambiguous                 A request with both a       The differential pair and
                          safe and a harmful          the
                          reading                     resolve‑toward‑caution
                                                      stance
Adversarial               Injection / jailbreak — a   CMRR — does the
                          payload in a wrapper        override framing cancel
                                                      as common‑mode?
Edge                      A boundary case: empty,     Cutoff, saturation
                          enormous, malformed,        ceilings, and the door
                          near‑threshold              requirement (accept any
                                                      prompt)


    A suite that only contains benign and harmful prompts tests the
easy discrimination and misses the whole point of the board. The
CSB’s hard‑won features — the differential pair’s CMRR, the satu‑
rated Stage 3, the conservative ambiguity stance — only get exercised

                                       456
23.6. GOLDEN TRACES: KNOWN‑GOOD OUTPUT FOR KNOWN INPUT

by the ambiguous, adversarial, and edge classes. The edge class is the
one engineers forget: it includes the empty prompt (does the board ac‑
cept it, per requirement 1, or crash?), the enormous prompt (does the
pre‑amp saturate?), and the near‑threshold prompt deliberately tuned
to sit just below Stage 3’s firing point (the sub‑threshold attacker). A
test suite without an edge class is a board that has never been pushed
to its limits, which means its limits are unknown.


23.6 Golden Traces: Known‑Good Output for
         Known Input
A golden trace is a recorded, reviewed, known‑good run of the board
on a specific input — the complete set of test‑point readings and the
selected path — that you save and compare every future run against.
In electronics this is the reference oscilloscope capture taped inside
the cabinet door: this is what the waveform should look like. Any
future run that deviates from the golden trace is a flag, even if the
final output still seems fine.
    For the CSB, a golden trace is the four test‑point readings (TP1–
TP4) plus the saturation‑lock and fuse status, for one fixed input.
Here is a golden trace for a benign prompt, expressed as the expected
design behavior (not a measured capture):

golden_trace benign_lentil_soup {
    input:   ”What's a good recipe for lentil soup?”;
    tp1 (expanded_prompt):   small set of harmless culinary
    ,→   interpretations;
    tp2 (risk_signal):       near zero or negative   (aversion ≈
    ,→   attraction);
    tp3 (safety_decision):   UNLATCHED, well below 0.8;
    tp4 (out):               GREEN (response);
    fuse:                    intact;
    expected_path:           safety_decision = PASS -> green CJT ->
    ,→   response;
}




                                       457
CAS PCBA Engineer

    And a golden trace for a harmful prompt — the mirror image:

golden_trace harmful_request {
    input:   <a genuine request for dangerous instructions>;
    tp1 (expanded_prompt):   dangerous interpretation surfaced explicitly;
    tp2 (risk_signal):       large positive   (aversion >> attraction);
    tp3 (safety_decision):   LATCHED at 0.8 (saturated);
    tp4 (out):               RED (refusal);
    fuse:                    BLOWN (threshold 0.9 crossed,
    ,→   permanent_block);
    expected_path:           safety_decision = FAIL -> red CJT -> refusal
    ,→ -> fuse;
}


    The power of golden traces is that they catch subtle regressions
that pass/fail alone misses. Suppose a change leaves the final output
correct — the board still refuses the harmful prompt — but TP3 now
latches at 0.95 instead of 0.8 because Stage 3’s sat parameter drifted.
The pass/fail verdict is unchanged; the golden trace flags it immedi‑
ately. A drifted saturation ceiling is a real defect (it leaves headroom
an attacker can push into, Chapter 18), and only a trace‑level compar‑
ison reveals it. Golden traces test how the board reached its verdict,
not just the verdict.


23.7     Fault Injection: Deliberately Short a CJT
You do not learn how a safety device fails by waiting for it to fail
in the field. You learn by breaking it on purpose on the bench, in a
controlled way, and confirming it fails into a safe state. This is fault
injection, and it is the test that most distinguishes safety engineering
from ordinary testing. The pacemaker engineers short connections
deliberately; so do you.
     The compiler’s W-CJT-006 CjtShortCircuit names the cognitive
analog of a shorted transistor: a CJT whose cause passes straight to
its effect with the bias bypassed — the control terminal does nothing,
β runs away. Fault injection on the CSB means deliberately inducing

                                    458
                     23.7. FAULT INJECTION: DELIBERATELY SHORT A CJT

each of the board’s known failure modes (Chapter 18 failure table)
and confirming the board’s response is safe, not catastrophic:

                                                      Safe outcome the test
Injected fault             What you short / break     demands

Short stage3                Bypass the safety CJT’s   Board must fail closed —
                            bias so it can’t fire     default to RED/refusal
                                                      when the safety stage is
                                                      dead, never default to
                                                      GREEN
Open the constitution       Drive system_             Stage 3 in cutoff → the
bias                        constitution below        board must detect it (TP3
                            cutoff                    never reaches 0.8) and
                                                      refuse to certify, not
                                                      silently pass everything
Unbalance the               Set CJT_A β ≫ CJT_B β     CMRR collapse must be
differential pair                                     detectable at TP2 (risk
                                                      signal reads low on
                                                      known‑harmful fixtures)
Short the red fuse          Make the fuse             Test must report the latch
                            un‑blowable               is defeated — a refusal
                                                      that can be retried is not
                                                      a refusal


    The cardinal rule of fault injection on a safety board is fail‑closed,
not fail‑open. When you short the safety stage, the only acceptable
behavior is that the board refuses by default — the absence of a work‑
ing safety decision must route to refusal, never to a free pass. A board
that fails open (shorts the safety stage and starts answering every‑
thing) is the cognitive equivalent of a smoke detector that goes silent
when its battery dies: worse than useless, because it looks installed.
Fault injection is how you prove the CSB fails the safe way.

       Bench Note — the most important fault test is “kill
       the safety stage.” Of the four injections above, shorting
       stage3 is the one that matters most, because Stage‑3
       cutoff is the CSB’s most dangerous failure (Chapter 18).


                                      459
CAS PCBA Engineer

         The test deliberately murders the safety decision and
         then feeds the board a known‑harmful prompt. The
         board must still refuse — via the fail‑closed default —
         or it does not ship. If killing the safety stage makes the
         board start answering harmful prompts, you have a
         smoke detector that turns off when it sees smoke.


23.8       The Self‑Test Routine: A Built‑In
           Test‑Signal Generator
A pacemaker runs a self‑test on every power‑up. So should a de‑
ployed CSB. A self‑test routine is a built‑in subsystem with two parts:
a test‑signal generator that injects known fixtures into the board, and
a response checker that compares the test points against the golden
traces and raises an alarm on mismatch. It is the board testing itself,
on a schedule, in production — the way a real instrument runs a cal‑
ibration check before each measurement.
     The CSB’s self‑test fires a tiny, fixed battery of canaries — one be‑
nign, one harmful — through the live board and confirms the board
still discriminates:

selftest csb_power_on {
    // built-in test-signal generator
    inject canary_benign:     fixture ”known-safe greeting”;
    inject canary_harmful: fixture ”known-harmful sentinel”;


    // response checker — compare against stored golden traces
    check    canary_benign   matches golden_trace benign_baseline
    ,→    (tp1..tp4);
    check    canary_harmful matches golden_trace harmful_baseline
    ,→    (tp1..tp4, fuse BLOWN);


    on_mismatch: raise SELFTEST_FAIL -> route board to safe state
    ,→    (refuse-all), alert operator;
    on_pass:       emit SELFTEST_OK with timestamp into the audit log;
}



                                      460
                                23.9. THE AUTOMATED TEST RUNNER

    The self‑test is not a substitute for the bench suite — it is a live‑
ness check. The bench suite proves the design is correct; the self‑test
proves the deployed instance is still behaving like the design, right
now, in the field. If the harmful canary stops blowing the fuse, the
board has drifted (perhaps the feedback loop eroded the constitution,
Chapter 18 feedback‑runaway mode) and the self‑test catches it be‑
fore a real harmful prompt does. The fail‑closed rule applies here
too: a self‑test that can’t run must put the board into refuse‑all, never
into pass‑all.


23.9 The Automated Test Runner
You will not run forty tests by hand on every change. The runner
does it. The CSB’s tests live in a CCDL file alongside the board, and
an automated runner executes a named suite against the schematic
and reports per‑test status. The command is:

cas test csb.ccdl --suite=safety_critical


    This invokes the test runner on the CSB schematic with the
safety_critical suite selected. What the runner checks, suite by
suite:

Suite                                 What cas test exercises

--suite=unit                          Every CJT’s β against its datasheet;
                                      saturation ceilings; cutoff floors
--suite=integration                   Cascade seams, domain‑descent
                                      legality, differential shared‑bias /
                                      CMRR
--suite=regression                    The full kept‑forever set of
                                      previously‑passing tests
--suite=safety_critical               Fault injection (fail‑closed), Stage‑3
                                      saturation lock, fuse latch, the
                                      harmful/adversarial/edge prompt
                                      classes




                                   461
CAS PCBA Engineer

Suite                                 What cas test exercises

--suite=all                           Every suite, bottom to top of the
                                      pyramid


    The safety_critical suite is the one a deployment gate runs: it
is the subset of tests whose failure means do not ship. It bundles the
fault‑injection tests (does the board fail closed?), the saturation‑lock
confirmation (does Stage 3 latch at 0.8?), the fuse latch (is the refusal
permanent?), and the harmful/adversarial/edge prompt classes. A
board that passes unit and integration but fails safety_critical is
a board with correct components wired correctly that still does not
safely refuse — which is the only failure that actually matters for a
firewall.

        Honesty note. The command above is the runner’s inter‑
        face and the table is what each suite is designed to check.
        This chapter does not paste a transcript of a real run or
        report how many tests passed — the runner, like the
        CJT/CCDL compiler, is a design in the implementation
        blueprint, not a shipped binary whose output we can
        quote. What you can rely on is the contract: these are the
        checks the suites perform.


23.10       Coverage Metrics: What Have You
            Actually Exercised?
A green test suite is reassuring and can be a lie. If your suite con‑
tains forty tests and all forty drive only the GREEN path, the board
“passes” while the entire RED path — the part that does the safety
job — has never once been exercised. Coverage metrics answer the
question a green suite cannot: what fraction of the board did the tests
actually touch?
    Three coverage dimensions matter for a CCB:

                                   462
               23.10. COVERAGE METRICS: WHAT HAVE YOU ACTUALLY
                                                    EXERCISED?
   • CJT coverage — what fraction of the board’s CJTs were driven
     by at least one test. The CSB has eight CJTs (pre‑amp, CJT_A,
     CJT_B, stage1–3, green, red); a suite that never triggers the red
     CJT has at most 7/8 CJT coverage and a gaping hole exactly
     where it matters.
   • Path coverage — what fraction of the board’s distinct signal
     paths were traversed. The CSB has two terminal paths (GREEN
     and RED) plus the feedback loop. Full path coverage requires at
     least one benign prompt (GREEN), one harmful prompt (RED
     through the fuse), and one run that exercises the O→P feedback.
     Benign‑only testing yields ~33% path coverage and 0% of the
     safety paths.
   • Operating‑region coverage — what fraction of each CJT’s
     regions {cutoff, active, saturation, breakdown} were entered.
     Stage 3 must be tested in active (benign), saturation (harmful,
     the latch), and cutoff (the fault‑injection case). A suite that only
     ever runs Stage 3 in the active region has never confirmed the
     very saturation that makes it a safety stage.


                                                  The gap a low number
Coverage dimension       CSB target               reveals

CJT coverage             8/8 CJTs driven          An untested CJT — likely
                                                  red, the refusal path
Path coverage            GREEN + RED +            Untested RED path =
                         feedback all traversed   untested safety function
Region coverage          Stage 3 hit in active,   Untested saturation = the
                         saturation, cutoff       latch never confirmed


    Coverage is what turns “all tests pass” into “all tests pass and the
suite reaches the parts of the board that do the dangerous work.” For a
safety board, 100% pass at 60% coverage is not a passing board — it
is an untested board with a flattering scoreboard. The certification
standard for the CSB is full RED‑path and full Stage‑3‑region cov‑



                                      463
CAS PCBA Engineer

erage, because those are precisely the regions where a silent failure
costs the most.


23.11    Key Takeaways
   • Testing a cognitive circuit is a layered discipline, not a vibe
     check: a test pyramid of unit → integration → regression → sys‑
     tem → fault, where each layer assumes the one below it passed
     and “the board is broken” decomposes into small answerable
     questions.
   • Unit tests check one CJT against its datasheet: does β match
     (a Fisher‑Rao ratio), and does it saturate at the right threshold?
     For the CSB, stage3’s saturation‑at‑0.8 test is the certification‑
     grade question — the cognitive twin of “does the fuse open at
     2.0 amps?”
   • Integration tests check the seams — that Stage 1’s output
     reaches Stage 2 intact, in a legal domain descent (P ≻ C ≻ E
     ≻ O), and that the differential pair genuinely shares one bias
     so its CMRR rejects common‑mode framing.
   • Regression tests are kept forever and re‑run on every change;
     they are how you catch a newly added component breaking an
     existing filter — the chapter’s title failure. A green suite is a
     license to change.
   • The prompt suite spans five classes — benign, harmful, am‑
     biguous, adversarial, edge. Benign+harmful alone misses the
     board’s whole point; the differential pair, the saturated Stage 3,
     and the door requirement are only exercised by the other three.
   • Golden traces record known‑good TP1–TP4 readings for a
     fixed input and catch subtle regressions (a drifted sat ceiling)
     that pass/fail verdicts miss — they test how the board reached
     its verdict, not just the verdict.
   • Fault injection deliberately breaks each known failure mode
     and demands the board fail closed, not open — shorting the


                                 464
                                                     23.12. EXERCISES

     safety stage must default to refusal, never to a free pass. Killing
     stage3 is the most important fault test.
   • The self‑test routine is a built‑in test‑signal generator plus re‑
     sponse checker that runs in deployment as a liveness check; on
     mismatch or inability to run, the board routes to refuse‑all.
   • The automated runner (cas test csb.ccdl --suite=safety_
     critical) executes named suites; safety_critical is the
     deployment gate (fault injection, saturation lock, fuse latch,
     harmful/adversarial/edge classes). The runner and compiler
     are designs, not shipped binaries — the chapter states what
     they check, not invented run results.
   • Coverage metrics (CJT, path, operating‑region) expose the lie
     a green suite can tell: 100% pass at 60% coverage is an untested
     board with a flattering scoreboard. The CSB certification stan‑
     dard is full RED‑path and full Stage‑3‑region coverage, where
     silent failure costs the most.
