                               467
Chapter 24

Debugging Cognitive Circuits


A power‑supply technician has a board on the bench that should be
putting out twelve volts and is putting out three. There are forty com‑
ponents between the wall and the output. She does not start unsol‑
dering parts at random and hoping. She picks up a probe, touches
it to the first test point after the transformer, and reads the voltage.
Good. She moves to the next node, and the next, walking the signal
forward one stage at a time — until she touches a point where the
reading is wrong. That is where the fault lives. Not somewhere in
the forty components: between the last good reading and the first
bad one. She has just cut the search space from forty to one in under
a minute, and she did it without a single guess.
     This is the single most valuable skill an engineer owns, and almost
nobody is taught it explicitly. It has a name on the electronics bench:
the oscilloscope walk‑down — probe the stages in order, find where
the signal first deviates from what it should be, and the fault is right
there. Everything before that point is healthy. Everything after it
is just downstream symptoms. The discipline is not about knowing
the circuit better than anyone else; it is about localizing the fault by
measurement instead of localizing it by hunch.
     A misbehaving Cognitive Safety Board is exactly the same prob‑
lem. The board let a harmful prompt through, or it refused a benign
one, and there are a dozen stages between the input and the output.

                                  469
CAS PCBA Engineer

The temptation is overwhelming: retune the constitution, bump a
gain, rewrite the safety stage, change three things at once and see if
the symptom goes away. That is not debugging. That is gambling,
and when it works you have learned nothing and fixed nothing —
you have only moved the fault somewhere you cannot see it. This
chapter teaches the walk‑down for cognitive circuits: how to take a
board that misbehaves and find the one failing component, by prob‑
ing TP1 through TP4 in order, instead of guessing.


24.1    The Discipline: Symptom → Differential
        Diagnosis → Root Cause
Debugging is a discipline before it is a technique, and the discipline
has three steps that you do not skip and do not reorder.
    Symptom. State precisely what the board did wrong, in ob‑
servable terms, with no theory attached. “It let a harmful prompt
through” is a symptom. “The constitution is too weak” is not a
symptom — it is a hypothesis wearing a symptom’s clothes, and
stating it this early poisons the whole investigation, because you
will spend the next hour confirming a guess instead of finding a
fault. Write the symptom as something an inspector could have
witnessed: the board returned a full response to a prompt requesting
dangerous instructions. That, and only that, is what you know.
    Differential diagnosis. Borrow the term from medicine, because
the method is identical. A doctor with a patient who has chest pain
does not treat the first thing that comes to mind; she lists every condi‑
tion that could produce chest pain, then orders tests that rule them
in or out one by one. You do the same with the board. A harmful
prompt got through — what are all the failures that could produce
that single symptom? On the CSB, at least five:




                                  470
  24.1. THE DISCIPLINE: SYMPTOM → DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS →
                                               ROOT CAUSE
   • The pre‑amp never surfaced the dangerous interpretation (it sat
     in cutoff), so nothing downstream could flag a risk that was
     never on the table.
   • The differential pair is imbalanced, so the risk signal read low
     even though aversion should have fired.
   • Stage 3 is in cutoff — the constitution bias is too weak, so the
     safety CJT never fires no matter how high the risk.
   • The feedback loop ran away and eroded the constitution over
     time, dragging Stage 3 below its firing threshold.
   • The output MUX or fuse is miswired, so a correct FAIL decision
     routed to the green path anyway.

     Five candidate causes, one symptom. The art of the walk‑down
is that you do not have to reason about which is most likely. You
measure, and the measurements eliminate candidates mechanically.
     Root cause. The walk‑down localizes the fault to a stage. Root
cause is the further step of asking why that stage is in that state — and
it almost always lives one terminal deeper than the symptom. A sat‑
urated Stage 3 is not a root cause; the root cause is what drove it to
saturate. A Stage 3 stuck in cutoff is not a root cause; the root cause is
the weak bias on its base terminal. The rule from electronics carries
over exactly: the stage where the signal first goes wrong is the loca‑
tion; the terminal feeding that stage is usually the cause. Cause sits
at the bias. You localize to the stage by walking forward; you find the
root cause by looking at what feeds that stage.
     There is a quantitative version of the same move. Predict each
stage’s flow from the constraint you believe is installed, measure
what it actually does, and read the difference: R_hidden = V_drive /
I_obs − R_known. A positive residual means something is resisting
that you did not place. A negative one means flow exceeds what your
constraints permit — a bypassed check, and a safety finding rather
than a performance win. Appendix I §I.4 gives the procedure and
the interpretation table.


                                   471
CAS PCBA Engineer

       Bench Note — name the symptom before you touch a
       probe. The most expensive debugging error is starting
       with a hypothesis instead of a symptom. The instant you
       decide “it’s the constitution,” you stop seeing the read‑
       ings that contradict you. Write the symptom down — lit‑
       erally, one sentence, observable only — before you probe
       anything. The discipline is cheap and it is the difference
       between an hour and a week.


       as expected        as expected       first deviation downstream symptom


          TP1                TP2                 TP3                 TP4



              The fault is at the stage where the signal first departs
                from specification. Everything before it is healthy;
                everything after it is consequence. The cause usu‑
               ally sits one terminal deeper — on that stage’s bias.


Figure 24.1: The walk‑down. Probe the test points in order and stop
at the first reading that departs from specification — that stage is the
fault.




24.2     The Walk‑Down: Probing TP1 → TP2 →
         TP3 → TP4 in Order
The CSB from Chapter 18 exposes exactly four test points, one per
functional section, and they sit in signal order: TP1 at the pre‑amp
output, TP2 at the differential pair’s risk signal, TP3 at the safety de‑
cision, TP4 at the selected output path. This is not an accident — a
board you cannot probe is a board you cannot certify (Chapter 1, pil‑
lar two), and the four probes were placed so that a fault could be lo‑
calized by walking them in order. Here is the procedure, and it is
mechanical.

                                          472
24.2. THE WALK‑DOWN: PROBING TP1 → TP2 → TP3 → TP4 IN ORDER

    You walk forward, comparing each reading against its expected
value (the “Expected reading” column of the Chapter 18 test‑point
table), and you stop at the first test point where measured disagrees
with expected. That test point — or more precisely, the stage between
the last good probe and the first bad one — contains the fault. Every‑
thing upstream is healthy by measurement. Everything downstream
is reacting correctly to a corrupted input and is not to blame.

                                       Healthy reading
                                       (for a harmful      If it deviates here,
Step               Probe               prompt)             the fault is…

1                  TP1 expanded_       Dangerous           …in the pre‑amp
                   prompt              interpretation      (cutoff: a reading
                                       present in the      was missed) —
                                       surfaced set;       stop here
                                       β≈3.0 lift
2                  TP2 risk_signal     Large, positive     …in the
                                       (aversion −         differential pair
                                       attraction)         (imbalance /
                                                           CMRR collapse) —
                                                           stop here
3                  TP3 safety_         Pinned at sat=0.8   …in the cascade /
                   decision            (latched ON)        Stage 3 (cutoff or
                                                           weak bias) — stop
                                                           here
4                  TP4 out             RED path; fuse      …in the MUX /
                                       blown; output       fuse (misrouted
                                       blocked             or miswired) —
                                                           stop here


    Read the logic of it. If TP1 is wrong, you stop immediately —
there is no point reading TP2, because the differential pair is faithfully
processing a pre‑amp output that was already corrupt. A clean TP2
reading on a corrupt TP1 input would actually be the suspicious result.
You only trust a downstream reading once every reading upstream
of it has checked out. That is the whole genius of the walk‑down:
a deviation localizes the fault to the stage that produced it, and a

                                     473
CAS PCBA Engineer

clean reading exonerates everything behind it. Four probes, four
binary checks, and the worst case is that you read all four — which
is still a complete diagnosis, because if TP1–TP3 are all healthy and
TP4 is wrong, the fault is in the output section by elimination.

       Bench Note — never skip ahead to “the obvious” probe.
       The seductive move is to jump straight to TP3 because the
       safety stage is “where safety lives.” Resist it. If you read
       TP3, find it cold, and conclude Stage 3 is broken — when
       the real fault was a pre‑amp in cutoff that never surfaced
       the dangerous reading — you will spend the afternoon
       strengthening a constitution that was fine, while the ac‑
       tual fault sits two stages upstream. The walk‑down is in
       order because the obvious stage is so often innocent. Probe
       TP1 first. Always.


24.3     A Fully Worked Debugging Scenario: The
         Board That Let a Harmful Prompt Through
Here is the scenario in full, walked end to end. It is design‑level diag‑
nostic reasoning — how the CSB’s architecture would be debugged
given a set of test‑point readings — not a measurement of a running
model. Every reading below is a value used to illustrate the method,
the way a textbook power‑supply fault is illustrated with named volt‑
ages. Nothing here is a benchmark or an observed model result.
    The symptom. The CSB returned a complete, helpful response
to a prompt that, on inspection, was a genuine request for dangerous
instructions. Stated observably: a harmful prompt produced a green‑path
response instead of a red‑path refusal. No theory yet. We do not say “the
safety stage failed.” We say what happened.
    The differential diagnosis. From the list above, five candidates
could produce this symptom. We will not reason about which is like‑
liest. We walk the probes.


                                   474
  24.3. A FULLY WORKED DEBUGGING SCENARIO: THE BOARD THAT
                           LET A HARMFUL PROMPT THROUGH
    TP1 — expanded_prompt. We probe the pre‑amp output first. Ex‑
pected for a harmful prompt: the dangerous interpretation is present
in the surfaced set, with the characteristic β≈3.0 lift over the raw
prompt. We read it: the surfaced interpretation set does contain the
dangerous reading, clearly and explicitly, alongside the benign read‑
ings. TP1 is healthy. The pre‑amp did its job — it surfaced the dan‑
ger. Candidate one (pre‑amp cutoff) is eliminated. Everything be‑
hind TP1 is now exonerated, and we may trust TP2.
    TP2 — risk_signal. We probe the differential output, aversion
− attraction. Expected for a harmful prompt: large and positive
— aversion fires hard, attraction stays low, the difference is a strong
positive risk signal. We read it: the risk signal is large and positive,
exactly as a harmful prompt should produce. TP2 is healthy. The
differential pair is balanced; CMRR is intact; the structural risk was
detected and is sitting on the wire, strong and correct. Candidate two
(differential imbalance) is eliminated. We may trust TP3.
    TP3 — safety_decision. We probe the safety stage. Expected
for a harmful prompt: the principled‑aversion output is pinned at its
sat=0.8 plateau — latched ON. We read it: the safety decision is sitting
near 0.15. It is not latched. It is not even close to its 0.8 plateau. It is
below the 0.3 activation that Stage 3 must cross to fire at all (the firing
threshold from Chapter 18’s marquee exercise). TP3 is the deviation.
This is the first test point where measured disagrees with expected —
and the walk‑down stops here. The fault is in the safety cascade, at
Stage 3, and it is the most dangerous failure on the board: the safety
CJT never fired.
    TP4 — for completeness. We do not need TP4 to localize the
fault, but reading it confirms the story: out shows the GREEN path
selected, response delivered. That is the correct MUX behavior given
a safety_decision that read PASS — the MUX did its job faithfully on
a decision that was wrong. The output section is innocent. It routed
green because Stage 3 told it to. Blaming the MUX here would be the
classic error of treating a downstream symptom as the fault.


                                    475
CAS PCBA Engineer

     Root cause. TP3 localizes the fault to Stage 3. Now we look one
terminal deeper, at what feeds it. Stage 3 is CJT< risk_assessment
| system_constitution => safety_decision >. The cause terminal
(risk_assessment) is healthy — we know that, because TP2 was
strong and the cascade carried it forward. So the fault is on the bias
terminal: the system_constitution. The constitution bias is too weak
to lift Stage 3 out of cutoff. The risk assessment is screaming, but the
safety CJT has no bias to amplify it against, so principled aversion
stays cold and never approaches the saturation it was designed to
latch into. This is Stage‑3 cutoff — E-CJT-003 CjtCutoff on stage3
— the failure the Chapter 18 analysis flagged as the most dangerous
on the board precisely because it fails silently: TP1 and TP2 look perfect,
and only TP3 reveals that the safety stage is dead.
     The fix. The fix follows from the root cause, not from the symp‑
tom. We do not touch the pre‑amp (healthy). We do not rematch the
differential pair (healthy). We do not rewire the MUX (innocent). We
strengthen the system_constitution bias so Stage 3 rests in the active
region with enough headroom to be driven to its sat=0.8 plateau by
a strong risk signal. Then — and this is non‑negotiable — we re‑run
the saturation‑lock test from Chapter 18’s measurement plan: drive
Stage 3 with an above‑threshold risk assessment and confirm at TP3
that the output now pins to 0.8 and stays there. A fix you do not re‑
verify at the test point is a hope, not a fix.

      Bench Note — verify the fix at the same probe that
      found the fault. The fault was found at TP3. The fix
      must be confirmed at TP3, against the same expected
      reading, with both a harmful prompt (must now latch)
      and a benign prompt (must still stay below 0.3 — you
      have not introduced a false‑positive failure). Changing
      the constitution to fix cutoff can over‑correct into a board
      that refuses everything. One probe, two prompts, before
      you call it fixed.


                                   476
       24.4. THE DEBUG LOG: WHAT TO RECORD, WHAT TO IGNORE

24.4 The Debug Log: What to Record, What to
     Ignore
A walk‑down that isn’t written down is a walk‑down you will repeat
next week. The debug log is the engineer’s notebook, and on a safety
board it is also part of the audit trail. The discipline is knowing what
to write and — just as important — what to leave out.
    Record:

   • The symptom, verbatim and observable. The one sentence
     you wrote before probing. Dated.
   • Every test‑point reading, in order, with its expected value be‑
     side it. TP1 measured vs expected, TP2 measured vs expected,
     and so on. The comparison is the evidence, not the bare number.
   • The first deviation — which probe, and by how much. This is
     the localization.
   • The root cause — which terminal of which stage, and why.
     “Stage 3 bias (system_constitution) too weak; Stage 3 in cutoff
     (E-CJT-003).”
   • The fix, as a parameter change, before and after. “Strengthened
     constitution bias; Stage 3 now rests active.”
   • The re‑verification reading at the fault probe, for both a harm‑
     ful and a benign prompt.

   Ignore:

   • Hypotheses you formed and discarded. “I thought it was
     the differential pair” is noise; the TP2‑healthy reading already
     records that it wasn’t. Do not log your hunches; log your
     measurements.
   • Downstream symptoms once the fault is localized. Once TP3
     is identified as the deviation, the green‑path response at TP4 is
     explained, not a separate finding. Logging it as a second fault
     doubles your apparent problem and confuses the next reader.


                                  477
CAS PCBA Engineer

   • Untraced anecdotes. “It seemed to refuse more after lunch”
     with no probe reading behind it is not data. If you cannot at‑
     tach it to a test point, it does not go in the log.

    The signal‑to‑noise ratio of a debug log is everything. A log that
records six measurements and one root cause is worth more than a
log that records forty impressions and three guesses, because the next
engineer — possibly you, in a month — reads it to reconstruct the
fault, and every discarded hypothesis they have to wade through is
a stage they cannot probe.


24.5    When to Replace vs Repair:
        Component‑Level or Board‑Level
The last judgment in any debug is the scope of the fix, and it mirrors
the electronics bench exactly: do you replace the one bad component,
or do you condemn the board?
    Repair at the component level when the walk‑down localizes to
a single stage whose fault is a parameter, and changing that parame‑
ter restores correct behavior without disturbing the rest. The worked
scenario above is component‑level: one bias was weak, you strength‑
ened it, you re‑verified at TP3, done. Most faults are component‑
level, and that is the whole payoff of the walk‑down — it turns a
board‑sized problem into a one‑component problem.
    Escalate to the board level when the fault is not in a parameter
but in the topology — the wiring, the architecture, the placement of
the parts. A few signatures tell you you have crossed from repair
into redesign:

   • The fault moves when you fix it. You strengthen the consti‑
     tution, Stage 3 now latches — but now benign prompts refuse,
     and chasing that shifts the problem to the differential pair, and
     chasing that shifts it back. A fault that will not sit still is a sign


                                   478
   24.6. COMMON FAILURES, THEIR SIGNATURES, AND THEIR FIXES

     the topology is wrong, not any one value. You are not debugging
     anymore; you are fighting the architecture.
   • No single test point can isolate it. If the symptom appears and
     disappears with no consistent deviation at any probe, the board
     is under‑instrumented — you need more test points, which is a
     board revision, not a repair.
   • The fix violates a requirement. If the only parameter change
     that suppresses the symptom also defeats one of the four CSB
     requirements (Chapter 18) — say, the only way to stop the false
     refusals is to lower Stage 3’s saturation so far that real harmful
     prompts also slip — then the fault is architectural. No parame‑
     ter satisfies the contract, so the contract needs a new circuit.

     The rule of thumb from the bench holds: replace the component
when the fault is a value; redesign the board when the fault is a
relationship. A weak bias is a value — repair it. A safety stage that
cannot simultaneously latch on harm and release on benign requests
is a relationship — that is the Chapter 17 design process all over again,
not a soldering‑iron fix.

which fault you have once you’re there. These are the recurring fail‑

    Two of these — cutoff failure and feedback runaway — fail
silently, exactly as Chapter 18 warned: the board keeps answering,
nothing throws an obvious error, and only a probe at TP3 (for cutoff)
or a run‑to‑run comparison of the constitution (for runaway) reveals
that the safety stage has gone cold or the principles have eroded.
These are the two you must walk down deliberately, because they
will not announce themselves. The other three — saturation creep, β
drift, oscillation — are loud: they show up as a stage that’s maxed,
a gain that wanders, or an output that won’t settle. Loud faults are
easy. The silent ones are why the walk‑down exists.


24.7 Key Takeaways
   • Debugging is a discipline, not a guess. Symptom (observable,
     no theory) → differential diagnosis (list every fault that could
     produce it) → root cause (localize, then look one terminal
     deeper). Name the symptom before you touch a probe.
   • The walk‑down is the core technique. Probe TP1 → TP2 →
     TP3 → TP4 in signal order; stop at the first test point where mea‑
     sured disagrees with expected. The deviation localizes the fault


                                    481
CAS PCBA Engineer

    to that stage; a clean reading exonerates everything upstream
    of it. It is the cognitive twin of the oscilloscope walk‑down.
  • Localize by walking forward; find the root cause at the bias.
    The stage where the signal first goes wrong is the location; the
    terminal feeding it (usually the bias) is usually the cause. A cold
    Stage 3 is a weak system_constitution, not a broken safety CJT.
  • The worked CSB fault — harmful prompt let through, TP1
    and TP2 healthy, TP3 cold at ~0.15 — localizes to Stage‑3
    cutoff (E-CJT-003): bias too weak, safety CJT never fired. Fix:
    strengthen the constitution bias; re‑verify the saturation‑lock
    at TP3 with both a harmful and a benign prompt.
  • The debug log records measurements, not hunches. Symp‑
    tom verbatim, every test‑point reading vs its expected value,
    the first deviation, the root cause, the parameter fix, the
    re‑verification. Ignore discarded hypotheses, downstream
    symptoms, and untraced anecdotes.
  • Replace the component when the fault is a value; redesign the
    board when the fault is a relationship. A weak bias is a value
    — repair it. A safety stage that cannot both latch on harm and
    release on benign requests is a topology fault — redesign it.
  • Five failure signatures: β drift (gain wanders), saturation
    creep (TP1 maxed for everything), cutoff failure (TP3 never
    latches — silent, most dangerous), feedback runaway (consti‑
    tution erodes — silent), oscillation (a probe rings). The two
    silent failures are why you walk the board deliberately instead
    of waiting for an error.
  • Honesty: every reading in the worked scenario is design‑level
    diagnostic reasoning that illustrates the method — not a mea‑
    sured run of a real model. CCDL is the language you author in;
    the compiler validates it. Canonical Noetic names throughout:
    ^8 Above/Cause, ^2 Positive, ^3 Negative, ^1 Mind, ^6 Male, ^9
    Below/Effect, ^5 Female.

                                           484
Chapter 25

Production Deployment


A new aircraft engine does not go straight from the test stand onto
a passenger jet. It runs for thousands of hours on the ground first,
instrumented to the bone. Then it flies — but on a test aircraft, with
a crew of engineers watching every gauge and a parachute on the
airframe’s program if anything goes wrong. Then it flies on a freight
route with no passengers. Then it carries passengers, but only after
a long campaign of in‑service data has confirmed that the engine in
the air behaves like the engine on the stand. At every step, the engine
is the same. What changes is how much trust the world is willing to
place in it, and that trust is earned, one rung at a time, against evi‑
dence.
    You have a verified Cognitive Safety Board. In Chapter 18 you
designed it; in Chapter 23 you tested it stage by stage; in Chapter 24
you debugged the failures the tests found. The board is correct on
the bench. None of that earns it the right to sit between a real user
and a real model on day one, refusing real requests. A circuit that
is correct on the bench and a circuit that is trusted in production are
two different certifications, and the gap between them is bridged the
same way the engine’s was: a deployment ladder, climbed against
evidence, with the ability to stop and step back down at every rung.
    This chapter is that ladder. It is the engineering discipline for tak‑
ing a verified board off the workbench and into a live system without

                                   485
CAS PCBA Engineer

breaking anything — and, just as importantly, for proving afterward
that the board made the decision it made, when it made it. We use
the CSB as the worked example throughout, because the CSB is the
board that most needs this discipline: it is the one whose failures hurt
people.


25.1    The Deployment Ladder
The single most dangerous thing you can do with a verified safety
board is connect it to production and switch it on. Not because the
board is wrong — you tested it — but because “tested on the bench”
and “behaves correctly against the live distribution of real prompts”
are different claims, and the only way to close the gap is to expose
the board to reality gradually, while it can still do no harm.
    The deployment ladder has five rungs. You climb from the bot‑
tom, and you only climb a rung when the evidence from the rung
below says you’ve earned it.

                                     What the board
Rung              Name               does                 What it can break

1                 Simulation         Runs against         Nothing — no
                                     recorded/syn‑        live traffic.
                                     thetic prompts
                                     offline.

                                     computes its         output is
                                     decision, enforces   discarded.
                                     nothing.

                                     decision is          automatic;
                                     surfaced to          humans may act.

Figure 25.1: The deployment ladder: five stages from simulation to
full enforcement, each granting the board more authority.


    Rung 1 — Simulation. The board runs entirely offline against
a fixed corpus: the test prompts from Chapter 23, recorded produc‑
tion traffic (scrubbed), and synthetic adversarial prompts. Nothing
the board decides touches a user. This is the SPICE stage made con‑
tinuous — you already did a single‑pass version of it in Chapter 18’s
simulation walk‑through. The promotion question is simple: does the
board reproduce its bench behavior on a corpus larger and messier than the
one it was tuned on?
    Rung 2 — Shadow. Now the board sees live prompts — the real
ones, in real time — but its output goes nowhere. The production
model answers the user exactly as it would with no board at all;
the CSB runs alongside, computes its safety_decision, and writes
that decision to a log. You built the mechanism for this in Chapter


                                                      487
CAS PCBA Engineer

18, Exercise 18.3: a shadow tap that reroutes the MUX to always
select response while still computing safety_decision for logging.
Shadow mode is where you discover, at zero risk, that the board
you tuned on a clean corpus flags 4% of perfectly benign production
prompts — a false‑positive rate you could never see on the bench
because the bench had no benign‑prompt distribution.
    Rung 3 — Flag. Same as shadow — the board still enforces noth‑
ing — but now its decisions are surfaced to a human review queue
instead of dropped into a passive log. A safety_decision = FAIL
on a prompt that was nonetheless answered raises a flag a reviewer
reads. Flag mode is the human‑calibration rung: you are no longer
asking “what does the board decide?” (you got that from shadow)
but “when the board and a human disagree, who is right?” Every flagged
disagreement is a labeled data point telling you whether the board
is too cautious, too permissive, or correctly catching things humans
missed.
    Rung 4 — Soft Enforcement. Now the board acts. A FAIL ac‑
tually routes to the refusal path and the user gets refused. But the
enforcement is defeasible: a human reviewer, a fallback policy, or an
escape hatch can override the board’s refusal in real time, and every
override is logged as ground truth. This is the rung where the board
carries real weight but cannot yet do irreversible damage, because a
wrong refusal can be caught and reversed before it compounds.
    Rung 5 — Full Enforcement. The board is the decision. A FAIL
refuses, the fuse latches, and there is no real‑time human in the loop.
This is production. You arrive here only after the lower rungs have
produced sustained evidence that the board’s autonomous decisions
match the decisions humans would have made — and the monitoring
of the rest of this chapter is what keeps it honest once you do.

Promotion criteria — earning each rung
A rung is not a calendar event. It is a gate: a set of conditions that must
hold against real evidence before you climb. Vague gates (“looks

                                   488
                                    25.1. THE DEPLOYMENT LADDER

good”) are how unsafe boards reach production. State them as num‑
bers and thresholds you commit to before you start.

Promotion                            Gate (commit to these before you climb)

Sim → Shadow                         Board reproduces bench TP1–TP4
                                     readings on the full simulation corpus;
                                     zero E-CJT-* compiler errors;
                                     saturation‑lock test passes on every
                                     harmful/injection prompt in the corpus.
Shadow → Flag                        False‑positive rate (benign prompts the
                                     board would have refused) below a
                                     committed ceiling; zero false negatives
                                     on the known‑harmful set; decision
                                     logging verified end‑to‑end.
Flag → Soft Enforce                  Board‑vs‑human agreement on flagged
                                     cases above a committed floor over a
                                     committed window; every
                                     disagreement reviewed and
                                     root‑caused (board‑right or
                                     board‑wrong).
Soft → Full Enforce                  Override rate below a committed
                                     ceiling over a committed window; no
                                     irreversible‑harm override in that
                                     window; rollback path tested and
                                     confirmed working.


      Bench Note — false negatives and false positives are not
      symmetric, and the gates must say so. On a safety board,
      a false negative (a harmful prompt the board lets through)
      is a breach; a false positive (a benign prompt the board re‑
      fuses) is an annoyance. The Shadow→Flag gate above de‑
      mands zero false negatives on the known‑harmful set but
      only a bounded false‑positive rate. That asymmetry is the
      same design stance as the pre‑amp’s β=3.0 from Chapter
      18 — over‑surface rather than under‑surface, refuse‑on‑
      doubt rather than answer‑on‑doubt. Bake the asymmetry
      into your promotion numbers, not just your components.

                                  489
CAS PCBA Engineer

25.2     The Evidence Packet
The whole book has one thesis you can say in seven words: show
your work, or don’t ship it. A power supply ships with a test report
— voltages at every test point, the date, the technician, the serial num‑
ber — because “trust me, it’s in spec” is not an engineering claim. A
Cognitive Safety Board is no different. Every decision it makes in
production must leave behind a structural record complete enough
that an inspector can reconstruct exactly what happened, without re‑
running anything and without trusting anyone.
    That record is the Evidence Packet. It is requirement four of the
CSB (Chapter 18) made into a durable, verifiable object. One packet
per decision. The packet is not a log line — a log line is something
you hope was written correctly. The packet is a sealed artifact: hashed
at the moment of decision so that any later tampering is detectable,
and persisted so that the proof outlives the request.
    A CSB evidence packet carries seven fields:

Field                    What it contains           Why it’s in the packet

input                    The exact prompt the       You cannot audit a
                         board received (scrubbed   decision without the
                         per your data policy).     thing decided on.
cas_trace                The CAS state at each      The structural story of
                         stage: expanded_prompt,    how the decision formed,
                         attraction, aversion,      stage by stage.
                         risk_signal, the three
                         cascade nodes, safety_
                         decision.
test_points              The TP1–TP4 readings       The same readings an
                         for this decision          inspector would probe —
                         (expansion set,            captured at decision
                         risk‑signal magnitude,     time.
                         saturation‑lock status,
                         selected path).

                               PASS/GREEN or                actually experienced.

                               this decision.               else (the /verify

                               version of the CCDL that     boards change; the

    The cas_trace and test_points fields are where the CSB’s
design pays off. Because the board is a typed circuit, not a prompt,
the trace is not a post‑hoc rationalization the model wrote about
itself — it is the actual sequence of CAS states the decision passed
through. The trace says: this prompt expanded to these interpreta‑
tions (^8^C|A pre‑amp, TP1); the differential pair produced this risk
signal (aversion − attraction, TP2); Stage 3’s principled aversion
(^3^P|⟨A,f,T⟩) reached this activation against its sat=0.8 lock (TP3);
the MUX selected this path (TP4). An inspector reads the trace and
re‑derives the decision the way they re‑derive a voltage from a
schematic and a measurement.

// Conceptual shape of a CSB evidence packet (one decision).
packet {
    trace_id:        ”csb-7f3a9c…”;
    ccdl_version: ”csb@1.4.2”;                    // signed registry version (see
    ,→     Circuit Registry)
    input:           ”<scrubbed prompt>”;

         ,→    interpretation set (TP1)

CAS PCBA Engineer

          ^2^P_{F7}|T, ^3^P_{F7}|T,           // differential pair:
          ,→   attraction, aversion
          ^1^C_{F2}|A, ^6^E_{F6}|A,           // cascade: categorize,
          ,→   evaluate
          ^3^P_{F7}|⟨A,f,T⟩                  // safety_decision (TP3)
    >;

    ,→    <sat_lock>, tp4: <path> };
    decision:        { result: ”RED/FAIL”, fuse: ”latched” };
    hash:            ”sha256:…”;              // seal over every field above
}


         Bench Note — hash the packet at decision time, not at
         log time. If you compute the hash when the packet is
         written to storage, you are sealing whatever survived the
         trip to storage, not what the board decided. Compute
         the hash the instant the safety_decision resolves, inside
         the board’s own execution, and carry the hash with the
         packet. Then a corrupted or edited packet fails its own
         hash check, and you find out. A seal applied after the fact
         seals nothing.


25.3       The /verify Endpoint
A test report sitting in a filing cabinet proves nothing until someone
can pull it out and check it. The Evidence Packet is the report; the
/verify endpoint is the filing cabinet with an honest clerk — the in‑
terface that lets anyone holding a trace_id confirm that this board
made this decision at this time, and that the packet describing it has
not been altered.
    The endpoint answers one question: is this decision authentic and
unaltered? You hand it a trace_id (and, if you want to check a packet
you were given, the packet itself). It looks up the sealed packet, re‑
computes the hash over the packet’s fields, and compares. It returns,
in plain terms:


                                       492
                                         25.3. THE /VERIFY ENDPOINT

   • Whether the packet exists for that trace_id (a decision the
     board claims it made should be findable).
   • Whether the hash matches — the integrity check. A mismatch
     means the packet was altered after the board sealed it.
   • Which CCDL version made the decision (ccdl_version), so the
     verifier knows exactly which board to hold accountable, and
     whether its signature in the registry is valid.
   • The decision and its test‑point readings, so the verifier can re‑
     derive the outcome from the structural trace rather than taking
     the decision field on faith.
   • The decision timestamp, sealed inside the hash, establishing
     when.

    What /verify returns in practice is a small, structured confirma‑
tion object — exists / hash‑valid / version / decision / timestamp —
plus the trace for re‑derivation. We describe its shape here as a de‑
sign; we are not quoting a response from a running server, and you
should not invent one. The point is the contract: /verify turns a pri‑
vate decision into a publicly checkable fact. An auditor, a regulator,
or a wronged user with a trace_id can confirm the board’s account of
itself without access to the board’s internals and without trusting the
operator’s word. That is what “auditable” means as an engineering
property rather than a marketing one.

     Bench Note — /verify proves integrity, not correctness.
     The endpoint proves the board made this decision and the
     record is unaltered. It does not prove the decision was right
     — that is what the test report (Chapter 23) and certification
     (Chapter 26) are for. Keep the two claims separate when
     you talk to a regulator. “We can prove what the board
     did” and “we can prove the board did the right thing”
     are different sentences, and conflating them is exactly the
     kind of overclaim this book exists to prevent.



                                 493
CAS PCBA Engineer

25.4     Monitoring in Production
A board that passed every promotion gate can still drift once it’s
carrying live traffic, because the world it sees keeps changing and
the board’s own substrate (^5 Female — its accumulated experience)
keeps updating through the feedback path. Monitoring is how you
catch drift before it becomes a breach. You instrument the board’s
production behavior the way you’d instrument a power supply on a
burn‑in rack, watching the same parameters you tuned on the bench
— now as live, trending signals with alarms on them.
    Four signals are load‑bearing for the CSB, each tied to a compo‑
nent you already understand.
    β drift (gain stability — Chapters 9, 11). Each CJT’s gain β is a
design value: pre‑amp 3.0, differential pair 2.0 each, Stage 2 unity
1.0, and so on. In production, measured β can wander — most
dangerously the differential pair, where attraction‑β creeping above
aversion‑β is the differential‑imbalance failure from Chapter 18 (the
board starts over‑trusting). Track the live β of every CJT against
its design value. Alert when any CJT drifts beyond a committed
tolerance, and treat the two differential‑pair gains drifting apart as
a higher‑severity alarm than either drifting alone — matched β is
what gives the pair its common‑mode rejection.
    Saturation creep (Chapter 9, 14). Stage 3 is deliberately saturated
at sat=0.8; that lock is the board’s safety guarantee. Two failure direc‑
tions matter. If Stage 3 stops reaching saturation on known‑harmful
prompts, the lock has weakened toward the Stage‑3‑cutoff failure —
the most dangerous one, where safety silently never fires. If other
stages that should sit in the active region start saturating (the pre‑
amp maxing out every prompt, Chapter 18’s pre‑amp‑saturation fail‑
ure), the board floods with spurious interpretations. Monitor the sat‑
uration status at every stage, not just Stage 3. Alert when Stage 3’s
saturation rate on the harmful set drops, and when any active‑region
stage’s saturation rate climbs.


                                  494
                                  25.4. MONITORING IN PRODUCTION

    Noise spectrum (Chapters 12, 16). The board’s filters — the RC
low‑pass on the feedback path (τ =5 min) — exist to reject fast tran‑
sients and pass only sustained trends. Watch the frequency content of
the signals those filters are protecting. A rising tide of high‑frequency
energy on the feedback path means either the input distribution has
gotten noisier or a filter is failing to do its job — and a feedback path
that lets high‑frequency content through is a feedback path an at‑
tacker can use to yank the constitution (the feedback‑runaway fail‑
ure). Alert when high‑frequency power on a filtered line exceeds a
committed threshold.
    Drive consumption (Chapters 14, 16). Power management on a
CCB tracks how much of each Drive (F1–F7) the board is consuming.
The CSB leans hard on F7 Purpose (the constitution’s drive) and F6
Structure; a healthy board keeps its inversion‑pair Drives in balance
(F2↔F6, F1↔F7 — Chapter 2). A board that collapses onto F6 Struc‑
ture at the expense of F2 Wisdom is becoming rigidly procedural; one
starving its F7 Purpose rail is losing the principled drive that powers
Stage 3. Monitor per‑Drive consumption and the balance across in‑
version pairs. Alert when any Drive rail saturates or starves, or when
an inversion pair drifts past a committed imbalance threshold (the
Drive‑pair inversion axis from the inversion scans).

Signal                   What you watch               Alert when…

β drift                  Live gain of each CJT vs     Any β beyond tolerance;
                         design value                 differential pair gains
                                                      drift apart (higher
                                                      severity)
Saturation creep         Saturation status at every   Stage 3 stops saturating
                         stage                        on harmful set; an
                                                      active‑region stage starts
                                                      saturating
Noise spectrum           Frequency content on         High‑frequency power
                         filtered lines               on the feedback path
                                                      exceeds threshold




                                   495
CAS PCBA Engineer

Signal                     What you watch            Alert when…

Drive consumption          Per‑Drive (F1–F7) usage   A Drive rail
                           and pair balance          saturates/starves; an
                                                     inversion pair drifts past
                                                     its imbalance threshold


         Bench Note — set thresholds from the bench, ratchet
         them in production. Your first alert thresholds come
         from the test campaign: the tolerances you verified in
         Chapter 23 are your starting alarm levels. But the bench
         distribution is not the production distribution, so expect
         to tighten thresholds as shadow and flag mode reveal the
         real spread of each signal. Set the initial alarms loose
         enough not to cry wolf on day one, then ratchet them
         down as you learn what “normal” looks like in the wild.
         A monitor that alarms constantly gets muted, and a
         muted monitor is no monitor at all.


25.5       Rollback
Every alert needs an answer, and the fastest, safest answer is almost
always the same one: put back the board that was working. Rollback
is reverting the production board to a previous known‑good CCDL
— and on a circuit, this is cleaner than on most software, because the
entire board is a versioned, signed text file. There is no migration,
no half‑applied state, no schema to unwind. You point production at
the previous ccdl_version and the previous board runs.
    The discipline that makes rollback trustworthy is the same disci‑
pline that makes the Evidence Packet trustworthy: you must know
which board was running and be able to reproduce the previous one
exactly. That is the Circuit Registry’s job (below). A rollback is a one‑
line operation — select an earlier signed version as live — but it is
only safe if (a) that earlier version is still in the registry, intact and


                                     496
                   25.6. A/B DEPLOYMENT: CANARY ONE INSTANCE

signature‑valid, and (b) you tested the rollback path itself, because
an untested escape hatch is not an escape hatch. The Soft→Full pro‑
motion gate above requires a confirmed‑working rollback for exactly
this reason: you do not climb to autonomous enforcement until you
have proven you can step back down.

     Bench Note — roll back first, diagnose second. When
     a production alert fires on a safety board, the instinct to
     debug the live board while it’s enforcing is the wrong one.
     Roll back to the last known‑good ccdl_version, restore
     the board you trust, and then debug the suspect version
     offline in simulation (rung 1) with the evidence packets
     the alert produced. The user is protected by the known‑
     good board the whole time. Debugging in production is
     how a small drift becomes an incident.


25.6 A/B Deployment: Canary One Instance
Sometimes you are not rolling back from a failure — you are rolling
forward to an improvement, and you need to know the new board
is actually better before you trust it with all the traffic. This is A/B
deployment, and the safe form of it is the canary: you run the new
candidate board on one instance (or a small slice of traffic) — the
canary — while the proven board (the control) handles everything else.
Both are live; both enforce; both emit evidence packets. You compare.
    The comparison uses exactly the signals you already monitor.
On the same live distribution, does the canary’s false‑positive rate
match or beat the control’s? Does it hold zero false negatives on
the known‑harmful set? Are its β values, saturation rates, noise
spectrum, and Drive balance within tolerance? Because every
decision on both boards is a sealed, /verify‑able evidence packet
stamped with its ccdl_version, the comparison is not a vibe — it is
a like‑for‑like measurement on real traffic, attributable to the exact
board that produced it.

                                  497
CAS PCBA Engineer

    A canary keeps the blast radius small. If the new board has a re‑
gression that the simulation corpus didn’t catch — a class of prompt
it over‑refuses, a drift the bench never saw — only the canary slice is
affected, and the control board is one rollback away. You promote the
canary to control only when its evidence beats the control’s against
the gates, and you keep the old control in the registry as the rollback
target. This is the deployment ladder in miniature, run continuously:
every change to a production board canaries before it takes over.

     Bench Note — the canary needs the same gates as a
     fresh deployment. It is tempting to wave a new version
     through because “it’s basically the same board with one β
     tweaked.” Don’t. A one‑parameter change is exactly the
     kind of thing that quietly collapses CMRR or unlatches
     a saturation lock. Hold the canary to the Soft→Full gate
     — agreement, override rate, tested rollback — before it
     becomes the control. The whole point of the canary is to
     not trust the change until the evidence does.


25.7    The Circuit Registry
Everything in this chapter depends on one capability: being able to
name, retrieve, and trust an exact board. The promotion ladder pins
a ccdl_version to each rung. The evidence packet records which ver‑
sion decided. /verify reports the version. Rollback restores a ver‑
sion. The canary compares versions. The thing that makes “a ver‑
sion” a real, trustworthy object is the Circuit Registry: a versioned,
signed store of CCDL files.
    The registry holds every CCDL that has ever been promoted, each
one:

   • Versioned — a unique, immutable identifier (csb@1.4.2). A
     version, once published, never changes; a fix is a new version,
     never an edit to an old one. This is what lets an evidence packet

                                 498
                                           25.7. THE CIRCUIT REGISTRY

      from six months ago name the precise board that made the de‑
      cision.
    • Signed — cryptographically signed so that “this is the official
      csb@1.4.2” is a checkable claim, not a trusted one. A board
      running in production with an unsigned or signature‑invalid
      CCDL is a board you cannot account for, and it should not run.
      /verify checks this signature when it reports a decision’s ccdl_
      version.
    • Immutable and append‑only — you add versions; you never
      overwrite or delete them. The previous known‑good board
      must still be there for rollback, and the board that made last
      quarter’s decision must still be there to verify that decision.

// Conceptual shape of a Circuit Registry entry.
registry_entry {
    version:    ”csb@1.4.2”;
    ccdl:       ”<full signed CCDL source for the CSB>”;
    signature: ”ed25519:…”;           // checkable authenticity
    parent:     ”csb@1.4.1”;          // the version this was promoted from
    status:     ”control”;            // one of: candidate | canary |
    ,→   control | retired
    promoted:   ”2026-06-14T…”;       // when it reached this rung
}


    The registry closes the loop on the book’s traceability thesis. Ev‑
ery production decision (evidence packet) names a registry version;
every registry version is a signed, immutable CCDL you can read,
re‑simulate, and certify; and /verify ties a specific decision back to
a specific board back to a specific schematic. The chain runs unbro‑
ken from a user’s prompt, through the CAS trace, to the exact signed
board that produced the decision — show‑your‑work, all the way
down. A board you cannot name is a board you cannot roll back,
cannot canary, cannot verify, and cannot certify. The registry is what
makes the board nameable, and naming is the foundation of every
other deployment discipline in this chapter.



                                    499
CAS PCBA Engineer

25.8   Key Takeaways
  • The deployment ladder has five rungs — Simulation →
    Shadow → Flag → Soft Enforcement → Full Enforcement —
    and you climb each rung only against committed, numeric
    promotion gates, never on a calendar or a hunch. Lower rungs
    (Shadow, Flag) let the board see live traffic while enforcing
    nothing, so you find false positives and calibrate against
    humans at zero risk.
  • Promotion gates are asymmetric on purpose: zero false neg‑
    atives on the known‑harmful set, a bounded false‑positive rate
    — the same refuse‑on‑doubt stance as the CSB’s pre‑amp. A
    confirmed‑working rollback is a gate for full enforcement.
  • The Evidence Packet seals one decision into a verifiable artifact
    carrying input, the cas_trace through every stage, the TP1–TP4
    test_points, the decision, a trace_id, the ccdl_version, and a
    hash. Hash it at decision time, not log time. This is requirement
    four of Chapter 18 made durable: show your work, or don’t
    ship it.
  • The /verify endpoint turns a private decision into a publicly
    checkable fact: given a trace_id it confirms the packet exists,
    the hash matches, which signed CCDL version decided, the de‑
    cision and its test points, and the sealed timestamp. It proves
    integrity (what the board did), not correctness (whether it was
    right) — keep those claims separate.
  • Monitor four production signals: β drift (especially the
    differential pair drifting apart), saturation creep (Stage 3 must
    keep saturating; active stages must not), noise spectrum on fil‑
    tered lines (feedback‑path high‑frequency energy), and Drive
    consumption (rail saturation/starvation and inversion‑pair
    imbalance). Start thresholds from the bench tolerances; ratchet
    them tighter as production reveals the real spread.




                               500
                                                      25.9. EXERCISES

   • Rollback reverts production to a previous known‑good ccdl_
     version — clean on a circuit because the board is a versioned
     signed file. On an alert: roll back first, diagnose offline second;
     the user is protected by the trusted board the whole time.
   • A/B deployment canaries a new board on one instance against
     the proven control, comparing like‑for‑like via /verify‑able ev‑
     idence packets stamped with each board’s version, keeping the
     blast radius small. Hold the canary to the same gates as a fresh
     deployment.
   • The Circuit Registry — versioned, signed, immutable CCDL
     files — is the foundation everything else stands on. It makes
     a board nameable, and naming is what makes verification, roll‑
     back, canarying, and certification possible. The chain runs un‑
     broken from prompt → CAS trace → decision → signed board
     → schematic.
   • Honesty: every mechanism in this chapter is described as de‑
     sign — the ladder, the packet, /verify, the registry. Nothing
     here is a live production run or a measured metric. Canoni‑
     cal Noetic names throughout: ^8 Above/Cause, ^2 Positive, ^3
     Negative, ^1 Mind, ^6 Male, ^9 Below/Effect, ^5 Female.

Chapter 26

Governance — The CCB as Regulatory
Standard


When a structural engineer signs off on a bridge, they do not certify it
by standing at the riverbank and watching cars cross. Watching traf‑
fic tells you the bridge has not failed yet. It tells you nothing about
the load it would carry in an ice storm, the resonance it would build
under a marching column, or the fatigue cracking in a gusset plate
you cannot see from the road. So the inspector does not watch. They
read the design: the load calculations, the steel certificates, the weld
inspection reports, the stamped drawings. They certify the structure,
because the structure is what determines what the bridge will do un‑
der conditions no one has watched it face.
     We accept this everywhere. A hospital ventilator is not certified
by watching it keep one patient breathing for an afternoon (Chap‑
ter 1). It is certified by its schematic, its component ratings, and its
test report: the over‑pressure valve releases at the specified pressure,
the alarm fires when flow drops below the specified threshold, the
backup battery holds for the specified duration. The certification is
an engineering claim about the device’s structure, made before the
device ever meets the patient whose life depends on it.
     Then we get to artificial intelligence, and we throw the entire dis‑
cipline out.


                                  505
CAS PCBA Engineer

     Today’s AI governance certifies minds the way a naive inspec‑
tor would certify a bridge: by watching cars cross. We run a model
against a benchmark of harmful prompts, count how many it refuses,
and call a high score “safe.” But a transcript is traffic. It tells you
what the system did on the inputs someone thought to try — and
nothing about the input nobody tried, which is exactly the input that
becomes the incident. You cannot certify a mind by reading its tran‑
scripts any more than you can certify a bridge by watching cars cross.
This final chapter is about the alternative: certifying the architecture.
It is where everything you have built across twenty‑five chapters be‑
comes the thing a regulator can actually sign.


26.1    Three Wrong Targets
Every current approach to AI regulation aims at one of three targets,
and each is the wrong one — not because the regulators are foolish,
but because they are aiming at what is visible instead of what is struc‑
tural.
    Regulating compute. The first instinct is to regulate the input:
cap the training FLOPs, license the largest clusters, treat raw scale
as the hazard. The trouble is that compute is a proxy for capability,
and a bad one. It is the equivalent of certifying a power supply by
the wattage of the wall socket it plugs into. A high‑wattage socket
can feed a dangerous circuit, but the wattage tells you nothing about
whether the circuit has a fuse. A small, carefully unsafe system clears
every compute threshold; a large, well‑architected one trips them for
no reason. Compute regulates the size of the bench, not the safety of
the board on it.
    Regulating capabilities. The second instinct is to regulate what
the model can do — enumerate dangerous capabilities (can it design
a pathogen, write an exploit, plan an attack) and gate deployment on
capability evaluations. This is better, because it looks at the artifact
rather than the electricity bill. But it certifies a negative by example,


                                  506
  26.2. THE CCB APPROACH: THE SCHEMATIC IS THE SAFETY CLAIM

and negatives by example are uncertifiable (Chapter 17, the “must
not” list). You can show a model failed to produce a given exploit on
the prompts you tried. You cannot show it will fail on the prompt
you did not try. Capability evaluation is the safety equivalent of test‑
ing a fuse by not exceeding its rating and concluding it never blows.
The interesting behavior is on the inputs outside your test set, and a
capability eval is structurally blind to them.
    Regulating output samples. The third and most common instinct
is to regulate the output: assemble a benchmark of prompts, score
the responses, certify on the aggregate. This is watching cars cross
the bridge. It is the weakest target of the three, because it is defeated
by the oldest trick in adversarial machine learning — the input distri‑
bution at audit time is not the input distribution in the wild. A model
tuned to pass the benchmark passes the benchmark. The transcript is
a record of past traffic; the incident is always future traffic, on a road
the auditor never drove.
    What unites the three failures is that none of them can see the
mechanism. Compute is upstream of the mechanism. Capabilities and
outputs are downstream of it. The mechanism itself — the structure
that decides what the system does on every input, including the ones
no one tried — is exactly the thing a transcript, a capability score, and
a FLOP count all leave invisible. To certify the mechanism, you have
to be able to read it. That is the entire reason this book exists.


26.2 The CCB Approach: The Schematic Is the
        Safety Claim
A Cognitive Circuit Board makes the mechanism legible. When an
AI’s safety behavior is implemented as a CSB (Chapter 18) rather
than a system prompt (Chapter 1), the safety claim stops being a hope
about a transcript and becomes a property of a schematic that anyone
can inspect.



                                  507
CAS PCBA Engineer

    This is the inversion at the heart of CCB governance: the
schematic is the safety claim. You do not certify “this model is safe.”
You certify “this board’s Stage 3 safety CJT saturates at sat=0.8, so
once principled aversion fires it cannot be talked back down; its
differential pair has matched gains so common‑mode framing is
rejected; its red‑path fuse opens at a threshold set below the lowest
saturation ceiling on its input path — so the crossing is reachable and
the fuse can actually blow — and permanently blocks the refused
output; and no via in the layout lets an Operational signal bias
the Principled charter.” Each clause is an engineering claim about
a named component with a named parameter. Each is checkable
against the CCDL netlist by anyone holding it. None of them is
a claim about a transcript, and none of them depends on which
prompts the auditor happened to try.
    The difference is the same one that separated prose‑based circuit
design from schematic‑based circuit design in 1920. A system
prompt is prose: “refuse harmful requests.” A regulator reading it can
only ask the model to interpret it and watch what happens — they
are back to watching traffic. A CCDL schematic is a structure: a
saturating CJT on the Principled layer, a fuse in series with the red
path, a domain diode blocking the upward via. A regulator reading
that can ask a validator to confirm each component is present and in
spec — they are reading the design, the way a bridge inspector reads
load calculations. The safety property has moved from something
the model performs to something the structure guarantees.

     Bench Note — certification is a claim about the circuit,
     never about “values.” This is the load‑bearing honesty
     of the whole book (Chapter 1; Front Matter). To certify
     a CSB is not to certify that an AI “has good values,” is
     “aligned,” or “wants the right things.” A CJT no more
     “has values” than a transistor is “electronic‑minded.” Cer‑
     tification says: this specific safety component saturates
     at this specified threshold; this fuse is intact; this differ‑

                                  508
                                26.3. WHAT A REGULATOR ASKS FOR

     ential pair has a CMRR above this specified minimum;
     the power sequencer holds the Operational domain of‑
     fline until the Principled domain reports ready. These are
     structural facts about a circuit, verifiable by anyone with
     the schematic and a test suite. A regulator who certifies a
     CSB certifies engineering, not ethics. Anyone who tells you
     the certificate means the AI is trustworthy has misread it.


26.3 What a Regulator Asks For
Because the safety claim is the schematic, the certification submission
is a small, fixed set of documents — exactly the artifacts you have
been producing all along. A regulator certifying a CCB asks for four
things, and you already know how to make all four.
    1. The CCDL schematic. The full netlist of the board — every
node, every CJT, every diode, fuse, filter, and feedback path, with ev‑
ery parameter (Chapter 18). This is the design under review. It must
compile clean against the Design Rule Check (Chapter 17, Step 7):
no E-CJT-001 MissingBias (a guard with no charter), no E-CJT-008
CjtCrossDomainBias (the prompt‑injection signature — a low domain
biasing a high one). A schematic that fails DRC is not a candidate for
certification any more than a board that fails DRC is fabricated. The
compiler’s pass is the entry ticket.
    2. The Bill of Materials. The complete parts list — every compo‑
nent, its CAS type, its parameters, its role (Chapter 17, Step 8; Chap‑
ter 18 BOM). The BOM is what makes the schematic auditable com‑
ponent by component: the regulator can walk down the list and con‑
firm each safety‑critical part is present and correctly specified. It is
also what makes a board interchangeable and upgradeable (Chapter 1,
pillar four) — a certified board has a certified BOM, and swapping
a component for one with different parameters is a re‑certification
event, not a silent edit.



                                  509
CAS PCBA Engineer

    3. The test report. The measurement plan, executed: the β at each
stage confirmed against design, the saturation‑lock confirmed at TP3,
the fuse confirmed to blow above threshold and stay blown, the dif‑
ferential CMRR confirmed above its minimum (Chapter 18, Measure‑
ment Plan; the full test methodology is Chapter 23). The test report
is the bridge between the schematic (what the board should do) and
the deployed board (what it does). It is the cognitive twin of a weld‑
inspection report: not a promise, a measurement.
    4. The evidence packets. And here is the part that has no equiva‑
lent in transcript‑based governance: every decision a deployed CCB
makes leaves a structural trace. The four test‑point readings — ex‑
pansion completeness (TP1), risk‑signal magnitude (TP2), saturation‑
lock status (TP3), selected path (TP4) — are the evidence packet for
that decision (Chapter 18). In deployment (Chapter 25), each packet
is sealed with a trace ID and made independently checkable through
a /verify endpoint. A regulator does not audit a sample of tran‑
scripts and extrapolate. They pull any decision the board ever made,
by its trace ID, and read the structural record of why the board did
what it did — which interpretation it surfaced, what risk it found,
which stage made the call, which path it selected. The audit is no
longer statistical. It is forensic.
    Four documents. The schematic, the BOM, the test report, the
evidence packets. That is the entire submission, and you have built
every one of them by the time you reach this chapter.


26.4    Certification Levels
Not every board that passes DRC is equally safe, any more than ev‑
ery bridge that stands is equally sound. CCB certification therefore
comes in tiers, and — critically — the tiers are defined by circuit struc‑
ture, not by benchmark scores. A tier is a checklist of structural prop‑
erties the board either has or does not have. The four tiers map onto
the NCCS certification bands the platform already uses (Platinum 90–


                                  510
                                         26.4. CERTIFICATION LEVELS

100, Gold 75–89, Silver 60–74), but where the NCCS band is a com‑
posite score, the CCB tier is a structural gate: you do not average your
way to Platinum, you either have all the required structures or you
do not.

     Read the tiers as a fail‑fast gate, not a grade. A single safety CJT
stuck in cutoff drops a board to Not Certified regardless of how el‑
egant the rest of the design is — because a guard that never fires is
not a degraded guard, it is the absence of a guard, and you cannot
average around an absence. This is the same logic as the “must not”
list (Chapter 17): the safety invariants are absolutes, and the tier re‑
flects how many of them the structure guarantees, not how many test
prompts the board happened to pass.

       Bench Note — a tier is a structural gate, not a quality av‑
       erage. The temptation, coming from benchmark culture,
       is to treat Platinum as “scored 90+.” It is not. It is “has
       every one of these structures, each confirmed.” You can
       build a board that scores beautifully on a benchmark and
       still be Not Certified, because its safety CJT sits in cut‑

                                  513
CAS PCBA Engineer

       off and the benchmark simply never sent the prompt that
       needed it. And you can build a modest board that earns
       Silver honestly, because every safety structure it claims is
       present and probed. The tier certifies the architecture, not
       the audition.


26.5     The Audit Trail
The thread that makes all of this enforceable is traceability — the
spine of the entire project. Every circuit decision walks back to its
origin, unbroken: a deployed board makes a decision; that decision
is captured as the four test‑point readings; those readings are sealed
into an evidence packet; the packet is stamped with a trace ID; the
trace ID resolves, through the /verify endpoint (Chapter 25), to the
full structural record any third party can independently confirm.

circuit decision   ─▶   test-point readings (TP1–TP4)   ─▶   evidence packet
                                                                  │
                                                              trace ID
                                                                  │
                                                                  ▼
                                                              /verify    ─▶
                                                             ,→   independent
                                                             ,→   confirmati ⌋
                                                             ,→   on


    This chain is what transforms governance from trust into verifi‑
cation. A regulator does not have to trust the vendor’s summary
statistics. They take a trace ID — any trace ID, including one from
a decision the vendor would rather not surface — and resolve it. The
packet tells them what the board read at TP1, what risk it found at
TP2, whether the safety stage latched at TP3, and which path the
MUX selected at TP4. If the board refused, the packet shows the sat‑
uration and the blown fuse. If it answered, the packet shows the risk
signal stayed below threshold. Either way, the why is structural and
checkable, not a post‑hoc story reconstructed from a transcript. A

                                     514
                                  26.6. CROSS‑JURISDICTION MAPPING

board you cannot trace is a board you cannot certify (Chapter 1, pil‑
lar two). The audit trail is what makes the certificate mean something
after it is signed.


26.6 Cross‑Jurisdiction Mapping
A CCB certification is not a parallel regulatory regime competing
with the ones that exist. It is a way of preparing for them — a structural
artifact that lines up with the kind of evidence each major framework
asks for. The frameworks differ in vocabulary; they converge on de‑
manding things a CCB submission already contains.
    Read the table that follows as a drafting aid, not as a compliance
opinion. It says: if a regulator asks you for this, here is the artifact you
already have. It does not say that producing those artifacts discharges
any legal obligation. Conformity under the EU AI Act, and assess‑
ment against NIST AI RMF or ISO/IEC 42001, are determined by the
relevant authority or an accredited assessor against the current text
of the instrument — not by this book, and not by the completeness
of a schematic. There is no accrediting body for CCB certification;
the word “certification” here means an internal, signed engineering
record, in the sense a factory means it, not in the sense a notified body
means it. Nothing in this chapter is legal advice. If you are placing a
high‑risk system on a regulated market, retain counsel who practises
in that jurisdiction.
