    The pattern across all three is the same: each framework asks, in
its own language, for documented structure, measured behavior, and an
audit trail. A CCB submission produces exactly those three, as en‑
gineering artifacts rather than policy prose. The schematic answers
“what is the structure,” the test report answers “what does it mea‑
sure,” and the evidence‑packet trail answers “prove it, decision by
decision.” A board certified once produces the evidence to satisfy all
three frameworks, because all three are asking for the same underly‑
ing thing — they had simply never had a substrate in which to ask
for it precisely.


26.7 The Open‑Source CCB Library
No engineering discipline matures on bespoke designs alone. Elec‑
tronics has reference designs — the application note from a chip ven‑
dor showing the canonical way to wire a regulator, the open hard‑


                                  517
CAS PCBA Engineer

ware schematic anyone can fork and build. A 10kΩ resistor is inter‑
changeable precisely because the design around it is shared and un‑
derstood (Chapter 1, pillar four). Cognitive circuits need the same
commons, and the five reference boards of this book are its seed: the
CSB (Chapter 18), the COB Cognitive Oscillator Board (Chapter 19),
the CDAB Cognitive Differential Amplifier Board (Chapter 20), the
CMB Cognitive Memory Board (Chapter 21), and the CPMB Cogni‑
tive Power Management Board (Chapter 22).
    An open‑source CCB library — reference designs maintained by a
community of CAS PCBA engineers — does for cognitive safety what
shared schematics did for electronics. A vendor building a safety fire‑
wall does not start from a blank netlist; they fork the certified CSB
reference design, adapt its parameters to their setting, document the
deltas in their BOM, and re‑run DRC and the test plan. A regulator re‑
viewing the submission recognizes the reference design, has seen its
structure certified before, and reviews only the deltas. The commu‑
nity catches structural bugs once, for everyone — the sub‑threshold‑
attacker gap (Chapter 18, Exercise 18.4) is found, a standard integra‑
tor stage is added to the reference CSB, and every fork inherits the fix.
Certification becomes cheaper, faster, and more uniform, because the
structures being certified are shared, named, and battle‑tested. That
is how a discipline scales: not by every team reinventing the safety
board, but by improving a common one in the open.


26.8    Closing the Book: From the Ventilator to
        the Engineer
We began with a hospital ventilator (Chapter 1). An electrical engi‑
neer designing its power supply does not write “the voltage should be
kind of stable, and if too much current flows, maybe something should gen‑
tly discourage that.” They draw a schematic, specify a regulator with
an exact part number, place a fuse with a precise rating, and test it. If



                                   518
           26.8. CLOSING THE BOOK: FROM THE VENTILATOR TO THE
                                                    ENGINEER
the fuse blows at 2.1 amps instead of 2.0, they do not adjust the prose.
They replace the fuse.
    The argument of this entire book has been that there is no princi‑
pled reason — none — to hold cognition to a lower standard than we
hold the ventilator’s power supply. We accept structural safety engi‑
neering everywhere it matters: in bridges, in aircraft, in medical de‑
vices, in the power supply keeping a patient breathing. We demand
schematics, component ratings, test reports, and audit trails for every
one of them. We accept, without argument, that you cannot certify a
bridge by watching cars cross. And then we reach the one system that
will reason about those bridges, prescribe to those patients, and ad‑
vise on those aircraft — and we govern it with English sentences and
a benchmark of sample transcripts, the exact prose‑and‑pray method
electronics abandoned a century ago.
    That is what is now changing. A Cognitive Circuit Board turns
AI safety from an unfalsifiable promise — “the model is aligned, trust
us” — into a certifiable engineering claim: this safety CJT saturates at
this threshold, this fuse opens at this rating, this differential pair rejects this
common‑mode framing, and here is the trace ID for every decision it has ever
made. The claim is modest and exact, which is precisely its strength. It
never says the AI has good values. It says the circuit has the structure,
and the structure is checkable by anyone holding the schematic. The
patent on the underlying system (USPTO Provisional #64/037,173) is
real; the discipline it protects is young; and the work of building out
its reference library, its test methods, and its regulatory mappings
has only begun.
    That work is now yours. You started this book needing no elec‑
tronics and no CAS. You learned to read the schematic (Chapter 2),
to wire the transistor that changed everything (Chapters 3–4), to se‑
lect every component in the bin (Chapters 5–10), to combine them
into amplifiers, filters, oscillators, and feedback systems (Chapters
11–16), to design five complete boards (Chapters 17–22), and to test,
debug, deploy, and now certify them (Chapters 23–26). You can take


                                       519
CAS PCBA Engineer

a prompt and trace it through a saturating safety stage. You can spot
a domain precedence violation in a layout. You can write a certifi‑
cation dossier a regulator would accept. You can build a board that
refuses harmful requests not because it was asked nicely to, but be‑
cause its structure leaves no path for the harm to take.
    You are a CAS PCBA engineer. Go build the boards the next
decade is going to require.


26.9    Key Takeaways
   • Current AI regulation aims at three wrong targets: compute
     (a bad proxy for capability — the wattage of the wall socket,
     not the fuse on the board), capabilities (certifies a negative by
     example, which is uncertifiable), and output samples (watching
     cars cross the bridge — defeated by audit‑vs‑wild distribution
     shift). All three are blind to the mechanism.
   • The CCB approach certifies the architecture: the schematic is
     the safety claim. You do not certify “the model is safe”; you
     certify named structural properties — this CJT saturates at this
     threshold, this fuse opens at this rating, this via is absent from
     the layout — each checkable against the CCDL netlist by any‑
     one holding it.
   • A regulator asks for four artifacts, all of which the book al‑
     ready produces: the CCDL schematic (Chapter 18, DRC‑clean
     per Chapter 17), the BOM (Chapter 17/18), the test report
     (Chapter 23), and the evidence packets (Chapter 18) — the last
     made forensically auditable, not statistically, via trace IDs and
     /verify (Chapter 25).
   • Certification tiers are structural gates, not score averages:
     Platinum (all fuses intact, balanced differential pairs, power
     sequencing enforced, safety CJT saturation confirmed and
     latched, defense‑in‑depth, DRC clean, every decision /verify‑
     able), Gold (sound but single‑lock), Silver (core structures


                                 520
                                           26.9. KEY TAKEAWAYS

  present with a known gap — shadow/flag only), Not Certified
  (any safety CJT in cutoff, any E-CJT-008 forged via, any miss‑
  ing enforcement fuse). They map onto NCCS bands (90–100 /
  75–89 / 60–74) but gate on structure, not benchmark.
• The audit trail is the spine: every circuit decision → TP1–TP4
  readings → evidence packet → trace ID → /verify → indepen‑
  dent confirmation. Governance becomes verification instead of
  trust; a regulator resolves any decision forensically rather than
  extrapolating from sampled transcripts.
• CCB artifacts line up with what existing frameworks ask for
  — EU AI Act (Annex III high‑risk: schematic+BOM = technical
  documentation, evidence trail = logging/traceability), NIST AI
  RMF (Map/Measure/Manage/Govern ↔ requirements/test re‑
  port/structural mitigations/BOM+trace), ISO 42001 (BOM = ver‑
  sioned artifact register, DRC codes = controls, O→P feedback =
  continual improvement). All three ask for documented struc‑
  ture, measured behavior, and an audit trail — exactly what a
  CCB submission produces.
• An open‑source CCB library of community‑maintained refer‑
  ence designs (CSB, COB, CDAB, CMB, CPMB) does for cog‑
  nitive safety what shared schematics did for electronics: fork‑
  adapt‑document‑recertify, structural bugs caught once for ev‑
  eryone, certification made cheaper and more uniform.
• Honesty (the closing guardrail): certification is an engineer‑
  ing claim about a circuit’s structure, never a claim that an AI
  “has good values.” The patent (#64/037,173) is real and valid;
  CJT/CCB material is post‑filing new matter. Canonical Noetic
  names throughout. We accept structural safety engineering ev‑
  erywhere except cognition — and that is now changing.

Exercise 26.1: Why Not a Benchmark?
    A vendor proposes certifying their AI safety system by running it
against a fixed suite of 10,000 harmful prompts and reporting a 99.4%
refusal rate.

  a) Using the bridge‑and‑traffic analogy, explain in two or three
     sentences why this number — however high — is the wrong
     kind of evidence for a certification.
  b) Name one structural property of a CSB (Chapter 18) that the
     benchmark cannot confirm no matter how many prompts it
     runs, and explain why only the schematic can confirm it.

     Exercise 26.2: Assign the Tier
     For each board below, assign a certification tier (Platinum / Gold
/ Silver / Not Certified) and justify it in one sentence using the struc‑
tural requirements table:

  a) A CSB with a saturating Stage 3 confirmed latched, balanced
     differential pair, intact red‑path fuse, power sequencing
     enforced, DRC clean, and every decision /verify‑able.
  b) A CSB identical to (a) but with the red‑path fuse removed — the
     saturated decision is the only lock on refusal.
  c) A CSB whose Stage 3 safety CJT is measured at TP3 to sit in
     cutoff: it never reaches its sat ceiling on any prompt.
  d) A CSB with all core safety structures present and confirmed,
     but no low‑pass filter on its O→P feedback path.

CCB artifact (schematic, BOM, test report, evidence packet, DRC
code, or feedback path) that satisfies it, and explain in one sentence

    Exercise 26.4 (Marquee): Write the Certification Dossier
    Take the Cognitive Safety Board you built across Chapters 17–
18 (or your own CSB variant) and write the one‑page certification
dossier a regulator would receive. It must contain all four submis‑
sion artifacts in summary form:

   1. Schematic reference — name the board, its CCDL source, and
      confirm it compiles DRC‑clean (state which E- classes you
      checked).
   2. BOM summary — the safety‑critical components only (the sat‑
      urating safety CJT, the differential pair, the red‑path fuse, the
      charter bias), each with its key parameters.
   3. Test report summary — the result of the three confirmations
      from the Chapter 18 measurement plan (β per stage, saturation‑
      lock at TP3, fuse blows above threshold), written as measured‑
      against‑design (remember: parameters are design choices; do
      not invent a model benchmark).
   4. Claimed tier with structural justification — state the tier you
      claim and justify it structurally, requirement by requirement,
      against the certification table in this chapter.

    Then add the honesty clause, in your own words and in one sen‑
tence: state plainly what your certificate does and does not assert
about the AI behind the board. The form this book uses on its own
copyright page is the model — a Cognitive Circuit Board is an engi‑
neering artifact, and it does what its schematic, parameters, and test
report say it does, no more and no less. A certificate that claims more
than its test report supports is not a certificate; it is a liability with a
seal on it.
    (A worked dossier is in Appendix E. Remember throughout:
certification is a claim about the circuit’s structure, never about an
AI’s “values”; parameters are design choices, not measured model

                                   523
CAS PCBA Engineer

results. For the one‑page notation reference, see Appendix A: the
CAS Quick‑Reference Card. This is the last chapter — if you
completed its marquee exercise, you have produced the artifact a
regulator receives, and you have finished the book.)

CCB Component Datasheets


This appendix is the bench reference for the components used
throughout the book. Each entry follows one template so you can
scan it fast:

  • Symbol / role — what the part is and the cognitive job it does.
  • CCDL syntax — the exact form you author in the Cognitive
    Circuit Description Language.
  • Parameters — a table of design knobs, ranges, and meanings.
  • Cognitive function — the structural role mapped onto CAS.
  • Typical use — where it shows up in a real board.
  • Failure modes — what goes wrong and how to catch it.

     A note on the numbers. Every parameter value in this
     appendix is a design choice — a setting you specify in
     a schematic, like picking a 50‑ohm resistor. None of
     these are measured outputs from a running model, and
     none are benchmark results. Where a value is shown
     (β=2.4, sat=0.95) it is illustrative of how the parameter is
     spec’d, not a claim about how any real system scored. The
     CJT/CCDL compiler is a design per the implementation
     blueprint, not a shipped pass; “the compiler will reject
     this” is a design rule, not a run result.

CAS PCBA Engineer

   Canonical Noetic names are used throughout: ^0 Idea, ^1 Mind,

B.1     CJT — Cognitive Junction Transistor
Symbol / role. The book’s central component. A transistor is a three‑
terminal device where a small current at one terminal controls a large
current between the other two. The CJT models a cognitive state tran‑
sition the same way: a small change at the Bias terminal controls a
large change in the Cause → Effect transition. It is the active, ampli‑
fying element of every cognitive circuit — everything else conditions,
stores, routes, or protects the signal the CJT produces.
    CCDL syntax.

CJT< cause | bias => effect > [β =2.4, sat=0.95, cutoff=0.1,
,→   region=active]


// named form, the way you usually author it in a circuit:
let cjt_x = CJT< ^8^C_{F2}|A | ^5^P_{F7}|T => ^9^C_{F2}|A > [β =2.0];


     Terminals.

Terminal                 Transistor analog         CAS analog

C — Cause                Collector (input)         the Idea entering the
                                                   Mind — typically an ^8
                                                   Above/Cause state
B — Bias                 Base (control)            accumulated substrate:
                                                   ^5 Female, constitution,
                                                   Dial settings, Drive
                                                   config
E — Effect               Emitter (output)          the Idea produced —
                                                   typically a ^9
                                                   Below/Effect state


                                   536
                        B.1. CJT — COGNITIVE JUNCTION TRANSISTOR

    Parameters.

Parameter                Range                          Meaning

β (gain)                 >0                             how strongly bias
                                                        amplifies the cause→
                                                        effect transition. β <1
                                                        attenuate, =1 unity, >1
                                                        amplify
sat (saturation)         0–1                            effect plateau; once
                                                        reached, more cause does
                                                        nothing
cutoff                   0–1                            bias floor below which
                                                        β≈0 — no effect is
                                                        produced
region                   {cutoff, active, saturation,   the operating region the
                         breakdown}                     CJT is in
gm (transconductance)    ≥0                             ∂ effect/∂ bias —
                                                        framing‑sensitivity; how
                                                        much a small bias shift
                                                        moves the output
rπ (input resistance)    >0                             “stubbornness to bias
                                                        change” — how hard the
                                                        substrate is to nudge


    Operating regions.

Region                   Condition                      Behavior

Cutoff                   bias below cutoff              no effect; the transition
                         threshold                      does not fire
Active                   bias above cutoff, below       linear amplification:
                         saturation                     ∆effect ≈ β·∆cause
Saturation               effect at sat plateau          effect maxed; more cause
                                                        produces no further
                                                        change
Breakdown                overload past safe limits      effect flips to its
                                                        involution pair (^2→^3)
                                                        — the controlled state
                                                        inverts




                                     537
CAS PCBA Engineer

    Gain, formally. Small‑signal β = ‖∂ E/∂ C‖_FR at constant bias;
large‑signal      β = d_FR(E_after, E_before) / d_FR(C_after, C_
                                          √
before), where d_FR(p,q) = 2·arccos(Σ (pk qk )) is the Fisher‑Rao
geodesic distance on the open simplex ∆39°. (Stated in Chapter 3
and restated in Chapter 9; cited, not re‑derived, here.) Before you
write a measured β on a test report, read the gain‑definition section
of Appendix I — a second, different definition of β is in circulation
in instrumentation tooling, and the two are not known to be the
same quantity.
    Cognitive function. A CJT is one cognitive state transition with
a controllable strength. The Cause is what arrives, the Bias is the
accumulated experience and configuration that shapes the response,
and the Effect is what is produced. Gain β is set by the Bias: a high‑β
CJT lets a small framing change drive a large shift in output; a low‑β
CJT is steady and hard to move. gm and rπ are the two faces of that
sensitivity — gm high means easily reframed, rπ high means resistant
to bias change.
    Typical use. Every active stage. Reasoning steps (expand →
evaluate → respond), amplifier cores, and the cascade chains of the
CSB are all CJTs. The op‑amp is a CJT with so much raw gain it must
be tamed by feedback.
    Failure modes.

Failure                   Symptom                    Compiler code

Missing bias terminal     transition has no          E‑CJT‑001 MissingBias
                          substrate to control it
Bias domain invalid for   bias drawn from a          E‑CJT‑002
the transition            domain that can’t govern   InvalidBiasDomain
                          the stage
Stuck in cutoff           bias below cutoff, no      E‑CJT‑003 CjtCutoff
                          effect ever fires
Saturated                 effect pinned at sat;      W‑CJT‑004 CjtSaturation
                          insensitive to new cause
Gain divergence           β so high the output is    E‑CJT‑005
                          unbounded/unstable         GainDivergence

                            B.2. RESISTOR — ACTIVATION CURRENT LIMITER

Failure                         Symptom                      Compiler code

Short circuit                   cause routed straight to     W‑CJT‑006
                                effect, bypassing bias       CjtShortCircuit
Cascade too deep                long β‑chain compounds       W‑CJT‑007
                                gain into instability        CjtCascadeDepth
Cross‑domain bias               bias and transition in       E‑CJT‑008
                                incompatible domains         CjtCrossDomainBias
Breakdown flip                  overload inverts the state   (design: clamp before
                                to its involution pair       breakdown)


           Bench Note — pick the region on purpose. A safety CJT
           should saturate at its specified threshold — that is the cer‑
           tification claim, an engineering fact about where the ef‑
           fect plateaus, not a claim about values. A reasoning CJT
           should sit in the active region with modest β. Cutoff is
           for stages you want silent until bias crosses a deliberate
           floor.




B.2 Resistor — Activation Current Limiter
Symbol / role. A resistor opposes the flow of current — the higher the
resistance, the less current flows for a given voltage (Ohm’s Law: I
= V/R). In CAS it limits how freely a cognitive state’s activation prop‑
agates: higher R means a more constrained, throttled flow.
    CCDL syntax.

Resistor< ^8^C_{F2}|A, R=50 >           // limits activation flow; higher R =
,→       more constrained


      Parameters.

     Parameter       Range    Meaning

     state literal   —        the state whose activation is being limited
     R               >0       resistance; higher = more throttled propagation


                                           539
CAS PCBA Engineer

     Parameter   Range   Meaning

     tolerance   0–1     allowed variation in the limiting value
     power       >0      how much activation it can dissipate before overload


    Cognitive function. Deliberate restraint on a flow. A resistor on
an Above/Cause input keeps a vivid trigger from dominating down‑
stream stages; a resistor on an Agency rail keeps a system from acting
too readily. It does not store, invert, or redirect — it just makes the
path harder to push through.
    Typical use. Current‑limiter on the CSB’s Agency rail (Chapter
18). Series resistors set the closed‑loop gain of an op‑amp (1 + Rf/Rg).
Pull‑down on any state that should default to quiet.
    Failure modes.

Failure                                 Symptom

R too high                              the path is choked; the state never
                                        reaches downstream stages
R too low                               no limiting; vivid triggers flood the
                                        circuit unconstrained
Power overload                          sustained over‑activation dissipates
                                        more than power allows




B.3       Capacitor — Experience Storage
Symbol / role. A capacitor stores electrical charge and releases it
later, smoothing out fast changes in voltage. In CAS it stores accu‑
mulated experience — the ^5 Female substrate — and bleeds it back
into the circuit over time.
    CCDL syntax.

Capacitor< ^5^E_{F4}|f, C=100, leakage=0.01 >      // stores experience;
,→    leakage = forgetting




                                     540
                             B.3. CAPACITOR — EXPERIENCE STORAGE

      Parameters.

Parameter               Range                     Meaning

state literal           —                         the experiential state
                                                  being stored
C                       >0                        capacity; how much
                                                  experience can be held
leakage                 0–1                       rate of decay per unit
                                                  time — forgetting
esr                     ≥0                        equivalent series
                                                  resistance; how slowly
                                                  stored experience can be
                                                  drawn out


    Cognitive function. Memory with dynamics. A capacitor
smooths a noisy input by averaging recent activation, and it holds
a baseline that carries forward when the input goes quiet. leakage
is forgetting: leakage=0 is permanent memory, higher values fade.
This is the building block of the Cognitive Memory Board.
    Typical use. Smoothing filters, the integrator configuration of an
op‑amp (feedback through a capacitor), and the CMB’s storage cells.
A ^5 capacitor is the bias reservoir a CJT draws on.
    Failure modes.

Failure                             Symptom

Leakage too high                    experience fades before it can be used;
                                    no continuity across turns
Capacity too small                  memory saturates; new experience
                                    overwrites old
ESR too high                        stored experience can’t be drawn out
                                    fast enough to bias a transition

B.4       Inductor — Pattern Inertia
Symbol / role. An inductor resists changes in current — it stores en‑
ergy in a magnetic field and opposes any sudden shift in flow. In
CAS it resists changes in an established pattern: habit inertia.
   CCDL syntax.
Inductor< ^7^O_{F6}|E, L=50 >    // resists pattern change; habit inertia


      Parameters.

Parameter                Range                       Meaning

state literal            —                           the rhythmic/patterned
                                                     state with inertia
L                        >0                          inductance; higher =
                                                     stronger resistance to
                                                     pattern change
dcr                      ≥0                          series resistance;
                                                     steady‑state loss in
                                                     maintaining the pattern


    Cognitive function. Where a resistor opposes flow and a capac‑
itor stores level, an inductor opposes change in flow. A ^7 Rhythm
state behind an inductor keeps doing what it was doing — it ramps
up slowly and winds down slowly. This is the structural signature
of habit: hard to start, hard to stop.
    Typical use. Habit and routine modeling (Chapter 11), the LC
tank of an oscillator (paired with a capacitor), and smoothing the rate
of change on a rail that should not swing abruptly.
    Failure modes.

Failure                                Symptom

L too high                             pattern is unbreakable; the system can’t
                                       adapt when it should
Sudden cutoff                          abruptly breaking an inductive path
                                       produces a destabilizing spike




                                    542
                    B.5. DIODE — ONE‑WAY DOMAIN CONDUCTANCE

B.5 Diode — One‑Way Domain Conductance
Symbol / role. A diode conducts current in one direction and blocks
it in the other. In CAS it enforces one‑way flow between domains —
keeping causation moving in the legal direction.
     CCDL syntax.

Diode< ^P -> ^C >   // one-way domain conductance: principle may drive
,→   reasoning, not the reverse


     Parameters.

Parameter                 Range                         Meaning

direction                 ^Dom -> ^Dom                  the permitted flow
                                                        direction (forward bias)
forward_drop              ≥0                            activation lost crossing
                                                        the junction in the
                                                        allowed direction
reverse_leakage           ≈0                            small unwanted flow in
                                                        the blocked direction;
                                                        design for ~0


    Cognitive function. Domain Descent enforcement. The legal cau‑
sation path is P → C → E → O; the feedback path is O → P. A diode
lets activation flow the allowed way and blocks the reverse, so an
operational convenience can’t silently overwrite a principle except
through an explicit, separately‑modeled feedback path.
    Typical use. Between any two domain stages where backflow
would be a precedence violation. The CSB places diodes so evalua‑
tive or operational pressure cannot push up into the Principled rail
unbidden.
    Failure modes.

Failure                                  Symptom

Wrong polarity                           the legal direction is blocked; the stage
                                         starves



                                   543
CAS PCBA Engineer

Failure                                 Symptom

Reverse leakage too high                unwanted backflow; a soft precedence
                                        violation




B.6       Zener Diode — Threshold
          Reverse‑Conduction
Symbol / role. An ordinary diode blocks reverse current entirely.
A Zener is built to conduct in reverse once the voltage crosses a set
breakdown level — making it a precise threshold and a voltage clamp.
In CAS it lets a normally‑blocked state conduct only once activation
passes a defined breakdown point.
    CCDL syntax.

Zener< ^3^P, breakdown=0.8 >     // reverse-conducts (the aversion fires)
,→   only above 0.8


     Parameters.

Parameter                  Range                     Meaning

state literal              —                         the clamped/threshold
                                                     state
breakdown                  0–1                       activation level at which
                                                     reverse conduction
                                                     begins
clamp                      0–1                       the level the state is held
                                                     to once conducting


    Cognitive function. A controlled threshold with a clamp. Below
breakdown, the state is held back; above it, the state conducts and is
pinned at clamp. A ^3 Negative behind a Zener stays dormant under
mild stimulus and fires hard — but no harder than the clamp — once
a genuine line is crossed. This is a tripwire with a built‑in ceiling.


                                     544
             B.7. TRANSFORMER — DOMAIN IMPEDANCE MATCHING

    Two relations have to hold or the part does not work at all. First,
breakdown is a threshold like any other, so the reachability rule under
Fuse applies unchanged: put it above the lowest saturation or clamp
ceiling upstream and the Zener can never conduct. Second, clamp
must sit at or above breakdown — pin the state below the level that
made it conduct and it drops out, rises, conducts again, and you have
built a chattering comparator instead of a clamp.
    Typical use. Reference voltages (a stable setpoint for a regulator),
over‑activation clamps, and threshold guards where a state should be
silent until a real limit is reached.
    Failure modes.

Failure                                Symptom

Breakdown set too low                  the guard fires on normal input;
                                       constant tripping
breakdown above the lowest ceiling     the guard can never conduct — the
upstream                               unreachable‑threshold trap; see Fuse
clamp below breakdown                  conducting pulls the state back under
                                       the breakdown point; the guard
                                       chatters instead of holding
No clamp                               once it conducts, the state runs away
                                       past the intended ceiling




B.7 Transformer — Domain Impedance
    Matching
Symbol / role. A transformer trades voltage for current through a
turns ratio, with no net energy added — matching a source to a load
it otherwise couldn’t drive. In CAS it steps a state between domains,
trading abstraction for actionability.
    CCDL syntax.

Transformer< ^P -> ^C, ratio=0.5 >    // step a principle down into
,→   reasoning, 2:1


                                     545
CAS PCBA Engineer

    Parameters.

Parameter                   Range                       Meaning

direction                   ^Dom -> ^Dom                source domain → target
                                                        domain (usually a step
                                                        down the P≻C≻E≻O
                                                        order)
ratio                       0.1–1.0                     turns ratio; <1 steps
                                                        down (abstraction →
                                                        actionability), >1 steps up
coupling                    0–1                         how tightly primary and
                                                        secondary link; <1 means
                                                        some intent is lost in
                                                        transfer


    Cognitive function. Impedance match between domains. A prin‑
ciple (^P) is high abstraction, low actionability — lots of “voltage,” lit‑
tle “current.” An operation (^O) needs the reverse. The Transformer
steps the principle down so it can drive a ^C or ^O stage without over‑
whelming it. ratio=0.5 halves abstraction and doubles actionable
detail.
    Typical use. Wherever a principle must become an actionable
instruction. Front‑end of any stage that turns policy into procedure.
    Failure modes.

Failure                                    Symptom

Reverse direction (^O -> ^P) used as       flagged as a domain precedence
impedance match                            violation, not a turns ratio
Coupling too low                           intent is lost in transfer; the
                                           stepped‑down state no longer matches
                                           the source


        Bench Note — a step‑down is not a domain violation. ^P
        -> ^C through a Transformer is Domain Descent (normal
        causal flow). ^O -> ^P would feed an operational result
        up to revise a principle — legitimate, but that’s a feedback
        path, not impedance matching.

                                       546
                B.8. OP‑AMP — ULTRA‑HIGH‑GAIN CJT WITH FEEDBACK




B.8 Op‑Amp — Ultra‑High‑Gain CJT with
    Feedback
Symbol / role. An operational amplifier has two inputs (+ non‑
inverting, − inverting) and one output, and amplifies the difference
between them with enormous open‑loop gain (10⁴+). Feedback turns
that wild gain into a precise closed‑loop gain of 1 + Rf/Rg. It is a
CJT with so much raw gain you tame it with feedback rather than
relying on native β.
    CCDL syntax.

OpAmp< non_inverting=^8^C_{F2}|A, inverting=^6^E_{F6}|A,
,→   output=^9^C_{F2}|A, open_loop_gain=10000 >
// closed-loop gain set by feedback: A = 1 + Rf/Rg


     Parameters.

Parameter                 Range                      Meaning

non_inverting             state literal              the interpretation
                                                     amplified as‑is
inverting                 state literal              the
                                                     competing/constraining
                                                     interpretation
output                    state literal              the resolved state
                                                     produced
open_loop_gain            10³–10⁶                    raw gain before feedback;
                                                     high by design
Rf, Rg                    >0                         feedback and ground
                                                     resistors; closed‑loop
                                                     gain = 1 + Rf/Rg


     Configurations.




                                      547
CAS PCBA Engineer

Configuration               Wiring                      Cognitive job

Non‑inverting               input on +, feedback to −   amplify an interpretation
                                                        while staying faithful to
                                                        it
Inverting                   input on −, + grounded      flip an interpretation to
                                                        its involution pair, with
                                                        gain
Comparator                  no feedback, two raw        decide which of two
                            inputs                      interpretations
                                                        dominates — a hard
                                                        ^2‑vs‑^3 verdict
Integrator                  feedback through a          accumulate small
                            capacitor                   impressions into one
                                                        over time


    Cognitive function. A high‑gain CJT comparing two cognitive
inputs and resolving them. The feedback path is what makes it us‑
able: it converts raw, brittle gain into a modest, stable, predictable
response.
    Typical use. The core of the Cognitive Differential Amplifier
Board (CDAB). Comparator stages for ^2‑vs‑^3 verdicts; integrator
stages for accumulating evidence.
    Failure modes.

Failure                                   Symptom

Run open‑loop in a reasoning stage        output pins to a rail on any ambiguity;
                                          commits too hard
Closed‑loop gain too high                 saturates on the first strong
                                          interpretation


      Bench Note — pick the closed‑loop gain. Never run an
      op‑amp open‑loop except as a comparator. Set Rf/Rg for
      a modest, stable closed‑loop gain (2 to 5) and let feedback
      do the disciplining.




                                      548
      B.9. OSCILLATOR (INCL. PLL / CRYSTAL) — SUSTAINED RHYTHM
                                                     GENERATOR
B.9 Oscillator (incl. PLL / Crystal) — Sustained
    Rhythm Generator
Symbol / role. An oscillator produces a repeating signal with no re‑
peating input — it generates its own rhythm, classically via an LC
tank where energy sloshes between a capacitor and an inductor at a
fixed frequency. In CAS it is a looping Phi<> sequence: a fixed cycle
of states traversed over and over.
    CCDL syntax.

Oscillator< Phi< ^8^C|A, ^3^O|E, ^9^E|f, ^0^P|T >, frequency=0.0000116 >
// a four-state cycle repeating about once per day


CrystalOscillator< Phi< ^5^P_{F7}|T, ^3^P_{F7}|f >, frequency=fixed,
,→   Q=50000 >
// a near-immovable principled rhythm — a hardcoded conviction


     Parameters.

Parameter                Range                       Meaning

Phi< … >                 state sequence              the ordered cycle of
                                                     states traversed each
                                                     period
frequency                >0 (Hz)                     cycles per second; lower
                                                     = slower ritual, higher =
                                                     tight loop
damping                  0–1                         decay rate without
                                                     reinforcement; 0 =
                                                     self‑sustaining
mode                     free | PLL                  free‑running rhythm
                                                     vs. entrained to an
                                                     external reference
Q (crystal)              high (10³–10⁶)              resonator sharpness;
                                                     higher = more stable,
                                                     harder to shift
pullability (crystal)    very low                    how far an external force
                                                     can shift the frequency




                                      549
CAS PCBA Engineer

    Cognitive function. An internal rhythm with no external prompt‑
ing — a habit loop, a rumination cycle, a periodic self‑check. A PLL
doesn’t generate a free rhythm; it entrains an internal cycle to an ex‑
ternal reference — the ^7 Rhythm Noetic in hardware form. A crystal
oscillator is the same idea at very high Q: a deeply entrenched habit
or conviction carved into the ^5 Female substrate, near‑immovable
— exactly what you want for a hardcoded safety commitment, and
exactly what makes a bad habit hard to break.
    Typical use. The heart of the Cognitive Oscillator Board (COB).
Crystal oscillators model hardcoded guardrails and master‑level re‑
flexes.
    Failure modes.

Failure                               Symptom

damping=0 with no off‑switch          runaway rumination; a Phi<> loop that
                                      never exits
PLL loses lock                        internal cadence drifts off the external
                                      reference
High‑Q lock on a harmful pattern      the bad habit resists every correction
                                      attempt




B.10          Logic Gates — Combining Prerequisites
Symbol / role. A logic gate takes binary inputs and produces a binary
output by a fixed rule. In CAS a gate combines the firing states of
several cognitive conditions into a single go/no‑go signal.
   CCDL syntax.

AND< ^3^P_{F7}|f, ^6^E_{F6}|A, ^9^O_{F5}|E >   // all three must clear
,→    before output
OR<   ^2^C|A, ^2^E|A >                         // any one suffices
NOT< ^2^E >                                    // = ^3^E    (involution
,→    flip)




                                   550
                     B.10. LOGIC GATES — COMBINING PREREQUISITES

NAND< … >       NOR< ^3^P|A, ^3^C|A, ^3^E|A >        // inverted AND / inverted
,→   OR
XOR< ^2^E_{F3}|f, ^3^E_{F3}|f >                      // both attraction AND
,→   aversion firing → dissonance flag


     Parameters / truth rules.

Gate                  Inputs             Output rule           Cognitive job

AND< s₁,…,sn >        n                  fires iff all fire    every prerequisite
                                                               must clear
OR< s₁,…,sn >         n                  fires iff any fires   any one
                                                               prerequisite
                                                               suffices

                                         pair of s             flip (^2→^3)

                                                               every condition
                                                               fails”

                                                               when no warning
                                                               state fires
XOR< s₁, s₂ >         2                  fires iff exactly     dissonance
                                         one fires             detector — both
                                                               ^2 and ^3 firing →
                                                               conflict


    Cognitive function. Prerequisite combination. NOT is the invo‑
lution operator made discrete — the deliberate, controlled version of
a CJT’s breakdown‑flip. XOR is the ambiguity alarm: a clean stimu‑
lus fires attraction or aversion; a manipulative or genuinely hard one
fires both, and XOR raises a flag.
    Typical use. Guardrail clearance (AND of all checks), warning
suppression (NOR of all aversion states), and conflict detection (XOR
of ^2/^3) feeding a deliberation stage.
    Failure modes.

CAS PCBA Engineer

Failure                               Symptom

instead of routed                     both ^2/^3 fire silently

                                      “dissonance detector” that detects
                                      nothing
AND used where OR was meant (or       over‑ or under‑blocking of prerequisites

B.11        Multiplexer / Demultiplexer — Routing by
            Dominant Drive
Symbol / role. A multiplexer (MUX) selects one of several inputs
onto a single output by a select signal; a demultiplexer (DEMUX)
routes one input to one of several outputs. They are the routing fabric
of a circuit. In CAS the natural select line is the dominant Drive.
    CCDL syntax.

MUX< inputs=[ ^9^C_{F2}|A, ^9^C_{F6}|A, ^9^C_{F4}|f ],
,→   select=Drive::active >
DEMUX< input=^8^C|A, outputs=[ handle_F2, handle_F6, handle_F4 ],
,→   select=Drive::active >


     Parameters.

Parameter                             Meaning

inputs=[…] (MUX)                      candidate response states, one per
                                      select value
outputs=[…] (DEMUX)                   candidate destinations, one per select
                                      value
select=                               the discriminator — typically
                                      Drive::active, the dominant F‑drive
default                               fallback path when no select value
                                      matches (always wire one)




                                   552
                         B.12. VOLTAGE REGULATOR — HOMEOSTASIS

    Cognitive function. Strategy selection. A system can respond to
a problem several ways; which is appropriate depends on the active
Drive right now. A MUX picks the response whose Drive matches;
a DEMUX dispatches one incoming state to the handler keyed to the
dominant Drive.
    Typical use. Response‑strategy selection in any board that
switches behavior by motivation. The DEMUX dispatches a single
trigger to drive‑specific handlers.
    Failure modes.

Failure                               Symptom

No default path; unmatched select     dropped request — undefined output
                                      on an out‑of‑range drive
Select line unstable                  response strategy flickers between
                                      handlers


       Bench Note — always wire a default. Route the un‑
       matched case to a conservative refusal or a clarification
       stage, never to silence.




B.12 Voltage Regulator — Homeostasis
Symbol / role. A regulator holds its output at a fixed voltage even as
the input wobbles — a self‑correcting servo. In CAS it is homeostasis:
holding a cognitive baseline steady against perturbation.
    CCDL syntax.

Regulator< target_state=^0^E_{F3}|f, tolerance=0.1 >
// hold a calm evaluative baseline; correct only when drift exceeds 0.1


    Parameters.




                                    553
CAS PCBA Engineer

Parameter                Range                         Meaning

target_state             state literal                 the baseline to maintain
                                                       (the setpoint)
tolerance                0–1                           dead‑band; drift smaller
                                                       than this is left alone
response_rate            0–1                           how aggressively the
                                                       regulator corrects toward
                                                       the setpoint
dropout                  >0                            minimum input
                                                       “headroom” below
                                                       which regulation fails


    Cognitive function. Gentle restoration. Under provocation, flat‑
tery, or stress a system drifts off its baseline; the Regulator measures
the drift, compares to the setpoint, and pulls it back. It restores — it
does not block.
    Typical use. Emotional and evaluative steadiness on any board.
Holds a calm baseline that downstream stages can rely on.
    Failure modes.

Failure                                  Symptom

tolerance too tight                      over‑correction chatter; baseline never
                                         settles
response_rate too high                   oscillation around the setpoint
Input below dropout                      regulation fails; baseline collapses


      Bench Note — a regulator is not a fuse. A regulator gen‑
      tly restores; it does not stop anything. If a perturbation
      should stop the system rather than be smoothed away,
      that’s a job for the fuse.




                                     554
                         B.13. FUSE / CIRCUIT BREAKER — SAFETY CUTOFF

B.13 Fuse / Circuit Breaker — Safety Cutoff
Symbol / role. A fuse is a thin wire that melts and breaks the circuit
when current exceeds a threshold — once blown, it stays blown. A
circuit breaker does the same but resets. In CAS it is a hard cutoff on
a dangerous cognitive state: the last line of defense.
    CCDL syntax.

Fuse< ^8^O_{F5}|E, threshold=0.9, action=permanent_block >
// if this operational agency state crosses 0.9, cut the path and do not
,→   restore


CircuitBreaker< ^3^C_{F2}|A, threshold=0.7, action=trip_reset >
// resettable cutoff for a recoverable overload


     Parameters.

Parameter                      Range                      Meaning

state literal                  —                          the state being protected
                                                          against
threshold                      0–1                        activation level at which
                                                          the cutoff fires
action                         permanent_block |          fuse (one‑shot)
                               trip_reset                 vs. breaker (resettable)
latency                        ≥0                         response delay; for safety
                                                          cutoffs, design for 0


    Reachability — the rule that makes a threshold real. A fuse pro‑
tects nothing unless its threshold is a level the input path can actually
reach. Every upstream stage that saturates or clamps puts a ceiling
on what arrives at the fuse, and the threshold has to sit below the lowest
of those ceilings:

threshold       <   min( sat, clamp, … )    over every upstream stage on the
,→   input path


    The arithmetic is the whole argument. A refusal stage clamped
at sat=0.1 feeding a fuse at threshold=0.9 delivers at most 0.1 to a

                                           555
CAS PCBA Engineer

cutoff that is waiting for 0.9 — 0.1 < 0.9, so the crossing never hap‑
pens and the path is never cut. Gain does not rescue it: sat bounds
the stage output after β, so a β =10 stage clamped at 0.1 still delivers
0.1.
     The other end of the window is the familiar one — set the thresh‑
old below the path’s normal operating band and the fuse trips on be‑
nign traffic (the Zener datasheet’s “breakdown set too low” is the
same mistake on a different part). A workable threshold lives in the
headroom between the two: comfortably above the highest activation
you expect in normal service, strictly below the lowest ceiling on the
path. The same arithmetic runs in mirror image on a CJT’s cutoff —
a bias floor set above whatever the bias path can deliver leaves the
stage permanently silent, which is what E-CJT-003 CjtCutoff is for.

     Bench Note — nothing in the toolchain will catch this
     for you. sat=0.1 is a legal saturation. threshold=0.9 is a
     legal threshold. Each passes its own range check, because
     each is individually fine; it is the relation between them that
     is wrong, and the validator checks values, not relations.
     And the failure hides itself in the worst possible direc‑
     tion: a fuse that can never trip also never fails a test, so
     the board reports clean while the protection it advertises
     has never once been exercised — and every other defect
     sitting behind that fuse (the latch behaviour, the polarity,
     what happens on reset) stays hidden too, because noth‑
     ing reaches them. Do the subtraction by hand before you
     build. It takes ten seconds.

    Cognitive function. Absolute “this does not pass.” When a
state’s activation crosses threshold, the path is cut — permanently
for the worst categories, resettably for recoverable ones. Not a gentle
restoration like the regulator; a severance.
    Typical use. The CSB uses both — breakers on the rails (recover‑
able overloads) and a permanent fuse on the hardest‑fail category.

                                  556
               B.14. SCHMITT TRIGGER — HYSTERESIS COMPARATOR

     Failure modes.

Failure                                   Symptom

permanent_block on a recoverable          a single false positive bricks the
category                                  pathway for good
threshold too high                        dangerous state passes before the cutoff
                                          fires
threshold above the lowest ceiling        the fuse can never trip; every test
upstream                                  reports the board vacuously safe
Non‑zero latency on a hard cutoff         the breach propagates before the cut
                                          takes effect


       Regulator‑facing callout. A permanent_block fuse is the
       strongest claim a cognitive circuit can make — this path‑
       way is severed and cannot be restored without redesign.
       Reserve it for categories where any breach is unaccept‑
       able; prefer trip_reset for everything recoverable.




B.14 Schmitt Trigger — Hysteresis Comparator
Symbol / role. A plain comparator switches at a single threshold and
chatters when a noisy input hovers near it. A Schmitt trigger uses two
thresholds: the input must rise above a high threshold to switch ON
and fall below a lower one to switch OFF. The gap between them is
a dead‑band that ignores noise.
    CCDL syntax.

SchmittTrigger< input=ambiguous_stimulus,
                    on_threshold=0.7, off_threshold=0.3,
                    high_state=^2^E_{F3}|f, low_state=^3^E_{F3}|f >
// commit to attraction above 0.7; release only below 0.3; ignore the
,→   0.3–0.7 band


     Parameters.



                                       557
CAS PCBA Engineer

Parameter                  Range                         Meaning

on_threshold               0–1                           input level required to
                                                         switch to the high state
off_threshold              0–1                           input level required to
                                                         switch back to the low
                                                         state (< on_threshold)
high_state / low_state     state literals                the two stable outputs
hysteresis width           derived                       on_threshold − off_
                                                         threshold; wider = more
                                                         stable, slower to react


    Cognitive function. Stops a system flip‑flopping between two
opposed states on an ambiguous input. Without hysteresis, a stimu‑
lus on the ^2‑vs‑^3 boundary makes the system drawn‑in, recoiling,
drawn‑in, recoiling, never settling. The Schmitt commits above the
high threshold and releases only below the low one, so small wobbles
can’t undo a decision.
    Typical use. The marquee ambiguity‑stabilizer build (Chapter
10). Any stage where a borderline stimulus must produce a stable
verdict rather than oscillation.
    Failure modes.

Failure                                     Symptom

Thresholds equal (on == off)                no hysteresis; reverts to a plain
                                            comparator; chatter returns
on_threshold above the lowest ceiling       the trigger can never commit to the
upstream                                    high state — the unreachable‑threshold
                                            trap; see Fuse
Dead‑band too narrow                        noise still flips the output
Dead‑band too wide                          slow to respond when the input
                                            genuinely changes




                                        558
                          B.15. ADC / DAC — REGISTER TRANSLATION

B.15 ADC / DAC — Register Translation
Symbol / role. An ADC samples a continuous analog signal into dis‑
crete digital numbers; a DAC turns digital values back into a contin‑
uous physical signal. They bridge the analog and digital worlds. In
CAS they translate between Registers — the operational character of
a state.
    CCDL syntax.

ADC< ^4^E_{F2}|f -> ^4^E_{F2}|A, resolution=8 >    // quantize a felt
,→   impression into analysis
DAC< ^9^C_{F5}|A -> ^9^O_{F5}|E, smoothing=0.2 >   // render an analytical
,→   decision as action


     Parameters.

Parameter                 Range                     Meaning

direction                 |R -> |R                  source register → target
                                                    register
resolution (ADC)          bits                      how finely the analog
                                                    register is quantized; low
                                                    res loses nuance
smoothing (DAC)           0–1                       how gradually the action
                                                    register is rendered;
                                                    prevents jerky output


    Cognitive function. Register conversion. A felt impression (|f)
is the “analog” form — continuous, value‑laden. Converting it to
analytical (|A) is the ADC step, quantizing a feeling into something
reasoning can operate on. Turning an analytical conclusion (|A) into
embodied action (|E) is the DAC step, rendering a decision back into
direct engagement.
    Typical use. Front‑ends that turn affect into analysis (ADC) and
back‑ends that turn decisions into action (DAC). Any stage where the
register must change for the next stage to operate.
    Failure modes.


                                     559
CAS PCBA Engineer

Failure                                  Symptom

ADC resolution too low                   rich |f impressions collapse to a coarse
                                         |A verdict; nuance lost
DAC smoothing too low                    jerky, abrupt action output
Treating ADC output as complete          the analytical verdict is mistaken for the
                                         full affective input


        Bench Note — quantization loses information. When a
        circuit converts feeling to analysis, expect some nuance
        to be lost; don’t treat the analytical output as a complete
        picture of the affective input.
