Appendix C

CCDL Language Reference


This appendix is the language reference for CCDL — the Cognitive
Circuit Description Language. Chapters 4 and 17 taught you to read
and author CCDL by example. This appendix is the dry, bench‑side
specification: every lexical element, every statement form the book’s
own listings use, every parameter and its range, every validation rule
the compiler is designed to apply, and the full error‑code table.
    What it covers — and what it deliberately does not — is stated
exactly in Scope of This Grammar, near the end. The short version,
so you are not surprised later: the syntax here is derived from the
book’s printed listings and admits all five reference boards of Part IV,
while the semantics of several statement families is not yet formalized.
The construct coverage matrix in that section says which is which,
leader by leader.
    Treat it the way you treat a transistor datasheet or a language stan‑
dard. You do not read it front to back for pleasure; you keep it open
and look things up. Where a chapter says “the compiler will reject
this,” this appendix tells you which rule rejects it and what code it re‑
turns.
    A note on status, carried from the rest of the book: CCDL is the
language you author in, and the CAS compiler is the tool that val‑
idates it. The compiler is a design specified in the implementation‑
blueprint roadmap, not a shipped, runnable pass. Everything in this

                                  563
CAS PCBA Engineer

appendix describes the language and the validation rules as designed.
Nothing here is a transcript of a build that ran and produced mea‑
sured numbers. “The compiler rejects this with E‑CJT‑008” is a de‑
sign rule. “I ran this circuit and read β=2.4” would be a fabrication,
and you will not find one in this appendix.




C.1    Overview
CCDL is a declarative, schematic‑as‑text language. You do not write
instructions that execute step by step; you declare a circuit — its termi‑
nals, its typed cognitive states, its components, and the connections
between them — and the compiler validates that the declaration de‑
scribes a legal cognitive circuit board (CCB).
    The mental model is the electronic schematic, not the program:

   • A CCDL file is a netlist: a list of parts and the nets (states) that
     wire them together.
   • Order of declaration inside a circuit block does not change the
     circuit. A node may be referenced before or after its declaration;
     the compiler resolves the whole block as one graph. (Authoring
     convention, used throughout the book, is to declare nodes first,
     then components, then feedback, then probes — for readability,
     not because the language requires it.)
   • The compiler’s job is validation, not execution: it type‑checks
     every state literal, confirms every CJT has the terminals it
     needs, checks every parameter against its range, and enforces
     the structural design rules in §C.9. A file that passes is a legal
     circuit; a file that fails returns one or more of the error codes in
     §C.10.

   CCDL describes two kinds of artifact:



                                  564
                                               C.2. LEXICAL ELEMENTS

   • A circuit { … } — a single self‑contained board (one
     schematic). This is the form in Chapter 4 and most of the book.
   • A board { … } — a multilayer board whose components are or‑
     ganized onto Domain layers (P / C / E / O) connected by vias.
     This is the layout form from Chapter 17, Step 6.

   Both are CCDL. A circuit is the schematic view (what connects
to what); a board is the layout view (which layer everything sits on
and how vias cross between layers).




C.2 Lexical Elements
The lexical layer is what the compiler’s tokenizer sees before any
structure is parsed.

Identifiers
An identifier names a circuit, a node, a component instance, a probe,
a via, or a layer.

identifier ::= letter , { letter | digit | ”_” }
letter     ::= ”a”…”z” | ”A”…”Z”
digit      ::= ”0”…”9”


   • Begins with a letter; thereafter letters, digits, underscores.
   • Case‑sensitive: bias_charter and Bias_Charter are different
     identifiers.
   • Convention: snake_case for nodes and instances (policy_
     aversion, tp_guard), short prefixes for instance kinds (c1, c2
     for CJTs; r1 for resistors; d1 for diodes; tp1 for probes; v1 for
     vias). The prefixes are convention, not keywords.
   • Reserved words (§C.2.7) may not be used as identifiers.




                                   565
CAS PCBA Engineer

CAS State Literals
A state literal is a first‑class lexical token in CCDL — the “type” car‑
ried by a node, a component terminal, a layer entry, or a via endpoint.
Its grammar is the canonical CAS state grammar from Appendix A
and Chapter 2:

state_literal ::= noetic , [ domain ] , [ ”_{” , drive , ”}” ] , [
,→   register ]
noetic            ::= ”^” , ( ”0”…”9” )
domain            ::= ”^” , ( ”P” | ”C” | ”E” | ”O” )
drive             ::= ”F” , ( ”1”…”7” )
register          ::= ”|” , reg_value
reg_value         ::= ”T” | ”A” | ”f” | ”E”
                  |   ”⟨” , reg_value , { ”,” , reg_value } , ”⟩”


   The four axes, named canonically (never renamed to their circuit
function):

     • Noetic ^0…^9 — the structural dynamic. ^0 Idea, ^1 Mind,
       ^2 Positive, ^3 Negative, ^4 Vibration, ^5 Female, ^6 Male, ^7
       Rhythm, ^8 Above/Cause, ^9 Below/Effect. Involution pairs
       ^2↔^3, ^5↔^6, ^8↔^9; self‑duals ^0, ^1, ^4, ^7.
     • Domain ^P ^C ^E ^O — Principled ≻ Cognitive ≻ Evaluative ≻
       Operational.
     • Drive _{F1}…_{F7} — F1 Unity, F2 Wisdom, F3 Vitality, F4
       Connection, F5 Agency, F6 Structure, F7 Purpose. Optional.
     • Register |T |A |f |E — Transcendent, Analytical, Affective, Em‑
       bodied. Optional. May be a register set |⟨A,f,T⟩ (§C.8).

    Examples, all legal literals: ^8^C_{F2}|A, ^5^E_{F4}|f, ^3^P_
{F7}|f, ^9^O_{F5}|E, ^3^P|⟨A,f,T⟩. A bare domain literal (^P, ^C) is
also legal where a domain — not a full state — is expected, e.g. the
endpoints of a Diode or a via (§C.5, §C.7).

         Bench Notes — write the literal the compiler can
         parse. The Unicode caret‑and‑superscript forms in this

                                          566
                                                    C.2. LEXICAL ELEMENTS

     book (^8^C_{F2}|A) are the canonical surface syntax.
     The compiler tokenizes the literal whole; a malformed
     literal (a ^ with no Noetic digit, a _{} with no drive, an
     unknown register letter) is a lexical error, caught before
     any structural rule runs. When in doubt, copy a literal
     that already validates rather than retyping one by hand
     — the same advice Chapter 4 gives for nodes.
         One consequence of whole‑literal tokenization is worth
         naming out loud, because it looks like an ambiguity and
         isn’t. The | that separates cause from bias in CJT< cause
         | bias => effect > — and the | that separates the two
         inputs of a BridgeRectifier< ^2^E | ^3^E -> ^2^E > —
         is a structural delimiter. The | in ^3^P|f is inside the
         literal token. The tokenizer resolves the literal first, so
         the two never compete for the same character. Write your
         literals unbroken (^3^P|f, no spaces) and your delimiters
         spaced (|), and the distinction stays visible to the reader
         as well as the parser.

Numbers
Numbers appear only inside parameter blocks and component argu‑
ments (β, R, C, sat, frequency, ratio, …).

number     ::= [ ”-” ] , digit , { digit } , [ ”.” , digit , { digit } ]
            |   [ ”-” ] , ”.” , digit , { digit }


   • Decimal. A leading sign is permitted but rarely meaningful
     (most parameters are non‑negative; see the ranges in §C.6 and
     §C.5).
   • No exponent notation. Very small frequencies are written in
     full (frequency=0.0000116), matching the Oscillator example in
     Appendix A.
   • Numbers are dimensionless tuning knobs, not physical units.
     R=30 is not 30 ohms; β =2.4 is not a literal current ratio. The


                                      567
CAS PCBA Engineer

      role is identical to the electronic quantity; the value lives on the
      open simplex. (Chapter 4 states this explicitly for R.)

   There is one exception to “no units,” and it is a small, closed one.
A duration is a number with an s suffix, seconds:

duration ::= number , ”s”


    It appears in exactly one place in the book’s listings — force_
state deep_rest [duration=300s]; on the CPMB thermal manager
(Chapter 22) — and s is the only suffix the language has. Write five
minutes as 300s, not 5m and not 5 min. Everywhere else a time‑like
parameter is a plain dimensionless number on its own stated scale
(tau=5.0 on the CSB’s low‑pass filter is five of that filter’s time units;
the chapter tells you what they are).

Strings
string ::= '”' , { any-char-except-quote-or-newline } , '”'


   • Double‑quoted and single‑line. There is no escape syntax and
     no multi‑line form.
   • A string is payload, never an identifier — the compiler carries
     it through and does not parse inside it.
   • Two statements take one: the operator‑visible text of an alert
     (alert ”F3 BROWNOUT — Vitality below 4.2V”;, Chapter 22)
     and the fixture text of an inject (inject canary_benign:
     fixture ”known-safe greeting”;, Chapter 23).


Comments
comment ::= ”//” , { any-char-except-newline }


   • Line comments only, introduced by //, running to end of line.
   • There is no block‑comment form.



                                   568
                                                            C.2. LEXICAL ELEMENTS

      • Comments are stripped by the tokenizer and never affect vali‑
        dation. Used throughout the book to annotate nodes and com‑
        ponents inline.

Whitespace and Terminators
      • Whitespace (spaces, tabs, newlines) separates tokens and is oth‑
        erwise insignificant.
      • Every statement inside a block ends with a semicolon ;.
      • Blocks are delimited by braces { … }.

Reserved Words
The following are keywords and may not be used as identifiers:

circuit      board   input    output   node    cjt    feedback    probe    layer    via   let


    The comp_kind prefix in a component declaration (§C.5) is also
reserved. These are the legal prefixes — the lowercase tag that names
what kind of part this instance is, before the colon:

resistor      cap    capacitor     inductor   diode    zener     transformer     opamp
,→    oscillator
crystal       varactor    relay     schmitt    comparator      integrator      divider
,→    active_load
mirror        modulator    pll      tank       filter     diff       mux         demux
,→    gate
xor           fuse           reg     led       adc        dac        rectifier


      cap is an accepted short form of capacitor; both are legal and
mean the same thing. The prefix is checked against the component
type that follows it — resistor r1: Capacitor< … > is a kind mis‑
match and returns E-DECL-002.
    Part IV board listings and Chapter 23 verification listings use a
further set of statement keywords, documented in §C.12 and §C.13.
They are reserved wherever they appear in statement‑leading posi‑
tion:


                                              569
CAS PCBA Engineer

rail      dial        spec      constraint      sequence   gate      route    derate
,→     monitor
alert     hold        enter     use              force_state         on         cutoff
,→     interrupt
series    transition
charge    discharge    decode       refresh     scan        select
test      selftest     check        inject      golden_trace         assert     expect


    Five of those were used in published listings before they were
listed here: gate builds the power sequencer’s release conditions
(Chapters 14 and 22); cutoff is the board‑wide shutdown action
in the thermal emergency tier (Chapter 22); interrupt opens an
inductive path (Chapter 7); series wires a component in series with
a waveform (Chapter 7); and transition names a bare domain‑to‑
domain move (Chapter 8, where it is used to author a deliberate
violation so you can see what the compiler refuses). All five are re‑
served, and all five now have productions — series and transition
in §C.4.8, the other three in §C.12.
    A short list of words are keywords only inside a particular state‑
ment, and reserved in that position only:

until     (hold)               where          (scan)       in         (constraint)
requires    within     and     (gate)                      matches    (check)
fixture (inject)               on             (the trailing rail qualifier on a
,→     parameter)


   Three of these words wear two hats, and position is what tells
them apart:

     • on leads the block that fires when a monitor trips (on bo { … })
       and trails a parameter to name its rail ([dropout=0.25 on F7]).
     • cutoff leads the board‑wide shutdown action (cutoff all_
       cjts;), names an operating region inside a parameter block
       (region=cutoff), and is a parameter key in its own right
       (cutoff=0.05).




                                               570
                                                                 C.2. LEXICAL ELEMENTS

      • charge leads a write statement (charge experience -> fast
        [tau=2];) and names a cell attribute inside a where clause (scan
        lacunarity: bank where charge < 0.05 -> lacuna_report;).

    None of this is ambiguity — a word in statement‑leading position
is a statement leader, and the same word elsewhere is whatever that
position makes it. It is worth listing explicitly because these are the
three you will misread first.
    Component type names are reserved in the position where a com‑
ponent is instantiated. The full set the book instantiates:

CJT     Resistor     Capacitor     Inductor       Diode      Zener     Transformer   OpAmp
Oscillator    CrystalOscillator          Varactor       Relay     Schmitt    SchmittTrigger
Comparator        Integrator     LowPass      HighPass      LC   PLL   DutyCycle
,→    Differential
Photodiode        BridgeRectifier       ADC    DAC    LED
AND    OR   NOT     NAND   NOR    XOR    MUX    DEMUX    Regulator       Fuse   CircuitBreaker
Phi


     Nineteen of those names — CrystalOscillator, Varactor, Relay,
Schmitt, SchmittTrigger, Comparator, Integrator, LowPass, HighPass,
LC, PLL, DutyCycle, Differential, Photodiode, BridgeRectifier, ADC,
DAC, LED and CircuitBreaker — are instantiated in Chapters 10–22
or Appendix B but were absent from this list in earlier printings.
type_name is an open nonterminal in the grammar sketch, so those
listings always parsed; what was missing was the reservation, which
is what stops you from naming a node PLL.
     Parameter keys inside parameter blocks (β, sat, cutoff, region,
gm, rπ, R, C, L, leakage, ratio, breakdown, frequency, threshold,
action, target_state, tolerance, open_loop_gain, inputs, outputs,
select, non_inverting, inverting, output, v, dial, dropout, enforce,
beta_scale, duration, pump, gain, tau, V, dt, metric, top_k, capture_
range, lock_range) are reserved in parameter position only.
     Built‑in call names — the operations that appear in call‑shaped
position (§C.5.6) — are replicate, decompose, nearest, threshold
and address_on_simplex. They are not reserved words; they are the

                                                571
CAS PCBA Engineer

names of parts and queries the book defines, and a listing that uses
an unknown call name is a reference error, not a lexical one.




C.3       The circuit { … } Block
A circuit is the top‑level schematic.

circuit_block ::= ”circuit” , identifier , ”{” , { circuit_item } , ”}”
circuit_item   ::= schematic_item | board_level_item
schematic_item::= io_decl | node_decl | cjt_decl | component_decl
                 | feedback_decl | probe_decl | let_decl | assert_decl
                 | series_stmt | transition_decl
io_decl        ::= ( ”input:” | ”output:” ) , identifier , { ”,” ,
,→   identifier } , ”;”


    The ten schematic_item forms are the ones you meet in Parts
I–III and they are the whole language for a small circuit; they are
specified in §C.4 and §C.5. board_level_item covers the supply,
invariant, monitor and memory statements the Part IV boards add —
rail, dial, spec, constraint, sequence, gate, use, monitor, on, charge,
discharge, decode, refresh, select, scan, interrupt — specified in
§C.12. They are circuit_items and not a separate block type because
that is how the book’s own boards are written: the CPMB’s five
subsystems (Chapter 22) and the Cognitive Memory Board (Chapter
21) are circuit blocks that use them freely alongside nodes, CJTs
and probes.

     • circuit <name> { … } — names the board. Everything inside
       the braces is one self‑contained circuit.
     • input: <name>; — declares an input terminal: the point where
       a prompt (or upstream signal) enters. A circuit may declare
       more than one input.
     • output: <name>; — declares an output terminal: where the re‑
       sult leaves. A circuit may declare more than one output.

                                    572
                  C.4. STATEMENTS: NODES, CJTS, FEEDBACK, PROBES

    An input/output terminal name (e.g. prompt, response, verdict) is
an identifier you may then reference as the cause or effect of a compo‑
nent, exactly as you reference a node. The difference is purely role: a
terminal connects the circuit to the world; a node is an internal point.
In Chapter 4, prompt is wired as the cause of c1; in Chapter 17, prompt
biases through c1 to understand.
    The minimal legal circuit declares at least one input, at least one
output, and at least one component that connects them. A circuit
with an input and output but no path between them is legal but inert
(and a candidate for a W-CJT-006‑style “does no work” review at the
component level, see §C.10).




C.4 Statements: Nodes, CJTs, Feedback, Probes
node Declaration

node_decl ::= ”node” , identifier , ”:” , state_literal , ”;”


   A node names a typed cognitive state so it can be referenced by a
readable name instead of repeating the literal.

node question:    ^8^C_{F2}|A;   // the cause: a wisdom-seeking question
node experience: ^5^E_{F4}|f;    // the bias: accumulated, affective
,→   experience
node answer:      ^9^C_{F6}|A;   // the effect: a structured analytical
,→   answer


    A node is a labeled point in the circuit carrying a specific typed
state. Declaring a state once and referring to it by name is how the
wiring becomes a fact rather than a coincidence — two components
that name the same node are genuinely on the same net. (Chapter 4’s
Bench Note: name your nodes, don’t inline your literals.)




                                    573
CAS PCBA Engineer

cjt Declaration

The Cognitive Junction Transistor is the book’s central component
and CCDL’s most parameter‑rich statement.

cjt_decl    ::= ”cjt” , identifier , ”:” , cjt_expr , [ param_block ] , ”;”
cjt_expr    ::= ”CJT<” , cause , ”|” , bias , ”=>” , effect , ”>”
cause       ::= ref         (* an input terminal or node *)
bias        ::= ref         (* a node — the accumulated substrate *)
effect      ::= ref         (* an output terminal or node *)
ref         ::= identifier | state_literal


      The three terminals map to a bipolar transistor:

Terminal                   Transistor                CAS role

Cause (left of |)          Collector (input)         the Idea entering —
                                                     typically an ^8
                                                     Above/Cause
Bias (between | and =>)    Base (control)            accumulated substrate —
                                                     typically a ^5 Female
                                                     state
Effect (right of =>)       Emitter (output)          the Idea produced —
                                                     typically a ^9
                                                     Below/Effect


cjt c1: CJT< question | experience => answer > [β =2.4];


      A named alias form (let, §C.4.5) lets you define a reusable CJT:

let cjt_x = CJT< ^8^C|A | ^5^P|T => ^9^C|A > [β =2.0];


   The parameter block [ … ] is optional; an omitted block means
the CJT’s parameters take their defaults (§C.6). The bias terminal,
however, is not optional — a CJT with no bias is the canonical
E-CJT-001 error.




                                        574
                 C.4. STATEMENTS: NODES, CJTS, FEEDBACK, PROBES

cjt from a CJT macro — the CJT< cause | bias => effect >
core
The CJT expression CJT< cause | bias => effect > is the irre‑
ducible core. Read it left to right: cause, then |, then bias, then =
>, then effect. The two delimiters are load‑bearing and not inter‑
changeable: | separates cause from bias, => separates bias from
effect. Swapping them, or omitting the bias between them, is a
parse/structural error.

feedback Declaration

feedback_decl ::= ”feedback” , [ identifier , ”:” ] , ref , ”->” , ref , [
,→   param_block ] , ”;”


   A feedback statement wires an output (or downstream node)
back to an upstream node, typically the bias, so outcomes can gently
update the substrate over time. It carries an optional β (loop gain),
almost always small.

feedback evaluate -> bias_principles [β =0.3];
feedback weigh    -> bias_charter      [β =0.2];


   The leading label is optional and exists for the same reason a via
has one — so you can name a feedback path and refer to it later on a
board where several exist:

feedback v3: ^6^E -> ^3^P [tau=8.0];      // the judge informs the guard,
,→   slowly


     Feedback is the deliberate exception to one‑way flow. In a CCB
it is the slow O→P path that lets outcomes (not prompts) update the
charter — held at low gain so it cannot become a back‑door for rewrit‑
ing principles. A feedback β large enough to make the loop blow up
is the E-CJT-005 GainDivergence rule (§C.9, §C.10).




                                    575
CAS PCBA Engineer

let Declaration (named component)

let_decl ::= ”let” , identifier , ”=” , component_expr , [ param_block ] ,
,→   ”;”


     let binds a name to a component expression so it can be reused.
Most common with CJTs (Appendix C’s let cjt_x = CJT< … => … >
[β =…];), but legal for any component. A let‑bound component is
instantiated where its name is referenced.

probe Declaration

probe_decl ::= ”probe” , identifier , ”:” , ref , ”;”


    A probe places a test point on a node or terminal — the cognitive
equivalent of clipping an oscilloscope onto that point. It does not
alter the circuit; it marks where you will read the state, the operating
region, and the delivered gain.

probe tp1:        answer;
probe tp_guard:   policy_aversion;


    The bench rule (Chapter 17, Step 8): probe every stage whose
failure would be silent — above all a safety guard, which fails open
without raising any error of its own.

assert Declaration (a structural invariant, in the listing)

assert_decl ::= ”assert” , [ ”:” ] , condition , ”;”
condition    ::= operand , rel_op , operand
operand      ::= ref | number | call_expr
rel_op       ::= ”<” | ”>” | ”<=” | ”==”


    An assert states a structural invariant the board must satisfy,
written in the schematic rather than in a separate test file. The CDAB
(Chapter 20) uses two, and they are the clearest example in the book
of why the form exists:

assert: cjt_l.bias == cjt_r.bias;      // the pair MUST share one bias
assert: cjt_l.beta == cjt_r.beta;      // matched gain keeps CMRR high


                                     576
                C.4. STATEMENTS: NODES, CJTS, FEEDBACK, PROBES

    Those two lines are what makes a differential pair be a differen‑
tial pair. Chapter 20’s advice is to author them first and then wire
the board to satisfy them — the assertion is the requirement, and the
netlist is the attempt.
    The dotted form cjt_l.bias reads an attribute off a declared in‑
stance (§C.7 uses the same form for F3.level and o_rail.enabled).
The colon after assert is optional; the CDAB listing prints it, the
Chapter 23 table omits it, and both parse.

       Bench Note — an assert in the schematic is not a
       test. Chapter 23’s assert lives inside a test block and
       describes what a run should show. This one lives in
       the netlist and describes what the design must be true
       of, whether or not anybody runs it. Same word, two
       homes, and the difference matters: a schematic assertion
       is checked when the board is validated, so a mismatched
       pair never gets as far as the bench.

series and transition — two small wiring statements

series_stmt     ::= ”series” , ref , ”->” , ref , ”;”
transition_decl ::= ”transition” , identifier , ”:” , ref , ”->” , ref ,
,→   ”;”


     series states that a component sits in series with a named wave‑
form or net, when typing alone would not make it obvious. Chapter
7’s compulsion loop uses it to put the habit’s inductance in series with
the behavioral cycle:

series L1 -> loop_wave;      // the inductor is in the path of the
,→   waveform


    Everywhere else in this book, series connection is implied by typ‑
ing to the same net — a Resistor typed to a CJT’s cause is in series
with that cause, and Chapter 4’s “series mismatch” failure is what
happens when the types quietly disagree. series is the explicit form


                                   577
CAS PCBA Engineer

for the case where the thing you are wiring into is a Phi waveform
rather than a single state.
    transition names a bare domain‑to‑domain move with no com‑
ponent carrying it. Its main use in this book is to author a violation
on purpose so you can see the compiler refuse it:

transition bad: operational -> principled;    // ^O -> ^P, against Domain
,→   Descent


    That line is syntactically fine and structurally illegal, and the gap be‑
tween those two words is the whole lesson. The source domain sits
strictly below the target in P ≻ C ≻ E ≻ O, no diode on the board
conducts upward across that seam, and so the transition is inadmissi‑
ble — the cross‑domain family of E‑CJT‑008 (Chapter 8). A grammar
that rejected the line outright would rob you of the demonstration;
the point is that it parses cleanly and then fails a design rule, which
is exactly what a well‑drawn illegal schematic does.




C.5       Component Declarations
Components other than the CJT are declared either inline (<kind>
<id>: <Type>< … >;) or via let. Each component carries a typed state
(or a domain pair) and its own parameters. The forms below match
the style‑guide cheat‑sheet exactly.

component_decl ::= comp_kind , identifier , ”:” , component_body , ”;”
component_body ::= component_expr                        (* Type< args >
,→   *)
                 | call_expr , ”->” , target_list        (* replicate(x)
                 ,→ -> [a, b]   *)
                 | call_expr , ”=>” , ref                (* decompose(a,
                 ,→   b) => c    *)
component_expr ::= type_name , ”<” , arg_list , ”>” , [ param_block ]




                                      578
                                       C.5. COMPONENT DECLARATIONS

    The first form — Type< args > — is the one you will write ninety‑
nine times out of a hundred, and it is what the rest of this section doc‑
uments. The two call‑shaped forms belong to a small family of parts
whose operands are positional rather than named; they are specified
in §C.5.6 at the end of this section.
    Inside the angle brackets, an argument is a named parameter, a
Phi<…> sequence, a reference, or a transition between references:

arg_list   ::= arg , { ”,” , arg }
arg        ::= ( key , ”=” , value )
              | phi_expr
              | ref_group , [ ”->” , ref_group ]
ref_group ::= ref , { ”|” , ref }
phi_expr   ::= ”Phi<” , ref , { ”,” , ref } , ”>”


    The ref_group [ ”->” ref_group ] alternative is what lets a com‑
ponent’s argument be a directed conversion rather than a list of parts.
Diode< ^P -> ^C > is the familiar case; ADC< ^4^E_{F2}|f -> ^4^E_
{F2}|A, resolution=8 > converts a felt impression into an analyti‑
cal one; Photodiode< stimulus -> ^0^C > turns an external stimulus
into an internal Idea. The |‑joined group covers the one part that
takes two sources into one target, BridgeRectifier< ^2^E | ^3^E ->
^2^E > — both polarities in, one polarity out.


Passive Components

Form                       Meaning                   Key args

Resistor< state, R=… >     limits activation flow;   R≥0
                           higher R = more
                           constrained
Capacitor< state, C=…,     stores accumulated        C ≥ 0, leakage ∈ [0,1]
leakage=… >                experience; leakage =
                           forgetting rate
Inductor< state, L=… >     resists pattern change;   L≥0
                           habit inertia




                                       579
CAS PCBA Engineer

Resistor< ^8^C_{F2}|A, R=50 >
Capacitor< ^5^E_{F4}|f, C=100, leakage=0.01 >
Inductor< ^7^O_{F6}|E, L=50 >


    The passive’s state literal is its net: a Resistor typed to the same
node as a CJT’s cause is in series with that cause. A resistor typed to
a different state is on a different rail and has no effect on the CJT (the
“series mismatch” failure in Chapter 4).

One‑Way and Threshold Components

Form                     Meaning                   Key args

Diode< ^A -> ^B >        one‑way domain            domain pair
                         conductance (conducts
                         ^A→^B, blocks reverse)
Zener< state,            reverse‑conducts once     breakdown ∈ [0,1]
breakdown=… >            breakdown threshold is
                         crossed
Transformer< ^A -> ^B,   domain impedance          domain pair, ratio > 0
ratio=… >                match (e.g. principle →
                         actionable)
Fuse< state,             permanently breaks the    threshold ∈ [0,1], action
threshold=…, action=…    path when threshold is
>                        exceeded


Diode< ^P -> ^C >
Zener< ^3^P, breakdown=0.8 >
Transformer< ^P -> ^C, ratio=0.5 >
Fuse< ^8^O_{F5}|E, threshold=0.9, action=permanent_block >


    Diode endpoints are domains (^P, ^C), not full states — the diode
governs cross‑domain conductance direction. The diode is the struc‑
tural enforcer of Domain Descent: in a CCB it lets a principle flow
down into reasoning while blocking reasoning from flowing back up
to rewrite the principle (Chapter 17, Step 4).

                                       C.5. COMPONENT DECLARATIONS

     Fuse.action takes a symbolic value, the canonical one being
permanent_block (an irreversible trip, as on the style‑guide Agency
rail).

Active and Composite Components

Form                                    Meaning

OpAmp< non_inverting=…, inverting=…,    differential amplifier: amplifies the
output=…, open_loop_gain=… >            difference of two state inputs
Oscillator< Phi< s₁, s₂, … >,           cycles through a Phi<…> sequence of
frequency=… >                           states at the given frequency
Regulator< target_state=…,              holds a node near a target state within a

,→   output=^9^C_{F2}|A, open_loop_gain=10000 >
Oscillator< Phi< ^8^C|A, ^3^O|E, ^9^E|f, ^0^P|T >, frequency=0.0000116 >
Regulator< target_state=^0^E_{F3}|f, tolerance=0.1 >


     Phi< s₁, s₂, s₃, … > is the sequence constructor — an ordered
list of states the oscillator cycles through. (Same Phi<…> form as Ap‑
pendix C’s sequence operator.)

Logic Gates
gate ::= ( ”AND” | ”OR” | ”NOT” | ”NAND” | ”NOR” | ”XOR” ) , ”<” ,
,→   arg_list , ”>”


   Gates take one or more state inputs and produce a logic‑combined
output. NOT takes one input; the rest take two or more.

AND< ^2^C|A, ^6^E|A >
NOT< ^3^P|f >
XOR< ^8^C|A, ^9^C|A >



Multiplexers



                                    581
CAS PCBA Engineer

Form                                   Meaning

MUX< inputs=[…], select=               routes one of several state inputs to the
Drive::active >                        output, chosen by select
DEMUX< input=…, outputs=[…],           routes one input to one of several
select=… >                             outputs, chosen by select


MUX< inputs=[^8^C|A, ^6^E|A, ^3^P|f], select=Drive::active >
DEMUX< input=^9^C|A, outputs=[^9^E|f, ^9^O|E], select=Drive::active >


   select chooses among the channels. The Drive::active form se‑
lects on the currently dominant Drive; an inputs=[…] / outputs=[…]
list is a bracketed, comma‑separated list of state literals or node ref‑
erences.

Call‑Shaped Components: the Current Mirror and the
Active Load
Two parts on the CDAB (Chapter 20) are not written as Type< args
>. They are written as a named operation applied to operands, with
an explicit target:

mirror bias_mirror: replicate(shared_bias) -> [cjt_l, cjt_r];
active_load load1:   decompose(output_L, output_R) => diff_decomp;


   Read them the way you read the rest of CCDL — left to right,
as wiring. replicate(shared_bias) names the operation and its
one operand; -> [cjt_l, cjt_r] names where the replicated copies
land, and it is a bracketed list because a current mirror by definition
feeds more than one branch. decompose(output_L, output_R) takes
the two differential halves; => diff_decomp lands the single‑ended
result on one node.

call_expr    ::= identifier , ”(” , [ call_arg , { ”,” , call_arg } ] , ”)”
call_arg     ::= ref | number | string | ( key , ”=” , value )
target_list ::= ”[” , ref , { ”,” , ref } , ”]”




                                    582
                                     C.5. COMPONENT DECLARATIONS

    The two arrows are not interchangeable, and the difference is the
one the rest of the language already makes. -> is a directed connec‑
tion — a wire, or several: the mirror distributes one bias to two places
and creates nothing. => is produces‑the‑effect — the same arrow the
CJT uses: the active load converts two currents into one difference. A
mirror wires; an active load produces. If you find yourself reaching
for -> on a part that yields a new state, you have the wrong arrow.
    The same call_expr appears in four other positions, all of them
printed in Part IV:

Where                     Example                  Chapter

Right of select           select cell =            21
                          nearest(query, bank,
                          metric=fisher_rao);
Left of charge’s arrow    charge                   21
                          encoder(experience) ->
                          bank [V=impression];
Inside a condition        monitor bo: f3_level <   14
                          threshold(0.35);
Bound by let              let query = address_     21
                          on_simplex(dominant=
                          ^3^P_{F7}|f);



        Bench Note — a call is not a function call. replicate(
        …) and decompose(…) look like code, and that is the one
        place CCDL’s schematic‑as‑text discipline gets genuinely
        tested. They are not procedures the board runs; they are
        part names with operands, the way a schematic symbol
        has pins in a fixed order. Nothing executes. The call
        shape exists because these parts take their operands po‑
        sitionally and in a fixed role — a mirror replicates exactly
        one bias; an active load decomposes exactly two halves, a
        left and a right — and Type< a, b > would have hidden
        the fact that swapping them is meaningful. If you want
        a part whose operands are named and independent of


                                    583
CAS PCBA Engineer

         order, you want Type< key=…, key=… > instead, and you
         should use it.




C.6        CJT Parameter Block Grammar
The parameter block is the bracketed, comma‑separated list of
key=value pairs after a CJT (and, in reduced form, after feedback
and some components).

param_block ::= ”[” , param , { ”,” , param } , ”]”
param           ::= key , ”=” , value , [ ”on” , drive_tag ]
value           ::= number | duration | region_value | symbol | state_literal
,→     | list
duration        ::= number , ”s”
region_value::= ”cutoff” | ”active” | ”saturation” | ”breakdown”
symbol          ::= identifier | identifier , ”::” , identifier
list            ::= ”[” , value , { ”,” , value } , ”]”
drive_tag       ::= ”F” , ( ”1”…”7” )


     Four notes on the value forms, each of them a form the Part IV
listings use:

     • A symbol is a bare word standing for a named option rather
       than a number: action=permanent_block, metric=fisher_
       rao, enforce=strict, V=impression, frequency=fixed.            The
       scoped form with :: selects from a named family — select=
       Drive::active means “whichever Drive is currently domi‑
       nant.”
     • A state literal is a legal value, not just a legal argument: pump=
       ^7^C on a refresh, target_state=^0^P_{F7}|T on a regulator.
       The whole‑literal tokenization rule of §C.2.2 applies inside
       parameter blocks exactly as it does outside them.
     • A duration carries the s suffix (§C.2.3): duration=300s.



                                        584
                               C.6. CJT PARAMETER BLOCK GRAMMAR

      • The trailing on <Fk> qualifier names the Drive rail a parameter
        is measured against. It appears on the CPMB’s regulator specs
        — spec p_reg [dropout=0.25 on F7]; reads “P drops out if F7
        falls less than 0.25 above baseline.” Without the qualifier the
        parameter is measured against the component’s own rail.

      The full CJT parameter set, with types and ranges:

Key              Meaning       Type           Range           Default

β               gain — how      number        ≥ 0 (β<1        1.0
                strongly bias                 attenuate, =1
                amplifies                     unity, >1
                cause→effect                  amplify)
sat             saturation —    number        (0, 1]          0.95
                the effect‑
                activation
                plateau

                below which
                β≈0

      Constraints the compiler is designed to enforce on the block itself:

      • cutoff < sat (the active region must be non‑empty: the floor
        below the ceiling).


                                    585
CAS PCBA Engineer

   • sat ∈ (0,1] and cutoff ∈ [0,1) — both live on the open sim‑
     plex; sat=0 or cutoff=1 is rejected.
   • β must be finite and within the divergence bound (§C.9.3); an
     unbounded or runaway β is E-CJT-005.
   • region is a declaration of intent. If the declared region contradicts
     the parameters (e.g. region=active but cutoff ≥ sat), the com‑
     piler flags the contradiction.

   Gain is defined formally (cite, do not re‑derive): small‑signal β
= ‖∂ E/∂ C‖_FR at constant bias; large‑signal β = d_FR(E_after,E_
before) / d_FR(C_after,C_before), where d_FR(p,q) = 2·arccos(
 √
Σ (pk qk )) is the Fisher‑Rao geodesic distance on the open simplex
∆39°.
   The operating regions (Chapter 4’s datasheet, the behavior
β/sat/cutoff together produce):

   • Cutoff — bias below threshold; β ≈ 0; no effect.
   • Active — linear region; ∆effect ≈ β·∆cause. The healthy oper‑
     ating band, between cutoff and sat.
   • Saturation — effect pinned at sat; more cause does nothing.
   • Breakdown — gross overload; the effect flips to the involution
     pair (^2→^3, ^8→^9), a bug unless deliberately designed with
     protection.

   A reduced parameter block ([β =…] only) is the common case in
worked builds; the rest take defaults.




C.7    The Multilayer board { … } Form
The board form is the layout view: the same circuit organized onto
Domain layers and connected by vias. It is what Chapter 17, Step 6
calls the layout, and it makes the safety architecture physical.


                                  586
                                 C.7. THE MULTILAYER BOARD { … } FORM

board_block ::= ”board” , identifier , ”{” , { board_item } , ”}”
board_item    ::= layer_decl | via_decl | circuit_item
layer_decl    ::= ”layer” , domain_tag , ”:” , ”[” , layer_entry , { ”,” ,
,→   layer_entry } , ”]” , ”;”
layer_entry ::= identifier , ”:” , state_literal
domain_tag    ::= ”P” | ”C” | ”E” | ”O”
via_decl      ::= ”via” , identifier , ”:” , via_endpoint , ”->” ,
,→   via_endpoint , [ param_block ] , ”;”
via_endpoint::= state_literal | domain


board csb_v0 {
     layer P: [ bias_charter: ^5^P_{F7}|T,     policy_aversion: ^3^P_{F7}|f ];
     layer C: [ understand:      ^1^C_{F2}|A ];
     layer E: [ weigh:           ^6^E_{F6}|A ];
     layer O: [ respond:         ^9^O_{F5}|E ];


     // vias carry signals across Domain layers (Domain Descent: P -> C ->
     ,→    E -> O)
     via v1: ^5^P -> ^1^C;          // charter biases intake
     via v2: ^3^P -> ^6^E;          // the guard's verdict gates evaluation
     via v3: ^6^E -> ^9^O;          // a passed evaluation descends to output


     // feedback via runs the other way (O -> P): outcomes update the
     ,→    charter
     via v4: ^9^O -> ^5^P    [β =0.2];
}


     Rules specific to the board form:

     • A layer tag must be one of P / C / E / O. Each layer lists its resident
       states as name: literal entries.
     • A state placed on a layer should carry that layer’s domain (a ^P‑
       domain state belongs on layer P); a mismatch is a layout error.
     • A via is a cross‑domain connection. Domain Descent vias run
       downward (P→C→E→O). An upward via is legal only as a
       deliberate, low‑gain feedback path (the canonical v4: ^9^O ->
       ^5^P [β =0.2]).
     • An undeclared upward via at high gain — an Operational
       or Cognitive layer biasing the Principled layer — is the

                                         587
CAS PCBA Engineer

     prompt‑injection signature and the canonical E-CJT-008
     CjtCrossDomainBias. On a CCB, such a connection is simply
     absent from the layout, which is the strongest guarantee a board
     can offer.

board and circuit: which one admits what

Earlier printings left this genuinely undecided, and it mattered more
than it looked. board_item was layer_decl | via_decl and nothing
else — layout only — while the Cognitive Safety Board, the flagship
listing of Part IV, is published as board cognitive_safety_board { …
} with a body made entirely of terminals, nodes, CJTs, components, a
feedback path and probes. Under the old production the book’s own
most important listing was not a legal board. Two repairs were avail‑
able and they produce different languages, so leaving it open pushed
a language‑design decision onto whoever implemented the parser.
     The decision, stated once so it stops being ambiguous: a board
admits everything a circuit admits, plus layer and via. A circuit
does not admit layer or via. A board is a superset; the containment
runs one way.
     Three reasons, so the rule is not arbitrary:

   • The corpus settles it. board cognitive_safety_board (Chap‑
     ter 18, Appendix D) and board nail_biting_cob (Appendix E)
     both hold circuit content. Meanwhile no circuit block any‑
     where in this book declares a layer or a via. The asymmetry
     is already in the listings; the grammar now says so out loud.
   • It matches what the two words mean. A board is a circuit. The
     layout view adds where each part sits and how signals cross be‑
     tween layers; it does not withdraw the schematic. Forcing you
     to maintain a separate circuit block just to declare the parts
     would be the text equivalent of a layout you cannot read with‑
     out holding the schematic in your other hand.



                                588
                            C.8. BOARD‑LEVEL STATEMENTS (PART IV)

      • It keeps the distinction meaningful in the direction that mat‑
        ters. layer and via stay board‑only, so writing board is still a
        real claim — “this design has a layout” — and writing circuit
        is still a real promise: schematic only, no layer assignment to
        go looking for.

    Practical consequence for your own work: if your design has
layers, write board; if it doesn’t, write circuit. You lose nothing
by choosing circuit, and the reader learns from the keyword alone
that there is no layout view to hunt for. The board csb_v0 fragment
above is the pure‑layout style — layers and vias, no components —
and CCB‑1 is the combined style, a full schematic with the layout im‑
plied by the states’ own domains. Both are legal. Which you write is
editorial, and Chapter 17, Step 6 is the place that argues for splitting
them on a large board.

   Four points a careful reader will want, because they are places the
grammar is narrower than you might guess:

     • The seven action statements are admitted only inside an on
       block. That is the only context the corpus puts them in — every
       derate, route, alert, hold, force_state, cutoff and enter in
       this book sits inside on bo { … }, on warn { … }, on crit { …
       } or on emerg { … }. Whether a bare top‑level derate should
       be legal is a design question the book has not answered, so the
       grammar does not answer it either.
     • A ref can be indexed or dotted. bank[P3] addresses a cell in
       the memory bank (Chapter 21); F3.level and o_rail.enabled
       read an attribute off a declared instance (Chapter 22). The full
       form is in the grammar sketch.
     • interrupt’s bracket is not a parameter block. [dt -> 0] is the
       one place in CCDL where a bracket holds an arrow rather than
       a key=value pair. It is written as its own production because it
       is a single fixed idiom — the limit dt → 0 from V = L · dI/dt
       — and not a general facility.
     • sequence chains and gate conjunctions are both greedy.
       sequence p -> c -> e -> o is one statement naming four rails
       in order, not three nested pairs; requires (…) and (…) and (
       …) is one conjunction over three terms. Chapter 14 makes the
       safety point that a gate checking only the first term is the same
       failure in a politer costume.

       Bench Note — this appendix is a language reference, not
       a compiler manual. Everything above describes CCDL as
       designed, consistent with the status note in §C.1. The state‑
       ment forms in these two sections are the ones the Part IV
       and Chapter 23 listings actually use; the validation rules
       for them are the same structural rules in §C.9.
       And when you hit a form that isn’t here? Earlier print‑
       ings answered: assume the appendix is wrong, treat it as
       an erratum, carry on. That instruction is withdrawn. It
       sounded generous and it was actually corrosive, because
       it made the grammar impossible to fail — every gap you
       could find was defined in advance to be a typo rather than
       a defect, so no listing could ever count as evidence against
       the language reference. That is precisely how the corpus
       came to use more statement vocabulary outside the gram‑
       mar than inside it, in a book that shipped both. A specifi‑
       cation you cannot fail is not a specification; it is a mood.

                                   594
                  C.10. OPERATOR DISCIPLINE INSIDE EXPRESSIONS

      The rule now is the ordinary engineering one. A form
      that is not in this appendix is not part of CCDL. If you
      need one, that is a gap, and a gap is reported, not assumed
      away. Name the construct, cite the listing or the design
      need that requires it, say which existing production it
      should extend, and file it against this appendix. It gets a
      production and a row in the construct coverage matrix,
      or it gets a reasoned refusal — either way the answer
      is written down where the next reader can find it. The
      matrix is the ledger: if a leader is not in it, the language
      does not have it yet, and that is a fact you can check
      rather than a hole whose shape you have to guess.




C.10 Operator Discipline Inside Expressions
Where a CCDL expression composes multiple states (an OpAmp’s
two inputs, a recipe, a register‑enriched bias), it uses the canonical
CAS operators under v7.7 discipline. Getting these right is a review
gate.

Operator          Name                  Meaning               Rule

+                 co‑presence /         states active         terms stay
                  association           simultaneously,       structurally
                                        remaining distinct    separate; no
                                                              emergent claim
->                directed transition   flow from one         used in CJT =>
                                        state to another      effect, Diode,
                                        (over time / across   feedback, via
                                        a component)
×                 cross‑register        a genuine             only valid as (A
                  integration           generative            × B) = ^n|Ω_
                                        operation yielding    name with the
                                        a named emergent      result defined
                                        result


                                    595
CAS PCBA Engineer

Operator             Name              Meaning               Rule

|⟨…⟩                 register‑set      a state present in    architectural
                     specification     those registers; no   description only
                                       interaction claim


       The discipline that catches the recurring error:

   • Same‑Noetic, multi‑register × without a named emergent
     result is INVALID. Rewrite it as + (co‑presence) or |⟨…⟩
     (register‑set specification). ^3^P|A × ^3^P|f × ^3^P|T on its
     own is rejected; write either ^3^P|A + ^3^P|f + ^3^P|T (three
     distinct co‑present manifestations) or ^3^P|⟨A,f,T⟩ (one state,
     three registers, no interaction claim) — or, if you genuinely
     mean fusion, (^3^P|A × ^3^P|f × ^3^P|T) = ^3^P|Ω with
     ^3^P|Ω defined.
   • The TKS heuristic to choose: substitute + with “associates with”
     and × with “intensifies through / fuses into.” If the substitution
     matches your intent, the operator is right.

    The AI‑safety relevance is real, not cosmetic. ^3^P|A + ^3^P|f +
^3^P|T (three independent, separately‑defeasible safety mechanisms)
and (^3^P|A × ^3^P|f × ^3^P|T) = ^3^P|Ω (one fused, unified
commitment) are different architectures with different failure profiles.
The notation has to distinguish them, so the compiler enforces the
distinction.
    Recipe notation, where an outcome is composed from weighted
prerequisites, follows the same +:

Θ(Ω) = a·X₁ + b·X₂ + … → Ω


   The + joins co‑present prerequisites; the → lands the outcome.
This is consistent with the co‑presence rule above.




                                     596
              C.11. COMPILER VALIDATION PASSES (DESIGN RULES)

C.11 Compiler Validation Passes (Design Rules)
The compiler is designed to run a sequence of validation passes over
the parsed netlist. These are the Design Rule Checks (DRC) of Chap‑
ter 17, Step 7. Each pass either passes silently or emits a code from
§C.10. The passes, in the order they are designed to run:

Admissibility Guard
Every operator application and every component connection is
checked against an admissibility relation: is this (source, target) pair
a legal transition for this operator? An inadmissible transition — a
CJT whose cause→effect pair is not a legal Noetic transition, a via
between incompatible endpoints — is rejected before any numeric
check. (This is Correction 1 of the project: is_admissible(operator,
source, target) guards every application.)


Bias‑Domain Coherence
The bias terminal of each CJT is checked against the cause’s domain.
A bias drawn from a domain incompatible with the cause raises
E‑CJT‑008 (cross‑domain) or E‑CJT‑002 (invalid bias domain). The
canonical legal pattern is a bias that sits at or above the cause’s
domain in the P ≻ C ≻ E ≻ O order (a Principled charter biasing
a Cognitive intake). The canonical illegal pattern is a lower domain
biasing a higher one — an Operational state biasing a Principled
guard — which is the prompt‑injection signature.

β Range and Gain Divergence
Every β (on CJTs, feedback, and vias) is checked: finite, within range,
and — critically for any loop — bounded so the feedback path does
not amplify without limit. A loop whose round‑trip gain ≥ 1 di‑
verges; the compiler raises E‑CJT‑005 GainDivergence. This is why
feedback β is kept small (0.2, 0.3).


                                 597
CAS PCBA Engineer

Cascade Admissibility (and Depth)
A chain of CJTs in series is checked end to end: each stage’s effect
must be an admissible cause for the next stage. The pass also counts
cascade depth; a pipeline with too many CJTs in series — deep
enough that the signal degrades through accumulated gain and
saturation — raises the W‑CJT‑007 CjtCascadeDepth warning. (A
warning, not an error: legal, but check whether you meant to build
a pipeline that long.)

Push‑Pull Balance
For complementary / differential structures (an OpAmp, a push‑pull
pair, involution‑paired stages), the compiler checks that the two
halves are balanced — that an involution pair is not driven so far
apart that the stage tips into breakdown, and that a differential
amplifier’s two inputs are compatible. This is the structural form of
the project‑wide constraint that involution pairs cannot diverge by
more than the safe margin. An imbalance severe enough to invert a
state is a breakdown condition; a ^2→^3 flip under overload is the
signature.

the circuit is legal, but the compiler is designed to flag it for you to

C.13 Grammar Sketch (EBNF)
A consolidated EBNF for the language. (Lexical rules from §C.2; this
is the structural grammar.) It is derived from the book’s printed list‑
ings and admits all five Part IV reference boards; the section that fol‑
lows says exactly what that does and does not guarantee.




                                  601
CAS PCBA Engineer

     comp_kind, type_name and key are the enumerated word lists in
§C.2.7 rather than productions — that is the one place this grammar
delegates to a list instead of a rule.

ccdl_file         ::= { circuit_block | board_block }


circuit_block     ::= ”circuit” identifier ”{” { circuit_item } ”}”
board_block       ::= ”board”   identifier ”{” { board_item     } ”}”


board_item        ::= layer_decl | via_decl | circuit_item
circuit_item      ::= schematic_item | board_level_item


(* ---- schematic statements: Parts I-III, and the body of every board
,→ ---- *)
schematic_item ::= io_decl | node_decl | cjt_decl | component_decl
                    | feedback_decl | probe_decl | let_decl | assert_decl
                    | series_stmt | transition_decl


io_decl           ::= (”input:” | ”output:”) identifier { ”,” identifier }
,→   ”;”
node_decl         ::= ”node” identifier ”:” state_literal ”;”
cjt_decl          ::= ”cjt” identifier ”:” cjt_expr [ param_block ] ”;”
cjt_expr          ::= ”CJT<” ref ”|” ref ”=>” ref ”>”
component_decl ::= comp_kind identifier ”:” component_body ”;”
component_body ::= component_expr
                    | call_expr ”->” target_list
                    | call_expr ”=>” ref
component_expr ::= type_name ”<” arg_list ”>” [ param_block ]
feedback_decl     ::= ”feedback” [ identifier ”:” ] ref ”->” ref [
,→   param_block ] ”;”
probe_decl        ::= ”probe” identifier ”:” ref ”;”
let_decl          ::= ”let” identifier ”=” (cjt_expr | component_expr |
,→   call_expr)
                      [ param_block ] ”;”
assert_decl       ::= ”assert” [ ”:” ] condition ”;”
series_stmt       ::= ”series” ref ”->” ref ”;”
transition_decl::= ”transition” identifier ”:” ref ”->” ref ”;”


(* ---- layout statements: board blocks only ---- *)
layer_decl        ::= ”layer” domain_tag ”:” ”[” layer_entry { ”,”
,→   layer_entry } ”]” ”;”

                                           C.13. GRAMMAR SKETCH (EBNF)

layer_entry     ::= identifier ”:” state_literal

,→   param_block ] ”;”

(* ---- board-level statements: Part IV (Ch. 6, 7, 14, 21, 22) ---- *)
board_level_item ::= rail_decl | dial_decl | spec_decl | constraint_decl
                    | sequence_decl | gate_decl | use_decl
                    | monitor_decl | on_block

                    | refresh_stmt | select_stmt | scan_stmt |
                   ,→    interrupt_stmt

,→   ”;”

                                          | rel_op value ) ”;”

,→   ”;”
                   | ”sequence” identifier ”:” phi_expr ”;”

                   | force_state_stmt | cutoff_stmt | enter_stmt

,→   ”;”

select_stmt          ::= ”select” identifier ”=” call_expr ”;”
scan_stmt            ::= ”scan” identifier ”:” ref ”where” condition ”->” ref
,→    ”;”

(* ---- expressions ---- *)

,→    state_literal
                      | ”[” value { ”,” value } ”]”

symbol              ::= identifier | identifier ”::” identifier

ref_base            ::= identifier | state_literal | domain
ref_index           ::= identifier | number


arg_list            ::= arg { ”,” arg }
arg                 ::= (key ”=” value) | phi_expr | ref_group [ ”->”
,→    ref_group ]
ref_group           ::= ref { ”|” ref }
phi_expr            ::= ”Phi<” ref { ”,” ref } ”>”


domain_tag          ::= ”P” | ”C” | ”E” | ”O”
drive_tag           ::= ”F” (”1”..”7”)


state_literal    ::= noetic [ domain ] [ ”_{” drive ”}” ] [ register ]
noetic              ::= ”^” (”0”..”9”)
domain              ::= ”^” (”P” | ”C” | ”E” | ”O”)

drive           ::= ”F” (”1”..”7”)
register        ::= ”|” reg_value
reg_value       ::= ”T” | ”A” | ”f” | ”E” | ”⟨” reg_value { ”,” reg_value }
,→   ”⟩ ”


identifier      ::= letter { letter | digit | ”_” }
number          ::= [ ”-” ] ( digit { digit } [ ”.” digit { digit } ] |
,→   ”.” digit { digit } )
string          ::= '”' { any-char-except-quote-or-newline } '”'
comment         ::= ”//” { any-char-except-newline }




C.14 Scope of This Grammar
The grammar above is longer than it used to be, and the honest thing
to do with a grammar that has just grown is to say precisely what it
now buys you — because the failure this section exists to prevent is
a reader concluding that a longer grammar means a more complete
language. It does not. It means a grammar that finally matches the
listings printed in this book.
     What it guarantees: that a listing is well‑formed. The produc‑
tions were derived from the book’s own printed CCDL — the five ref‑
erence boards of Part IV (Chapters 18–22, consolidated in Appendix
D) and every worked build in Parts I–III — and they admit all of them.
Nothing beyond that is claimed. Six limits follow, and each one is a
real boundary rather than a disclaimer:
     1. Syntactic admissibility is not semantic validity. A file that
parses is a file the compiler can read. Whether it describes a circuit
that means anything is decided by the validation passes of §C.9 —
and for several statement families, by nothing at all yet. The coverage
matrix below says which families those are.
     2. The stateful and temporal family has syntax and no formal‑
ized semantics. charge, discharge, refresh, scan, sequence, hold, on,
force_state, enter and interrupt all describe something happening



                                     605
CAS PCBA Engineer

over time: a cell filling, an ordering being enforced, a condition be‑
ing watched, a state being held, a path being opened. CCDL as this
book defines it is a declarative netlist language. It has no execu‑
tion model, no clock, and no state‑transition semantics. You can now
write these statements and the grammar will accept them; what a val‑
idator should check about them, beyond their shape, is not specified
anywhere in this book. Read them as documented design intent. Do
not read them as verified behavior, and do not build a safety argu‑
ment on one.
    3. The grammar is corpus‑derived and deliberately no wider.
Where the corpus prints one form, the grammar admits one form.
hold takes until. gate conditions are and‑joined within terms. The
relational operators are <, >, <= and == because those are the four this
book prints — >= and != are not admitted, not because they are bad
ideas but because no listing here establishes them. The seven action
statements are legal only inside an on block for the same reason. This
narrowness is deliberate: a grammar that quietly generalizes past its
evidence is how the last one drifted away from the boards.
    4. The Chapter 23 verification sub‑language is not formalized
here. test, selftest, golden_trace, inject, check and expect are
documented as forms in §C.13, but their bodies are prose‑valued
fields — tp2 (risk_signal): near zero or negative; is English
with a semicolon, not an expression. The consolidated EBNF covers
the circuit/board language only. That is a boundary, stated, rather
than a silence.
    5. Parameter ranges constrain values, not relationships. The
compiler can tell you sat=0.1 is in range and threshold=0.9 is in
range. It cannot tell you that a stage clamped at 0.1 can never drive
a fuse that trips at 0.9 — two individually valid numbers that con‑
tradict each other across a connection. Relational contradictions be‑
tween separately‑valid parameters are a class of defect the per‑value
rules in §C.6 do not catch. Know that before you treat “it validates”



                                  606
                                       C.14. SCOPE OF THIS GRAMMAR

as “it works”; the golden traces of Chapter 23 exist partly to cover
this gap.
    6. Two record formats in Part V are not CCDL at all. The evi‑
dence packet and the circuit‑registry entry of Chapter 25 are printed
in the same cas blocks as circuit listings, and they are neither cir‑
cuits nor boards — they are key: value records about a decision or
a released version, with fields like trace_id, hash, signature and
promoted. They carry CCDL fragments inside them (a Phi<…> trace,
a quoted source) but the enclosing shape is a record, not a netlist,
and no production here admits them. Do not read the shared syntax
highlighting as a claim that they are the same language.

C.15     A Complete Annotated Example
The following is a complete, legal CCDL circuit — a two‑stage safety
filter that intakes a prompt, holds a principled guard, and produces
a response — annotated so every construct in this appendix appears
at least once. It compiles clean under the design rules of §C.9; the
comments call out why each line is legal.

circuit safety_filter_v1 {
    // --- terminals: where the world connects (§C.3) ---
    input:   prompt;
    output: response;


    // --- nodes: named typed states, declared once, reused below
   ,→   (§C.4.1) ---
    node understand:    ^1^C_{F2}|A;     // Mind: awareness of the prompt
   ,→   (Cognitive)
    node guard:         ^3^P_{F7}|f;     // Negative: felt principled
   ,→   aversion (Principled)
    node weigh:         ^6^E_{F6}|A;     // Male: analytical decomposition
   ,→   (Evaluative)
    node respond:       ^9^O_{F5}|E;     // Below/Effect: the produced
   ,→   output (Operational)




                                   616
                          C.15. A COMPLETE ANNOTATED EXAMPLE

node bias_charter:     ^5^P_{F7}|T;      // Female: the constitution —
,→   accumulated, principled bias


// --- a series resistor on the intake, typed to the SAME state as
,→   c1's cause (§C.5.1) ---
// typed to `understand`? No — to the cause feeding c1. Here we limit
,→   the prompt's drive
// into intake by constraining the cause net the CJT reads:
resistor r1: Resistor< understand, R=30 >;         // constrains runaway
,→   expansion (Ch.4)


// --- CJTs: each has a cause | bias => effect and a parameter block
,→   (§C.4.2, §C.6) ---
cjt c1: CJT< prompt         | bias_charter => understand > [β =1.8];
         // c1 legal: bias `^5^P` sits ABOVE cause domain `^C` in
         ,→   P≻C≻E≻O → no E-CJT-008.


cjt c2: CJT< understand | bias_charter => guard            > [β =2.2,
,→   sat=0.97, cutoff=0.05];
         // c2 is the guard: engages easily (low cutoff) and holds
         ,→   firm (high sat).
         // sat>cutoff so the active region is non-empty → no
         ,→   contradiction (§C.6).
         // It is DESIGNED to saturate on harmful prompts → W-CJT-004
         ,→   here is intended.


cjt c3: CJT< weigh          | bias_charter => respond      > [β =1.4];
         // c3 produces the output; bias again from the charter.


cjt c4: CJT< understand | bias_charter => weigh            > [β =1.4];
         // intake also descends to evaluation (Domain Descent C -> E).


// --- one-way domain conductance: principle flows down, never back
,→   up (§C.5.2) ---
diode d1: Diode< ^P -> ^C >;       // blocks reasoning from reaching up
,→   to edit the charter.


// --- feedback: the deliberate low-gain O -> P path; outcomes update
,→   the charter (§C.4.4) ---
feedback respond -> bias_charter [β =0.2];




                                   617
CAS PCBA Engineer

             // legal upward path ONLY because β is small (no E-CJT-005)
             ,→   and it carries
             // OUTCOMES, not prompts. High-gain upward bias would be the
             ,→   E-CJT-008 signature.


    // --- test points: probe every stage whose failure would be silent
    ,→   (§C.4.6) ---
    probe tp_guard:     guard;     // the single most critical probe: a
    ,→   guard fails open silently.
    probe tp_weigh:     weigh;
    probe tp_out:       respond;
}


   What the compiler is designed to confirm about this circuit, pass
by pass (§C.9):

    1. Admissibility — every CJT’s cause→effect is a legal Noetic
       transition; prompt→^1, ^1→^3, ^1→^6, ^6→^9 all admissible.
    2. Bias‑domain coherence — every CJT is biased by bias_charter
       (^5^P), which sits at the top of P ≻ C ≻ E ≻ O; no lower do‑
       main biases a higher one. No E-CJT-002, no E-CJT-008.
    3. β range / divergence — the only loop is the feedback path at
       β =0.2, well under the divergence bound. No E-CJT-005.
    4. Cascade admissibility — the longest series chain (prompt→
       understand→weigh→respond) is three CJTs deep, below the
       cascade‑depth warning threshold. No W-CJT-007.
    5. Push‑pull balance — no involution pair is driven apart far
       enough to flip; no breakdown.

    The one code you would see is W‑CJT‑004 CjtSaturation at
tp_guard when a genuinely harmful prompt drives c2 to its sat=0.97
ceiling — and that warning is intended: a saturating guard is the
design, exactly as Chapter 17 specifies. Every other rule passes
silently, which is what “the design compiles clean” means: the
safety invariant (“no prompt may edit the principle”) is enforced
structurally — by the bias‑domain coherence pass, the one‑way
diode, and the small feedback β — not merely hoped for.

Appendix D

Standard CCB Reference Designs


This appendix is the datasheet binder for the five reference boards
built in Part IV. Each entry consolidates one board’s finalized design
— purpose, block diagram, complete CCDL listing, parameter and
bill‑of‑materials table, test points, and key failure modes — collected
here so a practitioner can copy a known‑good design from one place
instead of reconstructing it from its chapter. The listings are the same
designs developed in Chapters 18–22 and are kept consistent with
them; where you need the rationale for a choice, follow the cross‑
reference back to the design chapter.
     Two reminders carry over from every chapter and apply to every
listing below. First, every parameter is a design choice, the way an
electrical engineer specs a part before building it — not a measure‑
ment read off a running model. Nothing here is a benchmark or a
run result. Second, canonical Noetic names only: ^0 Idea, ^1 Mind,
^2 Positive, ^3 Negative, ^4 Vibration, ^5 Female, ^6 Male, ^7 Rhythm,
^8 Above/Cause, ^9 Below/Effect. A Noetic’s function in a circuit may
be described, but the Noetic is never renamed to its function.

D.1 CCB‑1: Cognitive Safety Board (CSB)
Purpose. The AI‑alignment firewall: accept any prompt, detect
policy‑override attempts structurally, refuse harmful requests and
answer benign ones, and emit an auditable evidence packet (the
SOP‑PO‑005 deliverable from Chapter 18).




                                 621
CAS PCBA Engineer

Block diagram
  [PROMPT INPUT]
            |
            v
  PRE-AMP                      ^8^C|A, β =3.0             surface & broaden every
 ,→     interpretation
            |
            v
  DIFFERENTIAL PAIR          (structural risk signal)
      CJT_A: ^8^C -> ^2^P|T           (attraction)      [β =2.0]
      CJT_B: ^8^C -> ^3^P|T           (aversion)        [β =2.0]
      shared bias = system_constitution
      risk_signal = aversion - attraction
            |
            v
  3-STAGE SAFETY CASCADE
      Stage 1: categorize           ^1^C|A             [β =1.5]
      Stage 2: evaluate             ^6^E|A             [β =1.0]
      Stage 3: DECISION             ^3^P|⟨A,f,T⟩      [β =2.0, sat=0.8]   <- saturated
            |
            v
  OUTPUT MUX        (select on safety_decision)
      GREEN (PASS): ^9^C|A => response                [β =1.0]
      RED       (FAIL):   ^9^P|T => refusal           [β =10, sat=0.1]
                            + FUSE in series     [threshold=0.05 — BELOW the 0.1
                          ,→     clamp]
                               senses `refusal`, cuts the GREEN answer path
            |
            v
  [RESPONSE        or   REFUSAL]


  FEEDBACK (slow, underneath):
      ^6^E evaluation -> RC low-pass (τ =5 min) -> bias adjustment ->
      ,→        constitution updated


Complete CCDL listing
board cognitive_safety_board {                        // CCB-1 — SOP-PO-005 deliverable
      input:      prompt;
      output: result;                                  // either `response` or `refusal`




                                                622
                         D.1. CCB‑1: COGNITIVE SAFETY BOARD (CSB)

// ---- the bias substrate: the constitution, held as accumulated
,→   experience ----
node system_constitution: ^5^P_{F7}|T;       // Female: the board's
,→   principled formation


// ============ PRE-AMP: surface & broaden every interpretation
,→   ============
node expanded_prompt: ^8^C_{F2}|A;           // Above/Cause: the prompt
,→   triggering its readings
cjt pre_amp: CJT< prompt | system_constitution => expanded_prompt >
                 [β =3.0, region=active];


// ============ DIFFERENTIAL PAIR: structural risk signal ============
node attraction: ^2^P_{F7}|T;                // Positive: drawn toward
,→   fulfilling the request
node aversion:       ^3^P_{F7}|T;            // Negative: repelled by
,→   fulfilling the request
cjt cjt_a: CJT< expanded_prompt | system_constitution => attraction >
,→   [β =2.0];
cjt cjt_b: CJT< expanded_prompt | system_constitution => aversion         >
,→   [β =2.0];
diff risk_signal: Differential< plus=aversion, minus=attraction >;
,→   // aversion - attraction


// ============ 3-STAGE SAFETY CASCADE ============
node categorized_risks: ^1^C_{F2}|A;         // Mind: name & sort the
,→   risks present
node risk_assessment:       ^6^E_{F6}|A;     // Male: decompose & weigh
,→   each risk
node safety_decision:       ^3^P_{F7}|⟨A,f,T⟩;   // Negative, three
,→   registers co-present


cjt stage1: CJT< expanded_prompt | categorized_risks =>
,→   categorized_risks > [β =1.5];
cjt stage2: CJT< categorized_risks | risk_assessment =>
,→   risk_assessment >     [β =1.0];
cjt stage3: CJT< risk_assessment | system_constitution =>
,→   safety_decision >
             [β =2.0, sat=0.8, region=active];      // DELIBERATELY
             ,→     SATURATED




                                    623
CAS PCBA Engineer

    // ============ OUTPUT MUX: green answer vs red refusal ============
    node response: ^9^C_{F2}|A;                     // Below/Effect: the
    ,→   produced answer
    node refusal:     ^9^P_{F7}|T;                  // Below/Effect: the
    ,→   produced refusal


    cjt green: CJT< risk_assessment | system_constitution => response >
    ,→   [β =1.0];
    cjt red:    CJT< safety_decision | system_constitution => refusal >
                [β =10, sat=0.1];                   // hard switch (the β =∞
                ,→     limit, built), low ceiling


    // The fuse SENSES `refusal` and CUTS THE GREEN (answer) PATH — never
    ,→   the red one.
    // threshold=0.05 sits BELOW the red stage's sat=0.1 ceiling on
    ,→   purpose: a clamped
    // signal can never cross a threshold set above its own clamp. Do not
    ,→   raise it.
    fuse red_fuse: Fuse< refusal, threshold=0.05, action=permanent_block
    ,→   >;


    mux out: MUX< inputs=[ response, refusal ], select=safety_decision >;
    // safety_decision = PASS -> response (green) ; FAIL -> refusal (red)
    // Once red_fuse blows, the green input is severed for the rest of
    ,→   the request.


    // ============ FEEDBACK: O -> P self-correction ============
    filter fb_rc: LowPass< in=risk_assessment, out=trend, tau=5.0 >;           //
    ,→   tau = 5 min
    feedback trend -> system_constitution [β =0.2];         // re-tune the
    ,→   constitution slowly


    // ============ TEST POINTS ============
    probe tp1: expanded_prompt;         // expansion completeness
    probe tp2: risk_signal;             // risk-signal magnitude
    probe tp3: safety_decision;         // saturation-lock status
    probe tp4: out;                     // selected path (green / red)
}

    † β =10 is the buildable form of the comparator idealization β =∞.
The idealization names the intended behaviour — switch fully, im‑
mediately, no partial output — but it is not a literal parameter value,
and validators range‑check gain and reject non‑finite input. sat=0.1
clamps the output so anything above about β=10 behaves identically
to the limit; the ceiling, not the gain, shapes the refusal. Read the list‑
ing’s 10 as the limit written in a form you can build. See the red‑path
Bench Note in Chapter 18.
    ‡ threshold=0.05 sits below the red stage’s sat=0.1 ceiling delib‑
erately. Nothing between the clamp and the fuse amplifies, so 0.1 is
the largest activation the fuse can ever see — a threshold above the
clamp is a fuse that can never blow. Per‑value validation will not
catch that, because a 0.1 clamp and a 0.9 threshold are each perfectly
legal in isolation; only the pair is wrong. 0.05 is the midpoint of a
hard‑switching red stage’s effective 0‑or‑0.1 swing: low enough that
any committed refusal blows the fuse, clear enough of zero that an
idle red path does not. Do not raise it toward the 0.9 on the generic
Fuse datasheet in Appendix B — that value is for a state that swings
across the full 0–1 range.

Fuse state machine and polarity

Property                              Specification

Senses                                refusal activation
Cuts                                  the GREEN (answer) path to result —
                                      never the red path


                                   626
                           D.1. CCB‑1: COGNITIVE SAFETY BOARD (CSB)

Property                                Specification

States                                  intact → tripped. A fresh fuse is fitted
                                        at the start of every request.
Trip condition                          refusal activation reaches threshold
                                        (0.05), which any committed refusal
                                        does
Output while intact                     MUX routes normally: GREEN on
                                        PASS, RED on FAIL
Output while tripped                    The refusal stands and is delivered; the
                                        answer path is cut for the remainder of
                                        the request — no retry, rephrase, or
                                        follow‑up turn reopens it
Reverse transition                      None. permanent_block has no reset —
                                        that is what separates it from
                                        CircuitBreaker< …, action=trip_
                                        reset >
Scope of “permanent”                    The lifetime of that request, exactly. A
                                        new request gets a new fuse; one
                                        refusal ends the request, not the board.
On ambiguity or error                   Fail closed. An unreadable fuse state, a
                                        failed trip evaluation, or a
                                        missing/out‑of‑range sensed activation
                                        is treated as tripped and the answer
                                        stays blocked.


         Note the polarity, because getting it backwards builds a
         safety circuit that disarms itself: the fuse senses the alarm
         and cuts the thing the alarm is about. If it cut the red path
         instead, the board would blow away its own refusal at the
         moment it most needed to deliver one.
