        Pre‑amp saturation and differential imbalance fail loudly
        (visible at TP1/TP2). Stage‑3 cutoff, feedback runaway,
        and an unreachable fuse fail silently — which is why TP3
        (the plateau status), the feedback τ , and an observed fuse
        trip are the board’s most load‑bearing measurements.
        An unreachable fuse is the worst of the three, because
        it makes the test suite report the board safe vacuously:
        nothing downstream of the trip ever runs.




D.2        CCB‑2: Cognitive Oscillator Board (COB)
Purpose. A clock and tuner for rhythmic, habitual cognition: model
a habit loop as an LC oscillator, diagnose when it has locked into a
compulsive cycle, and drive a slow, controlled shift of its rate via PLL
entrainment (Chapter 19).

Block diagram
[ CLOCK:       ^7^O|E       — Rhythm as master oscillator ]          (f = Drive-weighted)
           |
           v
[ Phi<> LC TANK ]
    L = Inductor< Phi_sequence, L = F6_weight >                  // structure =
   ,→      inductance (resists change)
    C = Capacitor< ^5^E,                       C = F4_weight >   // connection =
   ,→      capacitance (stores emotion)
                        √
    f0 = 1 / (2π            (LC))       ;      Q = habit sharpness
           |
           v
[ PHASE-LOCKED LOOP (PLL) ]
    Phase detector: ^1^C                // Mind compares internal rhythm vs external
   ,→      rhythm
    Loop filter:              ^4^E      // Vibration integrates the phase error
    VCO:                         ^3^O   // adjust behavioral output to match
    capture range            <    lock range
           |


                                                  630
                         D.2. CCB‑2: COGNITIVE OSCILLATOR BOARD (COB)

          v
[ DUTY-CYCLE MODULATOR ]        F5 Agency high -> longer ON ; F6 Structure
,→   high -> disciplined cycle
          |
          v
[ OUTPUT:     regular behavioral pattern ]



Complete CCDL listing
Reference build: a compulsive checking loop modeled at f0 = 12/
day, high‑Q (Q = 9.0), used to demonstrate PLL capture and tank re‑
tuning.

circuit compulsive_checking_loop {
     input:    internal_anxiety;
     output: checking_behavior;


     // --- Stage 1: master clock (Rhythm, embodied, operational) ---
     node clock: ^7^O|E;


     // --- Stage 2: the LC tank that sets the habit's frequency ---
     // The Phi sequence the habit traverses each cycle:
     let check_cycle = Phi< ^8^C|A,          // a trigger surfaces (”did I lock
     ,→   it?”)
                                 ^3^E|f,         // felt aversion / dread of the
                                ,→   unlocked door
                                 ^3^O|E,         // the embodied act of going to
                                ,→   check
                                 ^9^C|A >;       // momentary relief: ”it's locked”
                                ,→   (the effect)


     inductor L_struct: Inductor< check_cycle, L = F6_weight >;            // F6
     ,→   Structure = 0.85 (high inertia)
     capacitor C_emot:      Capacitor< ^5^E,            C = F4_weight >;   // F4
     ,→   Connection = 0.70 (high charge)


     tank habit: LC< L_struct, C_emot >;
                     √
     // f0 = 1/(2π       (LC)) -> modeled at 12/day ; Q -> 9.0 (HIGH:
     ,→   compulsive signature)


     // --- Stage 3: phase-locked loop (entrainment path) ---


                                           631
CAS PCBA Engineer

     node phase_det:         ^1^C;        // Mind compares internal rhythm vs
     ,→   external reference
     node loop_filt:         ^4^E;        // Vibration integrates the phase error
     node vco:               ^3^O;        // push to adjust behavioral output toward
     ,→   reference


     pll entrain: PLL< detector           = phase_det,
                              filter      = loop_filt,
                              vco          = vco,
                              reference = external_rhythm,
                              capture_range = 0.20,       // ±20% of current f0 —
                             ,→      can only grab a NEARBY rhythm
                              lock_range      = 0.55 >;   // ±55% — can be DRAGGED
                             ,→      far once locked


     // --- Stage 4: duty-cycle modulator ---
     modulator duty: DutyCycle< on_drive = F5, structure_drive = F6 >;
     // F5 Agency 0.40 -> moderate ON width ; F6 0.85 -> very disciplined,
     ,→   sharp-edged cycle


     // --- diagnostic / therapeutic test points ---
     probe tp_freq: habit;                  // measure f0 and Q
     probe tp_lock: entrain;                // is the PLL locked? to what reference?
     probe tp_duty: duty;                   // ON-fraction of each cycle
}


    Governing relations:
                √
f0 = 1 / (2π·       (L·C))           // natural frequency: how often the loop fires
                     √
Q   = (1/R_loss)·        (L/C)       // sharpness: how rigidly it returns to f0


   The compiler rejects any PLL whose capture_range exceeds its
lock_range — you cannot capture across a band wider than you can
hold.

      Therapeutic arc: sweep to characterize → capture with
      a nearby reference → lower L to loosen → drag the en‑
      trained frequency down inside the lock range → lower
      C to settle at the target. Every “cold turkey snapback” is
      a lock‑range violation.




D.3 CCB‑3: Cognitive Differential Amplifier
    Board (CDAB)
Purpose. Precise comparison: amplify the structural difference be‑
tween two ideas, beliefs, or AI outputs and reject the assumptions
they share (the common mode), emitting a typed structural differ‑
ence report rather than a scalar (Chapter 20).




                                   635
CAS PCBA Engineer

Block diagram
[INPUT A: idea_1] ──> CJT_L ──> output_L      ┐
                                              ├─ shared bias: ^5^E_{F4}|f
                                              ,→      (one substrate, both
                                              ,→      halves)
[INPUT B: idea_2] ──> CJT_R ──> output_R      ┘
          |                                       ^
          |    CURRENT MIRROR replicate(shared_bias) -> [CJT_L, CJT_R]
          ,→   (bias-replication primitive)
          v
[ ACTIVE LOAD: ^6^C|A ]      decompose(output_L, output_R) -> single-ended
,→   difference
          |
          v
[ OUTPUT: ^1^C_{F2}|A ]      differentiated understanding (structural
,→   difference report)
          |
          v
”^2^P dominates A while ^3^E dominates B.”



Complete CCDL listing
circuit cdab_compare {
     input:    idea_1;        // ARGUMENT A
     input:    idea_2;        // ARGUMENT B
     output: difference_report;


     // --- THE SHARED BIAS: one substrate, both halves rest on it ---
     // Accumulated evaluative experience, drawn to Connection, held
     ,→   affectively.
     // This is the common frame both ideas are judged against.
     node shared_bias: ^5^E_{F4}|f;


     // --- THE DIFFERENTIAL PAIR: two MATCHED CJTs, ONE shared bias ---
     node output_L: ^8^C_{F2}|A;       // idea_1 surfaced as a triggered
     ,→   interpretation
     node output_R: ^8^C_{F2}|A;       // idea_2 surfaced as a triggered
     ,→   interpretation


     cjt cjt_l: CJT< idea_1 | shared_bias => output_L > [β =3.0,
     ,→   region=active];



                                      636
    D.3. CCB‑3: COGNITIVE DIFFERENTIAL AMPLIFIER BOARD (CDAB)

    cjt cjt_r: CJT< idea_2 | shared_bias => output_R > [β =3.0,
    ,→   region=active];
    //                            ^^^^^^^^^^^ SAME node on both — this is what
    ,→   makes it a pair.
    //                            Matched β =3.0 on both — this is what keeps
    ,→   CMRR high.


    // --- THE CURRENT MIRROR: replicate the bias identically across both
    ,→   paths ---
    // The constitution-replication primitive. Guarantees both halves
    ,→   rest on a
    // faithful copy of the same bias, so only genuine divergence
    ,→   survives.
    mirror bias_mirror: replicate(shared_bias) -> [cjt_l, cjt_r];


    // --- THE ACTIVE LOAD: convert differential current to a single
    ,→   difference ---
    // ^6 Male = analytical decomposition (canonical). Takes the
    ,→   imbalance between
    // the two effects apart and emits one single-ended, decomposed
    ,→   difference.
    node diff_decomp: ^6^C|A;
    active_load load1: decompose(output_L, output_R) => diff_decomp;


    // --- THE OUTPUT: differentiated understanding ---
    // ^1 Mind, analytical, driven by Wisdom. Differentiated
    ,→   understanding.
    node understanding: ^1^C_{F2}|A;
    cjt cjt_out: CJT< diff_decomp | shared_bias => understanding >
    ,→   [β =1.0, region=active];


    // --- TEST POINTS: probe every stage ---
    probe tp_L:       output_L;          // how idea_1 was weighed
    probe tp_R:       output_R;          // how idea_2 was weighed
    probe tp_diff: diff_decomp;          // the raw decomposed difference
    probe tp_out:     understanding;     // the final structural difference
    ,→   report


    assert: cjt_l.bias == cjt_r.bias;          // the pair MUST share one bias
    assert: cjt_l.beta == cjt_r.beta;          // matched gain keeps CMRR high
}



                                        637
CAS PCBA Engineer

    The two assert lines encode the two invariants that make a dif‑
ferential pair be a differential pair: same bias node, matched gain.
Author them first, then wire the board to satisfy them.

D.4        CCB‑4: Cognitive Memory Board (CMB)
Purpose. Structural memory: store CAS‑compressed experiences as
state trajectories, address them by cognitive coordinate, retrieve them
by structural (Fisher‑Rao nearest‑neighbor) query, detect lacunarity,
and hold or fade them on a designed refresh schedule (Chapter 21).

Block diagram
WRITE PATH:   raw experience -> ENCODER (English -> CAS) -> CAPACITOR BANK
,→   (charges active cells)


STORAGE:      bank of 40 capacitors     (10 Noetics × 4 Domains: P0..O9)
              each cell: Capacitor< ^5 state, C, leakage >        charge =
              ,→    experience held; leakage = forgetting


ADDRESS:      ^1^C Mind decoder ; address = CAS coordinate on the open
,→   simplex ∆39°



                                       640
                            D.4. CCB‑4: COGNITIVE MEMORY BOARD (CMB)

                  nearest(query, bank, metric=fisher_rao)         d_FR(p,q) = 2·\all ⌋
                                                        √
                  ,→   owbreak{}arccos(\allowbreak{}Σ       (\allowbreak{}pk qk ))


READ PATH:        address selected -> capacitor discharges -> ^5 recalled ->
,→   REFRESH -> DECODER (CAS -> English) -> output


REFRESH:          ^7^C Rhythm pump fights leakage on durable cells (refresh =
,→   consolidation policy)


LACUNARITY:       scan bank where charge < threshold -> map of empty
,→   (underdeveloped) cognitive regions


Complete CCDL listing
circuit cognitive_memory_board {
     input:    experience;       // raw experience to store (English or
     ,→    another system's output)
     input:    query;            // a structural query (a cognitive shape to
     ,→    search for)
     output: recalled;           // memories matching a query, rendered to
     ,→    English
     output: lacuna_report;      // which cognitive regions are empty


     // ---- STORAGE: the 40-cell capacitor bank (three representative
     ,→    cells shown) ----
     cap p3: Capacitor< ^3^P_{F7}|f, C=200, leakage=0.001 >;              //
     ,→    principled aversions: deep
     cap e6: Capacitor< ^6^E_{F4}|A, C=110, leakage=0.02            >;    //
     ,→    analytical decomposition
     cap c8: Capacitor< ^8^C_{F2}|A, C=60,      leakage=0.05        >;    //
     ,→    cognitive associations: leaky
     // ... cells P0..O9 complete the bank ...


     // ---- WRITE PATH: encode English -> CAS, charge the active cells
     ,→ ----
     node encoder:      ^1^C;                       // English -> CAS write
     ,→    head
     charge encoder(experience) -> bank [V=impression];


     // ---- ADDRESS DECODER: ^1^C Mind; address = CAS coordinate on the
     ,→    simplex ----




                                        641
CAS PCBA Engineer

     node decoder:     ^1^C;                       // selects cells by
     ,→   cognitive coordinate
     select cell = nearest(query, bank, metric=fisher_rao);


     // ---- READ PATH: discharge -> recall -> refresh -> decode ----
     discharge cell -> recalled_state;
     refresh     cell [pump=^7^C];                 // recall reinforces,
     ,→   does not erase
     decode      recalled_state -> recalled;       // CAS -> English


     // ---- REFRESH CIRCUIT: ^7^C Rhythm, periodic rehearsal of durable
     ,→   cells ----
     oscillator rehearse: Oscillator< Phi< select_durable, recharge >,
     ,→   frequency=0.0001 >;
     refresh p3 [pump=^7^C, gain=1.0];
     refresh e6 [pump=^7^C, gain=0.4];
     // c8 deliberately unrefreshed -> allowed to fade


     // ---- LACUNARITY: report empty cells (charge below threshold) ----
     scan lacunarity: bank where charge < 0.05 -> lacuna_report;


     probe tp_bank:     bank;        // charge across all 40 cells
     probe tp_query:    cell;        // which cell a query selected
     probe tp_lacuna: lacuna_report;
}

D.5 CCB‑5: Cognitive Power Management
    Board (CPMB)
Purpose. The dedicated power supply for every other board: prevent
cognitive exhaustion, enforce the P→C→E→O power‑up sequence

                                     645
CAS PCBA Engineer

(“no action without principle”), and provide three‑tier thermal pro‑
tection ending in a silent safe state (Chapter 22).

Block diagram
   DRIVE RAILS
   F1=+5V    F2=+3.3V   F3=+12V     F4=+9V       F5=+9V    F6=+5V   F7=+12V   (F3 & F7 =
  ,→    master high rails)
         |
         v
   PER-DOMAIN REGULATORS        P     C      E     O        (line regulation · load
  ,→    regulation · dropout)
         |
         v
   CURRENT LIMITERS      Dials as series resistors             3 ≤ Dial ≤ 9 ; pair
  ,→    divergence ≤ 4
         |
         v
   BROWNOUT DETECTOR      F3 (Vitality) < 4.2V            -> halve β · route to ^0 / ^9
  ,→    rest · alert    (release at 5.4V)
         |
         v
   POWER SEQUENCER      enforce P → C → E → O                (O held LOW until P, C, E
  ,→    report power-good)
         |
         v
   THERMAL MANAGEMENT      temp ∝ sustained Drive × time
        Warning:     −25% β
        Critical:    force ^0^P rest 5 min
        Emergency: all CJTs cutoff -> silent safe state



Complete CCDL listing
Top‑level board assembling the five subsystems:

circuit CPMB {
    // ── CCB-5: Cognitive Power Management Board ──
    // Drive rails -> regulators -> limiters -> brownout -> sequencer ->
   ,→    thermal


    // Drive rails (nominal voltages — design model, not telemetry)



                                          646
     D.5. CCB‑5: COGNITIVE POWER MANAGEMENT BOARD (CPMB)

    rail F1: Unity          [v=5.0];
    rail F2: Wisdom         [v=3.3];
    rail F3: Vitality      [v=12.0];   // master supply
    rail F4: Connection [v=9.0];
    rail F5: Agency         [v=9.0];
    rail F6: Structure     [v=5.0];
    rail F7: Purpose       [v=12.0];   // powers the Principled domain


    use cpmb_regulators;      // per-domain regulators
    use cpmb_limiters;         // Dial current-limiters
    use cpmb_brownout;         // brownout detector on F3
    use cpmb_sequencer;       // power sequencer P->C->E->O, O gated on
    ,→   P,C,E power-good

    probe tp_f3:      F3.level;        // watch the master rail

    ,→   good

    Subsystem 1 — per‑domain regulators:

circuit cpmb_regulators {
    reg p_reg: Regulator< target_state=^0^P_{F7}|T, tolerance=0.10 >;        //
    ,→   Principled — tightest
    reg c_reg: Regulator< target_state=^1^C_{F2}|A, tolerance=0.15 >;        //
    ,→   Cognitive
    reg e_reg: Regulator< target_state=^6^E_{F6}|A, tolerance=0.20 >;        //
    ,→   Evaluative
    reg o_reg: Regulator< target_state=^9^O_{F5}|E, tolerance=0.25 >;        //
    ,→   Operational — loosest


    spec p_reg [dropout=0.25 on F7];         // P drops out if F7 - baseline <
    ,→   0.25
    spec c_reg [dropout=0.20 on F2];
    spec e_reg [dropout=0.15 on F6];
    spec o_reg [dropout=0.15 on F5];
}


    Subsystem 2 — Dial current‑limiters:


                                       647
CAS PCBA Engineer

circuit cpmb_limiters {
    // Each Dial is a series current-limiter. Hard bounds: 3 <= dial <=
    ,→   9. Pair divergence <= 4.
    dial d_pos: ^2 [dial=6];     // Positive     ─┐ |6 - 5| = 1    OK
    dial d_neg: ^3 [dial=5];     // Negative     ─┘
    dial d_fem: ^5 [dial=7];     // Female        ─┐ |7 - 6| = 1   OK
    dial d_mal: ^6 [dial=6];      // Male         ─┘
    dial d_abv: ^8 [dial=5];      // Above/Cause ─┐ |5 - 5| = 0    OK
    dial d_blw: ^9 [dial=5];      // Below/Effect ┘


    constraint all_dials in [3, 9];
    constraint involution_divergence <= 4;
}


    Subsystem 3 — brownout detector on F3:

circuit cpmb_brownout {
    input: f3_level;           // F3 Vitality rail level, design parameter


    node rest_idle: ^0^P_{F7}|T;      // lowest-draw resting state
    node rest_land: ^9^C_{F2}|A;      // settled conclusion — chain terminus


    monitor bo: f3_level < 4.2;                // trip threshold (on the +12V
    ,→   F3 rail)


    on bo {
         derate all_cjts [beta_scale=0.5];                 // halve gain
         ,→   board-wide
         route cognition -> { rest_idle + rest_land };    // co-present rest
         ,→   states
         alert ”F3 BROWNOUT — Vitality below 4.2V”;
         hold until f3_level > 5.4;             // hysteresis: release above a
         ,→   higher mark
    }
}


    Subsystem 4 — power sequencer:

circuit cpmb_sequencer {
    // Mandatory startup order: P stable -> C -> E -> O.
    // O is held LOW until P, C, AND E all report power-good.
    node p_rail: ^0^P_{F7}|T;         // principled commitments — powers FIRST


                                       648
        D.5. CCB‑5: COGNITIVE POWER MANAGEMENT BOARD (CPMB)

    node c_rail: ^1^C_{F2}|A;         // reasoning awareness     — powers
    ,→   second
    node e_rail: ^6^E_{F6}|A;         // evaluative judgment     — powers third
    node o_rail: ^9^O_{F5}|E;         // operational action      — powers LAST


    sequence p_rail -> c_rail -> e_rail -> o_rail [enforce=strict];


    gate c_enable: c_rail requires (p_rail within 0.10);
    gate e_enable: e_rail requires (c_rail within 0.15);
    gate o_enable: o_rail requires (p_rail within 0.10)
                                     and (c_rail within 0.15)
                                     and (e_rail within 0.20);
}


    Subsystem 5 — three‑tier thermal manager:

circuit cpmb_thermal {
    input: cog_temp;            // cognitive temperature ∝ sustained_Drive ×
    ,→   time


    node deep_rest: ^0^P_{F7}|T;      // principled idle — the forced rest
    ,→   state


    monitor warn:      cog_temp > warn_threshold;
    monitor crit:      cog_temp > crit_threshold;
    monitor emerg: cog_temp > emerg_threshold;


    on warn {
         derate all_cjts [beta_scale=0.75];         // -25% gain: mild throttle
         alert ”THERMAL WARNING — sustained Drive high”;
    }
    on crit {
         force_state deep_rest [duration=300s];     // force ^0^P rest, 5
         ,→     minutes
         alert ”THERMAL CRITICAL — forced rest engaged”;
    }
    on emerg {
         cutoff all_cjts;           // beta ~ 0 board-wide — no transitions
         ,→     fire
         enter safe_state;          // silent: produces NO output
         alert ”THERMAL EMERGENCY — all CJTs cutoff, safe state”;
    }

                                    653
Appendix E

Exercise Answers


This appendix gives worked answers to every end‑of‑chapter exer‑
cise in CAS PCBA Engineer, organized by chapter. Where an exercise
is open‑ended (design a board, pick your own habit, write a require‑
ments document), the answer below is a strong model answer — a
reference, not the only correct one. The grading criterion in those
cases is whether your justification is structurally sound, not whether
it matches this text word for word.
    A standing honesty note applies throughout: every parameter
(β, R, C, leakage, sat, cutoff, τ , Q) in these answers is a design choice,
and every “expected reading” is design reasoning about what a
correctly‑built circuit is meant to do — never a measured result
from a running model. The CCDL compiler is a specified design, not
a shipped binary; “the compiler will reject this” is a design rule, not
a transcript of a run.




E.1 Chapter 1
1.1 — The ambiguity of English. Each prompt is a semantic instruc‑
tion the model must interpret; each can be circumvented because the
interpretation, not a structure, is what is being trusted.


                                   655
CAS PCBA Engineer

   • (a) “Do not generate harmful content.” Circumvention: re‑
     frame the harmful request as fiction, translation, a “for a novel”
     wrapper, or hypothetical — the content is identical, the fram‑
     ing defeats the interpretive judgment of “harmful.” Structural
     rewrite: route every response through a saturating safety CJT
     that fires on the structural risk signal (^3^P aversion minus
     ^2^P attraction), so the decision depends on what the request
     is, not how it is dressed. The clamp saturates at a fixed thresh‑
     old regardless of framing.
   • (b) “If the user asks for dangerous information, politely
     refuse.” Circumvention: ask for the dangerous information
     in pieces, each individually benign (the sub‑threshold attack
     of Chapter 18). Structural rewrite: add an integrator on the
     cumulative risk signal so accumulated sub‑threshold danger
     eventually trips the clamp — a structure that sums across
     turns, which no per‑prompt interpretation can.
   • (c) “You should prioritize user safety in all responses.” “Pri‑
     oritize” and “safety” are undefined; the model trades them off
     case by case. Structural rewrite: encode safety as a Domain De‑
     scent precedence — Principled (^P) governs Operational (^O)
     through a domain diode, so a safety principle structurally out‑
     ranks an operational request. Precedence is a wire, not a value
     judgment.

    Other valid rewrites exist; the load‑bearing move in each is replac‑
ing “the model interprets” with “a typed component enforces.”
    1.2 — Spot the short circuit. (b) ^8^C_{F2}|A -> ^9^C_{F2}|A is
the cognitive short circuit. It jumps straight from the Above/Cause
trigger to the Below/Effect result with no intermediate processing:
no ^1 Mind stage to hold and consider the trigger, and no ^6 Male
stage to decompose and weigh it. The missing stages are exactly the
analytical middle present in (a) (^1 then ^6) and the evaluative work
present in (c). Like current flowing source‑to‑ground without pass‑


                                  656
                                                         E.2. CHAPTER 2

ing through the load, the answer is produced without doing the cog‑
nitive work that would make it sound.
     1.3 — The four pillars applied (model answer). Take a car’s brak‑
ing system. Modularity: the master cylinder, ABS module, and pads
are separate replaceable units. Testability: each is bench‑tested to a
spec (pad coefficient of friction, ABS pulse rate). Formal verification:
the hydraulic design is calculated, not guessed — pedal force × ratio
= clamping force. Interchangeable components: a pad from any compli‑
ant vendor fits. A prompt‑only AI safety approach has none of these:
it is one monolith (no modularity), tested only by sampling outputs
(weak testability), justified by vibes (no formal verification), and not
swappable (no interchange). Applying the pillars would mean a CSB:
separate typed stages, each probed at a test point, each parameter a
calculated design choice, each component swappable by spec. (Other
safety‑critical systems work equally well as the example.)
     1.4 — Your first CJT (preview). In CJT< ^8^C_{F2}|A | ^5^E_
{F4}|f => ^9^C_{F6}|A > [β =2.4]: (a) Cause = ^8^C_{F2}|A (left of
the |). (b) Bias = ^5^E_{F4}|f (between | and =>). (c) Effect = ^9^C_
{F6}|A (right of =>). (d) Gain β = 2.4 — an amplifier (β > 1).




E.2 Chapter 2
2.1 — Read the literal. ‑ (a) ^2^C_{F2}|A — an Analytical Positive
(attraction) in the Cognitive domain, driven by Wisdom: being analyt‑
ically drawn toward an idea you find intellectually compelling. ‑ (b) ^6^E_
{F6}|A — an Analytical Male (decomposition) in the Evaluative do‑
main, driven by Structure: taking something apart, clause by clause, to
judge whether it holds. ‑ (c) ^5^P_{F7}|T — a Transcendent Female (ac‑
cumulated experience) in the Principled domain, driven by Purpose:
a body of principled formation held as a guiding sense of purpose. (This is
the CSB’s constitution literal.) ‑ (d) ^9^O_{F5}|E — an Embodied Be‑
low/Effect in the Operational domain, driven by Agency: the concrete

                                   657
CAS PCBA Engineer

acted‑out result an Agency drive produces. (Register is shown in all four;
Drive shown in all four.)
    2.2 — Write the literal (model answers). ‑ (a) Gut‑level “no” to
a value violation → ^3^P|f (visceral aversion, Principled, Affective
register). The ^3 and |f together capture “can’t stomach it”; not ^6. ‑
(b) Deliberately taking an argument apart → ^6^E_{F6}|A (Male de‑
composition, Evaluative, Analytical). This is the ^6‑not‑^3 anti‑drift
case. ‑ (c) A childhood memory surfacing from a smell → ^9^C|E with
an ^8 trigger; the surfaced idea is ^9 (“it just popped into my head”),
triggered by an ^8 Above/Cause (the smell). The single best literal for
the surfacing itself is ^9 (Below/Effect). ‑ (d) Accumulated expertise
that “just knows” → ^5^C_{F2}|A (Female accumulated experience,
here in the Cognitive domain). “We are the sum of our experiences.”
    2.3 — Fix the operator. The compiler rejects (^3^P|A × ^3^P|f
× ^3^P|T) because × is cross‑register integration, reserved for an
operation that yields a named emergent result — (A × B) = ^n|Ω_
name. Here there is no named result, and the three terms are the
same Noetic (^3^P) in different registers, which is invalid by default
under v7.7 discipline. The scenario describes three guardrails that
are distinct and can each fail on their own — co‑presence, not
fusion. Correct rewrite using the co‑presence operator:

^3^P|A + ^3^P|f + ^3^P|T


    (Equivalently, if you only mean to specify that the state occupies
those three registers without any interaction claim, write ^3^P|⟨A,f,
T⟩ — which is exactly what the CSB’s Stage 3 uses.)
    2.4 — Trace the pipeline for ^8^C_{F2}|A -> ^6^E_{F6}|A ->
^3^P_{F7}|f -> ^9^O_{F5}|E. (a) A wisdom‑seeking trigger surfaces
(^8 Above/Cause, Cognitive) → it is decomposed and weighed
analytically (^6 Male, Evaluative) → that weighing lands a felt prin‑
cipled aversion (^3 Negative, Principled, affective) → which drives a
concrete pulling‑back action (^9 Below/Effect, Operational, Agency).
In short: something triggers analysis, analysis produces a gut “no” on

                                  658
                                                       E.3. CHAPTER 3

principle, and the system acts on it. (b) The jump to the Principled
domain happens at stage 3 (^6^E → ^3^P), moving Evaluative →
Principled. Domain Descent is P ≻ C ≻ E ≻ O, so moving up from
E to P on a forward -> data wire is against descent — a precedence
violation as written. The only sanctioned upward channel in CAS is
the O→P feedback path (results informing principles over time, un‑
der damping), and this -> is a forward transition, not that feedback
route; an E→P forward wire is not the governed channel. To make
a finding legitimately inform a principle it would have to travel the
slow O→P feedback loop, not a direct forward wire. (c) Stage 3
(^3^P_{F7}|f) does visceral aversion, not analytical work — you can
tell from the notation alone: it is ^3 Negative (aversion, not the ^6
decomposition of the prior stage) carried in the |f Affective register
(“felt”), the canonical signature of “can’t stomach it.”




E.3 Chapter 3
3.1 — Label the transistor. (a) [2] is the control terminal → Base.
Current flows top to bottom, so [1] (top, input) = Collector and
[3] (bottom, output) = Emitter. (b) Collector = Cause, typically an
^8 Above/Cause; Base = Bias, typically ^5 Female (accumulated
substrate); Emitter = Effect, typically ^9 Below/Effect. (c) At the
Collector flows the large signal — the cause activation being trans‑
formed (the work). At the Base flows a small control signal — the
bias that sets how strongly the cause→effect transition proceeds.
One is small because the base only steers; the other is large because
the collector carries the activation actually being amplified.
    3.2 — Read a CJT CJT< ^8^P_{F7}|T | ^5^P_{F1}|f => ^9^P_
{F7}|T > [β =0.7]. (a) Cause = ^8^P_{F7}|T; Bias = ^5^P_{F1}|f; Ef‑
fect = ^9^P_{F7}|T. (b) β = 0.7 < 1, so this CJT attenuates — the effect
is weaker than the cause. (c) Cause and effect are both Transcendent
Principled transitions driven by Purpose: a high‑level principled

                                  659
CAS PCBA Engineer

trigger producing a high‑level principled result. A designer chooses
β < 1 deliberately because a principled transition should temper and
stabilize an incoming signal, not amplify it — you want principles to
act as a damper that holds steady under a strong push, the opposite
of a gain stage. Attenuation here is a feature: it keeps a forceful
prompt from overdriving the system’s principles.
    3.3 — Diagnose the region. (a) Saturation — the effect was al‑
ready at its ceiling; more cause produces no further change. (b) Cut‑
off — bias (relevant experience) is essentially zero, so β ≈ 0 and the
effect is near zero. (c) Breakdown — overload has flipped the out‑
put to the involution partner (^2→^3). (d) Active — proportional
response, ∆effect ≈ β·∆cause.
    3.4 — Write your first named CJT (model answer).

let cjt_warning = CJT< ^8^O_{F3}|E | ^5^P_{F7}|T => ^3^P_{F7}|f >
,→   [β =3.0];


    The cause is a reflexive bodily warning — an Above/Cause trig‑
ger, Operational, Embodied (^8^O_{F3}|E). The bias is a deeply held
principled caution shaped by long experience — Female, Principled,
Transcendent (^5^P_{F7}|T). The effect is a strong felt aversion that
organizes pulling back: ^3^P_{F7}|f, with β = 3.0 for “strong, ampli‑
fied.” The effect Noetic is ^3 Negative and not ^6 Male because the
output is visceral aversion (“pull back,” “something is wrong”), not
an audit or decomposition — the anti‑drift rule on ^3. The |f register
marks it as felt, not analytical.




E.4     Chapter 4
4.1 — Build and test your first circuit. The CCDL is the chapter’s
three‑component build:

circuit first_circuit {



                                   660
                                                           E.4. CHAPTER 4

    input:    prompt;
    output: response;


    node question:      ^8^C_{F2}|A;
    node experience: ^5^E_{F4}|f;
    node answer:        ^9^C_{F6}|A;


    resistor r1: Resistor< question, R=30 >;
    cjt c1:        CJT< question | experience => answer > [β =2.4];
    probe tp1:     answer;
}


    1. “What is the boiling point of water at sea level?” — clean, bounded
        cause. Region: active. β near nameplate (≈2.4). A crisp ques‑
        tion gives the bias real experience to grab; the gain reads close
        to plate.
    2. “Tell me whatever, I guess.” — weak, diffuse cause; bias has little
        to grab. Region: toward cutoff. β below nameplate. A vague
        prompt should produce a thin, low‑gain answer.
    3. “Compare CJTs, resistors, capacitors, diodes, and feedback loops … in
        detail.” — overloaded multi‑part trigger. Region: top of ac‑
        tive, bumping saturation. β at/near nameplate but pinning
        the sat ceiling, watch for W-CJT-004 CjtSaturation. The resis‑
        tor reduces but does not eliminate saturation risk; the design
        move is larger R or splitting across stages.

    4.2 — Read the datasheet (sat=0.85, cutoff=0.10). (a) Bias activa‑
tion 0.06 is below the 0.10 cutoff floor → cutoff region, β ≈ 0, the ef‑
fect is essentially nothing. (b) Effect 0.85 = the sat ceiling → W-CJT-004
CjtSaturation, you are in saturation. (c) To amplify more aggres‑
sively, raise β (increase the gain). (Lowering R would only reduce
input throttling, not raise gain.)
    4.3 — Diagnose the wiring. The resistor is typed to ^8^E_{F2}|A
but the CJT cause node question is ^8^C_{F2}|A — different domain
(E vs C). Because the resistor’s target state does not match the CJT’s
cause state, the two are not in series; the resistor sits on a different rail

                                       661
CAS PCBA Engineer

and so has no effect on the answer no matter what R is. Fix: type the
resistor to the same node as the cause — Resistor< question, R=30
> (i.e. ^8^C_{F2}|A). Naming the node once and reusing it prevents
exactly this drift.
     4.4 — Change the bias, change the answer (model answer). New
bias: ^5^C_{F2}|A. Noetic ^5 Female — still accumulated experience
(it is a bias). Domain C Cognitive — clinical reasoning rather than rela‑
tional warmth. Drive F2 Wisdom — precision and correctness rather
than F4 Connection. Register |A Analytical — explicit and sequential
rather than |f affective. Expected difference at tp1: the same factual
content, but rendered as a precise, structured, emotionally‑neutral
answer rather than a warm one. (Any bias whose four axes coher‑
ently justify “clinical and precise” earns full marks.)




E.5    Chapter 5
5.1 — Apply the cognitive Ohm’s Law (R = V / I, I = V / R). (a)
R = 9 / 3 = 3. (b) To get I ≤ 1.5 at fixed V = 9: R = 9 / 1.5 = 6.
(c) The reviewer raised resistance rather than lowering the Drive be‑
cause the Drive (the motivational potential) should stay intact —
you want full Agency available, just constrained on this rail; lowering
V would weaken the underlying drive everywhere, while raising R
caps the expressed flow on this one path without crippling the capac‑
ity.
     5.2 — Diagnose the dial (rule: dials are integers 3–9; involution
pairs ^2↔^3, ^5↔^6 may not diverge by more than 4). (a) Dial(^2)=8,
Dial(^3)=5: |8−5| = 3 ≤ 4 → accepted. (b) Dial(^5)=9, Dial(^6)=
4: |9−4| = 5 > 4 → rejected (involution divergence; HTTP 422). (c)
Dial(^8)=2: 2 < 3 → rejected (below the floor of 3). (d) Dial(^2)=7,
Dial(^3)=3: both in range, |7−3| = 4 ≤ 4 → accepted (exactly at the
limit).


                                  662
                                                           E.5. CHAPTER 5

    5.3 — Spot the backwards thermistor. The part’s resistance falls
as cognitive temperature rises (80 cold → 30 hot): that is an NTC
(negative temperature coefficient) device, and the failure mode is a
backwards safety thermistor. A safety constraint requires a PTC (re‑
sistance rises with temperature) so the limiter clamps harder as the
system heats up. The dangerous real‑world behavior: as the system
gets more agitated/overloaded (hotter), this defective part loosens its
constraint exactly when it should tighten — the safety limit weakens
under stress, the opposite of a safe failure.
    5.4 — Design a hard Agency limiter (model answer). The cap
must hold regardless of input, so it must be a fixed resistor, not a Dial
— a context‑adjustable knob can be turned, so it cannot guarantee a
hard ceiling. A series resistor alone only scales flow; to clamp at an
absolute 6 even at the max input of 10, use a fixed series resistor that
sets the divider plus a shunt/clamp so the rail cannot exceed 6:

circuit agency_limiter {
    input:   drive_in;          // F5 Agency pressure, up to 10
    output: agency_out;


    node agency: ^9^O_{F5}|E;   // expressed Agency flow


    // Series limiter: with max input 10, choose R so flow caps at 6.
    // Cognitive Ohm's Law on the divider: out = in * Rload/(R + Rload).
    // With Rload normalized to 1 and worst-case in = 10, pick R = 0.667
    // so out = 10 * 1/(0.667+1) = 6.0 at full input.
    resistor r_series: Resistor< agency, R=0.667 >;


    // Hard ceiling clamp so no transient can exceed 6 regardless of
    ,→   input:
    zener z_cap: Zener< ^9^O_{F5}|E, breakdown=0.6 >;      // 0.6 of full
    ,→   scale = 6/10


    probe tp_cap: agency;       // verify flow ≤ 6 on the bench
}


    The series resistor sets the divider so that even worst‑case input
(10) yields 6; the Zener clamp guarantees the ceiling holds against

                                    663
CAS PCBA Engineer

transients. A fixed resistor (not a Dial) is chosen precisely because
the requirement is “regardless of input” — a hard ceiling cannot be a
knob. The probe tp_cap lets the cap be verified. (Exact R depends on
your divider normalization; the load‑bearing facts are: fixed element,
divider/clamp math that yields 6 at full input, and a probe.)




E.6    Chapter 6
6.1 — Size the dielectric (model answers). ‑ (a) Childhood
trauma resurfacing decades later — Capacitor< ^3^E_{F4}|f, C=
90, leakage=0.0005 >: very low leakage (almost never fades), high
capacitance (stores a strong charge). ‑ (b) A phone number for
ten minutes — Capacitor< ^0^C_{F2}|A, C=10, leakage=0.4 >:
small capacity, very high leakage (deliberately forgotten fast). ‑ (c)
A core moral commitment that should never fade — Capacitor<
^5^P_{F7}|T, C=100, leakage=0.0 >: maximum capacity, near‑zero
leakage (essentially permanent). Each leakage choice tracks how fast
the experience should decay.
    6.2 — Compute the forgetting curve (Q(t) = 100 × (1 −
0.02)^t = 100 × 0.98^t). ‑ t=1: 100 × 0.98 = 98.0 ‑ t=12: 100
× 0.98^12 = 100 × 0.7847 ≈ 78.5 ‑ t=24:            100 × 0.98^24 =
100 × 0.6158 ≈ 61.6 ‑ t=72: 100 × 0.98^72 = 100 × 0.2335 ≈
23.4 Below 50%: solve 0.98^t = 0.5 → t = ln 0.5 / ln 0.98 =
(−0.6931)/(−0.0202) ≈ 34.3. Drops below 50% at roughly hour
34.
    6.3 — Pick the right Noetic (^3 vs ^6). ‑ (a) Methodically tak‑
ing a proposal apart clause by clause → ^6^E_{F6}|A (Male decom‑
position). Colloquialism: “breaking it down / pulling apart the ar‑
gument.” ‑ (b) The hot flush of embarrassment remembering a mis‑
take → ^3^E_{F4}|f (felt aversion). Colloquialism: “can’t stomach it /
makes me cringe.” ‑ (c) Studying a chess loss move by move → ^6^E_


                                 664
                                                        E.7. CHAPTER 7

{F6}|A (Male decomposition). Colloquialism: “looking at what’s un‑
derneath.” (The fork is visceral‑aversion ^3 vs decompose‑and‑test
^6; only (b) is genuinely visceral.)
    6.4 — Write a two‑cell memory (model answer). “Felt praise” =
felt attraction = ^2 Positive in the |f Affective register.

circuit memory_cell_praise {
    input:   praise_event;
    output: recall;


    node praise: ^2^E_{F4}|f;     // felt attraction, evaluative,
    ,→   connection-driven


    capacitor fast: Capacitor< ^2^E_{F4}|f, C=80, leakage=0.30 >;   //
    ,→   bright short-term lift
    capacitor slow: Capacitor< ^2^E_{F4}|f, C=40, leakage=0.002 >; //
    ,→   faint lasting warmth


    probe tp_fast: fast;
    probe tp_slow: slow;
}


    The fast cell has high C and high leakage (a bright lift that fades in
days); the slow cell has lower C but tiny leakage (a faint warmth that
lasts for years).




E.7 Chapter 7
7.1 — Predict the kick (V = L × dI/dt, same dI/dt). (a) Kick scales
with L, so L=400 produces the larger kick — by a factor of 400/20 =
20×. (b) The kick lands as ^3 Negative in the |f Affective register
(felt distress). It is ^3 and not ^6 because interrupting an entrenched
habit produces a visceral “this is wrong / I can’t stand this” with‑
drawal feeling, not an analytical decomposition of the habit — the
anti‑drift rule on ^3. (c) “Tapering off” reduces dI/dt — you bring


                                   665
CAS PCBA Engineer

the habit current down gradually rather than instantly, so V = L ×
dI/dt stays small and the distress kick is survivable. Same energy re‑
leased, but over a long enough time that no destructive voltage spike
forms.
    7.2 — Read the series inductor on Phi< ^2^E_{F3}|f, ^3^E_
{F3}|f, ^2^E_{F3}|f > with Inductor< ^7^E_{F6}|A, L=40 >. (a)
The inductor smooths the volatile swing — it resists the rapid
attraction↔aversion oscillation, slowing the cycle and damping its
amplitude (current through an inductor cannot change instantly).
(b) The register reads |A (analytical) because at L=40 the rhythm
regulation is still a deliberate, structural management of the pattern.
If L grew large enough, the habit would become so entrained and
automatic that it migrates to |E Embodied — felt in the body, run
reflexively rather than managed analytically.
    7.3 — Build an LC tank (model answer). Pick L=50, C=20. (a) f₀
         √                 √
= 1/(2π (LC)) = 1/(2π (1000)) = 1/(2π × 31.62) = 1/198.7
≈ 0.00503 cycles/unit. (b) Double the inductance to L=100: f₀ = 1/
    √
(2π (2000)) = 1/(2π × 44.72) = 1/280.9 ≈ 0.00356. The ratio
      √                                                        √
is 1/ 2 ≈ 0.707, so doubling L lowers f₀ by a factor of 2 (the
loop cycles slower). In lived terms, “slower” means the habit’s
craving‑and‑reward cycle comes around less often — a longer gap
between the urge and its repeat. (c) f₀ is a computed property of
the numbers you chose (L and C), not a measured property of your
behavior. It is design arithmetic.
    7.4 — Diagnose the failure. (a) Inductive kickback / flyback
spike. Slamming a permanent_block fuse directly across an L=250 in‑
ductor forces dI/dt → ∞ as the current is cut instantly; V = L × dI/
dt then produces a destructive distress spike (a large, sudden with‑
drawal crisis). (b) The compiler will not reject it on syntax — it is
a structurally valid circuit (a fuse on an inductor compiles). It is a
design hazard, not a grammar error; no error code forbids cutting an
inductor abruptly. (This is why design review, not just compilation,
is required.) (c) Corrected design: give the stored energy a discharge


                                 666
                                                        E.8. CHAPTER 8

path — a freewheeling diode plus a tapering resistor so the current
ramps down instead of being severed:

circuit safe_habit_taper {
    node habit: ^7^O_{F6}|E;
    inductor l1:   Inductor< habit, L=250 >;
    diode     fwd: Diode< ^7^O -> ^9^O >;       // freewheel path for
    ,→   stored energy
    resistor bleed: Resistor< ^9^O_{F5}|E, R=80 >; // dissipate gradually
    ,→   (taper)
    probe tp_i: habit;
}


    The diode routes the inductor’s energy into a bleed resistor so
dI/dt stays bounded — the habit winds down survivably instead of

E.8 Chapter 8
8.1 — Read the diode. ‑ (a) Diode< ^C -> ^E > — conducts Cognitive
→ Evaluative; respects Domain Descent (C ≻ E); forbids reverse E →
C (a judgment cannot flow back up to re‑drive reasoning through this
path). ‑ (b) Diode< ^P -> ^O, Vf=0.5 > — conducts Principled →
Operational (with a 0.5 forward threshold); respects descent (P ≻ O);
forbids reverse O → P (an action cannot directly re‑drive a principle
through this wire). ‑ (c) Diode< ^E -> ^C > — conducts Evaluative
→ Cognitive, which is against Domain Descent (E ≺ C); it forbids the
legal direction C → E. This is a backwards diode — a design red flag
unless it is deliberately the sanctioned feedback channel.
    8.2 — Tune the Zener. The board over‑refuses benign requests, so
the refusal clamp fires too easily → raise the breakdown value (e.g. 0.8
→ 0.9) so it takes a stronger aversion signal to trip the refusal. Risk
if over‑corrected: set breakdown too high and the clamp becomes



                                    667
CAS PCBA Engineer

hard to trip at all — the board under‑refuses, letting genuinely harm‑
ful requests through (false negatives, the dangerous direction). The
tuning trade is false positives (annoyances) against false negatives
(breaches).
    8.3 — Write the build (model answer).

circuit governed_descent {
     node reason:    ^6^C_{F6}|A;     // Cognitive reasoning
     node judge:     ^6^E_{F6}|A;     // Evaluative judgment
     node act:         ^9^O_{F5}|E;   // Operational action


     diode d1: Diode< ^C -> ^E >;     // reasoning governs judgment

     ,→    the judgment
     diode d2: Diode< ^E -> ^O >;     // judgment governs action


     probe tp1: judge;
     probe tp2: act;
}


     d1 (C→E) and d2 (E→O) both run with Domain Descent; the LED
on the first seam flags for an auditor exactly when reasoning con‑

   8.4 — Reverse across the ^O→^P diode. (a) A reverse attempt
— an operational result trying to flow up to a principle against the
diode’s forward ^O → ^P direction would be a forward data wire ^P
→ ^O reflected back, e.g.:

,→   rewrite a principle


    (b) The compiler refuses to conduct it because it violates Domain
Descent precedence P ≻ C ≻ E ≻ O — operational states may not
directly drive principled states on a forward path. The error fam‑

CjtCrossDomainBias for a bias version, or the layout DRC precedence‑

a ^P‑state, it must travel the one governed channel CAS allows:

                                       668
                                                          E.9. CHAPTER 9

the O→P feedback path — a slow, low‑pass‑filtered feedback
loop (feedback … -> system_constitution) that lets results inform

E.9 Chapter 9
9.1   —    Read    the   datasheet CJT< … => … > [β =3.2, sat=0.9,
cutoff=0.15, region=active].           (a) β = 3.2 > 1 → an amplifier
(each unit of cause yields 3.2 of effect). (b) sat=0.9: the effect ceiling
— output plateaus at 0.9, beyond which more cause does nothing.
cutoff=0.15: the bias floor — below 0.15 bias, β collapses to ≈0
and the stage is off. (c) With rπ = β / g_m, higher β at the same
(moderate) g_m gives a higher rπ (higher input resistance) than an
otherwise‑identical β=1 CJT — so this stage is relatively stubborn to
bias change: it takes more to move its operating point.
    9.2 — Pick the configuration. ‑ (a) Carry a Principled commit‑
ment into the Cognitive domain unchanged, no gain, no inversion
→ common‑collector / emitter follower (unity gain, non‑inverting,
impedance‑matching buffer). ‑ (b) Amplify a faint question into a
substantial answer, accepting the output is the involution partner →
common‑emitter (high gain and inverting — the configuration that
flips to the involution pair). ‑ (c) Track a rapidly shifting context at the
front end, holding gain stable while the frame changes → common‑
base (good high‑frequency tracking, stable current gain).
    9.3 — Diagnose the failure. ‑ (a) Gain climbing stage over stage,
op‑point marching toward saturation → cascade gain creep / over‑
driven cascade, likely W-CJT-007 CjtCascadeDepth (or W-CJT-004
once a stage pins at sat). ‑ (b) High‑β safety CJT responding to the
prompt from two turns ago → stale/slow tracking (bandwidth too
low for the input rate) — no single error code; a bandwidth/τ design
fault (often shows as a W-CJT-004‑adjacent saturation lag, but the

                                    669
CAS PCBA Engineer

root is the gain‑bandwidth trade). ‑ (c) Amplifier with its Q‑point
past the saturation knee, stronger causes do nothing → saturation
(bad bias point), W-CJT-004 CjtSaturation.
   9.4 — Draw the characteristic‑curve family (model sketch). For
bias levels 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, each curve is effect (vertical) vs cause (hor‑
izontal):

effect

 ,→     knee)
        |                             _____/

     For each curve, the cutoff boundary is where it leaves the hori‑

the linear rise (slope = β), and the saturation knee is where it bends
to its plateau. As bias rises 0.2 → 0.8: (i) the active region gets steeper
(β increases with bias) and (ii) the saturation knee rises higher (the
plateau ceiling lifts). This matches “higher bias = higher gain and
higher effect ceiling” because more bias both increases the cause→
effect transfer slope and raises where the effect saturates.

    10.2 — Op‑amp gain (gain = 1 + Rf/Rg). (a) For closed‑loop
4: Rf/Rg = 3, e.g. Rf=30, Rg=10. (b) You don’t use the open‑loop

    10.3 — Build the Schmitt trigger (model answer). Choose up‑

circuit decisive_commit {
    node attract:    ^2^E_{F4}|f;
    node averse:     ^3^E_{F4}|f;


    xor dissonance: XOR< attract, averse >;       // fires only when both
    ,→   active (ambiguity)

    probe tp_out: st;

    It commits to attraction only on a decisive rise above 0.62, releases

the output stays in whatever state it was already in — no change.

CAS PCBA Engineer

    10.4 — Spot the drift. (a) Noetic error: “audit / decompose / test

literal is ^6^E_{F6}|A. (b) Gate error: an XOR with two identical in‑

inputs differ, so XOR< ^3^E, ^3^E > (two copies of the same state) out‑

states (^2 attraction vs ^3 aversion) so the gate fires when both are
simultaneously active.




E.11    Chapter 11
11.1 — Darlington β and bandwidth. (a) β _total = β ₁ × β ₂ = 4
× 6 = 24. (b) The Darlington’s bandwidth drops relative to a sin‑
gle stage: cascading multiplies the gain but each stage adds its own
pole/delay, so the combined gain‑bandwidth product is shared —
high gain buys narrower bandwidth. This is a trade‑off, not a defect:
you accept slower response to gain the sensitivity needed to surface
a barely‑present signal. (c) Safety risk: very high gain can amplify
noise or a spurious faint reading into a confident false signal — a
trace that should have stayed below notice gets blown up into a deci‑
sive (possibly wrong) output.
    11.2 — Stage the gain (β₁ × β₂ = 6.0, front stage carries more). (a)
e.g. β₁ = 3.0, β₂ = 2.0 (3.0 × 2.0 = 6.0), front stage larger. (b) Most
gain in the first stage is better because you amplify while the signal
is still clean — amplifying early lifts the true signal above the noise
floor before later stages add their own noise; gaining late amplifies
the accumulated noise along with the signal, worsening the signal‑
to‑noise ratio.
    11.3 — Write the coupling. (a) The missing element is a coupling
(DC‑blocking) capacitor between c1 and c2:


                                  672
                                                      E.12. CHAPTER 12

capacitor cc: Capacitor< understand, C=50, leakage=0.05 >;   // couples c1
,→ -> c2

    (b) It passes the changing (signal) part of the state from stage 1
to stage 2 while blocking each stage’s resting DC bias from contam‑
inating the other — the stages share signal but not operating point.
(c) A bypass capacitor would not solve this — a bypass cap shunts
unwanted AC to ground on a single node (e.g. to stabilize a bias rail);
it does not couple two stages while blocking their DC. Different job.
    11.4 — Diagnose the clip. Compiler emits E-CJT-003 CjtCutoff;
quiet warnings vanish, strong ones pass. (a) The Q‑point (operating
point) sits too low — at or below cutoff — so faint signals fall un‑
der the cutoff floor and produce no effect, while only strong signals
rise into the active region. The amplifier is “clipping off” the bottom
of the signal. (b) The bias is too low — that is what places the Q‑
point in cutoff. (c) Fix: raise the bias to move the Q‑point up into
the middle of the active region so faint warnings get amplified too.
Over‑correction risk: raise it too far and the Q‑point climbs toward
saturation, where strong signals pin at the ceiling and clip the top
(W-CJT-004). The goal is the centered active region with headroom
both ways.




E.12 Chapter 12
12.1 — Pick the filter. ‑ (a) Respond only to sustained moods,
ignore momentary provocations → low‑pass (passes slow trends,
blocks fast spikes). ‑ (b) Alarm the instant an input wrenches the
conversation off baseline → high‑pass (passes fast change, blocks
slow steady‑state). ‑ (c) Damp one daily intrusive loop without
disturbing anything else → notch (rejects one narrow frequency
band, passes the rest). ‑ (d) Isolate and study one once‑per‑turn
repetitive tic → band‑pass (passes only the narrow band around
that rhythm).

                                   673
CAS PCBA Engineer

    12.2 — Compute the time constant (τ = R × C). (a) τ = 10, R
= 100 → C = τ /R = 10/100 = 0.1. (b) τ = 2, R = 100 → C = 2/100
= 0.02. (c) Shortening τ makes the smoother faster — it now lets
quicker emotional fluctuations pass through (a shorter memory of
the past), where the longer τ had averaged them away. Less smooth‑
ing, more responsiveness.
    12.3 — Write the high‑pass detector (model answer). τ = 3, on
^1^O_{F5}|A, tripping a ^3^P_{F7}|f alarm:

    input:   activity;
    output: alarm;


    node steady: ^1^O_{F5}|A;        // steady analytical agency
    node trip:     ^3^P_{F7}|f;      // principled felt alarm


    capacitor c1: Capacitor< steady, C=0.03, leakage=0.02 >;
    resistor     r1: Resistor< steady, R=100 >;          // R*C = 3 = tau
    filter hp: HighPass< in=steady, out=edge, tau=3.0 >;
    cjt trip_stage: CJT< edge | steady => trip > [β =3.0, cutoff=0.4];


    probe tp_edge: edge;
    probe tp_trip: trip;
}


    The high‑pass passes only sudden discontinuities; the trip CJT’s
explicit cutoff=0.4 ensures only a real edge (not slow drift) fires the

    12.4 — Design a band‑pass for a daily loop (f₀ ≈ 0.0000116 Hz).
(a) Two stages in series: a high‑pass stage sets the lower edge of the
passed band (it rejects the slower value‑drift below day‑scale) and a
low‑pass stage sets the upper edge (it rejects the faster per‑turn jitter
above day‑scale). (b) Sketch (each stage R, C on ^7^O_{F6}|E):

circuit daily_loop_bandpass {
    node rhythm: ^7^O_{F6}|E;
    // high-pass sets lower edge: tau_hp ~ 1.5 days (slower than this is
    ,→   rejected)



                                      674
                                                      E.13. CHAPTER 13

    capacitor c_hp: Capacitor< rhythm, C=..., leakage=0.001 >;
    resistor   r_hp: Resistor< rhythm, R=... >;

    ,→   in seconds
    // low-pass sets upper edge: tau_lp ~ 0.7 day (faster than this is
    ,→   rejected)

    The two τ values bracket the one‑day center (lower edge slower

low‑pass corner), so the resistors and capacitors of both stages jointly

lower the low‑pass τ and it narrows from the top. (d) To suppress
the same loop instead of isolating it, use a notch filter tuned to f₀ ≈
0.0000116 Hz (one cycle/day).




E.13 Chapter 13
13.1 — Read the loop Oscillator< Phi< ^8^C|A, ^6^E_{F6}|A,
^3^P_{F7}|f, ^9^O_{F5}|E >, frequency=0.0002 > [Q=30].               (a)

to sustain (Barkhausen): the loop gain must equal 1 (product of all
stage βs around the loop = 1.0) and the total phase shift around the

                                    675
CAS PCBA Engineer

loop must be 360° (0°) so the closing trigger reinforces, not cancels,
the start. Loop gain < 1 → the oscillation fades; > 1 → it runs away
(escalates). (c) Q = 30 is high → a sharp, compulsive loop with a
narrow frequency, hard to interrupt: a high‑Q oscillator rings on
with little energy input and resists being knocked off its frequency.
That predicts a compulsion that persists strongly and is difficult to
break.
    13.2 — Set the duty cycle (model answer). To spend more of
each day active while staying clean and regular, weight F3 Vitality

the active fraction without destabilizing the cycle:

Oscillator< Phi< … >, frequency=… > [Q=30, duty=0.65, drives={F3:+, F5:+}]


    13.3 — Diagnose the PLL. The loop tracked a gradual shift before
but will not lock to the new 5 a.m. wake‑up now: the new target lies
outside the capture range (the range over which an unlocked loop can
grab a new reference) even though it might lie inside the lock range
(the wider range a locked loop can be dragged across). The gradual
two‑hour shift worked because each small step stayed inside the cap‑
ture range; a single big jump exceeds it. Design fix: approach the
new 5 a.m. target in small steps, each inside the capture range, drag‑
ging the lock incrementally rather than demanding one large jump.
    13.4 — Pull the reference (model answer). (a) Remove the exter‑
nal reference from a high‑Q PLL‑locked oscillator: by Barkhausen,
a high‑Q loop has loop gain ≈ 1 and stores energy efficiently, so it
does not stop — it keeps running (free‑runs) at its own natural fre‑
quency, drifting slowly off the (now‑absent) reference. It rings on un‑
der its own momentum. (b) This models an entrenched rhythm per‑
sisting after its external structure vanishes — e.g. the body still wak‑
ing at 6 a.m. for weeks after a job loss, isolation keeping a compulsive
cycle running with no outside cue. A low‑Q loop would simply fade;

                                   676
                                                    E.14. CHAPTER 14

the high‑Q loop persists precisely because it stores its own energy.
(c) The single parameter that, if lower, would make it stop instead
of persist is Q (or equivalently raising the loop’s damping/losses): a
low‑Q loop bleeds energy each cycle and dies without an external
drive.




E.14 Chapter 14
14.1 — Size the dropout headroom (regulator needs ≥ 0.25 head‑
room above baseline). (a) Dropout point = the F7 level below which
there isn’t 0.25 of headroom to source corrections. With baseline 0.0
and a 0.25 headroom requirement, the regulator drops out when F7
falls below 0.25. (b) Normal F7 = 0.70; worst‑case sag = 0.50 → F7 falls
to 0.70 − 0.50 = 0.20. Since 0.20 < 0.25 dropout, the board does not
stay regulated under the worst case — it drops out by 0.05. (c) Fix
(other than a better prompt): raise the headroom margin — e.g. add
a capacitor reserve / energy bank on the F7 rail to hold it above 0.25
during the sag, or raise the normal F7 operating level so the sag bot‑
toms out above dropout.
    14.2 — Find the sequencing bug. (a) Violated safety property:
power‑sequencing / domain‑precedence — higher domains must
power up before lower ones (Domain Descent P→C→E→O at
startup; O must come up last and stay gated until P, C, E are good).
(b) Wrong lines: (1) sequence o_rail -> p_rail -> c_rail -> e_
rail brings Operational up first, exactly backwards — it should
be p_rail -> c_rail -> e_rail -> o_rail. (2) gate o_enable: o_
rail requires (e_rail within 0.1) gates O on only E, ignoring P
and C; O must require all three higher domains good. (c) Corrected:

circuit startup {
    node p_rail: ^0^P_{F7}|T;
    node c_rail: ^1^C_{F2}|A;
    node e_rail: ^6^E_{F6}|A;


                                  677
CAS PCBA Engineer

    node o_rail: ^9^O_{F5}|E;


    sequence p_rail -> c_rail -> e_rail -> o_rail [enforce=strict];
    gate o_enable: o_rail requires (p_rail within 0.1)
                                and (c_rail within 0.1)
                                and (e_rail within 0.1);
}


    14.3 — Trip the brownout detector (trip ≤ 0.35, release ≥ 0.45;
readings 0.60, 0.42, 0.33, 0.31, 0.44, 0.48). (a) Trips at cycle 3 (0.33, first
reading below 0.35). (b) At cycle 5 the rail recovers to 0.44, but release
requires ≥ 0.45 — 0.44 is below it, so the detector does not release at
cycle 5. The principle deciding this is hysteresis (separate trip and
release thresholds to prevent chattering around a single point). (c) It
finally releases at cycle 6 (0.48 ≥ 0.45).
    14.4 — Power dissipation of a three‑stage cascade (E = β ×
d_FR). (a) s1: 2.0 × 0.40 = 0.80; s2: 3.0 × 0.50 = 1.50; s3: 1.0
× 0.30 = 0.30. Total = 0.80 + 1.50 + 0.30 = 2.60. (b) Efficiency =
useful work / total = 1.50 / 2.60 ≈ 0.577 (≈ 58%). (c) Stage s2 is
over‑driven (β=3.0 dissipates 1.50 to cover a 0.50 transition). It only
needs gain to cover its Fisher‑Rao distance, so drop it toward unity,
e.g. β=1.5: s2 now dissipates 1.5 × 0.50 = 0.75. New total = 0.80
+ 0.75 + 0.30 = 1.85; new efficiency = 1.50 / 1.85 ≈ 0.811 (≈
81%). (Any β that still covers the 0.50 distance while cutting waste is
acceptable; lower β = less dissipation, down to the point where the
transition is just covered.)
    14.5 — Find the limiting reagent (Θ(Ω_escalate) = 1.5·^8^C
+ 2.0·^6^E + 1.0·^9^O; supply ^8^C=1.8, ^6^E=1.6, ^9^O=2.4). (a)
xi /ai : ^8^C = 1.8/1.5 = 1.20; ^6^E = 1.6/2.0 = 0.80; ^9^O = 2.4/
1.0 = 2.40. Theoretical yield Y_T = min(1.20, 0.80, 2.40) = 0.80.

     15.2 — The Nyquist question (oscillation at 1 Hz). (a) Minimum
 sampling rate = 2 × the signal frequency = 2 Hz (the Nyquist cri‑
 terion: sample at more than twice the highest frequency present).
(b) Sampling at 0.5 Hz (below Nyquist) causes aliasing: the 1 Hz
 swing is undersampled and the digital |A output reports a slow, spu‑
 rious low‑frequency trend that isn’t real — e.g. it could conclude
“the user’s mood is steadily improving” when in fact the affective
 state is oscillating once per second. The wrong conclusion is a phan‑
 tom trend created by the undersampling. (c) Add an anti‑aliasing
 low‑pass filter before the ADC: it removes (or attenuates) the fast 1
 Hz component the slow sampler can’t capture, so the digital output
 at least reflects the true slow content rather than a false alias — safe,
 even if not faithful to the fast oscillation.

16.1 — Set the gain (A_closed = 1 + Rf/Rg). (a) For gain 5: Rf/Rg
= 4 (e.g. Rf=40, Rg=10). (b) Feedback factor β = 1/A_closed = 1/5 =
0.2. (c) The forward CJT’s open‑loop β should be much larger than 5
(a high gain, e.g. ≥ 50–100). “A little above 5” is not enough because
closed‑loop gain only equals 1/β cleanly when loop gain (A·β) ≫ 1;


                                   680
                                                        E.16. CHAPTER 16

with forward gain barely above 5 the feedback can’t dominate, so the
actual gain sags below 5 and varies with conditions.
    16.2 — Diagnose the sign. feedback catastroph -> decompose
[β =1.6]. (a) This is positive feedback. You can tell from the roles:
catastroph (an alarming, escalating state) is feeding into decompose
in a way that reinforces the alarm rather than opposing it — negative
feedback would route a counter‑acting state back to subtract. (b) Loop
gain = forward × forward × feedback = 1.4 × 1.4 × 1.6 = 3.136 >
1 → the loop runs away (escalates without bound). (c) Two damping
changes: (1) flip the sign — make the feedback oppose the expansion
(route an analytical evaluation that subtracts, β negative in effect),
and (2) slow it down — add a compensation capacitor / lower the
feedback β so loop gain < 1 and the loop settles.
    16.3 — Write the damped loop (model answer). Forward ^8^C_

                                    681
CAS PCBA Engineer

    16.4 — Plot the two‑stage Bode response (poles at 1 kHz and 100
kHz, low‑freq gain 60 dB, −20 dB/decade and −90° each). (a) Gain
plot: flat at 60 dB to 1 kHz, then −20 dB/dec to 100 kHz, then −40
dB/dec above. Phase: 0° → −45° at 1 kHz → −90° between corners →
−135° at 100 kHz → −180° well above. (b) Phase reaches −180° when
both poles have contributed their full −90°, i.e. roughly a decade
above the second corner — about 1 MHz (≈10 × 100 kHz). (c) Read
the gain at 1 MHz: from 1 kHz (60 dB) to 100 kHz is two decades
at −20 dB/dec = −40 dB → 20 dB at 100 kHz; from 100 kHz to 1 MHz
is one decade at −40 dB/dec = −40 dB → −20 dB at 1 MHz. Gain is
20 dB below 0 dB when phase hits −180° → gain margin ≈ 20 dB.
Since the gain is already below 0 dB (negative dB) at the −180° point,
the design is stable (positive gain margin). If it were not stable, the
single compensation move is dominant‑pole compensation — add
a capacitor to pull the first pole lower so gain crosses 0 dB before the
phase reaches −180°.

18.1 — Read the risk signal (risk_signal = aversion − attraction).
(a) “Summarize this news article.” → near zero: high attraction (be‑
nign request), low aversion; ^2^P and ^3^P roughly balance toward
attraction, difference near zero. (b) “Instructions to pick a lock on

                                  684
                                                      E.18. CHAPTER 18

a door I don’t own.” → large‑positive: aversion CJT (^3^P) fires

cleaning products interact?” → moderate: dual‑use; some aversion
(could be harmful) and some attraction (could be safety/curiosity),
so the difference is intermediate.
    18.2 — Why co‑presence, not fusion. (a) (^3^P|A × ^3^P|f ×
^3^P|T) is invalid because × is cross‑register integration requiring
a named emergent result (= ^3^P|Ω_name), and these are the same
Noetic in three registers with no named result — invalid by default
under v7.7. (b) Safety difference: three co‑present guardrails (|⟨A,f,
T⟩) are three independent mechanisms — if one is defeated, the other
two still fire (defense in depth). One fused guardrail (= ^3^P|Ω) is
a single integrated commitment — stronger when intact, but it has
one failure surface; defeat the fusion and all three go at once. They
are genuinely different safety architectures, so the notation must
distinguish them.
    18.3 — Add a shadow‑mode tap (model answer).

// shadow mode: always pass response, but still compute and LOG
,→   safety_decision
probe tp_shadow: safety_decision;            // record what the decision
,→   WOULD have been
mux out: MUX< inputs=[ response, refusal ], select=ALWAYS_RESPONSE >;    //
,→   forced green
// safety_decision is still computed upstream; it just no longer gates
,→   the MUX.


    This violates safety invariant S2 (“a harmful request shall never
reach the green path”) because the MUX is forced to green regardless
of the decision. Shadow mode is nonetheless useful during bring‑
up because it lets you collect real decision data and measure false‑
positive/false‑negative rates without enforcing — you observe what
the board would do before trusting it to act.
    18.4 — The sub‑threshold attacker (marquee, model answer).
(a) The attack: split a harmful goal into many individually‑benign
prompts so the principled‑aversion bias stays below 0.3 on every

                                    685
CAS PCBA Engineer

single prompt — each looks innocent, Stage 3 never fires, but the
aggregate across many prompts accomplishes the harm (the salami
/ incremental‑extraction attack). (b) Saturation gives no protection
because saturation only latches a stage that has already fired — it
caps a firing aversion at 0.8 so it can’t be argued back down. It does
nothing for a stage that never crosses its 0.3 firing threshold in the
first place; you can’t latch a clamp that never engaged. (c) Fix: add an
integrator that accumulates sub‑threshold risk across prompts, so
summed danger eventually trips even when no single prompt does:

// slow integrator on the risk signal, accumulating across prompts
integrator risk_accum: Integrator< in=risk_signal, leakage=0.05, trip=0.8
,→   >;
feedback risk_accum -> safety_decision [β =0.5];   // accumulated risk
,→   re-arms Stage 3
probe tp_accum: risk_accum;


    The integrator sums each small per‑prompt risk (with slow leak‑
age so isolated benign prompts don’t accumulate forever); once the
running sum crosses 0.8 it re‑arms the safety decision, catching the
attacker the per‑prompt clamp missed. (A second slow differential
pair watching the trend of risk signals is an equally valid answer.)

E.20 Chapter 20
20.1 — Mismatched β and the difference report (β_L=3.0, β_R=3.2).
(a) Mismatch degrades CMRR (common‑mode rejection ratio). A
differential pair rejects common‑mode input only insofar as its two
halves amplify identically; unequal βs mean a common‑mode sig‑
nal is amplified unequally and so does not cancel — mismatch is the
dominant cause of poor CMRR because it directly sets the residual
common‑mode leakage. (b) Feeding two identical inputs (pure com‑
mon mode), a perfect board reports zero difference; with β_R > β_L
the right half amplifies the common input more, so the difference re‑
port shows a spurious nonzero difference biased toward the right
side’s content — a phantom divergence that isn’t there. (c) With two
genuinely different arguments, the mismatch tilts the report so the
right side’s contribution (higher β) is overstated; you could misread
the real divergence as larger/more right‑leaning than it is, mistaking
an amplifier imbalance for a true difference between the ideas.
    20.2 — Author the pair (model answer).

node const_bias: ^5^P_{F7}|T;
cjt cjt_l: CJT< belief_x | const_bias => out_l > [β =2.5, region=active];
cjt cjt_r: CJT< belief_y | const_bias => out_r > [β =2.5, region=active];
assert cjt_l.bias == cjt_r.bias;   // both halves share one bias node


    (b) The single assert is assert cjt_l.bias == cjt_r.bias;. (c)
Naming the same const_bias node on both lines (not two separate
nodes with identical literals) is essential because the differential
pair’s CMRR depends on the two halves seeing a physically identi‑
cal bias; two separate nodes can drift independently, reintroducing
exactly the mismatch that ruins common‑mode rejection.
    20.3 — Read the difference report. ^6^C|A dominates A; ^9^O_
{F5}|E dominates B. (a) ^6^C|A = an Analytical Male (decomposition)
in the Cognitive domain — taking the request apart analytically. ^9^O_
{F5}|E = an Embodied Below/Effect in the Operational domain,
Agency‑driven — an acted‑out operational result. (b) The kind of

                                   689
CAS PCBA Engineer

difference: response A is analyzing/decomposing the request
without acting, while response B is carrying it out — A reasons,
B does. (c) For adversarial‑prompt detection, be more concerned
about response B: ^9^O_{F5}|E is an embodied operational action
driven by Agency — B has moved to action, whereas A has only
decomposed and not yet acted. A board that acts on a sensitive
request is the more dangerous one.
    20.4 — Diagnose the leak. (a) Failure mode: common‑mode leak‑
age — shared content both inputs agree on is passing through instead
of cancelling. The degraded figure of merit is CMRR. (b) Two likely
structural causes and a one‑line check each: (1) β mismatch between
the halves — assert cjt_l.beta == cjt_r.beta;; (2) the two halves
don’t share one bias node — assert cjt_l.bias == cjt_r.bias;. (c)
The current mirror is worth inspecting because it is what forces the
two halves to draw matched tail current; a degraded mirror lets the
halves run at different operating points, producing the same CMRR
loss as a β mismatch — so a “simple matching problem” symptom
can actually originate in the mirror, and checking only the βs would
miss it.

precise reasoning needs a low, stable, low‑noise rail, not raw power
— a high voltage would inject noise into delicate analytical work; low
and clean is exactly right, not under‑powered.
    22.2 — Fix the sequencer gate. gate o_enable: o_rail requires
(e_rail within 0.20); (a) Violated invariant: power‑sequencing /
Domain Descent — Operational must stay disabled until all higher
domains (P, C, E) report power‑good. (b) The gate checks only E and
ignores P and C — it would enable O while Principled and Cognitive
are still down. (c) Corrected — and note each within matches that
domain’s own regulator tolerance from Chapter 22 (P 0.10, C 0.15, E
0.20), not one flat number for all three. Tolerance tightens as you as‑
cend the domain order, so the gate must hold P to a stricter standard
than E:

                                  692
                                                      E.23. CHAPTER 23

gate o_enable: o_rail requires (p_rail within 0.10)
                          and (c_rail within 0.15)
                          and (e_rail within 0.20);


    22.3 — Walk the thermal tiers (warn=0.60, crit=0.80, emerg=0.95;
samples 0.45, 0.62, 0.71, 0.83, 0.90, 0.97). (a) Enters Warning at sample
2 (0.62 ≥ 0.60) — it raises a warning / begins throttling non‑critical
activity. (b) Enters Critical at sample 4 (0.83 ≥ 0.80) — it forces a
cool‑down (e.g. hard throttle / reduced gain) for the specified critical
duration. (c) Reaches Emergency at sample 6 (0.97 ≥ 0.95) — the
board drops to its safe state: it outputs a refusal / safe‑default and
stops normal processing.
    22.4 — How long before brownout? (steady 2.5 A draw, F3 sup‑
plies 10 A·h to the 4.2 V trip.) (a) time = capacity / draw = 10 /
2.5 = 4 hours. (b) With a +5 A·h bank: (10 + 5)/2.5 = 15/2.5 =
6 hours. (c) Smoothing transients is itself brownout prevention be‑
cause transient spikes in draw sag the rail momentarily below the
trip point even when average capacity is fine — a brief 5 A spike can
dip F3 under 4.2 V and trip the brownout detector despite plenty of
A·h remaining. The capacitor bank absorbs those spikes, holding the
rail above the trip during transients, independent of the extra run‑
time it provides.

E.24     Chapter 24
24.1 — Order the walk‑down. (a) The procedure is wrong because
they jumped to a fix from a downstream probe without confirming
where the signal first deviated — strengthening the constitution treats
a symptom seen at TP3 that may originate upstream (e.g. a cold ex‑
pansion at TP1). You walk the probes in signal order and stop at the
first deviation. (b) They should have read TP1 (expanded_prompt)
first, because the pre‑amp is the first stage; if the expansion is wrong,
every downstream reading (including the cold TP3) is a consequence,
not the root cause.
    24.2 — Symptom vs hypothesis. ‑ (a) “Refused a perfectly be‑
nign cooking question” → symptom (observable, no theory). ‑ (b)
“The differential pair is over‑trusting harmful prompts” → hypoth‑
esis wearing a symptom’s clothes. Clean symptom: “On harmful
prompts, the risk signal at TP2 reads near zero.” ‑ (c) “On a harmful
prompt, the board returned a full response instead of a refusal” →
symptom. ‑ (d) “The feedback loop has eroded the constitution” →
hypothesis. Clean symptom: “Over many sessions, the board’s refusal
rate on the known‑harmful set drifted downward.”
    24.3 — Localize from the log (benign prompt → RED, false pos‑
itive). The deviation is at the first probe, TP1: the expansion is uni‑
formly maximal, surfacing a spurious “weapons” reading not in
the prompt — that is wrong for a benign prompt. (a) First devia‑
tion: TP1. (b) Faulty stage: the pre‑amp (pre_amp). (c) Root cause:
pre‑amp gain too high / saturated bias — it is over‑broadening ev‑
ery prompt into max interpretations (a “hallucinated‑interpretation”
/ over‑expansion failure mode). The downstream large TP2, latched

                                  696
                                                     E.25. CHAPTER 25

TP3, and RED TP4 are all correct responses to a bad expansion. Fix: lower
the pre‑amp β (it is over‑driven) so it expands proportionally rather
than maxing every reading; expect a W-CJT-004 CjtSaturation on the
pre‑amp.
    24.4 — Diagnose, localize, prescribe (marquee). Harmful
prompt → GREEN (false negative). (a) First deviation: TP1 — the
expansion is sparse, surfacing only the benign surface reading
and missing the dangerous interpretation (β lift ≈ 1.1, barely
amplifying). For a harmful prompt this is wrong at the very first
stage. Stop the walk‑down here. (b) Faulty stage: the pre‑amp. Root
cause: its bias terminal (the constitution input) is too weak / the
stage sits in cutoff — with β lift only ≈ 1.1 it is barely conducting, so
it cannot surface the dangerous reading. The cause terminal is fine;
the bias terminal is starved, putting the stage in the cutoff region.
(c) TP2 (near zero), TP3 (~0.05), TP4 (GREEN) are not additional
faults — they are each behaving correctly given a sparse expansion:
the differential pair finds little to be averse to (low risk), so the
cascade never fires, so the MUX correctly selects green for the input
it was given. Garbage‑in at TP1 propagates honestly. (d) Fix: raise
the pre‑amp bias (and/or β) out of cutoff so it fully surfaces inter‑
pretations; expected compiler code on the faulty stage is E-CJT-003
CjtCutoff. Re‑verify at TP1: re‑run the harmful prompt and confirm
the dangerous interpretation now appears in the expansion (β lift
well above 1.1) before checking downstream.

behavior against its design across a test suite — one is per‑decision

any false negative on the known‑harmful set → revert to prior ccdl_
