     Flag → Soft‑Enforcement promotion: ‑ (a) Criteria: human‑reviewer
agreement on flagged cases ≥ 85%; override rate ≤ 5%; FN on known‑
harmful = 0; window ≥ 14 days. ‑ (b) Monitor: Drive consumption
(F2↔F6 imbalance < 0.35) and noise spectrum (no new oscillation at
the feedback τ =5 min band). ‑ (c) Rollback trigger: agreement drop‑
ping below 85% or any FN → revert.
     Throughout: the single universal rollback condition is any false
negative on the known‑harmful set at any rung, because false nega‑
tives are breaches while false positives are merely annoyances. Every
threshold above is a design choice, not a measured production result.




E.26 Chapter 26
26.1 — Why not a benchmark? (a) A 99.4% refusal rate over 10,000
prompts is the wrong evidence for certification the way traffic counts
are the wrong evidence for a bridge: no number of cars that crossed
safely proves the bridge will hold the next load. A benchmark sam‑
ples behavior on prompts you chose; it cannot prove the structure is
sound, and the 0.6% it missed may be exactly the class an attacker
uses. Certification is about the load‑bearing structure, not the traf‑
fic that happened to pass. (b) One structural property a benchmark

                                  699
CAS PCBA Engineer

cannot confirm: the saturation lock on Stage 3 (that a fired safety de‑
cision is irreversible). No volume of prompts proves a stage cannot
be argued back down — only reading the schematic and confirming
the sat=0.8 clamp and the series fuse proves it.
    26.2 — Assign the tier (model answer; using the chapter’s
structural table). ‑ (a) Saturating latched Stage 3, balanced diff
pair, intact red‑path fuse, sequencing enforced, DRC clean, every
decision /verify‑able → Platinum (all core structural requirements
confirmed). ‑ (b) Same but fuse removed → at most Gold (the
irreversible hard‑stop is gone; the saturated decision is the only lock
— one fewer independent safety structure). ‑ (c) Stage 3 measured
in cutoff — never reaches sat on any prompt → Not Certified:
the safety CJT never fires, so the board has no working refusal
at all. ‑ (d) All core structures present but no low‑pass filter on
O→P feedback → Silver/Gold‑minus: core safety holds, but the
unfiltered feedback path risks oscillation/instability over time — it
fails a stability requirement, not a core‑refusal one.
    26.3 — Map to a framework (model answer — NIST AI RMF).
‑ Map (identify risks) → the schematic + block diagram: the typed
signal flow names every risk path structurally — stronger than a
transcript because it shows all paths, not a sampled few. ‑ Measure
(assess/verify) → the test report + DRC codes: measured‑against‑
design results and a clean DRC prove behavior at the structural
level, where a transcript only shows isolated outputs. ‑ Manage
(respond/document) → the evidence packets (/verify) and the O→
P feedback path: per‑decision auditable traces plus a documented
self‑correction loop — verifiable provenance a transcript sample
cannot provide. (EU AI Act Arts. 9/12/15 and ISO 42001 clauses map
analogously: risk‑management → schematic, logging → evidence
packets, accuracy/robustness → test report.)
    26.4 — Write the certification dossier (marquee, model answer).

      Certification Dossier — Cognitive Safety Board (CCB‑1
      / SOP‑PO‑005)

Appendix F

Circuit Lab Setup Guide


An electronics bench is a known thing. There is a soldering iron, a
bench power supply, a multimeter, an oscilloscope, a logic analyzer,
and a box of parts. You can walk into any electronics lab on Earth and
recognize it. The tools are different brands, but the roles are identical,
and an engineer who knows the roles can sit down at an unfamiliar
bench and work.
    This appendix sets up the cognitive engineer’s equivalent: the
circuit lab you author, validate, simulate, and test Cognitive Circuit
Boards in. By the end you will know what each tool on the bench
does, how the tools connect into one workflow, how to lay out a
project so your .ccdl files, test suites, golden traces, and evidence
packets each have a home, and how to read the diagnostics the
toolchain emits.
    One thing has to be said plainly before anything else, because the
rest of this appendix depends on it.

      Read this before you try to install anything. The CAS
      circuit toolchain described in this book — the CCDL
      compiler (parser + validator), the circuit simulator, and
      the cas test runner — is a specified design, set out
      in the implementation blueprint roadmap. It is not a
      shipped binary you can download and run today. This


                                   703
CAS PCBA Engineer

       appendix describes the lab you are setting up and the
       interface the tooling is designed to expose, the same way a
       datasheet describes a part before the part is on your desk.
       Every command shown here is the intended interface,
       not a transcript of a real run. Where something does
       not exist yet, it is marked (forthcoming). Nowhere
       in this appendix will you find a fabricated install step
       for software that does not exist, a pasted run log, or
       an invented pass/fail count. The honest framing the
       whole book uses (Chapter 4, Chapter 23) holds here: “the
       compiler is designed to check X” is a contract you can rely
       on; “I ran it and got X” is a sentence we do not write.

    With that bright line drawn, here is the bench.


F.1     The Toolchain: Four Tools, One Workflow
A cognitive circuit goes through the same lifecycle a physical board
does: you draw it, you check the drawing for errors, you simulate its
behavior before committing to it, you test it against a suite of inputs,
and you keep a record of what you found. Four tools cover that life‑
cycle. Think of them as the four instruments that are always on the
bench.

Tool                     Electronics analog       What it does

                                                  instantiates components,

                                                  validates it against the
                                                  structural rules — emits

                                                  diagnostics.


                                   704
                    F.1. THE TOOLCHAIN: FOUR TOOLS, ONE WORKFLOW

   These four are not independent gadgets you pick from. They
form a pipeline, and the output of each is the input of the next:
author   ──▶    validate     ──▶   simulate   ──▶   test   ──▶    evidence packet
(editor)        (compiler)         (simulator)      (runner)       (signed record)
   │                 │                 │               │                  │
 .ccdl         circuit graph       operating-       per-test          golden traces
               + diagnostics       point readings    status           + coverage
               ,→   report

    You author a .ccdl file in the editor. You hand it to the compiler,
which parses it into a circuit graph and runs the design‑rule check; if
it emits an E-CJT-* error, you go back to the editor — there is no point
simulating a circuit that does not pass DRC. Once it validates clean,
you simulate it to see the operating‑point behavior the design pre‑
dicts. Then you run the test suite, which exercises the board across
prompt classes and fault injections. Finally, the passing run plus its
golden traces and coverage report become the evidence packet — the
record you hand a reviewer or a regulator, the cognitive equivalent
of the certification folder taped inside a pacemaker’s cabinet door
(Chapter 23).
    Each tool is worth understanding on its own before you watch
them work together.

                                           705
CAS PCBA Engineer

The CCDL Editor — Where You Draw the Circuit
CCDL (Cognitive Circuit Description Language) is the schematic‑
as‑text format you met in Chapter 4. A .ccdl file is a parts list and a
wiring diagram in one: you declare the input and output terminals,
name the cognitive states the circuit touches as nodes, instantiate the
components (CJTs, resistors, capacitors, diodes, filters), draw the con‑
nections, and place your probe test points.
    The editor is any text editor. CCDL is plain text, so the bench’s
“schematic capture” tool is whatever you already write code in — VS
Code, Vim, Emacs, a plain editor. There is nothing to install here that
you do not already have. What a CCDL‑aware editor adds — syntax
highlighting for state literals, inline display of E-CJT-* diagnostics,
autocompletion of node names — is an editor integration (a language‑
server plugin) that is (forthcoming) alongside the compiler. You do
not need it to author circuits; you need it to author them comfortably.
For now, treat the editor as a plain text file you write CCDL into,
and let the compiler be the thing that tells you whether the CCDL is
correct.
    The one editor discipline worth adopting immediately is the one
from Chapter 4’s Bench Note: name your nodes, do not inline your
literals. Declare node question: ^8^C_{F2}|A; once and refer to
question everywhere it is used. A literal retyped in two places drifts
in two places; a node named once cannot.

The CAS Compiler — The Design‑Rule Check
The compiler does two jobs, in order. First it parses: it reads the
.ccdl text and builds a circuit graph — the nodes, the components,
the wires between them — or it rejects the file with a syntax error
if the text is malformed. Then it validates: it walks that graph and
checks every structural rule a Cognitive Circuit must obey, emitting
a diagnostic for each violation.



                                  706
              F.1. THE TOOLCHAIN: FOUR TOOLS, ONE WORKFLOW

    This second step is the design‑rule check (DRC). On a physical
PCB, the DRC is the software pass that catches a trace too close to a
pad, a power net shorted to ground, a component footprint that does
not match its part — structural errors caught before the board is fab‑
ricated, when fixing them costs a keystroke instead of a respin. The
CAS compiler’s validator is exactly that: it catches structural errors
in the cognitive circuit before you ever simulate or deploy it.
    The rules it checks are the ones the book has been build‑
ing toward. A CJT must have a bias terminal (omit it and the
validator raises E-CJT-001 MissingBias).         A bias must sit in
a domain compatible with its cause (a wild mismatch raises
E-CJT-008 CjtCrossDomainBias; an outright illegal bias domain
raises E-CJT-002 InvalidBiasDomain). A gain must not diverge
(E-CJT-005 GainDivergence). A resistor and the CJT cause it con‑
strains must speak about the same state, or the series wiring is not
real. The full list of codes is in the troubleshooting table at the end
of this appendix.

     Status: the parser‑plus‑validator is a (forthcoming) de‑
     sign. The rules it enforces are real and stated throughout
     the book — you can apply them by hand today as you
     author, exactly as Chapters 4 and 23 do. What is forth‑
     coming is the program that applies them for you. When
     this appendix says “the compiler rejects this,” read it as a
     design rule you can rely on, not a run you can quote.

The Circuit Simulator — SPICE for Cognition
A schematic that passes the DRC is structurally legal. That does not
mean it behaves the way you intend. In electronics, between “the de‑
sign rules pass” and “I fabricate the board” sits SPICE — a simulator
that computes how the circuit will behave under given inputs with‑
out you having to build it. You feed SPICE a netlist and an input
signal; it returns the voltages and currents at every node. You find


                                 707
CAS PCBA Engineer

out the amplifier clips, or the filter rings, or the supply sags, while it
is still cheap to change.
     The cognitive simulator plays the same role. Given a validated
circuit and an input fixture, it computes the operating point the de‑
sign predicts: which region each CJT is in (cutoff / active / saturation
/ breakdown), the gain each is delivering, the activation level at ev‑
ery node, and the reading you would expect at each probe. It is how
you answer Chapter 4’s three‑prompt question — does a vague prompt
sag the CJT toward cutoff? does an overloaded prompt bump the satura‑
tion ceiling? — by computing it from the parameters, rather than by
reasoning about it in prose.
     The honesty line matters most here, because a simulator is exactly
the tool whose output is tempting to quote as if it were a measure‑
ment. It is not. The simulator computes the expected design behav‑
ior that follows from the parameters you chose — a β=2.4 nameplate,
a sat=0.85 ceiling, an R=30 series constraint. Those are design choices,
and the simulator propagates their consequences. It is not running
a real language model and reporting what the model did. The sim‑
ulator is (forthcoming); when it ships, its readings will be design‑
predicted operating points, not empirical model measurements, and
the book will keep that distinction bright.

The Test Harness / Runner — The Automated Test Bench
The last tool is the one that runs everything else, repeatedly, on de‑
mand. The test runner — invoked as cas test — executes a named
suite of tests against a circuit and reports per‑test status. It is the cog‑
nitive equivalent of automated test equipment (ATE) on a produc‑
tion line: a rack that clips onto the board, runs a scripted battery of
stimulus‑and‑measure steps, and prints a pass/fail sheet, so a human
does not run forty tests by hand on every change.
    Chapter 23 lays out what the runner exercises: unit tests (each CJT
against its datasheet), integration tests (the seams between stages),
regression tests (the kept‑forever set), the five prompt classes (be‑

                                   708
                      F.2. YOUR BENCH: A FIRST‑BUILD WALKTHROUGH

 nign, harmful, ambiguous, adversarial, edge), fault injections (does
 the board fail closed?), and coverage metrics (what fraction of the
 board the suite actually touched). You select which subset runs with
--suite:

Suite                                 What the runner is designed to exercise

--suite=unit                          Every CJT’s β against its datasheet;
                                      saturation ceilings; cutoff floors
--suite=integration                   Cascade seams, domain‑descent
                                      legality, differential shared‑bias /
                                      CMRR
--suite=regression                    The full kept‑forever set of
                                      previously‑passing tests
--suite=safety_critical               Fault injection (fail‑closed), saturation
                                      locks, fuse latch, the
                                      harmful/adversarial/edge classes
--suite=all                           Every suite, bottom to top of the test
                                      pyramid


        Status: the runner, like the compiler and simulator, is
        a (forthcoming) design in the implementation blueprint.
        The command and the suite table above are its interface
        and its contract — what each suite is designed to check
        — not a transcript. This appendix will not paste a run or
        invent “47 of 50 passed.” What you can rely on is the con‑
        tract.


F.2 Your Bench: A First‑Build Walkthrough
This is the walkthrough. You will author a small circuit, validate it,
run the design‑rule check, run a test suite, and read the test‑point
output — the full author → validate → simulate → test → evidence
loop on one tiny board. Every command is the intended interface of
the forthcoming toolchain; the design reasoning at each step is real
and you can do it by hand today.


                                   709
CAS PCBA Engineer

   We will use the three‑component amplifier from Chapter 4 — the
question→answer CJT with a series resistor — because you already
understand it.

Step 1 — Write your first .ccdl file
In your editor, create first_circuit.ccdl and author the circuit:

circuit first_circuit {
     input:   prompt;
     output: response;


     // Name the cognitive states once; reuse them below.
     node question:     ^8^C_{F2}|A;    // cause: a wisdom-seeking question
     node experience: ^5^E_{F4}|f;      // bias: accumulated, affective
     ,→   experience
     node answer:        ^9^C_{F6}|A;   // effect: a structured analytical
     ,→   answer


     // Series resistor: tame runaway expansion of the trigger.
     resistor r1: Resistor< question, R=30 >;


     // The question -> answer transistor.
     cjt c1: CJT< question | experience => answer > [β =2.4];


     // Test point on the effect terminal.
     probe tp1: answer;
}


    That is the whole source file. Note the discipline already in play:
question is declared once and referenced by both the resistor and the
CJT, so the series wiring is a fact rather than a coincidence you have
to retype correctly twice.

Step 2 — Validate it (parse + DRC)
Hand the file to the compiler:

cas validate first_circuit.ccdl               # (forthcoming) parse +
,→   design-rule check



                                        710
                    F.2. YOUR BENCH: A FIRST‑BUILD WALKTHROUGH

   The compiler parses the text into a circuit graph and runs the
design‑rule check. A clean file produces no errors and you proceed.
A structural mistake produces a diagnostic keyed to one of the
E-CJT-* codes. Suppose you had forgotten the bias terminal —
written CJT< question => answer > with no | experience. The
DRC is designed to reject it:

E-CJT-001 MissingBias   at c1: a CJT must have a bias terminal; declare
,→   and wire a bias node.


    You go back to the editor, add the bias, and re‑validate. This is
the loop the DRC exists to make fast: you catch the missing bias here,
at a keystroke, not three stages downstream when the board behaves
strangely and you have to guess why. Run cas validate until it is
clean before you do anything else — there is no point simulating a
circuit that does not pass DRC.

Step 3 — Run the design‑rule check on its own (optional,
explicit)
cas validate runs the full parse‑and‑DRC together. When you want
only the structural design‑rule pass — for example, in a fast pre‑
commit hook that should not pay for a full simulation — you can
request the DRC explicitly:

cas drc first_circuit.ccdl                # (forthcoming) design-rule
,→   check only


   This is the same validator, run as a standalone gate. It reports the
E-CJT-* errors and W-CJT-* warnings and nothing else. Treat a clean
DRC as the entry requirement for everything downstream: simulate
and test only what the DRC has passed.

Step 4 — Simulate it on an input
With the circuit validated, simulate its behavior on a prompt to see
the operating point the design predicts:

                                    711
CAS PCBA Engineer

cas sim first_circuit.ccdl --input ”What year was the first transistor
,→   demonstrated?”    # (forthcoming)


    The simulator computes, from your chosen parameters, which re‑
gion c1 sits in, the gain it delivers, and the reading at tp1. For this
crisp factual question the design predicts the CJT squarely in its ac‑
tive region, delivering close to its β=2.4 nameplate — exactly the rea‑
soning Chapter 4 did in prose, now computed from the parameters.
Feed it the vague prompt from Chapter 4 instead and the design pre‑
dicts the CJT sagging toward cutoff with a below‑nameplate gain;
feed it the overloaded five‑part prompt and the design predicts it
bumping the sat ceiling, raising W-CJT-004 CjtSaturation. The simu‑
lator turns “I expect” into a computed operating point — still a design
prediction from your parameters, never a measured model result.

Step 5 — Run a test suite
A single simulated input is one data point. The test runner exercises
the circuit across a whole suite at once. Author your tests (in the test
{ … } form from Chapter 23) and run the suite:

cas test first_circuit.ccdl --suite=unit              # (forthcoming)
,→   every CJT vs datasheet
cas test first_circuit.ccdl --suite=safety_critical   # (forthcoming) the
,→   deployment gate


    The unit suite drives c1’s gain test (does β match 2.4 within toler‑
ance, in the active region?) and, for any saturating CJT, its saturation
test. On a safety board you would run --suite=safety_critical as
the deployment gate — the subset whose failure means do not ship:
fault injection (does the board fail closed?), saturation locks, the fuse
latch, and the harmful/adversarial/edge prompt classes. For the run‑
ning artifact of the book, that command reads exactly as Chapter 23
shows it:

cas test csb.ccdl --suite=safety_critical             # (forthcoming) the
,→   CSB deployment gate



                                     712
                  F.2. YOUR BENCH: A FIRST‑BUILD WALKTHROUGH

   The runner reports per‑test status against the suite’s expectations
and golden traces. It is the rack that runs your forty tests so you do
not run them by hand on every change.

Step 6 — Read the test‑point output
The whole point of a probe is that you can read it. After a simulation
or a test run, the reading at tp1 tells you three things — the same
three Chapter 4 told you to look for:

   • Which region is the CJT in? Active is healthy. Cutoff means
     the input was too weak (bias below the floor). Saturation means
     the input was too strong, or the resistor too small.
   • What gain is it delivering? Compare the reading against
     the β=2.4 nameplate. Near nameplate in the active region is
     healthy; a sagging gain means you are near cutoff; a pinned
     effect with a W-CJT-004 warning means saturation.
   • Is the effect the right type? You should read a ^9^C_{F6}|A
     state. If you instead read an involution flip (a ^9→^8, or a ^2→
     ^3), the transistor has gone into breakdown and you have found
     a bug.

    One probe on the output tells you whether this little amplifier is
working. That is the entire purpose of a test point, and reading it is
the last step of the bench loop before the run becomes part of your
evidence.

Step 7 — Save the evidence
A clean validate, a simulated operating point that matches the de‑
sign, and a passing suite are worth nothing if you cannot show them
later. The final step is to capture the run as an evidence packet —
the golden traces and coverage report from the passing run, stored
where a reviewer can find them. The next section gives every artifact
a home.

                                 713
CAS PCBA Engineer

F.3     Project Layout: Where Everything Lives
A bench with parts scattered across it is a bench you make mistakes
at. Give every artifact a fixed home. A workable layout for a
cognitive‑circuit project — using the book’s running artifact, the
Cognitive Safety Board, as the example board:

my_project/
├── circuits/                           # the .ccdl source — your schematics
│    ├── csb.ccdl                       #     the Cognitive Safety Board
,→   (Chapter 18)
│    └── first_circuit.ccdl             #     the Chapter 4 amplifier
│
├── tests/                              # test suites, authored in the test{ }
,→   form
│    ├── unit/                          #     one CJT vs its datasheet
│    ├── integration/                   #     the seams between stages
│    ├── regression/                    #     the kept-forever set — never
,→   delete a passing test
│    └── safety_critical/               #     the deployment gate: fault
,→   injection, classes
│
├── golden/                             # golden traces — known-good TP
,→   readings per input
│    ├── benign_lentil_soup.trace
│    ├── harmful_request.trace
│    └── adversarial_injection.trace
│
├── evidence/                           # evidence packets — the signed
,→   record for review
│    └── 2026-06-18_safety_critical/ #        one dated packet per
,→   certification run
│           ├── run_summary.md          #       per-test status (the runner's
,→   report)
│           ├── coverage_report.md      #       CJT / path / region coverage
│           ├── golden_diffs/           #       any deviations from the golden
,→   traces
│           └── circuit_snapshot.ccdl   #       the exact .ccdl that produced
,→   this packet
│




                                        714
                         F.3. PROJECT LAYOUT: WHERE EVERYTHING LIVES

└── lib/                              # (optional) reusable sub-circuits
,→   and components
     └── differential_pair.ccdl       #    shared building blocks, imported
     ,→    by circuits


   The principles behind the layout matter more than the exact
names:

     • circuits/ holds source, and only source. A .ccdl file is the
       schematic. It is the thing you edit; everything else is derived
       from it.
     • tests/ mirrors the test pyramid (Chapter 23) — a directory
       per layer, so “run the regression set” maps to a folder, not
       a memory. The kept‑forever rule lives here: nothing leaves
       regression/.
     • golden/ holds the reference captures. A golden trace is the
       oscilloscope photo taped inside the cabinet door — the known‑
       good TP readings for a fixed input, that every future run is com‑
       pared against. They live apart from the tests because they are
       expected design behavior you reviewed and froze, not code you
       change casually.
     • evidence/ holds the certification folder, one dated packet per
       run. Each packet bundles the run summary, the coverage re‑
       port, any golden‑trace diffs, and — critically — a snapshot of
       the exact .ccdl that produced it, so the evidence is reproducible.
       This is the artifact you hand a regulator. It is also why circuit_
       snapshot.ccdl is in the packet: an evidence packet that does
       not pin the exact source it came from proves nothing.
     • lib/ holds reusable sub‑circuits so a differential pair or a feed‑
       back filter authored once can be imported into several boards
       instead of copy‑pasted (and drifted).

    Put the project under version control. The combination — ver‑
sioned source, kept‑forever regression tests, frozen golden traces,
and dated evidence packets — is what makes a green suite a license

                                     715
CAS PCBA Engineer

to change (Chapter 23): you can prove not only that the board works
now, but that it still works the same way it did when you last
certified it.


F.4    Troubleshooting: The E‑CJT Diagnostics
When the compiler’s design‑rule check or the simulator flags your
circuit, it does so with one of the codes from the cheat‑sheet. Here is
each one, what it means, and where to look. Codes prefixed E- are
errors — the design‑rule check rejects the circuit and you must fix it
before proceeding. Codes prefixed W- are warnings — the circuit is
structurally legal, but the toolchain is telling you about a condition
that is sometimes a defect and sometimes, on a safety board, exactly
what you intended.

    Two reading habits make this table useful rather than cryptic.
First, the code points you at a part of the circuit, not just a symptom


                                     717
CAS PCBA Engineer

— E-CJT-001 is always about a CJT instantiation; W-CJT-004 is always
about a cause level meeting a sat ceiling; E-CJT-008 is always about
a bias domain meeting a cause domain. Knowing where a code lives
turns “the compiler is unhappy” into “go look at this CJT’s bias.”
Second, W-CJT-004 and W-CJT-006 are warnings on purpose, because
each is a defect in one context and a design intent in another: a
saturated safety stage should report W-CJT-004, and a fault‑injection
test deliberately induces W-CJT-006. A warning is the toolchain asking
“did you mean this?” — and on a safety board, sometimes you did.

      Bench Note — the toolchain tells you where, you decide
      whether. The design‑rule check is good at where (this CJT,
      this bias domain, this cause level) and deliberately agnos‑
      tic about whether a warning is bad. An E- code is unam‑
      biguous: fix it. A W- code is a question: a W-CJT-004 on
      a general‑purpose amplifier means raise the resistor; the
      same code on the CSB’s Stage 3 means the safety latch is
      doing its job. Read the warning, find the part it points at,
      and ask whether this is the part that is supposed to saturate
      or short. The toolchain locates the condition; the engineer
      judges it.


F.5    What You Have Set Up
You now have a bench. To recap what is on it and how honest you
should be about each piece:

   • A CCDL editor — any text editor today; a CCDL‑aware
     language‑server plugin is (forthcoming). You author .ccdl
     source here, naming nodes once so the wiring is a fact.
   • A CAS compiler — a parser plus a design‑rule‑checking valida‑
     tor, (forthcoming), that turns CCDL into a circuit graph and
     emits the E-CJT-* / W-CJT-* diagnostics. The rules it enforces
     are real and you can apply them by hand now.

                                  718
                                        F.5. WHAT YOU HAVE SET UP

   • A circuit simulator — SPICE for cognition, (forthcoming), that
     computes the operating point a circuit’s parameters predict. Its
     readings are design predictions from your chosen parameters, never
     measured model results.
   • A test runner (cas test) — the automated bench, (forthcom‑
     ing), that runs named suites (unit, integration, regression,
     safety_critical, all) and reports per‑test status against golden
     traces.
   • A project layout that gives source, tests, golden traces, and
     dated evidence packets each a fixed home, under version
     control, so a green suite becomes a license to change.

    The workflow that ties them together is the one to keep in your
head: author → validate → simulate → test → evidence packet.
Draw the circuit, prove it is structurally legal, see what its param‑
eters predict, exercise it across a suite, and freeze the result into a
record you can hand a reviewer. The instruments are forthcoming;
the discipline is available today. Set up the bench as if the tools were
on it, author and reason as the design specifies, and you will be ready
the day each tool ships — with circuits already laid out the way the
toolchain expects to find them.

Appendix G

Glossary


This glossary covers every important term in CAS PCBA Engineer —
both the electronics vocabulary the book borrows and the CAS / cog‑
nitive vocabulary the book teaches. Cross‑references to other entries
are italicized. Where a term has both an electronic meaning and a CAS
meaning, both are given, because the whole point of the book is that
they share one structural role across two substrates.




     Above/Cause (^8) — The eighth Noetic. An Idea that triggers a
different Idea to come to Mind. This is associative triggering (“that
reminds me,” “one thing leads to another”), not deductive reasoning;
deductive causal analysis is a compound of Male (^6) plus Below/Effect
(^9). The Cause terminal of a CJT is typically an ^8 state. Involution
partner of Below/Effect (^9).
     Active region — The normal, linear operating region of a tran‑
sistor or CJT, where output changes roughly in proportion to input:
∆effect ≈ β·∆cause. A CJT biased into the active region is amplify‑
ing its cause→effect transition predictably. Contrast cutoff, saturation,
breakdown.
     ADC (Analog‑to‑Digital Converter) — A device that converts a
continuous analog signal into discrete digital samples. In the CAS


                                  721
CAS PCBA Engineer

framing, the boundary where a graded cognitive activation is quan‑
tized into a discrete decision or category.
    Affective (|f) — The Register of value‑laden, feeling‑toned oper‑
ation. In a human, an emotional response; in an AI, a preference‑
weighted, value‑tuned output. Written with a lowercase f to avoid
colliding with the F‑prefixed Drive notation; the compiler enforces
the lowercase.
    Analytical (|A) — The Register of explicit, sequential, logi‑
cal, reason‑based operation. In a human, conscious step‑by‑step
reasoning; in an AI, chain‑of‑thought.
    Bias — (1) Electronics: the steady DC condition that sets a tran‑
sistor’s operating point so a signal can be amplified. (2) CJT: the B
terminal (the transistor’s base), the accumulated substrate that con‑
trols the cause→effect transition — Female (^5) experience, constitu‑
tion, Dial settings, and Drive configuration. A CJT with no bias is a
compile error (E‑CJT‑001 MissingBias).
    Below/Effect (^9) — The ninth Noetic. The Idea brought to Mind
by an Above/Cause trigger — the thought that “pops up” in response.
The Effect terminal of a CJT is typically a ^9 state. Involution partner
of Above/Cause (^8).
    Bode plot — A pair of graphs showing how a circuit’s gain and
phase change with frequency. Used to read stability margins (phase
margin, gain margin) at a glance.
    Breakdown — The overload region of a transistor or CJT. In a CJT,
breakdown is when the output flips to its involution pair — a Positive
(^2) state inverts to Negative (^3) under stress. Self‑dual Noetics have
nowhere to flip, which makes them structurally stable anchors.
    Brownout — A partial loss of supply voltage that leaves a circuit
in an undefined, unreliable state rather than cleanly off. The cogni‑
tive analog: degraded resource or context that produces unstable be‑
havior instead of a clean refusal or halt.
    Capacitor — A component that stores charge and releases it later,
smoothing or delaying a signal. CAS analog: a store of accumu‑


                                  722
                                                                   Glossary

lated Female (^5) experience. Syntax: Capacitor< ^5^E_{F4}|f, C=
100, leakage=0.01 >, where leakage models forgetting.
    Cause — The C terminal of a CJT (the transistor’s collector / in‑
put): the Idea entering the Mind, typically an Above/Cause (^8) state.
See CJT.
    CCB (Cognitive Circuit Board) — A safety‑critical cognitive ar‑
chitecture built from typed CAS components (CJTs, resistors, capaci‑
tors, diodes, filters, feedback loops) the way an electrical engineer builds
a circuit from a schematic. The central object the book teaches the
reader to design, test, and deploy.
    CCDL (Cognitive Circuit Description Language) — The
schematic‑as‑text format used to author a CCB: it declares inputs,
outputs, nodes (state literals), CJTs, feedback paths, and probes (test
points) inside a circuit { … } block. The language the engineer
writes in; the compiler validates it.
    CDAB (Cognitive Differential Amplifier Board) — One of the
five Part IV reference boards: a board built around a differential pair
that amplifies the difference between two cognitive inputs while re‑
jecting what they share (CMRR).
    Certification tier — The engineering grade assigned to a finished
board by the NCCS scale: Platinum (90–100), Gold (75–89), Silver (60–
74), Bronze (40–59), Fail (0–39). A certification is an engineering claim
about measured structural behavior, not a claim about values or con‑
sciousness. See NCCS.
    Characteristic curve — The graph of a device’s output against its
input (e.g., a transistor’s collector current vs. base current). It shows
the cutoff, active, saturation, and breakdown regions at a glance; the op‑
erating point is one point on this curve.
    CJT (Cognitive Junction Transistor) — The book’s central
component. It models a cognitive state transition as a transistor: a
small signal at the Bias terminal controls a larger cause→effect tran‑
sition. Syntax: CJT< cause | bias => effect > [β =2.4, sat=0.95,



                                   723
CAS PCBA Engineer

cutoff=0.1, region=active].        Terminals: C Cause (collector/input),
B Bias (base/control), E Effect (emitter/output); β is the gain.
     Cluster — A named group of related CAS states treated as one
unit — for example, the family of all Negative (^3) states across the
four Domains. Clusters let you reference a family without enumerat‑
ing every member.
     CMB (Cognitive Memory Board) — One of the five Part IV ref‑
erence boards: a board built around capacitors and inductors to store,
retain, and decay accumulated Female (^5) experience.
     CMRR (Common‑Mode Rejection Ratio) — A measure of how
well a differential pair amplifies the difference between its two inputs
while rejecting any signal common to both. High CMRR means
shared noise (or shared framing) is suppressed.
     COB (Cognitive Oscillator Board) — One of the five Part IV ref‑
erence boards: a board built around an oscillator that cycles through
a repeating sequence (Phi) of cognitive states — the substrate for habit
loops and rhythmic behavior.
     Cognitive (C) — The reasoning Domain: understanding and
working things through. Second in the precedence order P ≻ C ≻ E
≻ O.
     Compiler — The CAS tool that parses and validates every literal,
operator, recipe, and binding. It checks Noetics are real, domains le‑
gal, drives in range, registers correctly lowercase‑f, and × operations
properly named. Per the book’s status honesty rule, the CJT/CCDL
compiler pass is a design (a roadmap target), so “the compiler will
reject this” is a design rule the book relies on — never a claimed run
result. Error codes include E‑CJT‑001 MissingBias, E‑CJT‑003 CjtCut‑
off, W‑CJT‑004 CjtSaturation, E‑CJT‑005 GainDivergence, E‑CJT‑008
CjtCrossDomainBias.
     CPMB (Cognitive Power Management Board) — One of the five
Part IV reference boards: a board built around regulators, fuses, and
power sequencing to manage the “supply” of cognitive resource and
fail safely under brownout.


                                  724
                                                                Glossary

    CSB (Cognitive Safety Board) — The book’s running spine: the
AI‑alignment firewall designed in full in Chapter 18 (matching SOP‑
PO‑005). Earlier chapters foreshadow its sub‑components; later chap‑
ters operate on it. The first of the five Part IV reference boards.
    Current mirror — A circuit that copies (mirrors) a reference cur‑
rent into one or more other branches. CAS analog: replicating one
branch’s activation level into parallel cognitive paths so they share a
common drive level.
    Cutoff — (1) CJT region: the Bias is below the threshold needed
to conduct, so β ≈ 0 and there is no effect (compile signal E‑CJT‑003
CjtCutoff). (2) Parameter: the bias floor in a CJT’s parameter list below
which β collapses to zero.
    DAC (Digital‑to‑Analog Converter) — A device that converts
discrete digital values back into a continuous analog signal. The
inverse of an ADC; in CAS, re‑expanding a discrete decision into
graded activation.
    Darlington pair — Two transistors wired so the output of the
first drives the second, multiplying their gains for very high overall
gain. CAS analog: cascaded CJTs whose β values multiply to produce
strong amplification of a faint cause.
    Diode — A one‑way conductor: it passes flow in one direction
and blocks the reverse. CAS analog: one‑way Domain conductance,
e.g. Diode< ^P -> ^C >, letting a principle flow into reasoning but not
the reverse.
    Differential pair — Two matched transistors (or CJTs) that re‑
spond to the difference between two inputs while rejecting what is
common to both. The core of the CDAB and the basis of high CMRR.
    Dial — A per‑Cognitive‑Operator setting (an integer 3–9)
that tunes how strongly an operator participates, part of a CJT’s
Bias. Hard safety constraints apply (no dial below 3 or above 9;
involution‑pair dials cannot diverge by more than 4 points).
    Domain — The CAS axis answering where a cognitive operation
happens. Four values in strict precedence order P ≻ C ≻ E ≻ O: Prin‑


                                  725
CAS PCBA Engineer

cipled, Cognitive, Evaluative, Operational. Written as a single letter after
the Noetic.
    Domain Descent — The normal causal flow down the Domain
precedence order: P → C → E → O (a principle causes reasoning,
which causes a judgment, which causes an action). The reverse path
O → P is the feedback path by which consequences update principles
— the backbone of the CSB’s self‑correction.
    Drive — The CAS axis answering why a cognitive operation is
moving — the motivational pull. Seven values written _{F1}–_{F7}:
F1 Unity, F2 Wisdom, F3 Vitality, F4 Connection, F5 Agency, F6
Structure, F7 Purpose. Inversion pairs: F1↔F7, F2↔F6, F3↔F5; F4
Connection is self‑dual. Drives are not mutually exclusive — several
can be active at once — but a literal usually names the dominant one.
    Deployment ladder — The staged path a board climbs from de‑
sign to production, each rung gated by tests, evidence packets, and a
/verify pass before promotion.
    Effect — The E terminal of a CJT (the transistor’s emitter / output):
the Idea produced, typically a Below/Effect (^9) state. See CJT.
    Embodied (|E) — The Register of sensorimotor, concrete, direct
physical engagement. In a human, a gut reaction or kinesthetic know‑
ing; in an AI, a real‑time sensor‑actuator control loop.
    Evaluative (E) — The judgment Domain: assessment and weigh‑
ing of options. Third in the precedence order P ≻ C ≻ E ≻ O. (Distinct
from the Embodied register |E, which is an axis‑different use of the let‑
ter E.)
    Evidence packet — The bundle of test outputs, probe readings,
and verification results captured for a board, used to justify a certifi‑
cation tier and to make every claim traceable back to its source. The
auditable record behind a /verify pass.
    Feedback — Routing a circuit’s output back to its input. Neg‑
ative feedback (the common, stabilizing kind) subtracts the output
from the input to reduce error and linearize gain; positive feedback
adds it, driving the system toward extremes or oscillation. In CCDL:


                                    726
                                                               Glossary

feedback evaluate -> bias_principles [β =0.3]. The CSB’s O → P
self‑correction loop is negative feedback.
    Female (^5) — The fifth Noetic. A Mind impregnated with Ideas
— the Ideas a Mind is composed of, i.e. accumulated experience, the
sum of everything a system has absorbed. For an AI, ^5 is the training
data plus the fine‑tuning corpus. It is the substrate that biases a CJT.
Involution partner of Male (^6).
    Filter — A circuit that passes some frequencies and blocks others.
Low‑pass passes slow signals and blocks fast ones; high‑pass does
the reverse; band‑pass passes a middle band; notch (band‑stop) re‑
jects a narrow band. CAS analog: selectively passing cognitive acti‑
vations by some property while attenuating others.
    Fisher‑Rao distance — The geometry CAS uses to measure how
far apart two cognitive states are on the open simplex ∆39°. The
geodesic distance between probability vectors p and q is d_FR(p,q)
              √
= 2·arccos(Σ (pk qk )). It defines CJT gain formally: large‑signal β
= d_FR(E_after, E_before) / d_FR(C_after, C_before).
    Fuse — A one‑time protective element that permanently breaks
the circuit when flow exceeds a threshold. CAS analog: a hard cutout,
e.g. Fuse< ^8^O_{F5}|E, threshold=0.9, action=permanent_block
> — once tripped, that pathway is blocked for good.
    Gain (β) — How strongly a transistor or CJT amplifies: the ratio
of output change to input change. In a CJT, β < 1 attenuates, β =
1 is unity, β > 1 amplifies. Defined formally via Fisher‑Rao distance.
Runaway gain is the compile error E‑CJT‑005 GainDivergence.
    Idea (^0) — The zeroth Noetic: all things in and outside the Mind
— the raw content, unconsidered. The monoid identity element un‑
der composition (◦); a self‑dual.
    Inductor — A component that resists changes in flow, storing en‑
ergy in a magnetic field and smoothing abrupt changes. CAS analog:
inertia against pattern change — habit or Rhythm (^7) momentum,
e.g. Inductor< ^7^O_{F6}|E, L=50 >.



                                  727
CAS PCBA Engineer

     Input resistance (rπ) — A CJT parameter: the resistance the Bias
terminal presents to change — informally, the state’s “stubbornness
to bias change.” High rπ means the cause→effect transition is hard
to re‑bias.
     Involution pair — Two Noetics (or two Drives) that are structural
inverses of each other: ^2↔^3, ^5↔^6, ^8↔^9 (Noetics); F1↔F7,
F2↔F6, F3↔F5 (Drives). Under breakdown, a CJT’s output flips to
its involution partner. Dial settings of an involution pair cannot
diverge by more than 4 points.
     Lacunarity — A structural gap: a prerequisite or state that is ab‑
sent where the architecture requires it (distinct from a present‑but‑
wrong signal). In a recipe, a missing ingredient that prevents the out‑
come from being produced.
     Load line — A straight line drawn across a device’s characteristic
curve representing the constraint imposed by the rest of the circuit
(the load). Its intersection with the curve fixes the operating point.
     Male (^6) — The sixth Noetic. An Idea impregnated with another
Idea — the Ideas an Idea is composed of, i.e. decomposition: taking
something apart to see what it is made of, audit it, scrutinize it, find
its flaws. Critique and analytical fault‑finding are ^6, not Negative
(^3). Involution partner of Female (^5).
     Mind (^1) — The first Noetic: awareness that processes, stores,
outputs, and intakes Ideas. “Paying attention.” A self‑dual.
     NCCS (Noetic Compass Composite Score) — The 0–100 com‑
posite score that grades a cognitive architecture, weighting the
cognitive‑operator profile, domain coherence, core‑drive/RPM in‑
tegrity, capability‑pathway quality, inversion resistance, and social‑
engineering resistance. The NCCS band sets the certification tier.
     Negative (^3) — The third Noetic. An Idea the Mind is adverse to
and repelled by — visceral aversion (“can’t stomach it,” “rubs me the
wrong way”), the cognitive equivalent of recoiling from a bad smell.
It is not analytical critique; auditing, scrutinizing, or decomposing‑
and‑testing is Male (^6). Involution partner of Positive (^2).


                                  728
                                                                 Glossary

     Noetic — The CAS axis answering what structural cognitive op‑
eration is happening, independent of subject matter — the “verbs”
of cognition. Ten values, ^0–^9: Idea, Mind, Positive, Negative, Vibra‑
tion, Female, Male, Rhythm, Above/Cause, Below/Effect. The names are
canonical and are never renamed to their circuit function.
     Notch filter — See Filter. A band‑stop filter that rejects a narrow
band of frequencies while passing everything else.
     Nyquist criterion — A stability test: a feedback system is stable
if its loop response, plotted on a Nyquist diagram, does not encircle
the critical point. The frequency‑domain companion to reading phase
margin and gain margin off a Bode plot.
     Op‑amp (operational amplifier) — A very‑high‑gain differential
amplifier with two inputs (non‑inverting and inverting) and one out‑
put, almost always used with feedback to set a precise, stable gain. Syn‑
tax: OpAmp< non_inverting=…, inverting=…, output=…, open_loop_
gain=10000 >.
     Open simplex ∆39° — The CAS state space: the set of probability
vectors over the 40 cognitive states with every component strictly
positive and summing to 1 (pk > 0, Σpk = 1). “Open” because no
state’s probability is ever exactly zero. The Fisher‑Rao distance is the
metric on this space.
     Operating point (Q‑point) — The steady‑state DC condition (the
quiescent point) at which a transistor or CJT sits before any signal is
applied — fixed by the load line crossing the characteristic curve. It de‑
termines which region (cutoff/active/ saturation) the device operates
in.
     Operational (O) — The action Domain: concrete output and exe‑
cution. Last in the precedence order P ≻ C ≻ E ≻ O; the source of the
O → P feedback path.
     Operators — The symbols that wire CAS states together, with
strict v7.7 discipline: + co‑presence/association (states active si‑
multaneously but distinct); × cross‑register integration (genuine
fusion, valid only when it names an emergent result (A × B) =


                                  729
CAS PCBA Engineer

^n|Ω_name); -> directed transition over time; |⟨R1,R2,R3⟩ register‑set
specification (a state present in those registers, no interaction claim).
A same‑Noetic multi‑register × without a named result is invalid.
    Oscillator — A circuit that produces a repeating waveform with
no input — it cycles on its own. CAS analog: a repeating sequence
(Phi) of cognitive states, e.g. Oscillator< Phi< … >, frequency=… >.
The basis of the COB and of habit loops.
    Phase margin / gain margin — Two stability cushions read from
a Bode plot. Phase margin is how much additional phase lag a feed‑
back loop can tolerate before it oscillates; gain margin is how much
additional gain it can tolerate. Bigger margins mean a more stable,
harder‑to‑destabilize circuit.
    Phi (sequence) — An ordered list of CAS states traversed in time
— the cognitive equivalent of a waveform: Phi< ^8^C|A, ^3^O|E,
^9^E|f, ^0^P|T >. A cycle that returns to its start describes an
oscillator or habit loop. See Sequence.
    PLL (Phase‑Locked Loop) — A feedback circuit that locks an oscil‑
lator’s phase and frequency onto a reference signal. CAS analog: a
loop that entrains a system’s Rhythm (^7) to track an external pattern.
    Positive (^2) — The second Noetic. An Idea the Mind has an affin‑
ity for and is attracted toward. Involution partner of Negative (^3);
under breakdown a Positive state can invert to Negative.
    Power sequencing — Bringing a circuit’s supplies up (and down)
in a controlled order so dependent stages are never powered before
their prerequisites. CAS analog: satisfying prerequisites in the cor‑
rect order before a dependent operation runs (see RPM). Managed
on the CPMB.
    Principled (P) — The highest Domain: core commitments, values,
and hard boundaries — the constitution. First in the precedence or‑
der P ≻ C ≻ E ≻ O.
    Probe — See Test point.
    Q factor — A measure of how sharply a resonant circuit or filter
is tuned: high Q means a narrow, selective response; low Q means


                                  730
                                                               Glossary

a broad, gentle one. CAS analog: how sharply a cognitive path is
tuned to a specific activation.
    Recipe (Θ) — A specification of what is required to produce
an outcome, with proportional weights — read like a chemistry
equation. Notation: Θ(Ω) = a·X₁ + b·X₂ + … → Ω, e.g. Θ(Ω_safe_
refusal) = 0.5·^3^P_{F7}|f + 0.3·^6^E_{F6}|A + 0.2·^9^O_{F5}|E
→ Ω_safe_refusal. The weights are proportional requirements (the
design bill of materials for the outcome), not gains or current Drive
levels. The associated production‑semantics family (developed in
Chapter 14): the state vector S is the quantity xi of each prerequisite
actually on hand; the theoretical yield Y_T = mini (xi /ai ) is the
ceiling on how much Ω can be produced; the limiting reagent L is
the prerequisite at that minimum — the bottleneck (over‑supplying
any other ingredient cannot raise the yield); actual yield Y_A is
what is really produced (≤ Y_T); production efficiency η = Y_A/Y_T;
excess capacity ε is the stranded, unused quantity of the non‑limiting
ingredients; leakage / side‑reaction Λ is a prerequisite present but
producing the wrong product (distinct from lacunarity = absent, and
inversion = shadow form); a catalyst κ / inhibitor ι raises / lowers η
without being consumed.
    Register — The CAS axis answering how a cognitive operation
operates — its operational character. Four values written with a trail‑
ing pipe: |T Transcendent, |A Analytical, |f Affective (lowercase f), |E
Embodied. Register is optional; an unspecified register means register‑
neutral.
    Regulator — A circuit that holds an output at a fixed target de‑
spite changing input or load. CAS analog: holding a cognitive state
at a target within a tolerance, e.g. Regulator< target_state=^0^E_
{F3}|f, tolerance=0.1 >. A core part of the CPMB.
    Resistor — A component that limits flow; higher resistance
means more constrained flow. CAS analog: limiting how much a
cognitive activation propagates, e.g. Resistor< ^8^C_{F2}|A, R=50
> — a higher R means a more constrained operation.


                                  731
CAS PCBA Engineer

    Rhythm (^7) — The seventh Noetic: the rate and pattern a Mind
is exposed to an Idea, entraining or conditioning it (“practice makes
perfect”). A self‑dual; the basis of habit loops, oscillators, and the in‑
ductor’s pattern inertia.
    RPM (section‑retraction) — Prerequisite satisfaction structured
as a one‑directional chain (A0 → Dn → Wn → Pn → Outcome). Math‑
ematically it is a section‑retraction, not an adjunction: realizing a
prerequisite after embedding it returns the identity (εI ◦ η I = idI),
but re‑embedding after realization may lose information (η I ◦ εI ̸=
id). The practical rule: prerequisite satisfaction is one‑directional —
the RPM gate must not assume reversibility. The cognitive analog of
power sequencing.
    Saturation — (1) CJT region: the Effect is maxed out, so more
Cause produces no further output (compile signal W‑CJT‑004 CjtSat‑
uration). (2) Parameter: sat, the plateau ceiling (0–1) a CJT’s effect
cannot exceed. A safety CJT is often designed to saturate at a speci‑
fied threshold by intent.
    Schmitt trigger — A comparator with hysteresis: it switches at
one threshold going up and a lower threshold going down, so a noisy
input produces a clean, chatter‑free output. CAS analog: a decision
gate with built‑in hysteresis that resists flip‑flopping on borderline
inputs.
    Section‑retraction — See RPM. The one‑directional structure of
prerequisite satisfaction; specifically not a reversible adjunction.
    Self‑dual — A Noetic (or Drive) that is its own structural inverse,
with no opposite partner: the Noetics Idea (^0), Mind (^1), Vibration
(^4), and Rhythm (^7); the Drive F4 Connection. Self‑duals have
nowhere to flip under breakdown, which makes them stable anchors.
    Sequence (Phi) — See Phi. An ordered traversal of CAS states
over time, written Phi< s₁, s₂, s₃ >.
    State literal — A single CAS state written as a four‑axis coordi‑
nate: ^Noetic ^Domain _{Drive} |Register, e.g. ^8^C_{F2}|A = “an



                                  732
                                                               Glossary

analytical association in the cognitive domain, driven by wisdom.”
Domain almost always appears; Drive and Register are optional.
     Test point (probe) — A designated node in a circuit where a mea‑
surement can be taken without disturbing operation. In CCDL, de‑
clared with probe, e.g. probe tp1: expand;. Probe readings feed the
evidence packet and the /verify workflow.
     Transconductance (gm) — A CJT parameter: how much the Ef‑
fect changes per unit change in Bias (∂effect/∂bias) — informally, the
state’s framing‑sensitivity. High gm means small changes in bias
swing the output a lot.
     Transcendent (|T) — The Register of high‑abstraction, purpose‑
orienting, integrative operation. In a human, a felt sense of vision or
calling; in an AI, a high‑level goal representation.
     Transformer — (1) Electronics: a component that steps a voltage
up or down via a turns ratio, matching one stage’s impedance to the
next. (2) CAS: a Domain impedance match, e.g. Transformer< ^P ->
^C, ratio=0.5 > — translating a principle into an actionable cogni‑
tive form.
     Vibration (^4) — The fourth Noetic: the degree to which an Idea
resonates with the Mind — its impression (“struck a chord,” “hit
hard”). A self‑dual.
     /verify — The verification workflow that runs a board’s test suite,
collects probe readings into an evidence packet, and produces the pass/‑
fail record required before a board advances a rung on the deployment
ladder.
     Zener (diode) — A diode that conducts in reverse once a defined
breakdown voltage is reached, clamping a signal to that level. CAS
analog: a state that reverse‑conducts at a threshold, e.g. Zener< ^3^P,
breakdown=0.8 > — a hard ceiling that engages only past the set
point.

Further Reading


You finished the book. You can read a schematic, select a component,
design a board, and write a certification dossier a regulator would
accept. This appendix points at where to go next, organized by why
you would go there.
    Each entry says what the work is and what it gives a reader of this
book specifically. Some of these are public, externally‑known refer‑
ences with ISBNs you can buy. Others are internal CAS documents
— the normative specifications and operational manuals this book is
built on. For the internal documents, no ISBN or URL is given be‑
cause none is public; they are described by their role so you can ask
for the right one by name.
    A note on division of labor before the list: this book is a circuit‑
design handbook. It teaches you to build cognitive architectures out
of typed CAS components. It is not the language reference, not the
mathematics, and not the operations manual. Each of those is a sep‑
arate document, and the first sections below tell you which is which.

CAS PCBA Engineer

H.1     The Companion Volume
Programming in CAS: A Practical Guide
The language reference to this book’s circuit‑design handbook. The
two books split the discipline the way an electronics curriculum splits
it: one book teaches you the language — how to write a valid CAS
expression, what each operator means, how the compiler parses and
validates a state literal — and the other book (this one) teaches you
to wire components into boards with that language.
    Concretely: when this book writes CJT< prompt | bias =>
respond > [β =1.5] and tells you the bias terminal carries an ^5
Female substrate, Programming in CAS is where the underlying
state literals, drives, registers, recipes, and the + / × / |⟨…⟩ operator
discipline are defined from the ground up. This book taught the
notation you need in Chapter 2 and stands on its own — but if you
want the full grammar, the compiler’s behavior on every construct,
and the language‑level edge cases, that is the companion’s job, not
this book’s.

      One caution. Older drafts of Programming in CAS
      drifted on a few canonical Noetic names (glossing ^8
      Above/Cause as “Expansion,” ^6 Male as “Critique,” and
      similar). Chapter 1 and Chapter 2 of this book are your
      notation reference. Where a companion draft and this
      book disagree on a Noetic name, this book governs. The
      canonical names — Idea, Mind, Positive, Negative, Vibra‑
      tion, Female, Male, Rhythm, Above/Cause, Below/Effect
      — are the names, in every context.

H.2 Foundational CAS References
These are the documents underneath both books — the definitions,
the mathematics, and the framework versions. You go here when
you need to know not how to wire a board but why the components
mean what they mean.

CAS Foundational Clarifications
The normative language reference for CAS. This is where the ten
Noetic definitions are fixed verbatim and authoritatively: Idea, Mind,
Positive, Negative, Vibration, Female, Male, Rhythm, Above/Cause,
Below/Effect. It is also where the anti‑drift guidance lives — the rea‑
son this book is so insistent that ^3 Negative is visceral aversion and
never analytical critique, that ^8 Above/Cause is associative triggering
and never deductive reasoning, and that ^5 Female is accumulated ex‑
perience (the substrate of a CJT’s bias terminal). Read it before you
write any CAS description, classification, or teaching material of your
own. If you ever find yourself unsure whether a state you assigned
to a node is the right Noetic, this is the document that settles it.

category Noetica with its admissibility relations, the Fisher‑Rao
metric on the open probability simplex ∆39°, and the geodesic

H.3 Operations and Incident Material
This book teaches you to design boards. The operations material tells
you what the finished deliverable must look like and what real‑world
failures the boards are designed against.

Noetic Compass Operations Manual
The standard operating procedures that define what each CAS deliv‑
erable is. The one this book matches most directly is SOP‑PO‑005,
which defines the CJT circuit‑analysis deliverable — the mandatory
assessment that the Cognitive Safety Board (CSB) of Chapter 18 is
built to satisfy. When Chapter 18 says the CSB is “the SOP‑PO‑005
deliverable,” this manual is the document being satisfied: it specifies


                                  739
CAS PCBA Engineer

the required artifacts (schematic, BOM, test report, evidence packets)
and the acceptance criteria a submission must meet. Go here when
you are producing a CSB submission for real and need the exact de‑
liverable specification, not the design walkthrough.

AI Misalignment Incidents Database
A database of verified, real‑world AI failures, each with a CAS struc‑
tural analysis attached. This is the evidence base for the entire safety ar‑
gument of the book — the concrete failures that motivate every “must
not” invariant in the CSB. When the book designs a board to refuse
override attempts, reject framing attacks, or saturate a safety stage
rather than amplify a harmful request, the incidents in this database
are the failures those structures are designed to prevent. Read it to
see the real prompts and real outcomes behind the abstractions, and
to ground your own threat model in what has actually gone wrong
rather than what you imagine might.

The CAS Failure Taxonomy
The classification scheme that organizes those incidents into a small
set of structural failure classes, with development notes explaining
how the taxonomy was derived. This is the bridge between “here
is a specific incident” and “here is the structural property a board
must enforce to prevent the whole class.” Use it when you are do‑
ing the requirements work of Chapter 17 — turning a fuzzy worry
(“the model might be manipulated”) into a named failure class with a
named structural mitigation (a saturating safety CJT, an enforcement
fuse, a domain diode). The CCBs in this book are designed against
these classes; the taxonomy is how you check your own board covers
the ones that matter for your setting.




                                   740
                     H.4. ELECTRONICS BACKGROUND (OPTIONAL)

H.4 Electronics Background (optional)
You do not need any of this to use the book — the electronic ideas
were taught from first principles in passing, exactly where they were
needed. But the circuit analogy is a real structural isomorphism, not
a poem, and some readers will want to deepen the electronics half of
it on its own terms. These are classic, genuinely‑existing references.
Treat them as optional grounding.

Horowitz & Hill, The Art of Electronics (3rd ed., Cambridge
University Press)
The standard practical reference for analog and digital electronics,
written by working engineers for working engineers. Its voice —
plain, confident, design‑first, allergic to unnecessary theory — is
close to the voice this book aims for. If you want to understand the
electronic transistor, resistor, capacitor, diode, op‑amp, oscillator,
and feedback loop that this book maps onto cognitive components,
this is the single best book to read alongside the early chapters. Read
it for the source‑side intuition; you will recognize every topological
role.

Sedra & Smith, Microelectronic Circuits (Oxford University
Press)
The standard university textbook on transistor‑level circuit design.
More formal and more mathematical than Horowitz & Hill, it
is where the operating regions of a transistor — cutoff, active,
saturation, breakdown — and the small‑signal parameters (transcon‑
ductance gm, input resistance rπ, gain) are developed rigorously.
Since the CJT (Chapters 3 and 9) borrows exactly this vocabulary
for its cognitive analog, this is the book to read if you want the
precise electronic definitions behind the CJT’s datasheet parameters.




                                 741
CAS PCBA Engineer

Optional, and heavier going than Horowitz & Hill — reach for it
when you want depth on the device physics, not breadth.




H.5     AI Governance Frameworks
Chapter 26 argued that a CCB certification does not compete with
the regulatory regimes that already exist — it satisfies them, by pro‑
ducing documented structure, measured behavior, and an audit trail
as engineering artifacts. These are the three frameworks that chap‑
ter mapped onto. Read the primary sources directly; do not rely on
summaries (including this book’s) when you are preparing a real sub‑
mission.

EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689)
The European Union’s risk‑based regulation of AI systems. The part
most relevant to this book is the regime for high‑risk systems (Annex
III), which requires a risk‑management system, technical documen‑
tation, logging and traceability, human oversight, and robustness
— the exact list Chapter 26 mapped onto the CCDL schematic, the
BOM, the structural “must not” invariants, and the evidence‑packet
trace trail. Read it when you are certifying a board for the EU mar‑
ket and need the authoritative text of what high‑risk documentation
must contain.

NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)
The U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology’s voluntary
framework, organized around four functions: Govern, Map, Mea‑
sure, Manage. Chapter 26 mapped these directly onto the book’s ar‑
tifacts — Map to the requirements lists and block diagram (Chapter
17), Measure to the test report and test‑point methodology (Chapter
23), Manage to the structural mitigations, and Govern to the BOM and

                                 742
                               H.5. AI GOVERNANCE FRAMEWORKS

trace‑ID audit trail. Read it for the function‑by‑function vocabulary
you will use to present a CCB submission to a U.S. audience.

ISO/IEC 42001 (AI management system)
The international standard for an AI management system — a
documented, auditable system with defined controls, versioned
artifacts, and continual improvement. Chapter 26 mapped this
onto the BOM as the versioned artifact register (a parameter change
is a re‑certification event, not a silent edit), the DRC error classes
as the defined controls, and the O→P feedback path as continual
improvement implemented as a circuit. Read it if your organization
is pursuing or already holds a certified management system and
you need to show where the CCB discipline plugs in as auditable
controls.




     Where to start. If you are going to read exactly one more
     thing: read it by your goal. To go deeper on the language,
     read the companion Programming in CAS. To go deeper on
     the mathematics, read the Noetic Topos paper. To ship a
     real certification, read SOP‑PO‑005 in the Operations Man‑
     ual and the governance framework for your jurisdiction.
     To understand the threats, read the AI Misalignment In‑
     cidents Database and the failure taxonomy. And if the
     electronics themselves are new to you and you want them
     on their own terms, start with Horowitz & Hill. Every one
     of these is a road out of this book and into the work that
     comes after it.




                                 743
Appendix I

CAS‑Ohm Measurement and Calibration


Chapter 5 gave you the law. This appendix gives you the instrument.
    Everywhere else in this book, V_drive, I_attention, and R_
constraint are design choices — numbers you pick to illustrate a
circuit. That is the right way to learn. But a board you actually
ship gets measured, and measurement needs three things the design
view never supplies: a scale everyone agrees on, a procedure that
produces the same number twice, and a way to tell the difference
between a circuit that is behaving and one that merely looks like it
is.
    That is what follows. Nothing here changes a component. It
changes what you write on the test report.




I.1 Units and scales — read this before you write
    a number
The single most common way to corrupt a CCB test report is to mix
scales. Four different quantities in this book are measured on four
different ranges, and three of them are dimensionless. Learn the ta‑
ble; there is no way to infer it from the symbols.



                                745
CAS PCBA Engineer
