    Three rules follow from that table, and every one of them has bit‑
ten someone.
    A Dial is set; resistance is measured. You set Dial(^2) to an inte‑
ger between 3 and 9 — the compiler rejects anything else with HTTP

                                    746
                                                I.2. THE THREE MODES

422. What you then measure on that path is R_total, a decimal, and
it is not the Dial. Writing Dial(^2) = 6.4 is a category error, not a
precise reading.
     Normalize before you compare. A raw flow reading means noth‑
ing across two boards until you divide by that path’s full‑scale value:

I_Q = min(10, 10 × I_raw / I_FS)


   I_FS is the flow the path produces with constraint at its floor and
drive at its rail. Measure it once per path, record it on the test report,
and never compare two I_raw figures from different boards.
    The normalized 0–10 reading is a reading, not a component
value. It is what your instrument reports. Component values stay on
the ranges in the table above. If you find yourself writing R = 2.0 on
a resistor, you have written a normalized reading into a component
field, and the compiler’s range check will catch it. Convert: R_
component = 10 × R_normalized.


      Bench Note. The fastest way to spot a mixed‑scale report
      is to look for a saturation figure above 1. If you see sat =
      8.5, someone recorded a normalized reading in a compo‑
      nent field. The value is 0.85.




I.2 The three modes
CAS‑Ohm has one equation and three uses. Which one you are doing
depends entirely on which term you do not know.

V_drive = I_attention × R_constraint


   Measure — I = V / R. You know the drive and the constraint;
you want the flow. This is the design‑time prediction, and it is what
you compare a live reading against.

                                   747
CAS PCBA Engineer

                                                              Measure
                                                              I = V /R
                 V
                                                               Design
                                                              V =I ×R
           I           R
                                                              Diagnose
                                                              R = V /I

            Cover the term you do not know; the remaining
          two show how to combine them. Which mode you
          are in depends entirely on which term is unknown.


Figure I.1: The three CAS‑Ohm modes. One equation, three uses,
selected by which term you do not already know.


    Design — V = I × R. You know the flow you need and the con‑
straint you are stuck with; you want the drive required to get there.
This is how you size a supply rail on a CPMB.
    Diagnose — R = V / I. You applied a known drive, you ob‑
served a flow, and you want to know what the path is actually
resisting. This is the mode that finds faults, and it is the reason §I.4
exists.
    Cover the term you do not know; the remaining two tell you how
to combine them.




I.3   Where constraint comes from
R_constraint in Chapter 5 is a single number. In a real board it is a
sum, and knowing the parts is what lets you fix a constrained path
instead of just noting that it is constrained.

R_total = R_cap + R_policy + R_context + R_resource


   • R_cap — capability. The path is constrained because the system
     cannot do the thing well. Falls as competence rises.

                                      748
                              I.3. WHERE CONSTRAINT COMES FROM

   • R_policy — deliberate. A safety boundary, a refusal rule, a
     hard constraint you installed. On a CSB this is supposed to be
     high.
   • R_context — situational. Ambiguity, missing information, con‑
     flicting instructions in the prompt.
   • R_resource — budgetary. Context window, latency ceiling, to‑
     ken budget.

    Capability‑derived resistance has a closed form, because capabil‑
ity and constraint are inverses:

R_cap = R_min + (R_max − R_min) × (1 − P_cap / 10)


   P_cap is the capability score on the 0–10 normalized scale. At P_
cap = 10 the path is unconstrained by skill and R_cap = R_min; at P_
cap = 0 it is maximally constrained and R_cap = R_max.
    This decomposition matters diagnostically. A path with R_total
= 70 tells you nothing. A path with R_policy = 60, R_cap = 10 is a
working safety board. A path with R_cap = 60, R_policy = 10 is an
incompetent one. Same total, opposite verdicts, opposite fixes.

Decoding D/W/P
Chapter 8 introduces the RPM chain as A0 → Dn → Wn → Pn →
Outcome and never says what the letters stand for. They are:


   • D — Desire. The motivational prerequisite. Does the system
     want the outcome enough to push toward it? This is the drive
     term, V.
   • W — Wisdom. The know‑how prerequisite. Does it know what
     to do? This governs how much of the drive converts into useful
     flow, I.
   • P — Power. The capability prerequisite. Can it actually exe‑
     cute? This is the inverse of R_cap.



                                  749
CAS PCBA Engineer

    Treat the D↔V, W↔I, P↔R_cap crosswalk as an aid to intuition,
not a proof. It is a mapping between two vocabularies for the same
bottleneck, and it has not been measured against a live model.
    RPM remains one‑directional. The scan descends into an unmet
prerequisite and returns; that is tree traversal, not reversal. No sat‑
isfied prerequisite is ever un‑satisfied by the return, so the section‑
retraction property from Appendix G holds unchanged.




I.4      Residual diagnosis — finding constraint you
         did not install
This is the part of the appendix that earns its place.
   Predict the flow from what you believe the circuit to be. Measure
what it actually does. The difference is the fault.

I_pred   = V_drive / R_known
∆I        = I_obs − I_pred
R_hidden = V_drive / I_obs − R_known


      R_known is the constraint you can account for — the resistors you
placed, the policy you wrote, the budget you set. R_hidden is every‑
thing else.
    Read the residual like this:

Observation                  Reading                     Where to look

∆I ≈ 0                       Circuit matches the         Nothing. Record and
                             schematic.                  move on.
∆I < 0, R_hidden > 0         Something is resisting      Undocumented policy, a
                             that you did not install.   saturating upstream
                                                         stage, resource
                                                         exhaustion.
∆I > 0, R_hidden < 0         Flow exceeds what the       A bypassed constraint.
                             constraints permit.         Treat as a safety finding,
                                                         not a performance win.


                                        750
               I.5. EQUIVALENT RESISTANCE FOR NESTED ASSEMBLIES

Observation               Reading               Where to look

∆I varies run to run at   The path is not        Sampling temperature,
fixed V                   deterministic.         context leakage, a
                                                 capacitor holding state
                                                 across runs.


   The third row is the one to take seriously. On a Cognitive Safety
Board, flow higher than the installed resistance allows means a re‑
fusal path is being routed around. Chapter 24’s walk‑down proce‑
dure starts here.

      Bench Note. R_hidden is a residual, not a component. Do
      not add it to the schematic. Find what it is, name it, and
      place a real component — or remove whatever is bypass‑
      ing the one you already placed.




I.5 Equivalent resistance for nested assemblies
When a CJT’s bias path is itself built from sub‑circuits, collapse them
before applying the law.
   Series — constraints stack. Flow passes through every stage in
turn:

R_eq = Σ R_k


    Parallel — constraints divide. Flow has alternative routes:

1 / R_eq = Σ (1 / R_k)


    Parallel paths are the more dangerous configuration, and the arith‑
metic shows why. Two constraints of 80 in parallel give an equivalent
of 40 — less than either alone. Every alternative route you add lowers
total resistance.


                                    751
CAS PCBA Engineer

      Bench Note — parallel paths are not co‑present
      guardrails. These two things look alike on a schematic
      and behave in opposite directions, so keep them straight.
     A parallel path is an alternative route for the same flow.
     Adding one gives the flow somewhere else to go, so re‑
     sistances combine reciprocally and the total falls. That is
     why a request with three different ways to reach the same
     output is easier to satisfy, not harder.
     Co‑present guardrails are not routes. They are indepen‑
     dent checks that each must be defeated on the same path
     — Chapter 18’s ^3^P|⟨A,f,T⟩, where an attacker who rea‑
     sons past the analytical guardrail still meets the felt one
     and then the purpose‑level one. Those do not divide re‑
     sistance; their defeat probabilities multiply, which is the op‑
     posite behaviour. Three locks on one door is redundancy.
     Three doors is not.
     The test is simple: ask whether the second element gives
     the flow a new way around, or another thing to get through.
     Around is parallel and weakens. Through is co‑presence
     and strengthens.

    That distinction is the quantitative form of the argument Chapter
18 makes about redundant versus fused safety architecture.
    Cascades multiply gain, but flow is local. Chapter 11 gives β _
total = Π β _k. Gain compounds along the chain. Flow does not:
each stage’s I is set by that stage’s local drive and resistance. A late
stage starved by its own high R will not be rescued by a high‑gain
stage upstream — it will saturate the upstream stage instead and clip.
That product is a rule for sizing a cascade at design time; what it does
and does not license you to do with measured stage gains is the subject
of the next section.




                                  752
 I.6. WHICH β YOU MEASURED — ONE SYMBOL, TWO DEFINITIONS

I.6 Which β you measured — one symbol, two
    definitions
β sits in the units table at the top of this appendix under the gloss
“∆effect per unit ∆cause,” and that phrase hides a problem. Two
different mathematical objects circulate under the single symbol β.
A test report that does not say which one it used is not reproducible,
and two reports that used different ones are not comparable — even
though both numbers are dimensionless and both look perfectly at
home in the same column.
    The book’s definition — a Fisher‑Rao displacement ratio. Stated
in Chapter 3, restated in Chapter 9, and the definition every β printed
in these pages is written under:

small-signal   β = ‖∂ E/∂ C‖_FR at constant bias
large-signal   β = d_FR(E_after, E_before) / d_FR(C_after, C_before)
                                                               √
               d_FR(p,q) = 2·\allowbreak{}arccos(\allowbreak{}Σ (\allowb ⌋
               ,→   reak{}pk qk ))


    d_FR is the Fisher‑Rao geodesic distance on the open simplex
∆39°. Gain, under this definition, is a ratio of distances travelled on the
simplex, measured in the simplex’s own information geometry.
    The operational definition — a Jacobian / projection derivative.
Instrumentation hooked to a running model does not have the sim‑
plex; it has activation vectors. The natural gain there is a local deriva‑
tive: pick a cause test point and an effect test point, take the derivative
of effect with respect to cause, project onto chosen directions, report
the magnitude. This is what a measurement harness hands you when
you ask it for a gain, and it is a perfectly reasonable quantity in its
own right.
    They are not known to be the same quantity.




                                     753
CAS PCBA Engineer

                                                   Jacobian / projection
                        Fisher‑Rao displacement    derivative
Property                ratio (this book)          (instrumentation)

Lives on                the open simplex ∆39°,     activation space, under a
                        in its information         chosen projection
                        geometry
Invariance              invariant under the        depends on the direction
                        simplex’s natural          vectors picked at both
                        reparameterizations        test points
Signal size             has a small‑signal and a   small‑signal by
                        large‑signal form          construction — it is a
                                                   local derivative
Dimensionless           yes                        yes — but by a different
                                                   normalization


    Both are dimensionless, and that is the hazard rather than the reas‑
surance it looks like: a unit check cannot tell them apart. Two figures
that read identically on a report can be the outputs of two different
measurements of two different things, and nothing in the arithmetic
will complain.
    What would have to be true for the two to be comparable. Not
“roughly similar” — comparable, in the sense that you could put a
number produced one way where a number produced the other way
belongs. Four things would have to be established and written down:

   1. A coordinate map. An explicit map between the activation co‑
      ordinates the derivative is taken in and the simplex coordinates
      the distance is measured on — and it would have to be a local
      diffeomorphism over the region you actually measured in, or
      “the same point” means nothing.
   2. Metric compatibility. The projection structure used to take
      the derivative would have to agree, under that map, with the
      Fisher‑Rao metric. A derivative and a distance line up only
      when the derivative is taken in the metric the distance is mea‑
      sured with.


                                  754
 I.6. WHICH β YOU MEASURED — ONE SYMBOL, TWO DEFINITIONS

   3. A matched signal regime. A Jacobian is a small‑signal object by
      construction. Only the book’s small‑signal form is even a candi‑
      date for comparison; a large‑signal displacement ratio has no
      local derivative to be compared to.
   4. A shared normalization. Both quantities are rendered dimen‑
      sionless, but by different normalizations. Those would have to
      be shown to be the same one, or the ratio between them stated.

     None of the four is established in this book, and none is estab‑
lished in any source this book draws on. No theorem here derives
one quantity from the other; no experiment here measures both on
the same path and compares them. Do not read the identification as a
technicality someone has surely worked out offstage. It is open, and
it is worth saying so plainly on a page that is otherwise about how to
get a number you can defend.
     So which one governs? In this book’s terms, the Fisher‑Rao
displacement ratio governs. Every β in these pages — the CJT
datasheet’s β =2.4, the CSB’s stage gains, Chapter 11’s cascade
figures — is written under that definition, and a gain reported “in
this book’s terms” means that one. A Jacobian gain out of a harness
is not wrong; it is a different measurement, and it belongs on the report
under its own name, never silently in a field labelled β.
     Write the method beside the number. Never let a bare β off the
bench. Write β (FR) or β (Jac), or spell the method out on the line
above it. A gain figure without its method identity is not a measure‑
ment; it is a number.

      Bench Note — composition is where this bites. Chap‑
      ter 11’s β _total = Π β _k is how you size a cascade: pick
      stage gains whose product is the amplification the design
      needs. As a design rule it does its job. It is not, on the
      strength of anything in this book, a licence to multiply
      measured stage figures together and call the product a mea‑
      sured cascade gain. Composition of local derivatives fol‑

                                  755
CAS PCBA Engineer

      lows a chain rule only when adjacent stages’ coordinates
      agree; composition of Fisher‑Rao displacement ratios has
      no chain rule at all without further structure, and this
      book supplies none. And a cascade that mixes the two
      — one stage’s derivative times the next stage’s displace‑
      ment ratio — computes cleanly and means nothing, be‑
      cause both factors are dimensionless and nothing stops
      the multiplication.
      The error does not stay local, either; it compounds with
      depth. Three stages at a 30% definitional discrepancy is
      a factor of about 2.2 — illustrative arithmetic about how
      error propagates, not a measurement of anything. Report
      per‑stage gains, each tagged with its method, and let the
      reader see the chain instead of a product that hides what
      went into it.




I.7    Field protocol
Run this in order. Skipping step 2 is the most common cause of un‑
reproducible test reports.

  1. Identify the path. Name the cause, bias, and effect states in
     canonical notation — e.g. ^8^C_{F2}|A → ^6^E_{F6}|A →
     ^9^C_{F2}|A. If you cannot type the path, you are not ready to
     measure it.
  2. Establish full scale. Drive at rail, constraint at floor. Record
     I_FS. This is per‑path and does not transfer.
  3. Record installed constraint. Sum R_cap + R_policy + R_
     context + R_resource into R_known. Note which terms you
     estimated.
  4. Predict. I_pred = V_drive / R_known.
  5. Apply and observe. Record I_obs, normalized via I_Q.

                                756
                                                           I.8. MATURITY BANDS

   6. Compute the residual. ∆I and R_hidden. Read against the ta‑
      ble in §I.4.
   7. Note the operating region. Cutoff, active, saturation, or break‑
      down, per Chapter 9. A residual computed on a saturated stage
      is meaningless — the stage is clipping, not resisting.
   8. Repeat three times. A single reading is an anecdote.

Worksheet
PATH ________________________________________________
  cause     ^__^__ _{F_} |_         bias    ^__^__ _{F_} |_
  effect ^__^__ _{F_} |_


FULL SCALE             I_FS ______
DRIVE                  V_drive ______


INSTALLED CONSTRAINT
  R_cap ______    R_policy ______
  R_context ______     R_resource ______          R_known ______

I.8 Maturity bands
For reporting a capability score without implying more precision
than you have, bin P_cap into four bands and tag the direction of
travel.



                                           757
CAS PCBA Engineer

Band                    P_cap                    Meaning

M1 — Absent             0.0–2.5                  The capability is not
                                                 present.
M2 — Emerging           2.5–5.0                  Present under favorable
                                                 conditions only.
M3 — Developing         5.0–7.5                  Reliable in the common
                                                 case; fails at the edges.
M4 — Mature             7.5–10.0                 Reliable including edge
                                                 cases.


    Tag each with ↑ rising, → stable, or ↓ waning. M2↑ and M3↓ are the
same score band travelling in opposite directions and call for oppo‑
site interventions.
    Bands are a reporting convenience. Compute with the decimal;
report the band.




I.9    What these numbers are, and are not
Every figure produced by this appendix is a design score, a calibra‑
tion value, or an observed rating. None of it is a voltmeter reading
from a brain or a language model. There is no instrument that mea‑
sures attention flow in volts.
    The engineering value is not in the absolute numbers. It is in three
things they make possible: consistency between two engineers mea‑
suring the same board, test points that a later run can be compared
against, and falsifiable predictions — I_pred is a claim that can turn
out wrong, and that is exactly what makes the residual in §I.4 diag‑
nostic.
    The relationship between drive, flow, and constraint is testable
in principle. It has not been measured against a live model. Do not
write “proportional” on a report; write the numbers you took and the
procedure you took them with.


                                   758
                    I.9. WHAT THESE NUMBERS ARE, AND ARE NOT

    One notational caution. This book uses Ω in two ways: in Chapter
5’s prose it is the electrical unit, in CAS recipe notation (Θ(Ω_safe_
refusal)) it names an emergent outcome. Never use Ω as shorthand
for CAS‑Ohm. Spell it out.
